WFO is the access host, not a third independent author; its duplicate Nicaragua/China/Panama text not counted again. Corrected vague 'this region' statement: Mesoamericana explicitly says introduced United States, native southern Mexico–Argentina/Antilles; retained regional caution without implying all American occurrences native. No invasion severity inferred.
previousDescription: Arrocillo is a coarse perennial grass that forms clumps with broad leaves and many spreading flowering branches. Small, rounded flower clusters line those branches. It grows in warm places such as clearings, plantations and other disturbed ground. Its natural distribution includes a broad area of the Americas, so a record in this region does not automatically mean the grass is an introduced species.

supportedClaims: Perennial to1.6m; broad soft-hairy young leaves; spreading numerous racemes, rounded1.25–1.5mm spikelets; tropical American native, Australian naturalized pasture.
Clumped perennial; paired rounded spikelets in4rows; open disturbed sites; southernMexico–Argentina/Antilles, introduced UnitedStates/OldWorld tropics.

proposedDescription: Arrow bamboo has upright canes and long, broad leaves that make it popular as a screen. Beneath the soil, spreading stems can carry new shoots well beyond the original planting. It can form dense patches where it escapes cultivation. Records from places including Maryland and New Zealand illustrate why its underground growth matters when assessing a planting near neighboring gardens or natural vegetation.
identification: Compare broad elongated leaves, cane sheaths, and spreading rhizomes with other running bamboos.
actions: Check the edge of a planting for new shoots and seek local bamboo-management guidance before removal; ordinary lawn broadleaf weed treatments do not target bamboo.

sources.title: Flora of New Zealand: Pseudosasa japonica
Maryland Extension: Running bamboo identification and management response

researchNotes: Full New Zealand flora description and Maryland Extension identification/management response read. Naturalized habitats and running rhizomes are supported. The response provides regional management guidance, not a controlled treatment trial.
previousDescription: Arrow bamboo forms a leafy screen of upright canes and long, broad green leaves. What happens below ground is just as important: running underground stems can send new shoots beyond the original planting. That habit has helped it escape gardens, with naturalized stands described beside rivers, roads, and woodland edges in New Zealand and reports of invasive growth in Maryland. An established patch is therefore more than the canes you can see. Identification and a plan for the underground growth are useful before attempting to remove or contain it.

proposedDescription: Arrowleaf elephant ear has large, arrow-shaped leaves held on long stalks that meet the leaf at its base. Thick underground growth and new shoots help it expand into patches. It favors warm, moist places and can grow along streams. In parts of Florida, escaped plants are considered invasive, where their large leaves and dense growth can crowd other vegetation.
identification: Look at the stalk attachment at the leaf base and the broad arrow-shaped blade; compare with Colocasia and native Peltandra before removal.
actions: Prevent a cultivated patch from escaping and avoid dumping live underground pieces near wetlands. Confirm identification before disturbing a wild patch.

sources.title: University of South Florida: Arrowleaf elephant's ear

researchNotes: NParks descriptive/habitat passages, UF IFAS regional assessment, and full USF identification/spread account read. NParks excludes flooded sites while USF records swamps, so habitat is limited here to moist streambanks. UF regional ratings and USF statewide listing differ; wording avoids a single nationwide status.
previousDescription: Arrowleaf elephant's ear makes a bold patch of tropical greenery, with large arrow-shaped leaves held on long stalks. The stalk joins the blade at its base, a useful clue when comparing plants commonly called elephant ears. Thick underground growth produces offsets, allowing colonies to expand in moist places such as streambanks. It has a long history as a cultivated tropical plant, but it can also escape. Florida assessments describe invasive behavior in some regions, where dense growth can crowd or shade native vegetation; those regional findings should not be treated as a universal status.

proposedDescription: Artist's pallet is grown for its heart- to arrow-shaped leaves, patterned in combinations of green, white, pink and red. It grows from underground tubers and produces small flowers grouped on a fleshy spike within a pale surrounding leaf-like structure. Native to tropical America, it is widely cultivated. Its colorful foliage is ornamental rather than edible, and the plant's tissues can cause irritation.
identification: Look for colorful arrow- or heart-shaped leaves with the stalk joining inside the blade; cultivated hybrids can complicate species identification.
actions: Keep the plant from being eaten and avoid contact with sap when handling damaged leaves or tubers.

sources.title: Kew Plants of the World Online: Caladium bicolor
NC State Extension Plant Toolbox: Caladium bicolor

researchNotes: Kew's full flora description and NC State descriptive/toxicity passages read. Cultivar variation and hybrid identification limits retained. No ecological harm inferred from cultivation.
previousDescription: Caladium is grown for leaves that can look hand-painted in green, white, pink, and red. The broad blades range from heart-shaped to arrow-shaped and rise on long stalks from underground tubers. Its flowers are much less conspicuous, carried on a fleshy spike within a pale bract. This tropical American plant is widely cultivated, with garden forms that vary greatly in color and shape. An ornamental caladium should not automatically be described as an invasive threat, but its sap and tissues do deserve care around people and pets because they contain irritating compounds.

proposedDescription: Diplosoma listerianum is a colonial sea squirt that forms thin, soft sheets over submerged surfaces. Many tiny filtering animals share the same gelatinous covering. Colonies grow on docks, boat hulls and natural surfaces, giving them opportunities to travel with marine traffic. They can cover other organisms as they spread, but the long history of transport makes the species' original native range difficult to establish.
identification: Look for a very thin, translucent colony with tiny individual openings and larger shared outlets; confirm with a marine specialist.

sources.title: Rhode Island Coastal Resources Management Council: Diplosoma listerianum identification card

researchNotes: Smithsonian's full descriptive/introduction passages and the complete Rhode Island identification card read. Smithsonian treats origin as unknown; the Rhode Island card's likely-European wording does not override that uncertainty. No eradication method prescribed.
previousDescription: What looks like a thin gelatinous film on a dock or boat hull may be a colony of tiny sea squirts. In Diplosoma listerianum, many individuals share a soft outer covering, drawing in seawater and filtering suspended food. Colonies spread across submerged surfaces rather than moving around as adults. That makes boat hulls and other fouled equipment important to its story. Similar sheet-forming tunicates can be difficult to separate by eye, and the species' long history of transport complicates claims about where every population originated.

proposedDescription: Polyandrocarpa zorritensis is a colonial sea squirt made up of small, club-shaped individuals connected by root-like strands. Each has its own outer covering and two openings used in filter feeding. Colonies occur on docks, boats and natural surfaces such as mangrove roots, and can overgrow neighboring organisms. It was described from Peru, but that alone does not establish where it originally evolved.
identification: Look for separate club-shaped individuals joined at their bases, sometimes coated with sand; distinguish from tunicates that form a continuous flat sheet.

sources.title: Salinity-mediated limitation of asexual reproduction in Polyandrocarpa zorritensis (2024)

researchNotes: Smithsonian substantive biology and impact account and the independent 2024 primary study's abstract/introduction read. The laboratory study supports budding and environment-dependent reproductive performance, not a field control method. Its Peru-native assertion conflicts with Smithsonian uncertainty, which is retained.
previousDescription: This sea squirt grows as a cluster of small, club-shaped animals, joined at their bases by rootlike strands. Each individual has its own tough covering and two openings through which it pumps and filters seawater. Colonies occur on docks, boat hulls, and natural surfaces such as mangroves. Introduced populations have been documented in several regions, and some colonies can overgrow other organisms. Its original home remains uncertain in the Smithsonian account, despite having first been described from Peru; the place where a species was named is not necessarily its native range. Experiments also show that salinity can limit its asexual reproduction, so success in one harbor does not predict equal growth in another.

proposedDescription: Ash whitefly feeds beneath the leaves of trees and shrubs, including pears, pomegranates and citrus. Adults are small and white; immature insects have distinctive waxy structures and may carry tiny droplets. Feeding and honeydew can harm foliage and encourage sooty mold. In California, introduced natural enemies greatly reduced a once-serious outbreak, making this species a notable example of successful biological control.
identification: Inspect leaf undersides for immatures with a wax band and droplet-tipped projections; flying white adults alone are not diagnostic.
actions: Check for natural enemies before treating. Avoid disrupting effective biological control with unnecessary broad-spectrum insecticides.

sources.title: University of Florida IFAS: Ash Whitefly

researchNotes: UF IFAS PDF biology and natural-enemy passages and UC IPM species and management passages read. California biological-control success is not assumed for every region; no location-level absence is inferred.
previousDescription: Ash whitefly can cover the undersides of leaves with tiny sap-feeding insects. Adults are pale and wax-dusted, but the settled young are more distinctive, with a thick wax band and a fringe of fine tubes ending in droplets. Ash is only one host; pears, pomegranates, citrus, and other broadleaved trees can also support it. Heavy infestations can leave sticky honeydew and harm foliage or fruit. Its history in California also shows the value of natural enemies: introduced parasitoids greatly reduced a once conspicuous pest problem.

proposedDescription: Ashy cinquefoil has small yellow flowers and leaves divided into five to seven toothed leaflets. Pale hairs on the undersides give the foliage a grayish cast, and hairy stems rise above the lower leaves. It favors dry, open places, including roadsides, grasslands and disturbed ground. This Eurasian plant has been introduced to parts of North America. Several yellow-flowered cinquefoils look similar, so the leaflet shape, gray undersides and hairs around the flowers are more useful together than flower color alone.
identification: Compare both sides of the leaflets and the hairs on stems, sepals, and the small bracts beneath flowers; check against Potentilla intermedia.

sources.title: Flora of North America: Potentilla inclinata
German Federal Agency for Nature Conservation FloraWeb: Potentilla inclinata

researchNotes: Full FNA page recovered through public HTTP after prior web502; morphology, habitat, introduced range and P.intermedia comparison all read. FloraWeb BfN full German morphology/habitat account independently read. Regional phenology and differing hair terminology (FNA distinguishes crisped hairs from cottony hairs, FloraWeb says gray-felted) resolved with plain pale/hairy undersides. No broad harmfulness or treatment claim.
previousDescription: Ashy cinquefoil has yellow flowers and divided, toothed leaves whose hairy undersides give them a grayish appearance. Its stems are also hairy and rise above the lower foliage. Native to Eurasia, it occurs in North American roadsides, fields and open woodland. Several cinquefoils have similar yellow flowers, so leaf shape and the gray undersides are useful details to examine together.

supportedClaims: Ascending/erect stems,5–7toothed leaflets, grayish undersides; dry disturbed sites/grasslands/woodlands; introducedNA, Eurasia; differences from P.intermedia.
15–50cm, hairy stems and gray hairy leaflet undersides, yellow petals, dry sandy open/roadside habitats.

proposedDescription: Ashy geckos are tiny lizards that shelter in leaf litter, beneath bark and among rocks or woody debris, often near buildings. Young animals have bold bands and bright reddish tails; adults become tan to rusty brown with pale speckling. Sphaerodactylus elegans has been introduced to Florida, where other small geckos can complicate identification. Observations from Cuba also describe these geckos hunting flies and ants around a house during daylight. Their changing colors and secretive habits make a clear photograph more useful than a fleeting glimpse.
identification: Photograph the back, head pattern, and tail without handling the animal; young and adult patterns differ substantially.

Independent evidence is deArmas's repeated daytime hunting observations, not background citations. Activity terminology differs: Heagy calls diurnal/crepuscular, deArmas primarily nocturnal but regularly seen by day; profile reports daytime observations without exclusive activity classification. previousDescription: Ashy gecko is a tiny lizard that hides among leaf litter, bark, rocks and sheltered spaces near buildings. Young animals have strong bands and reddish tails, while adults become more muted and speckled. It has been introduced to Florida, where it can be confused with other small geckos. The change in pattern as it grows means young and adult animals may look surprisingly different.

S.elegans repeatedly observed hunting mainly flies/ants indoors byday over severalyears; juvenile13mmSVL documented trapped in decorative glass.
Florida nonindigenous status and2007neonate specimen; supports regional context, not independent full ecological account.

proposedDescription: Ashy pipewort forms a small tuft of very narrow leaves in wet ground. Slender stalks lift rounded, button-like flower heads above the foliage; these may look gray, yellowish or greenish rather than showy. Eriocaulon cinereum occurs in damp valleys and rice fields, including introduced populations recorded in California and Louisiana. Before flowering, its leaves can resemble a small grass. Mature heads are much more useful for recognition, although their tiny flowers still need close examination to distinguish this plant from other pipeworts.
identification: Photograph the basal leaves and mature flower heads; tiny floral details may be needed to separate pipewort species.

sources.title: Flora of North America: Eriocaulon cinereum

previousDescription: Ashy pipewort grows as a small tuft of narrow leaves on wet ground. Thin stalks rise above the leaves and end in compact, button-shaped flower heads. It occurs in wet margins and rice-growing settings, where plants without flowers may resemble a small grass. The round heads are a more useful recognition feature than the leaves alone.

Narrow leaves, multiple slender stalks, subglobose yellow-green heads, minute floral distinctions; ricefields/valleys/dampsoil.

proposedDescription: Asia minor bluegrass, Polypogon fugax, is a loosely tufted annual with a compact flower head that may be pale green or tinged purple. Fine, short bristles edge the tiny flower clusters. Its stems can bend near the base and sometimes root at lower joints, while the leaves are often rough to the touch. It grows in moist places, including disturbed ground and farmland margins. Despite its common name, it belongs to Polypogon rather than Poa, and mature spikelets help separate it from similar grasses.
identification: Examine a mature seed head and individual spikelets with magnification; do not identify it from leaf color or common name.

previousDescription: Asia minor bluegrass is an annual grass with a narrow, compact flower head lined with fine bristles. Its leaves feel rough, and lower stem joints may take root where they touch suitable ground. It grows in damp, disturbed places. proposedDescription: Asian bush mosquito has pale-banded legs and golden markings on its back. It uses small pools of water, including rock pools, tree holes, tires and other containers, and can thrive in relatively cool, wooded settings near homes. Its ability to use artificial containers helps it spread. The species can carry pathogens under some conditions, but finding it does not establish local disease transmission.
identification: Golden thorax markings and banded legs suggest the species, but separation from other Aedes mosquitoes requires close examination.
actions: Empty, cover, or remove unnecessary water-holding containers. Use personal bite protection and local mosquito-control guidance for water that cannot be drained.

sources.title: University of Florida IFAS: Asian Bush Mosquito
University of Illinois Division of Research Safety: Mosquitos

researchNotes: UF IFAS biological, disease-limit and prevention passages plus Illinois's species and prevention sections read. Laboratory competence and uncertain U.S. field transmission are explicitly distinguished; no diagnosis or local disease claim.
previousDescription: Asian bush mosquito develops in small collections of water, from rock pools and tree holes to discarded tires and garden containers. Adults have golden markings on the upper body and pale bands on their dark legs. The species tolerates cooler conditions than many familiar container mosquitoes, helping it use wooded and residential settings. Females take blood meals, but a mosquito's capacity to carry a virus in a laboratory should not be confused with proof that it is causing local disease transmission. Around a home, reducing water-holding containers is a practical way to reduce breeding opportunities.

proposedDescription: Asian chestnut gall wasp causes rounded swellings on the buds, leaves and shoots of true chestnut trees. These galls start green or pink and later become woody and brown, sometimes remaining after the wasps have left. Heavy infestations can reduce shoot growth and nut production. The adult wasp is tiny, so the galls are usually the first sign people notice.
identification: Look for rounded swellings on Castanea leaves and young shoots; distinguish fresh soft galls from old dry ones.
actions: Have unusual chestnut galls identified and seek local guidance before pruning or treatment. Avoid moving suspect nursery plants to new sites.

sources.title: University of Florida IFAS: Asian Chestnut Gall Wasp
UK Forest Research: Oriental chestnut gall wasp

researchNotes: UF IFAS biology, damage and management passages and UK Forest Research identification, life-cycle and movement guidance read. True chestnut hosts are explicit; no unsupervised parasitoid release or jurisdiction-independent quarantine rule.
previousDescription: Asian chestnut gall wasp is usually noticed through the growth it causes rather than through the tiny adult wasp. Rounded green or pink galls develop on chestnut buds, leaves, and shoots, sheltering the larvae inside. Later, the galls turn brown and woody and may remain attached after the insects have left. Repeated gall formation can disrupt growth and flowering and reduce nut production. This pest attacks true chestnuts in Castanea, and its management has included carefully studied biological control; an old gall is not proof that a living wasp is still inside.

proposedDescription: Asian citrus psyllid is a small sap-feeding insect often seen with its body tilted upward as it feeds on tender citrus growth. Young insects are yellow-orange and produce curled, waxy tubes. Feeding can distort new leaves, but its greater importance is its ability to transmit the bacteria associated with citrus greening disease. Identifying the insect accurately helps distinguish that risk from ordinary leaf damage.
identification: Check tender citrus shoots for tilted mottled-brown adults, yellowish young, and curly white wax; confirm suspect insects or disease symptoms.
actions: Report suspected psyllids or citrus-greening symptoms through local agricultural authorities where reporting is requested. Do not move suspect citrus plants or cuttings while seeking guidance.

USDA APHIS: Citrus greening and Asian citrus psyllid

researchNotes: UC IPM identification and disease passages and USDA APHIS prevention/reporting material read. Psyllid presence is separate from disease diagnosis. Readers are directed to local authorities rather than a claimed nationwide movement ban.
previousDescription: Asian citrus psyllid often feeds with its rear end raised from a citrus leaf, giving the tiny insect a distinctive tilted posture. Yellow-orange young cluster on tender growth and produce curled white wax tubes. Feeding can distort shoots, but the greater concern is transmission of the bacteria associated with huanglongbing, or citrus greening. Infected trees can decline and produce poor fruit, and there is no cure for the disease. A psyllid sighting does not prove a tree is infected, but it is a good reason to follow local citrus plant-health guidance promptly.

proposedDescription: Asian cockroach usually lives outdoors in leaf litter, mulch and similar sheltered places. It closely resembles the German cockroach, but flies readily and is attracted to lights, especially around dusk. Adults may enter buildings from outside. That behavior matters when interpreting a sighting: one flying into a lit room does not necessarily indicate the kind of indoor infestation associated with its lookalike.
identification: Look for a small tan cockroach with two dark stripes behind the head; flight and attraction to light help distinguish it, but similar species need comparison.
actions: Reduce unnecessary light attraction near doors and windows. Seek identification before choosing a pest treatment.

researchNotes: Texas A&M full biology account and UGA's species-specific identification/lighting guidance read. UF IFAS was search-only and is not counted toward the two-source gate. The profile describes an outdoor species without claiming indoor establishment is impossible.
previousDescription: An Asian cockroach near a porch light may have flown in from the garden. Although it closely resembles the German cockroach, this species usually lives outdoors in shaded leaf litter, mulch, and similar shelter. Adults fly readily and are attracted to light, particularly around dusk. Those habits explain why one can appear indoors without the building supporting the kind of established infestation associated with German cockroaches. Correct identification changes the response: reducing attraction and access around a building can be more useful than treating it as an indoor kitchen pest.

proposedDescription: Asian copperleaf is an annual plant with upright stems and toothed, oval leaves. Young growth may be reddish. Broad, heart-shaped structures surround the small flowers and developing fruit, providing a useful identification feature. Native to Asia, it has been recorded as a weed in parts of the American Midwest, where it can grow and produce seed beneath a crop canopy.

researchNotes: Read Iowa State's full species account and the Illinois Extension identification PDF. The latter is separately authored with a collaborating Iowa State contributor; descriptions and field concerns were compared rather than counted as two unrelated experiments. No nationwide severity or herbicide-resistance generalization.
previousDescription: Asian copperleaf is a small annual plant that can blend into a garden bed or crop field until its flowers develop. Its upright stems carry toothed, oval leaves, often with reddish young growth. Look especially for the broad, heart-shaped leafy bracts around the flowers and fruits; several native copperleaf relatives look similar before flowering. Introduced from eastern Asia, it has become a concern in some Midwestern fields because it can grow beneath crop canopies and produce seed for future seasons.

proposedDescription: Asian drill snail has a thick, ridged shell, commonly about one to two inches long. It lives among shells, gravel and mud around oyster beds, where it bores through the shells of its prey. Small oysters are especially vulnerable, although it also eats other shellfish. Native to the northwestern Pacific, it has traveled with oyster shipments. Clusters of bright yellow, bottle-shaped egg capsules can offer another clue to its presence.

Omitted disputed introduction dates and universal ecological-impact claims.
previousDescription: Asian drill snail is a marine snail with a thick, ridged shell, often around one to two inches long. It lives around shell, gravel and muddy oyster habitats and feeds by boring through the shells of other animals. Native to the northwestern Pacific, it has traveled with oyster shipments. Its feeding makes it a concern where introduced populations overlap with shellfish beds.

proposedDescription: Asian flatsedge is an annual sedge of muddy river margins, ditches and fields. Its narrow leaves grow below branched flower clusters surrounded by longer, leaf-like bracts. The small yellow-brown scales in those clusters have green, pointed midribs. Originally associated with East Asia, it has also been recorded as a field weed in Europe. Close flower details help distinguish it from similar sedges.

previousDescription: Asian flatsedge is a small, grasslike annual that grows in muddy places, including riverbanks, ditches, and cultivated fields. Several upright stems rise together above narrow leaves. At the top, branching flower clusters are overtopped by long, leaflike bracts; the tiny spikelets have yellow-brown scales with pointed green midribs. Native to eastern Asia, it has appeared as an introduced field weed in parts of Europe. Close inspection of the flowering head helps separate it from similar sedges.

proposedDescription: Asian kelp is the brown seaweed widely known as wakame. It has a broad blade with a clear central rib and a ruffled reproductive structure near the base. It grows on rocks as well as ropes and boat hulls, which can help it reach new coasts. Cultivated as food, it is also invasive in some temperate regions, where dense growth can change the habitat available to other marine life.

It attaches to rocks but also grows on ropes, docks, and boat hulls. Cultivated as food in Asia, it has reached many other temperate coasts. Dense growth can shade other seaweeds, although its effects vary between places. The ruffled base is especially helpful when distinguishing mature plants from native kelps.

proposedDescription: Asian longhorned beetle is a large, glossy black beetle with white spots and long, banded antennae. Its pale larvae feed beneath the bark of hardwood trees, then tunnel deeper into the wood. Maples are among its hosts, and heavy feeding can eventually kill a tree. Round exit holes, chewed egg-laying marks and coarse sawdust-like material are useful signs. Native to Asia, it most likely reached the United States in wood packaging.

Native to Asia, it has reached other regions through wood packaging, making careful identification of beetles and tree damage especially important.

proposedDescription: Asian marsh snail is a tiny brown snail with a blunt, cone-shaped shell, reaching only about five millimeters. It lives among vegetation high in salt or brackish marshes, where the ground is not continuously underwater. A field study in Japan found it concentrated in middle and upper tidal areas. Native to Japan and Korea, it has also been recorded in Oregon. Smithsonian reports no observed Oregon impacts, which does not establish that impacts are absent.

proposedDescription: Asian marshweed looks quite different above and below the water. Its submerged leaves are finely divided and arranged in whorls around the stem; leaves emerging into the air are firmer and toothed. Small pink to violet flowers appear above the surface. This Asian aquatic plant has been sold for aquariums and apparently escaped cultivation in the southeastern United States. Some stem fragments can root and regrow, while dense stands can shade and crowd other aquatic plants.

proposedDescription: Asian mustard begins as a rough-leaved rosette before sending up branching stems with small, pale yellow flowers and long seed pods. In southwestern North America, it can grow quickly after winter rain and compete with native desert wildflowers. It comes from the Mediterranean region and nearby parts of Asia. Its ability to spread through open desert habitat makes it more than an ordinary roadside weed in affected areas.

previousDescription: Sahara mustard is a fast-growing annual that can turn desert ground into a dense patch of mustard after favorable winter rain. It begins with a rough, deeply lobed rosette, then sends up mostly leafless stems bearing small pale-yellow flowers and slender seedpods. Originally from the Mediterranean region and nearby parts of Asia, it has spread into southwestern North American dunes, washes, and scrub. Early growth lets it compete with native wildflowers for water and space before those plants finish their own short season.

proposedDescription: Asian nakedwood is a sprawling evergreen shrub with shiny, toothed leaves, small greenish-yellow flowers and rounded seed capsules. Its seeds can float and tolerate salty conditions, helping it move through coastal environments. Native to parts of the Old World tropics, it has become invasive in Florida's coastal habitats, where its climbing and spreading growth can cover other vegetation.

previousDescription: Latherleaf is a sprawling evergreen shrub that can scramble over neighboring vegetation. Shiny oval leaves with toothed edges, small yellow-green flowers, and round seed capsules help identify it. Its buoyant, salt-tolerant fruits and seeds suit a life along tropical shores. The plant is native in parts of the Old World tropics but invasive in coastal southern Florida, where its long branches can form dense tangles over native vegetation. A low roadside shrub can therefore be the beginning of a much larger patch.

proposedDescription: Asian needle ant is a dark ant with paler legs and antenna tips. It often nests in damp wood, leaf litter or beneath stones and feeds on termites and other small animals. Established in parts of the eastern United States, it can displace native ants, including species that disperse plant seeds. It also has a painful sting. Newer references usually call it Brachyponera chinensis.

It often nests in damp leaf litter, rotting logs, mulch, or spaces beneath stones, and feeds on termites and other small animals. Introduced from Asia, it occurs in eastern U.S. forests as well as gardens and buildings. It can displace native ants, including ants that disperse plant seeds. It also delivers a painful defensive sting when pressed against skin. Newer references use the name Brachyponera chinensis.

proposedDescription: Asian pigeonwings is a tropical vine with striking blue flowers that have pale centers. Its leaves are divided into oval leaflets, and flat pods follow the flowers. Widely known as butterfly pea, it is grown ornamentally and for flowers used to color foods and drinks. It can live as a perennial in warm climates, climbing over nearby supports and vegetation.

previousDescription: Butterfly pea is a slender climbing vine best known for its large blue flowers, usually with a pale yellow center. Its leaves are divided into several oval leaflets, and the flowers give way to long, flattened pea pods. It is a perennial in warm climates and is also grown as a seasonal garden plant. The flowers have a long history as a blue food coloring. Cultivated vines sometimes grow wild in disturbed ground, but that alone does not establish harmful ecological effects.

proposedDescription: Asian ponysfoot forms a low green carpet of small, rounded to kidney-shaped leaves. Its creeping stems root as they spread, while tiny greenish-white flowers sit close to the ground and are easy to miss. Fine hairs, especially beneath the leaves, help with identification. It has been grown as a lawn substitute and can occur among lawn grasses. Related Dichondra species look similar, and regional references warn that this scientific name has sometimes been applied inconsistently.

Geographic-origin statements vary across regional sources, so origin and broad invasive status remain omitted. This resolves the descriptive second-source gap without asserting that every regional specimen was correctly identified.
previousDescription: Asian ponysfoot is a low, creeping plant with small kidney-shaped leaves. Its stems spread across the ground, forming a mat, and its tiny greenish to white flowers are easy to overlook. It has been used as a lawn substitute. Fine hairs and other small features help distinguish it from related Dichondra species; the common name alone is not a reliable guide to its native range.

proposedDescription: Asian shore crab has a square shell with three small teeth along each front side. Lifted rocks in the intertidal zone reveal the sheltered spaces it uses between tides. It eats both plant material and small animals, including shellfish. Native to the western Pacific, it has established along parts of the eastern United States. Some invaded rocky shores support dense populations, where its feeding and competition can affect other members of the shore community.

proposedDescription: Asian soybean rust is a fungal disease that can cause tan or reddish leaf spots and tiny spore-producing bumps, especially on leaf undersides. Wind carries the spores between living host plants, including soybean and kudzu. Warm areas with suitable hosts can help the fungus survive between crop seasons. Under favorable wet conditions, severe infections can cause early leaf loss and reduce seed production.

It first shows as small tan or reddish-brown leaf spots, with tiny spore-producing pustules that are easiest to see under magnification. Wind can carry those spores over long distances, while living hosts such as kudzu help the fungus persist in warm regions. Wet, humid weather favors infection. Severe disease strips leaves and reduces seed production, although its importance varies greatly by place and season.

proposedDescription: Asian spiderflower is a sticky, hairy annual with bright yellow flowers and leaves usually divided into five leaflets, though some have three. The slender stems can reach about three feet, with long, narrow seed pods developing among the upper leaves. Glandular hairs give the plant its noticeably sticky surface and help distinguish it from other yellow-flowered herbs. Older botanical accounts call it Cleome viscosa; this catalog retains Arivela viscosa for the same species.

proposedDescription: Asian swamp eels historically grouped as Monopterus albus have long, smooth, scaleless bodies, small eyes and greatly reduced fins. They breathe air and shelter in muddy wetlands, ponds and slow-moving waters, feeding on small aquatic animals. Research has revealed several genetically distinct forms within this group. This overview describes their shared biology; it does not establish the identity of individual U.S. populations. Florida records now assigned to M. javanensis should not automatically be attributed to M. albus.

The retained catalog ID is unchanged; specimen/occurrence assignments and any final ICZN ruling remain unverified and require separate taxonomic work. The profile explicitly states this scope, so occurrence uncertainty alone no longer blocks a conservative biological description.

proposedDescription: Asian swordfern has long, arching fronds made up of many narrow leaflets. Flat, dark brown scales on the leaf stalks are among the features used to distinguish it from similar ferns. It can form dense stands in sheltered places and spreads through spores. In Florida, introduced populations can displace native vegetation, making accurate identification important where several swordferns grow together.

previousDescription: Asian swordfern forms tall, arching fronds lined with many closely spaced leaflets. The dark brown, flat-lying scales on mature frond stalks are useful clues when comparing it with similar native swordferns. It grows in sheltered places and can form dense stands; Florida botanists have documented it displacing other vegetation. Because several native and introduced ferns share the same familiar garden names, an identification should include the stalk scales and leaflet details. Like other ferns, it reproduces by spores rather than seeds.

proposedDescription: Asian tapeworm is a parasite that lives in the intestines of freshwater fish. It infects carp, minnows and many other hosts, and can reduce growth or harm young fish. Moving infected fish, including bait, can help it reach new waters. It is not identified by the fish's appearance alone; examining the parasite or using genetic methods is needed to distinguish it reliably.

sources.title: USGS: Asian fish tapeworm detection study
Rave et al. (2025): Asian fish tapeworm in Parodon magdalenensis

researchNotes: Read the USGS detection-study abstract and substantive sections of the independent 2025 primary Colombian host study. The former is an abstract page, not a claim to have read its entire journal article. Both contain substantive research evidence. Broad host range does not imply equal severity in every host.
previousDescription: Asian fish tapeworm is a parasite that lives inside the intestine of freshwater fish. Carp and minnows are well-known hosts, but researchers have found it in many other kinds of fish too. It is usually hidden from casual observation; identification uses the worm's attachment structures and, increasingly, DNA tests. Infections can interfere with growth and are especially concerning in young fish. Moving infected fish, including live bait, can carry the parasite into new waters and connect an aquaculture problem with native-fish conservation.

proposedDescription: Asian tiger mosquito is black with white-banded legs and a single white stripe down its back. It bites during the day and breeds in small water-filled containers such as tires, buckets and plant trays. Eggs laid just above the waterline can survive dry periods. That combination has helped this Asian species travel with goods and establish around homes in many other regions.

sources.title: University of Florida IFAS: Asian tiger mosquito
CDC: Life Cycle of Aedes Mosquitoes

researchNotes: Read UF's species account and CDC's Aedes life-cycle page. UF's older geographic and disease summaries were not used for current distribution or transmission claims; description focuses on identification, breeding, and household relevance.
previousDescription: Asian tiger mosquito is a small black mosquito with white-banded legs and a single white stripe down its back. Females often bite during the day, especially around morning and late afternoon. Its young develop in small water-filled spaces such as tires, buckets, and flowerpot trays, while eggs attached just above the waterline can survive drying. Native to Asia, it has traveled widely with human commerce. Its close association with homes makes ordinary containers important places to understand and interrupt its life cycle.

proposedDescription: Asian tiger shrimp is a large shrimp with bold bands across its body. Young animals use estuaries and mangroves, while adults breed in marine waters and feed near the bottom, often at night. Native to the Indo-Pacific and widely farmed for food, it has been found along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts of the United States. Its presence raises questions about effects on native species, which require local evidence.

sources.title: FAO: Cultured aquatic species fact sheet, Penaeus monodon

researchNotes: Read Smithsonian's full species account and FAO's cultured-species biology page. Historical aquaculture figures omitted. U.S. ecological concerns are qualified rather than presented as established effects everywhere.
previousDescription: Asian tiger shrimp is a large coastal shrimp with alternating dark and pale bands across its body. Young shrimp use estuaries and mangrove areas, while adults breed in marine water and often feed at night over the bottom. Native to the Indo-Pacific, it is widely raised for food and has appeared in other coastal regions, including U.S. Atlantic and Gulf waters. Its size and predatory diet raise questions about interactions with local shrimp and other animals; those concerns should be separated from demonstrated effects at a particular site.

proposedDescription: Asian waterwort is a tiny, creeping herb of wet mud and shallow water. Its delicate, branching stems carry small leaves and can produce roots at the joints, helping it spread over damp ground. Field observations describe it in rice fields, irrigation channels and other persistently wet cultivated places. It closely resembles other waterworts, especially Elatine triandra. The stalks beneath its flowers and fruits, together with other small botanical details, are more reliable identification clues than its low-growing shape alone.

The flora is brief but contains a substantive diagnostic comparison with E. triandra; the independent Niger report documents habit, rooting and observed habitats with botanical identification. Earlier IISc text and failed FNA access are replaced by these directly read sources. Local Niger crop effects are not generalized to US ecological impact.
previousDescription: Asian waterwort is a tiny, creeping plant of wet mud and shallow water. Small leaves and flowers grow along its delicate stems, often making it inconspicuous among larger wetland plants. It occurs in places such as rice fields and river margins. Several waterworts are similar, so flower and seed details can be important when deciding whether a record truly belongs to this species.

Floral similarity makes casual identification unreliable.

Roots at nodes.
Observed rice-field, irrigation-channel and wet-garden habitats; botanical identification attributed in report.

proposedDescription: Asiatic clam has a rounded, roughly triangular shell marked by strong concentric ridges, usually yellowish to brown. It filters tiny particles from freshwater and can also feed on organic material in the sediment. Rapid growth and reproduction can build dense populations that alter food and nutrient conditions. Large numbers may clog water intakes. Effects on native mussels vary among places, so the presence of this clam alone does not establish why a native population has declined.

previousDescription: Asiatic clam is a freshwater clam with a rounded, roughly triangular shell marked by strong ridges. Shells range from yellowish to brown. It filters particles from the water and can reach high densities, changing food and nutrient conditions and competing with native mussels. Large populations may also clog water-intake equipment, making it important to both aquatic ecosystems and water infrastructure.

Suspension and deposit feeding, dense populations and industrial intake fouling.
Native-bivalve impacts vary; taxonomic names of invasive lineages remain provisional.

proposedDescription: Asiatic dayflower opens vivid blue flowers that usually last only a day. Each flower has two large blue petals and a much smaller pale one. Its leaves wrap around the stems, which can take root where they touch the ground. Native to East Asia, it grows in disturbed places and can become a crop weed, spreading through patches of moist, suitable soil.

sources.title: Iowa State University Extension: Asiatic dayflower
North Carolina State Extension: Asiatic dayflower

researchNotes: Read Iowa State and NC State accounts. Combined short-lived flowers, sheathing leaves, rooting stems, and crop relevance; avoided a universal regional invasive designation.
previousDescription: Asiatic dayflower is a sprawling annual whose bright blue flowers open for only a day. Two large blue petals sit above a much smaller pale petal, while smooth, pointed leaves wrap around the stem in a sheath. Stems touching the ground can root and help a patch spread. Originally from eastern Asia, it now grows in fields, gardens, and other disturbed places. It can compete with crops or nearby vegetation, and its ability to survive some common herbicides makes correct identification useful.

proposedDescription: Asiatic dock has large lower leaves and upright flowering stems that rise above the surrounding vegetation. It grows along rivers, in meadows and in disturbed ground, where seeds and spreading underground stems can help it form patches. Research in Central Europe found that light and shallow burial strongly influenced seedling emergence, helping explain establishment in gaps and disturbed soil. It has expanded in parts of Europe, but those regional findings do not establish its effects in every place it occurs.

This replaces the earlier inaccessible PMC shell. APHIS and the paper share some background literature, but the authors' light, salinity and burial experiments supply independent primary biological evidence. Sources differ in labeling the life cycle perennial versus biennial; omitted that label rather than silently choosing. European spread is geographically bounded and no US impact claim is inferred.
previousDescription: Asiatic dock is a perennial with large lower leaves and tall flowering stems. It grows in places such as river margins, meadows and disturbed fields. Both seeds and spreading roots can help it establish dense patches. It has expanded in parts of Europe outside its earlier range, where its size and persistent root growth can make established stands difficult to displace.

Seed and rhizome reproduction.
Expansion and reported dense growth in parts of Europe.
Original light, salt, nitrate and sowing-depth experiments.

Authors infer establishment in vegetation gaps and disturbed surface soil; abstract labels life cycle biennial.

proposedDescription: Asiatic garden beetle is a small, cinnamon-brown beetle with a rounded shape resembling a coffee bean. Adults hide during the day and feed on leaves at night. Underground, the pale, C-shaped grubs feed on roots and can damage seedlings. Introduced from Asia, it occurs in the United States, where the larvae have also become a concern in some corn-growing areas.

sources.title: University of Maine Extension: Asiatic garden beetle
Michigan State University: Asiatic garden beetle in Michigan field crops

researchNotes: Read Maine Extension's identification account and MSU's primary field-crop observations. Older range limits were omitted. Maladera formosae is retained as the requested ID; older literature often uses M. castanea.
previousDescription: Asiatic garden beetle is a small cinnamon-brown scarab with the rounded shape of a coffee bean. Adults hide during the day and emerge at night to chew leaves; their pale, C-shaped grubs feed underground on roots and young seedlings. Both stages use many garden and crop plants. Introduced from Asia, it has caused damaging infestations in some U.S. corn fields as well as landscapes. This two-part life cycle explains why ragged foliage and weak seedlings can point to the same insect.

proposedDescription: Asiatic witchweed is a parasitic plant that attaches to the roots of grasses, including crops such as corn and sorghum. Its narrow, hairy leaves and small flowers appear above ground, while the connection to its host remains hidden below. Seeds can persist in soil for a long time. That persistence helps explain the long-running monitoring and control efforts around infestations in the Carolinas.

sources.title: USDA APHIS: Witchweed biology and eradication program assessment
Southern Illinois University: Striga asiatica in the U.S.A.

researchNotes: Read APHIS's biology/parasitism section and SIU's annotated primary observations of attachment, self-pollination, seeds, and effects on maize. Historical Carolinas program context is not presented as a current quarantine map.
previousDescription: Asiatic witchweed is a small flowering plant with narrow leaves, coarse hairs, and flowers that may be red, yellow, white, or purple. Much of its effect begins before it appears above ground: the young plant attaches to grass roots and draws resources from its host. Crops such as corn and sorghum can be badly weakened. Its dustlike seeds can remain in soil for years, which is why introduced populations in the Carolinas have required persistent monitoring and control rather than a single season of weeding.

proposedDescription: Asparagus beetle is a small, dark beetle with pale spots and reddish edges. Both adults and grayish larvae feed on asparagus. Dark eggs are often laid upright on the plant, and feeding can scar spears or strip foliage. It differs from the orange, spotted asparagus beetle, so noticing the adult's color pattern helps connect damage with the correct species.

sources.title: University of Wisconsin Vegetable Entomology: Asparagus beetle
University of Minnesota Extension: Asparagus beetles

researchNotes: Read Wisconsin Vegetable Entomology and Minnesota Extension species accounts. Distinguished common and spotted asparagus beetles and their damage patterns. No automatic pesticide recommendation.
previousDescription: Common asparagus beetle is a small, dark beetle marked with pale spots and reddish edges. Both adults and their plump grayish larvae feed on asparagus, while rows of upright, dark eggs may be visible on the spears. Feeding can scar the edible shoots and damage the leafy summer growth that supports the next crop. The orange, black-spotted asparagus beetle is a different species. Checking the adult's markings and the affected plant parts helps connect a beetle sighting with the damage in a garden.

proposedDescription: Asparagus fern is a flowering plant with fine, feathery-looking growth. The narrow green structures that resemble leaves are modified stems; its true leaves are much smaller. True Asparagus densiflorus has upright, closely branched growth, with small white to pinkish flowers that can develop into red berries. It grows naturally on sandy ground in southeastern Africa. Garden names are often mixed with Asparagus aethiopicus, so an arching plant sold as a Sprengeri asparagus fern may represent that related species instead.

Flora Zambesiaca provides a distinct true-densiflorus morphology and habitat; PlantNET states that densiflorus was formerly misapplied to aethiopicus in Australia. Wisconsin conflates names/cultivars, so only shared modified-stem, flower and berry biology is used from it, not Sprengeri identity, sexual system or invasion status. SANBI attempts remained blocked. Replaced the mixed upright-to-arching description with the accepted botanical concept; existing catalog ID is retained.
previousDescription: Asparagus fern has fine, feathery-looking growth, but it is a flowering plant rather than a true fern. What look like tiny leaves are modified stems. Small pale flowers can be followed by red berries, and cultivated forms range from upright plumes to arching sprays. Names are sometimes confused with the related Asparagus aethiopicus, so garden labels alone may not establish the exact species.

proposedDescription: Aspen leafblotch miner spends its larval life inside the leaves of aspens and cottonwoods. Young larvae feed on sap, while later stages remove internal leaf tissue and leave a visible blotch. Silk can draw the mined area into a raised fold. The insect also pupates within its mine before emerging as a tiny moth. These altered patches on leaves are often easier to notice than the adults; a leaf mine still needs careful identification because other insects make similar marks.

The Turkish study reports one generation whereas other regions may have more; no universal generation count was added. MassMoths was also read but is unnecessary to meet the two-source threshold. No non-native or invasive designation is inferred from plant feeding.
previousDescription: Aspen leafblotch miner spends its larval stage inside the leaves of aspens and cottonwoods. Early feeding uses sap, while later feeding removes internal leaf tissue and produces a visible blotch. Silk can draw the mined area into a raised fold. The adult moth is tiny, so the pale, altered patches on leaves are often a more noticeable sign than the insect itself.

proposedDescription: This asthmaweed, Conyza bonariensis, is an annual or short-lived plant with narrow, hairy, gray-green leaves. Its many small flower heads release seeds carried by fine, fluffy hairs. Originally from South America, it grows in fields, orchards and along roads in other regions. Wind dispersal helps it reach newly disturbed ground, where a small plant can develop into a much-branched seed producer.

previousDescription: Hairy fleabane, also called asthmaweed, is a fast-growing annual or biennial with narrow leaves and a covering of grayish hairs. Branching stems carry many small flower heads that develop fluffy, wind-carried seeds. It grows in orchards, fields, roadsides, and other open, disturbed places. Native to South America, it has become a widespread agricultural weed elsewhere, where it competes for water and other resources. Its hairy foliage and branching pattern help separate it from similar fleabanes, though close comparisons are often needed.

proposedDescription: Asthmaweed develops upright, leafy stems carrying many tiny flower heads in a broad, branching cluster. Narrow leaves and the nearly hairless bracts around the heads help distinguish this species from some similar fleabanes. Its small fruits carry fine, pale bristles. It grows in disturbed places, including roadsides and river margins. Modern treatments place Conyza floribunda in Erigeron as Erigeron floribundus; older records sometimes mix it with E. sumatrensis, so those records need a name check.

Fine bristles help its seeds travel on the wind. Records include openings in coastal live-oak habitat in Texas. References may place these plants in Conyza or Erigeron, making scientific-name cross-checks useful when comparing information about them.

proposedDescription: Athel tamarisk is a large evergreen tree with fine, jointed-looking branches and tiny, scale-like leaves. Its deep roots and tolerance of dry, salty conditions have made it useful for shelter plantings. Outside cultivation, it can spread along waterways. In parts of Australia, dense stands have altered river habitats and soil conditions, showing how a tree valued for protection from wind can become a problem in the wrong setting.

sources.title: Oregon State University Landscape Plants: Tamarix aphylla

researchNotes: Read Oregon State's tree description and Queensland's biology/impacts page. Australian river-system effects are explicitly regional; a planting does not establish a U.S. invasive outcome.
previousDescription: Athel tamarisk is a large evergreen shrub or tree with a spreading crown and fine, jointed branchlets. Its tiny leaves hug the twigs, and clusters of pale pink to white flowers appear among the foliage. Deep roots and tolerance of drought and salty soils made it useful for shade and shelter in dry landscapes. It can also escape cultivation. In parts of Australia, dense riverbank infestations have altered water flow and soil salinity, illustrating why a hardy planted tree can become a management concern in some settings.

proposedDescription: Atlantic ivy is an evergreen vine that can carpet the ground or climb trees. Young growth has lobed leaves, while mature flowering growth has less-divided leaves and produces fruit eaten by birds. Stems can also root as they spread. Introduced populations in the Pacific Northwest can dominate forest ground cover and add weight to trees. It is closely related to, but distinct from, English ivy.

sources.title: Washington State Noxious Weed Control Board: English and Irish ivy

researchNotes: Read Oregon State's ivy account and Washington's species/cultivar-specific findings page. The latter explicitly includes H. hibernica 'Hibernica'. Shared ivy traits are described without asserting that every cultivar has identical status.
previousDescription: Atlantic ivy, often called Irish ivy, is an evergreen climbing vine that can also make a thick carpet across the ground. Young shoots carry lobed leaves; flowering shoots have less-divided leaves and produce berries. Rooting stems expand a patch locally, while birds can carry seeds farther away. In invaded Pacific Northwest woodlands, dense ivy can cover native understory plants and add weight to trees. It closely resembles English ivy, and the species or cultivar should be confirmed when interpreting local weed guidance.

proposedDescription: Aucuba whitefly is a tiny sap-feeding insect that uses many host plants, including citrus and ivy. Its dark, oval immature stages sit on leaves and are easier to examine with magnification. Plants moved through trade can carry it between locations. A California assessment reported no significant known impacts at that time, so detection should be distinguished from evidence of serious damage.

researchNotes: Read CDFA's 2022 assessment and Seljak's primary study, especially the A. aucubae section on pages 4-5. Identification relies on slide-mounted immature cases. Dated absence of reported damage is not proof of permanent harmlessness.
previousDescription: Aucuba whitefly is a tiny plant-feeding insect found on a wide range of trees and shrubs, including citrus, ivy, and ornamental evergreens. Its immature stages stay on leaves; the late immature cases are small, dark, and oval, and reliable identification requires magnification. Trade in infested plants can move it between regions. California's 2022 assessment reported no known significant economic or environmental damage there, while European observations likewise found limited injury. Finding the insect and demonstrating damage to its host are separate questions.

proposedDescription: Australasian geranium is a low-growing perennial with hairy, rounded leaves divided into lobes. Its small pink flowers have paler centers and usually appear singly or in pairs. Thickened roots support the plant in moist places such as gullies, creek margins and forested ground. The modest flowers and creeping or spreading growth can make it less conspicuous than familiar garden geraniums.

sources.title: Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney PlantNET: Geranium homeanum
Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria: Geranium homeanum

researchNotes: Read PlantNET and independently authored Flora of Victoria treatment. Both support a perennial, sprawling plant of moist habitats; no U.S. impact claim was added.
previousDescription: Australasian geranium is a low, sprawling perennial with coarse hairs and rounded leaves cut into several broad lobes. Small flowers, pink toward the tips and paler at the base, appear singly or in pairs. A thickened, branching root supports growth from season to season. In Australia it is associated with moist places such as creek banks, wet gullies, and forest margins. Its modest flowers and leaf shape help distinguish it from the more conspicuous plants commonly sold as garden geraniums.

proposedDescription: Australian backyard mosquito has white-banded legs, a pale ring on its mouthparts and lyre-shaped markings on its back. It breeds in small water collections, including tree holes and containers around homes. Adults may bite during the day in shaded places. Originally associated with Australasia, it has also been detected in California, where container habitats can provide suitable places for it to reproduce.

sources.title: Northern Territory Department of Health: Common mosquitoes, Aedes notoscriptus
Santa Barbara Mosquito and Vector Management District: Australian backyard mosquito

researchNotes: Read the NT Department of Health's species section and the Santa Barbara vector district's own detection/biology report. Kept diagnostic white proboscis band and container breeding; avoided inferring local human disease transmission.
previousDescription: Australian backyard mosquito is a dark mosquito with white-banded legs, pale lyre-shaped markings on its back, and a white ring around the middle of its long feeding tube. Its young use tree holes and rain-filled containers, including plant trays, buckets, and drains. Females bite people and other animals, sometimes during the day in shade. Recent detections in California show how this adaptable mosquito can become a neighborhood concern. Its markings matter because it closely resembles other introduced Aedes mosquitoes.

proposedDescription: Australian brake is a fern with large fronds divided into many narrow green segments. Brown stalks rise from a short base, and lines of spore-producing structures form along the undersides of the leaf edges. It grows naturally in Australasian forest and stream habitats and is also cultivated. Looking beneath a mature frond can reveal features that are less obvious from its overall shape.

sources.title: Flora of New Zealand: Pteris tremula
Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney PlantNET: Pteris tremula

researchNotes: Read Flora of New Zealand and PlantNET botanical treatments. Natural habitat, frond form, and sori were compared. Cultivation or escape does not by itself establish invasive harm.
previousDescription: Australian brake is a large, lacy fern whose fronds divide repeatedly into narrow green segments. Brown stalks rise from a short, scaly base, and the fronds can move delicately in a breeze. Lines of spore-producing structures run near the underside edges of fertile segments. It grows in sheltered forest, streamside, and garden settings and has been cultivated beyond its Australasian range. Looking beneath a frond provides useful identification details that are easy to miss when seeing only its feathery outline.

proposedDescription: Australian cheesewood is an evergreen tree with glossy, wavy-edged leaves and fragrant white flowers. Orange capsules open to expose sticky seeds that birds can carry away. Native to eastern Australia, it has become weedy in some places outside its natural range. Its attractive foliage and scent explain its garden use, while bird-dispersed seeds help it move beyond planted sites.

sources.title: Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria: Pittosporum undulatum

researchNotes: Read Stanford's observed tree account and Flora of Victoria's treatment. PIRSA returned navigation without substantive species text and was not used. Victoria's account explicitly distinguishes original native range from later expansion.
previousDescription: Australian cheesewood, or sweet pittosporum, is a shrub or tree with glossy leaves edged in gentle waves. Fragrant creamy-white flowers are followed by orange to yellow-brown capsules that open around sticky seeds. Birds help move those seeds away from planted trees. Although native to parts of eastern Australia, it has spread beyond its earlier range and become an environmental weed in some Australian forests and coastal scrub. Its familiar garden appearance can therefore mean different things depending on the local setting.

proposedDescription: Australian eelgrass is a freshwater plant with long, ribbon-like leaves rooted in the bottom. It spreads through runners and can form dense underwater beds. Female flowers reach the surface, and their stalks coil after pollination. Despite the common name, it is not a marine seagrass. Introduced populations occur in places including California's Delta, where its underwater growth can change the structure of aquatic habitat.

sources.title: California Department of Parks and Recreation: Ribbon weed identification
Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney PlantNET: Vallisneria australis

researchNotes: Read California's ribbon-weed identification sheet and PlantNET's species treatment. Distinguished freshwater Vallisneria from marine eelgrass and avoided transferring other Vallisneria species' impacts.
previousDescription: Australian eelgrass, also called ribbon weed, is a freshwater plant with long, strap-shaped leaves rising from the sediment. Underground runners connect neighboring plants into tall underwater meadows. Small female flowers reach the surface on slender stalks, which coil back underwater after pollination. Despite the name eelgrass, it is not a marine seagrass. Introduced populations have been documented in California's Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta, where distinguishing it from other ribbonlike aquatic plants helps track changes in submerged vegetation.

proposedDescription: Australian fingergrass is easiest to recognize by its little windmill-shaped seed heads. Usually six to nine slender branches spread almost horizontally from the top of a stem, with the florets turning dark as they mature. Narrow leaves form a low, dense clump beneath flowering stems that can reach about knee height. Native to Australia, it grows on varied soils and flowers in response to rain. The detached seed heads can tumble in the wind, helping scatter seed.

These provide separate detailed botanical and growth/dispersal observations despite both being NSW institutions. Corrected the earlier wording: mature florets/spikelets darken, not necessarily the supporting branches. Accounts call it perennial versus biennial/short-lived perennial; avoided an unnecessarily rigid lifespan. No US impact or weed-status claim is inferred.
previousDescription: Australian fingergrass has a seed head shaped like a small windmill, with narrow branches spreading outward in a roughly horizontal plane. It forms low clumps with narrow leaves, and the flowering branches darken as they mature. Native to Australia, it responds to rainfall and grows on a range of soils. The spoke-like head is its clearest feature when seen among other grasses.

proposedDescription: Australian lovegrass is a loosely tufted perennial with narrow leaves and open, branching flower heads. Small, layered flower clusters sit along the fine branches, and hairs near the leaf joints can help with identification. It is native to eastern and southeastern Australia, where it grows in woodland and pasture settings. It should not be confused with other lovegrasses that have different ranges and impacts.

researchNotes: Read Kew GrassBase and PlantNET botanical descriptions. Used broad, concordant morphology rather than incompatible exact floret-count ranges. Did not transfer the reputation of other Eragrostis species to this one.
previousDescription: Australian lovegrass, also known as paddock lovegrass, is a slender perennial that grows in loose tufts. Narrow leaves sit below an open, branching flower head made of many small, neatly stacked spikelets. A tiny fringe of hairs where the leaf meets the stem provides another identification clue. Native to eastern and southeastern Australia, it occurs in woodland and native pasture. Several unrelated concerns are attached to other plants called lovegrass, so the scientific name matters when deciding what a local observation means.

proposedDescription: Australian redcedar can become a very large rainforest tree, with leaves divided into pointed leaflets and new growth often tinged red or pink. Older trees develop rough bark and may have broad buttresses at the base. Woody fruits release winged seeds. Its valuable timber led to extensive historical logging, and trees growing in open sites can look quite different from tall forest-grown specimens.

Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney PlantNET: Toona ciliata

researchNotes: Read ANBG's horticultural account and PlantNET's botanical treatment. The earlier draft's Botanic Gardens palms URL is unrelated and has been excluded. No U.S. invasive designation inferred from seed production.
previousDescription: Australian redcedar is a large deciduous rainforest tree with long leaves divided into many pointed leaflets. New foliage can flush reddish pink, while mature trunks develop scaly bark and substantial buttress roots. Small pale flowers are followed by woody capsules that release winged seeds. Its rich-colored, workable timber made it historically valuable and led to extensive logging in Australia. The shape also changes with its surroundings: forest trees can grow tall and straight, while open-grown trees develop broader spreading crowns.

proposedDescription: Australian redclaw crayfish is a large freshwater crayfish, often blue-green, with a distinctive red patch on the claws of mature males. It comes from northern Australia and nearby regions, using streams, lakes and seasonally changing waters. Widely farmed for food, it can escape cultivation. It eats a variety of plant and animal material, making its establishment relevant to the waters and species it encounters.

The field guide supports male claw markings and regional pest context; feeding-trial findings are not presented as a wild impact experiment.
previousDescription: Australian redclaw crayfish is a large freshwater crayfish, usually mottled blue-green. Mature males have a soft, bright red patch along the outer edge of each large claw, a useful identification clue. It uses tropical streams, lakes, and billabongs in its native northern Australian range and is also farmed for food. It eats a varied diet that includes naturally occurring pond organisms and plant material. Movement for aquaculture has taken it beyond its home waters, where escaped populations can interact with local species.

proposedDescription: Australian saltbush is a low, spreading plant that can form a mat over dry or salty ground. Its gray-green leaves have a fine coating, especially beneath, and its seed-bearing structures become fleshy and red. It has been planted for forage and erosion control. Animals can spread its seeds, and it has established outside cultivation in places including coastal California.

previousDescription: Australian saltbush is a low, spreading perennial that can form broad mats above a deep woody root. Small gray-green leaves often look dusted underneath, and the seed is enclosed in fleshy reddish structures. Native to Australia, it was introduced elsewhere for uses including forage and erosion control. It tolerates dry and salty ground and has colonized disturbed coastal habitats in California. Animals can carry its seeds, helping explain how a plant close to the ground can establish new patches some distance away.

proposedDescription: Australian teatree is a shrub or small tree with gray-green leaves, white flowers and persistent woody seed capsules. Older plants may have twisted trunks and textured bark. Native to coastal southeastern Australia, it has been planted as a screen and windbreak and has become invasive in some other regions. Newer botanical references may list it as Gaudium laevigatum rather than Leptospermum laevigatum.

previousDescription: Australian teatree is a shrub or small tree with gray-green leaves, white flowers, and flat-topped woody seed capsules. Older plants can develop wonderfully twisted trunks and shaggy bark. Native to coastal southeastern Australia, it tolerates salt spray and has been planted as a screen or windbreak. It has also naturalized beyond its original range and become weedy in some regions. Recent botanical treatments may use Gaudium laevigatum, so both names are helpful when matching observations with planting records or identification guides.

proposedDescription: Australian tortoise beetle is a rounded brown beetle, often mottled with darker marks, that feeds on eucalyptus. Adults and larvae chew the leaves, leaving curved or semicircular notches along the edges. Adults commonly feed at night and shelter beneath loose bark during the day, a habit also documented in Chilean field collections. Introduced populations occur in California. Established, well-cared-for trees often tolerate feeding, although heavy defoliation can add stress; finding beetles does not by itself show how seriously a tree is affected.

California damage severity and tree tolerance are supported by UC, not extrapolated from the Chilean collection. Retained that established trees often tolerate feeding, not a guarantee of harmlessness.

Adults commonly feed at night and shelter beneath bark during the day. Introduced populations occur in California. Mature trees can often tolerate some feeding, so the presence of beetles and the severity of damage should be assessed separately.

proposedDescription: Australian tubeworm lives inside a hard, pale tube attached to a submerged surface. A feathery crown reaches into the water to collect tiny food particles, then withdraws into the tube when disturbed. It favors sheltered brackish places such as estuaries, lagoons and docks. Many generations can build tangled, reef-like colonies, although reefs do not form everywhere it occurs. It also grows on boat hulls and structures. Despite its common name, an Australian native origin remains uncertain.

The failed MDPI paper is not counted as read. Both accounts treat Australian origin as possible, not established. Reef development is explicitly conditional; no reef is assumed at every occurrence.

A feathery crown extends from each tube to collect food, while large colonies can form reef-like structures on submerged surfaces. It also grows on boats and marine infrastructure, which can help it travel. Despite its common name, its original native range is uncertain; the name should not be treated as proof of an Australian origin.

proposedDescription: Australian waterbuttons is a small, low-growing plant with finely divided leaves and tiny flower heads that look like buttons. The heads are cream to pale yellow and lack the showy outer petals of many daisies. Slender stems may lie along the ground or turn upward, and can root where they touch suitable soil. Look for it in lawns, roadsides, open grassland and other disturbed places. Its modest size can make the button heads easier to notice than the plant beneath them.

proposedDescription: Austrian pine has stiff, dark green needles held in pairs. Young trees are often roughly pyramid-shaped, while older trees develop broader crowns, deeply furrowed bark and brown cones. Native across parts of Europe, northwestern Africa and western Asia, it has been widely planted for screens and windbreaks. Its paired needles and mature bark are useful features when comparing it with other planted pines.

previousDescription: Austrian pine is a substantial evergreen with stiff, dark green needles held in pairs. Young trees form a dense pyramid, while older trees develop a broad, rounded or flattened crown above stout branches. Brown cones point outward from the shoots, and mature bark becomes deeply furrowed. Native across parts of southern Europe, northwest Africa, and western Asia, it has been widely planted for screens and windbreaks. Its paired needles are a practical first clue, while cone and bark details help distinguish it from other pines.

proposedDescription: Austrian yellowcress is an upright perennial with small, four-petaled yellow flowers and toothed leaves that clasp the stem. Rounded seed pods follow the flowers. It can spread through both seeds and creeping roots, allowing patches to expand in damp fields, pastures and river margins. In parts of the western United States, dense growth can compete with other vegetation, including desirable pasture plants.

previousDescription: Austrian yellowcress is an upright perennial in the mustard family, with small four-petaled yellow flowers and toothed leaves that partly clasp the stem. Its nearly round seedpods help separate it from mustards with long, narrow pods. It grows along moist riverbanks and in disturbed places such as pastures, roadsides, and fields. Creeping underground roots allow a patch to expand as well as spread by seed. In parts of the western United States, it competes with desirable forage and native vegetation.

proposedDescription: Autumn olive is a spreading deciduous shrub with silvery foliage, fragrant pale flowers and small red fruits dotted with pale scales. Native to Asia, it was widely planted in the United States for landscaping and erosion control. Birds and small mammals carry its seeds into fields, roadsides and woodland edges. Its roots can add nitrogen to the soil, helping it grow on poor ground. In North Carolina and other affected regions, dense growth can crowd surrounding vegetation.
identification: Alternate leaves with silvery scales; pale tubular flowers; red, speckled fruit.
actions: Avoid planting where invasive. Small seedlings can be pulled with their roots; check for regrowth.

proposedDescription: Autumn zephyrlily is a small bulb-forming perennial with narrow green leaves and white, crocuslike flowers. Blooms rise above the grassy foliage in summer and autumn, often following rain. It comes from South America and is grown widely as an ornamental in borders and containers. The plants form compact clumps, and offsets develop around the original bulbs. In mild climates the leaves may remain green; in colder places the bulbs need protection from winter freezing.
identification: Clumps of narrow leaves; solitary white flowers with six petal-like segments and orange stamens.

proposedDescription: Chenopodium hircinum is an annual herb from South America and a wild relative of quinoa. Its upright stems branch near the base, carrying alternate leaves that often have three uneven lobes. A pale, mealy coating and an unpleasant smell are useful supporting clues. The tiny whitish-green flowers grow in clusters along narrow spikes. Leaf shape varies considerably, so a familiar-looking leaf alone is not enough to separate it from other goosefoots; mature seeds can be important for identification.

proposedDescription: Avocado is an evergreen tree from tropical America, grown for fleshy fruits with a single large seed. Its broad leaves form a dense crown, while small greenish-yellow flowers appear in branching clusters. Fruit size, skin texture and ripening season vary considerably among cultivated varieties. The trees grow best in warm, sunny places with good soil drainage. Avocados have been cultivated in the Americas since before European contact and remain an important orchard crop in tropical and subtropical regions.
identification: Large alternate leaves; clusters of small greenish-yellow flowers; fleshy fruit surrounding one large seed.
actions: Use healthy planting stock and avoid poorly drained sites. Ask local extension staff to diagnose unexpected decline.

Adults and spiny young gather beneath avocado leaves, where their feeding creates pale patches that can turn brown. Dark specks of waste and clusters of eggs are useful clues on the lower leaf surface. The insect also uses some other plants in the laurel family. Heavy infestations can cause early leaf drop, exposing fruit and branches to sun; small populations may cause little lasting damage.
