Young mobile stages move to new feeding sites, while infested nursery plants can carry established colonies farther afield. Several related scales look very similar, so a microscope is usually needed to confirm the species.

proposedDescription: Bald brome is a short-lived grass that grows as a loose tuft or sometimes as a single upright stem. Its leaves and lower sheaths are hairy, while the flower clusters carry several pale-green, many-flowered spikelets with slender bristles. It is native across a broad temperate range from the Azores and Europe into Asia, and has been introduced elsewhere. Although its common name suggests a hairless plant, the floral details, rather than the absence of leaf hairs, are important for identification.
identification: Hairy leaves and sheaths; pale many-flowered spikelets with straight bristles on a relatively compact flower cluster.
actions: Photograph mature flower heads and leaf sheaths; confirm against a regional grass key before removal.

proposedDescription: Balfour's touch-me-not is an annual with upright, branching stems and two-toned pink and white flowers. Each flower has a narrow spur extending behind it, and the pointed leaves have regularly toothed edges. Native to the western Himalayas, it has been grown as a garden ornamental and sometimes escapes into disturbed ground. In Victoria, Australia, botanical accounts describe localized dense stands near old gardens. Its smooth stems and modest flower size help separate it from some larger, more familiar balsams.
identification: Hairless stems, alternate toothed leaves and pink-and-white flowers with a slender straight spur.
actions: Confirm the species and remove unwanted seedlings before seed capsules mature; avoid moving seed-bearing garden material.

proposedDescription: Ballmustard is an annual mustard-family plant of fields, meadows and disturbed ground. Small yellow flowers are followed by rounded fruits, giving the seed-bearing stems their distinctive beadlike appearance. Native to Eurasia, it has spread into parts of northern North America, including New England. The seeds can be difficult to separate from harvested canola or mustard because they are similar in size. That makes it relevant as an agricultural weed even where it is less conspicuous than larger flowering plants.
identification: Small yellow mustard flowers and rounded fruits; confirm mature material with a regional flora.
actions: Use clean seed and avoid carrying mature seed-bearing plants between fields; seek local advice for crop infestations.
researchNotes: Read both cited accounts directly. Regional and taxonomic scope retained; no national invasive designation inferred.

proposedDescription: Balloon vine is a tendril-climbing plant named for its inflated, papery fruit capsules. The green capsules become brown as they mature, enclosing black seeds with a pale heart-shaped mark. Divided leaves and small white flowers grow along branching stems that scramble over nearby plants. It occurs across tropical and subtropical regions in thickets, river margins and disturbed ground. In parts of the southeastern United States, introduced growth can cover surrounding vegetation, but its native and introduced status varies around the world.
identification: Inflated three-chambered capsules and black seeds marked with a white heart; climbing tendrils and divided leaves.
actions: Check local status and keep seed-bearing vines out of dumped garden waste; remove unwanted growth before capsules mature.
researchNotes: Native-range complexity explicit; not characterized as universally nonnative. Omitted questionable flower measurement in NC State account.

proposedDescription: Balloon-flower is a perennial grown for buds that swell like small balloons before opening into broad, five-pointed bells. The flowers face outward or upward above leafy stems, appearing in late spring and summer. Native to eastern Asia, the plant returns from a fleshy root system that can be easily damaged by disturbance. It is commonly grown in sunny or partly shaded borders with well-drained soil. Its unusual unopened buds are usually the easiest feature to recognize.
identification: Balloonlike unopened buds; open bell-shaped flowers with five pointed lobes.
actions: Confirm the plant before removing a garden escape; avoid scattering seed from unwanted plants.
researchNotes: Ornamental profile with no demonstrated invasive-impact claim.

claims: Bud and flower shape, fleshy roots and cultivation
Eastern Asian native range and perennial habit

proposedDescription: Balsam woolly adelgid is a tiny sap-feeding insect hidden beneath white, woolly wax on true fir trees. Colonies settle on bark and branches, where their feeding can cause swollen twigs, distorted growth and declining crowns. Susceptibility varies among fir species: Fraser fir in the southern Appalachians and subalpine fir in the western United States can suffer severe damage. Introduced from Europe, the insect reproduces without mating in North America. Its small size means an infestation may go unnoticed until tree symptoms develop.
identification: White woolly spots on true-fir bark; swollen twig nodes and declining growth are warning signs.
actions: Inspect true firs and consult local forestry staff about suspect colonies; avoid transporting infested trees or branches.
researchNotes: Regional effects distinguished; Douglas-fir is not a true fir. Omitted disputed alternate-host detail unnecessary to overview.

proposedDescription: Balsampear, also called bitter melon, is a fast-growing annual vine with curling tendrils and deeply lobed leaves. Yellow flowers develop into bumpy or ridged fruits that change from green to orange when ripe. The mature fruit splits open, exposing seeds wrapped in bright red flesh. Cultivated varieties are familiar vegetables in many warm regions, while smaller-fruited forms may grow outside gardens. The plant thrives in heat and humidity and can climb supports or spread across the ground.
identification: Lobed leaves, yellow flowers and warty fruit that turns orange and splits into curling sections.
actions: Keep unwanted vines from setting seed. Do not assume ripe fruit or seeds are safe to eat because immature cultivated fruit is used as food.
researchNotes: Native origin omitted because sources use different broad ranges; no medicinal efficacy claims.

claims: Annual vine, tendrils, leaves, ripening fruit and ripe-part toxicity

proposedDescription: This bamboo, also known as timber bamboo or Phyllostachys bambusoides, is a tall woody grass native to central and southern China. Its green canes carry long branches and pointed leaves that are bright green above and blue-green beneath. Young cane sheaths can be pinkish with purple mottling, a useful seasonal detail. It has a long history in cultivation, and its eventual size varies greatly with climate and growing conditions. The scientific name is more informative than the catalog's general label Bamboo.
identification: Green canes, long branches, two-toned leaf surfaces and pinkish, purple-mottled young cane sheaths.
actions: Confirm species before planting or removal, and monitor the edge of an established planting for spread.

proposedDescription: Bamboo armored scale is a small scale insect that can remain well hidden on its host. Recorded colonies occupy the tight space between a bamboo leaf stalk and the stem, so an ordinary glance at the leaves may miss them. The species was originally described from Asian bamboo and has since been reported in other regions, including Saint Lucia. Closely related scales require microscopic comparison, making the host and concealed feeding site useful search clues rather than a complete identification.
identification: Inspect the junction of bamboo leaf stalks and stems; a specialist must confirm microscopic scale characters.
actions: Keep suspect bamboo plants separate and seek identification before moving them to another site.

proposedDescription: Bamboo pit scale is a tiny sap-feeding insect found on bamboo leaves and stems. Females are elongated and yellowish, sheltered beneath a translucent cover that can blend into the plant. A fringe of pale wax may help reveal a colony. Observers in the Canary Islands found it on both leaf surfaces and stems, sometimes in large groups. It was considered a minor pest in that setting, so the number of scales alone should not be treated as proof of serious damage.
identification: Oval translucent covers with pale wax fringes on bamboo stems or leaves; color alone is unreliable.
actions: Inspect new bamboo carefully and isolate suspect plants pending specialist identification.

proposedDescription: Bamboo powderpost beetle develops inside cut bamboo, where both adults and larvae make feeding tunnels. The insects can attack culms during processing, storage or use, turning internal tissue into fine powder and reducing the material's strength. Eggs are laid inside the bamboo, and the young remain concealed as they grow. Fresh powder and small exit holes may reveal an infestation before the beetles themselves are noticed. Research in Japan documents it as an important pest of dried bamboo products.
identification: Fine powder and exit holes in bamboo are clues; collect an adult for expert identification because other borers leave similar signs.
actions: Set suspect bamboo products apart and obtain pest identification; avoid moving visibly infested material.

proposedDescription: Stigmaeopsis celarius is a tiny bamboo-feeding spider mite that lives beneath silk shelters on leaves. The dense, oval roofs cover small colonies and help protect them from predators. Behavioral experiments found that adults defend these nests and that larger groups provide stronger protection. Several related bamboo mites look similar and older reports used this name more broadly. Webbing beneath a bamboo leaf is therefore a useful place to look, but microscopic examination is needed to identify the species reliably.
identification: Bamboo leaf mites require microscopic identification; webbing or leaf damage alone cannot confirm this species.
actions: Photograph affected leaves and obtain specialist identification before treatment or plant movement.

proposedDescription: Banana aphid is a small, shiny brown to nearly black insect that feeds on banana sap. Colonies produce sticky honeydew, which can attract ants and support black sooty mold. Its greatest importance is as a carrier of banana bunchy top virus, rather than the feeding injury alone. Winged forms can disperse to other plants. Older accounts assigned aphids from ginger and several other hosts to this species, but modern research separates many of those populations as Pentalonia caladii.
identification: Shiny reddish-brown to black aphids on banana; winged individuals have conspicuously dark wing veins.
actions: Inspect banana planting material and seek local plant-health advice for aphids or bunchy-top symptoms; do not distribute suspect plants.

proposedDescription: Banana bud moth is a small brown moth whose caterpillars tunnel inside stems and other plant tissues. Despite its name, it attacks many plants, including palms, dracaenas, bananas and other tropical ornamentals. The pale caterpillars have a brown head and produce piles of fine plant waste held together with silk. Infested stems may weaken or collapse, and empty pupal cases can project from the tunnels. Damaged or stressed plants are especially attractive places for the nocturnal adults to lay eggs.
identification: Silk-bound powdery waste and projecting pupal cases; pale caterpillars with brown heads inside damaged stems.
actions: Inspect plants for frass and wounds, reduce avoidable plant stress, and seek advice on containing confirmed infestations.

proposedDescription: Pestalotiopsis disseminata is a fungus reported from many kinds of plants, sometimes causing blight, cankers or fruit decay and sometimes living within apparently healthy tissue. Symptoms depend on the host and growing conditions, so a spotted leaf alone does not identify it. A banana disease reference lists this species with fruit rot, while other Pestalotiopsis species are associated with banana leaf spots. Modern diagnosis combines microscopic characters with genetic evidence because older identifications based only on appearance can be unreliable.
identification: No reliable naked-eye diagnosis; laboratories compare fungal structures and DNA.
actions: Have unexplained plant disease diagnosed before choosing treatment; avoid sharing suspect propagation material.

proposedDescription: Banana passionflower is a climbing vine with three-lobed leaves, hanging pink flowers and elongated fruits that ripen yellow. Often called banana poka in Hawaii, it can climb high into forest vegetation and spread across tree crowns. Birds and pigs disperse its seeds there. The vine is native to the Andes and was long confused with another banana passionfruit, Passiflora mollissima. Its vigorous growth is a serious problem in some Hawaiian forests, where it can smother the plants supporting it.
identification: Three-lobed leaves, pendent pink flowers and elongated yellow-ripe fruits; confirm against similar passionflowers.

proposedDescription: Banded cichlid is a deep-bodied South American fish from the upper Orinoco and upper Negro river regions. Dark vertical markings cross the body, but the pattern must be interpreted carefully because several related fishes are sold as severums. In the modern identification of Heros severus, one middle body bar is shortened rather than extending fully between the upper and lower fins. Older aquarium and biological accounts can mix it with other Heros species, making confirmed identity especially important.
identification: Deep body and vertical bands; precise bar pattern and other characters require comparison with related Heros species.
actions: Never release aquarium fish. Obtain a specialist identification for wild records or uncertain aquarium stock.

proposedDescription: The banded elm bark beetle is a small Asian beetle that now occurs in North America. Adults are reddish brown with a darker band across the wing covers. Its pale, legless larvae tunnel beneath the bark of stressed elms, interrupting the tissues that move food through the tree. The beetle can also carry the fungus responsible for Dutch elm disease. Tree condition matters: in Utah, attacks on the common Siberian elm often cause little damage when disease is absent.
identification: Reddish-brown adults roughly 3–4 mm long with a dark wing band; white legless larvae and branching galleries beneath elm bark.
actions: Keep elms healthy and arrange assessment of dying branches or trees; do not move infested elm wood.

proposedDescription: Barbados aloe is an evergreen succulent with a rosette of thick, pointed leaves edged with small pale teeth. The leaves store water and contain the clear gel familiar from cosmetic products. Mature plants can send up tall stalks bearing tubular yellow to orange flowers, while young offsets form beside the parent plant. It is widely grown in pots and warm-climate gardens, where freely draining soil is important. The yellow latex near the leaf surface differs from the inner gel and should not be casually consumed.
identification: Thick toothed leaves in a basal rosette; offsets around the base; tubular flowers on tall stalks.
actions: Avoid overwatering and dispose of unwanted offsets responsibly; do not eat the leaves or latex.
researchNotes: No medicinal efficacy or current regulatory claim taken from Cambridge historical use account. NCSU vague invasive claim omitted without a named affected region.

proposedDescription: Barbados gooseberry is a climbing cactus with ordinary-looking, slightly fleshy leaves. Paired hooked spines help its branches catch surrounding plants, while older stems carry clusters of longer spines. Fragrant white or pale-yellow flowers are followed by round yellow to orange fruits. Native to tropical America, it has escaped from gardens in places such as eastern Australia, where heavy, tangled growth can smother other vegetation. Broken stems and even leaves can regrow, making dumped garden material a source of new plants.
identification: Leafy climbing cactus with hooked branch spines, longer clustered trunk spines and round yellowish fruit.
actions: Handle with protective gloves; contain all fragments and ask local weed staff about disposal where it has escaped.
researchNotes: Kew taxonomy and range are independent of the NSW applied weed-management synthesis. No US-wide invasive status asserted.

proposedDescription: Barbados nut is a spreading shrub or small tree native to tropical America. Its broad leaves have three or five pointed lobes, and small yellow-green flowers develop into rounded capsules that split as they mature. The dark seeds contain oil used in industrial products and investigated as a fuel source. The plant tolerates drought and relatively poor soil, which has encouraged cultivation far beyond its native range. Despite the common name, its seeds are not edible nuts and can cause poisoning.
identification: Alternate broad leaves with three or five pointed lobes, yellow-green flowers and yellowish capsules containing dark seeds.
actions: Keep seeds away from children and animals; prevent unwanted seedlings around cultivated plants.

proposedDescription: Barbary fig is a large, branching cactus grown for its fleshy fruit. Its flattened, oval pads are stems, often forming a small tree with a distinct trunk. Many cultivated plants lack long spines, but small irritating bristles can still be present. Yellow flowers develop into rounded fruits that change color as they ripen. The species comes from Mexico and has been carried widely in cultivation. In New South Wales it sometimes escapes into surrounding vegetation, spreading through seeds and fallen stem pieces.
identification: Large flattened oval pads on a shrubby or tree-like cactus; yellow flowers and fleshy fruit; spines vary greatly.
actions: Use gloves when handling; collect fruit and contain discarded pads where escape is a concern.

proposedDescription: Barbed goatgrass is a winter annual grass closely related to wheat. Its stiff, narrow leaves and short seed heads become especially noticeable when the very long bristles spread from the developing seeds. Native from the Mediterranean region into central Asia, it grows in California grasslands, rangelands and oak woodlands, including some dry, shallow soils. The bristles catch on clothing and animal fur, helping seeds travel. They can also lodge around livestock mouths or eyes, reducing the usefulness of affected pasture.
identification: Short cylindrical seed heads with exceptionally long, spreading bristles; narrow rigid leaves and hairy leaf sheaths.
actions: Clean attached seed heads from clothing and equipment before leaving affected ground; obtain local advice before treating pasture.

proposedDescription: Barberton daisy is a perennial from southern Africa with bold daisy-like flower heads held above a low rosette of leaves. The leaves are elongated and often deeply lobed, while the flowers usually have red outer rays surrounding a darker center. This species helped give rise to the many hybrid gerberas sold as bedding plants and cut flowers. It favors bright conditions and moist but well-drained soil; saturated soil can damage its roots. In colder climates it is commonly grown seasonally or protected from frost.
identification: Lobed leaves in a basal rosette with solitary large daisy heads on upright stalks; garden hybrids vary widely in color.
actions: Keep the crown at soil level and avoid waterlogged soil; verify local status before treating a garden escape as invasive.

proposedDescription: Cryptocarenus heveae is a very small, dark-brown bark beetle recorded in South America. At roughly two millimeters long, it is difficult to recognize without a microscope. A specialist key uses details of the forehead, including a shallow depression and small central bump, to separate it from similar beetles. Researchers have caught it in ethanol-baited traps in a mixed Brazil-nut and rubber plantation in the southern Amazon. That finding documents its presence there, but does not by itself show which trees it was using.

proposedDescription: The black stem borer is a tiny ambrosia beetle from eastern Asia that has become a pest of orchard and nursery trees in North America. proposedDescription: Barnyardgrass is a variable annual grass common in damp, disturbed ground and cultivated fields. Its flattened stems may spread near the ground before turning upward, carrying broad, flat blades. The branched seed head is crowded with small spikelets and may have a purplish cast. One useful clue is the absence of a small membrane or fringe where the leaf blade meets its sheath. Introduced from Eurasia into North America, it is a familiar agricultural weed of irrigated fields, ditches and rice-growing areas.

proposedDescription: Basil downy mildew is caused by Peronospora belbahrii, a microscopic water mold that infects basil. Leaves often turn yellow between the main veins, while gray to purple downy growth develops underneath. Symptoms may begin low on the plant and spread upward, making a healthy-looking crop decline quickly in humid conditions. The pathogen can arrive on seed or infected plants, and its spores travel through the air. Yellowing alone can resemble a nutrient problem, so the leaf underside provides an important clue.
identification: Yellow areas bounded by leaf veins with gray-purple downy growth underneath; a diagnostic laboratory can confirm uncertain cases.
actions: Choose resistant varieties and tested seed, allow air movement, avoid wetting foliage and remove confirmed infected plants.

proposedDescription: Basket plant is a fleshy perennial from Mexico that forms clusters of broad, glossy leaves. Long flowering stalks rise from the upper leaf bases and carry small, fragrant white flowers. Some cultivated forms have pale or purple markings, so leaf color alone is unreliable. Grown as an ornamental groundcover, it has escaped into hammocks and disturbed places in central and southern Florida, where it can displace existing vegetation. A plant growing outside cultivation should be assessed in its local setting before removal is planned.

The blossoms attract bees, including large carpenter bees, and flowers may be followed by distinctly beaked capsules.

actions: Check local weed status before planting or sharing it. For escaped vines, obtain a plan that addresses the persistent roots and keeps cut material out of natural areas.

proposedDescription: Bent-grass nematode is a microscopic roundworm that develops inside abnormal growths in grass flower heads. These elongated galls replace developing seeds and can be concealed by the surrounding flower parts. Bentgrasses are the best-known hosts, and a modern study also confirmed the species in fowl bluegrass beside a Wyoming river. Older accounts assigned many other grasses to this nematode, but some of those records belong to different species. Accurate identification therefore depends on examining the nematodes, not just noticing damaged seed heads.
identification: Unusually elongated flower parts and seed-replacing galls are useful warning signs. Microscopic and, where needed, DNA examination are necessary for species identification.
actions: Do not distribute suspect grass seed lots. Ask a seed-testing or plant diagnostic laboratory to examine galls and advise on cleaning or disposal.
researchNotes: Strong taxonomy caveat: older A. agrostis sensu lato host and bacterial-toxicity accounts cannot be transferred indiscriminately. Roubtsova/Subbotin 2020 molecularly confirmed Poa palustris; Eisenback/Roane 2006 is an independent morphology-based grass-gall study, but its A. stolonifera host record predates the narrow modern synthesis. Nemaplex repeats both lineages and is not a third independent experiment. No chemical, hot-water or burning prescription.

proposedDescription: Agrostis castellana is a perennial bentgrass with fine, gray-green leaves and upright flowering stems. It forms tufts linked by slender underground stems, while its flower head spreads into a delicate branching shape and often narrows as it ages. The tiny flower clusters may be greenish or purple, with some bearing slender awns and others lacking them. Native around the Mediterranean and nearby Atlantic islands, it has been introduced elsewhere, including New Zealand, where it is known as dryland browntop.
identification: Look for fine gray-green leaves, underground spreading stems and an open flower head with a mixture of awned and awnless flower clusters. A grass key is needed.
actions: Have flowering material identified before managing an unfamiliar patch. Check local guidance and avoid moving seed or soil from unwanted stands.
researchNotes: Catalog Bentgrass is nonspecific; dryland browntop is supported by Edgar and Connor. Independent New Zealand flora and Kew/WCVP support morphology and range. No US invasive status inferred and no traits copied from unrelated Agrostis entries or old synonym descriptions.

proposedDescription: Lachnagrostis filiformis is a fine-leaved grass native to Australia, often growing on poorly drained or seasonally wet ground. Its loose, airy flower head branches widely above a tuft of narrow leaves, and the small green or purplish flower clusters carry bent bristles. At maturity, the stem commonly breaks beneath the flower head, allowing it to move away from the parent plant. Plants may behave as annuals or persist longer, and closely related grasses can be difficult to separate.
identification: Look for an open, often drooping flower head, narrow leaves and tiny bent awns. Mature heads may break away; a botanical key is needed for close relatives.

proposedDescription: Bermuda buttercup is a bulb-forming perennial from southern Africa, with bright yellow flowers held above a loose cluster of leaves. Each leaf has three heart-shaped leaflets, often dotted with purple. Despite its common name, it is a wood sorrel rather than a true buttercup. In California it grows during the cooler, wetter part of the year and retreats to underground bulbs as weather warms. Those bulbs allow patches to return and can spread the plant when contaminated soil is moved.
identification: Look for three heart-shaped leaflets, clustered yellow flowers on leafless stalks and small underground bulbs. Distinguish it from low, creeping wood sorrels.
actions: Avoid moving soil from infested patches. Where removal is appropriate, collect bulbs carefully and revisit the area, since cutting off leaves alone leaves bulbs alive.
researchNotes: UC's California biology is kept regional; the same article includes O. corniculata, whose seed-based spread and management were not transferred. proposedDescription: Bermudagrass is a low, wiry perennial grass that grows most actively in warm weather. It spreads through runners above ground and underground stems, both able to root and form new plants. Narrow leaves and fingerlike branches radiating from the tip of each flower stalk help distinguish a flowering patch. It is widely grown as turf, yet the same spreading growth makes it a persistent weed in gardens and planting beds. In cooler conditions the foliage turns brown as the grass becomes dormant.
identification: Check for rooting runners, underground stems, a fringe of white hairs where leaf meets sheath and three to seven fingerlike flower-head branches.
actions: Keep runners and contaminated soil out of beds where it is unwanted. Remove spreading stems repeatedly and monitor regrowth; fragments left in moist soil can root.
researchNotes: Species-specific UC IPM account and Utah State pest guide were read; no genus-level hybrid-turf facts used. Utah phenology is regional, so exact dormant months omitted. UC and USU are independently authored institutional guidance, with USU's own photographed specimens.

proposedDescription: Bhutan pine is an evergreen mountain tree from the Himalayan region, also known as Himalayan pine. Its long, gray-green needles grow in bundles of five and hang downward on older shoots, giving the branches a soft, drooping appearance. Long, resinous cones hang from stalks, while bark changes from smooth gray-green on young wood to darker, fissured scales with age. The species is grown as an ornamental beyond its native range and generally favors sunny sites with well-drained soil.
identification: Count five needles per bundle and look for long, drooping needles and long-stalked, resinous cones. Compare mature cones with other five-needle pines.
actions: Document needles, cones and overall form to confirm identification. Assess local planting or naturalization status before deciding whether any management is needed.
researchNotes: Oregon State horticultural observations and Kew/WCVP are independent sources. Common name Bhutan pine refers here to P. wallichiana; no claim about P. bhutanica. proposedDescription: Bicolored trailing ants are tiny, shiny ants with a dark head and abdomen contrasting with a much lighter middle section. Workers are less than two millimeters long and often forage on trees, shrubs and around buildings in warm climates. Colonies occupy small cavities, including spaces in twigs and bark, and may contain several queens. The ants take insects and sweet foods, including honeydew from plant-feeding bugs. Their small nests can travel with nursery plants and other material moved by people.
identification: Use magnification to check the dark head and abdomen, pale middle and two-part waist. Confirm a collected specimen because other small household ants can look similar.
actions: Inspect nursery plants and small cavities before moving them. Indoors, remove accessible food and seek species identification before selecting a targeted control.

proposedDescription: Bighead carp are large freshwater fish with oversized heads, low-set eyes and irregular dark blotches along their bodies. Rather than hunting larger prey, they strain tiny organisms and other food from the water. Introduced from Asia for pond management, they escaped into rivers and now occur in parts of the Mississippi River system. identification: The eyes sit low on a very large head. Dark body blotches and a belly ridge extending only from the vent to the pelvic fins help distinguish it from silver carp.
actions: Do not move live fish between waters. Photograph a suspected catch and contact your state fisheries agency for identification and handling instructions.

proposedDescription: Bigheaded ants get their name from the unusually large heads of their larger workers, which forage alongside many smaller ants. These small brown ants nest in soil, lawns and sheltered spaces beneath paving or pots, often leaving loose piles of sand. They feed on insects and sweet liquids such as honeydew. Established in many warm regions, including Florida, their large colonies can displace other ants and become a persistent household nuisance. identification: Look for two distinct worker sizes, with conspicuously large heads on the larger workers. Have an expert confirm the species.
actions: Seek identification before treating. For an established infestation, coordinate with neighboring properties and use locally approved bait or professional guidance.

proposedDescription: Birch leafminer is a small sawfly whose young feed between the upper and lower surfaces of birch leaves. proposedDescription: Black carp is a large, dark fish with broad scales and powerful teeth deep in its throat that can crush snails and mussels. Brought from Asia for use in fish farming, it escaped into waterways and now reproduces in the Mississippi River basin. Its appetite raises concern for native freshwater mollusks, many of which already face other threats.
