proposedDescription: Coastal burnweed is an upright, short-lived herb with narrow, regularly toothed leaves and clusters of small cylindrical flower heads. Unlike a showy daisy, its heads lack a ring of spreading ray petals. Botanists now commonly treat this plant as Senecio minimus, while Erechtites minimus remains a name used in older records. It occurs naturally in Australia and New Zealand, including moist forest settings, so its presence there should not automatically be interpreted as an alien invasion.
identification: Look for narrow stem leaves with toothed bases that clasp the stem, small cylindrical heads and no showy ray flowers. Closely related Senecio species can require examination of head bracts and mature fruits.
actions: Photograph leaf bases, flower heads and the whole plant. Confirm the identification and local native status with a herbarium before considering management.
researchNotes: Flora of New Zealand explicitly links Erechtites minimus to Senecio minimus; independent Flora of NSW supplies morphology and wet-forest context. Database ID retained. Native occurrence is distinguished from introduced occurrence elsewhere.

sources.title: Flora of New Zealand: Senecio minimus

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Flora of New Zealand / Manaaki Whenua
claims: Erechtites minimus is a synonym of Senecio minimus.
Erect annual or short-lived perennial with toothed clasping leaves and no ray florets.
The species belongs to New Zealand's indigenous flora.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney / Flora of NSW
claims: Erect herb with narrow, regularly toothed, stem-clasping leaves.
Small cylindrical heads occur in branched clusters.
Native Australian populations colonize wet forest settings.

proposedDescription: Coastal wattle is a dense shrub or small tree with narrow, leathery leaf-like structures and round golden flower heads. Its most striking feature appears when the pods open: each dark seed is surrounded by a fleshy orange to scarlet loop. Native to coastal Western Australia and South Australia, it has been planted elsewhere for shelter and dune stabilization. Outside its native range it can become invasive; South African conservation assessments identify it as a threat to sensitive coastal plant habitat.
identification: Look for narrow phyllodes with three or four main veins, spherical yellow flower heads and thick pods that twist after opening. The conspicuous red-orange structure around each dark seed is especially useful.
actions: Record pods, seeds and foliage when seeking confirmation. Check local native status and land-management guidance before planting or removing coastal wattles, particularly in dune or conservation areas.
researchNotes: VicFlora supplies independent morphology and native Australian range. SANBI's original Erica occulta assessment documents a specific conservation threat from A. cyclops, not a global impact estimate or current legal category.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria / Flora of Victoria
claims: Dense shrub or small tree with narrow multi-veined phyllodes and golden globular flower heads.
Seeds have fleshy orange-to-scarlet surrounding structures.
Native to coastal Western Australia and South Australia.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: South African National Biodiversity Institute, Turner and Oliver assessment
claims: Acacia cyclops infestations are identified as a threat to Erica occulta habitat on the southern Agulhas Plain.
Cleared invasive vegetation requires ongoing management at the assessed locality.

proposedDescription: Coatbuttons carries little daisy-like heads on long, wiry stalks above a low tangle of hairy stems and coarsely toothed leaves. A yellow center is bordered by just a few short white, cream or pale yellow rays, giving each head its button-like appearance. The plant is native to tropical America and is now widespread in warm regions elsewhere. It readily occupies bare and disturbed soil, where sprawling stems can form small patches between taller plants.
identification: Look for rough-hairy, toothed leaves, long solitary flower stalks and a small yellow-centered head with only a few short, often three-toothed pale rays. Mature fruits carry feathery bristles.
actions: Photograph the flower head from above and the leafy stems below it. Confirm uncertain plants with a local flora or extension service and note whether the patch is in disturbed ground or natural vegetation.
researchNotes: Kew-hosted tropical floras provide detailed morphology and native range; the Indian Institute of Science herbarium independently documents abundant occurrence on disturbed soil in India. No medicinal efficacy or universal invasive impact is asserted.

sources.title: Kew: Tridax procumbens, tropical flora descriptions
Indian Institute of Science Herbarium JCB: Tridax procumbens

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Flora of the Cayman Islands and Flora of Tropical East Africa
claims: Hairy sprawling plant with coarsely toothed leaves.
Long-stalked heads have yellow disc florets and a few short pale rays.
Native to tropical America and introduced widely in the Old World tropics.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Indian Institute of Science Herbarium JCB, Indian regional floras
claims: The plant is widespread and abundant where soil is disturbed.
Indian records document occurrence across multiple regions outside its native American range.

proposedDescription: Cochineal cactus grows into a branching shrub or small tree, with flattened green pads and slender scarlet flowers. Despite its often nearly spineless appearance, the pads can carry tiny irritating bristles. Native to Mexico, it has been planted widely in warm regions and sometimes grows beyond cultivation. It also has a long history as a host for insects used to produce cochineal dye. Its presence in a garden is different from an established wild population, so records need that context.
identification: Look for elongated, flattened green pads and red flowers with conspicuously projecting stamens. Other prickly pears can look similar; photograph flowers and the whole plant.
actions: Avoid bare-handed handling. If a plant is spreading outside cultivation, photograph it and ask a local plant specialist to confirm its identity before removal.
researchNotes: Kew accepts Opuntia cochenillifera; Nopalea cochenillifera remains the queue identifier. The reviewed sources support cultivation and naturalization, not a blanket claim of ecological harm throughout the United States.

sources.title: Indian Institute of Science: Opuntia cochenillifera

claims: Mexican origin, pad and flower morphology, cultivation and cochineal history.
Independent regional flora documents its widespread occurrence outside the Americas.
Independent description of branching pads, red flowers and easy rooting of pads.

proposedDescription: Cockroach berry is a prickly, short-lived member of the nightshade family, with broad leaves, white star-shaped flowers, and round fruits that turn orange-red. It grows in disturbed ground in warm, moist regions, including places outside its native tropical American range. The bright fruit can make it conspicuous along a roadside or neglected patch, but appearance alone is not a safe guide to edibility. Similar prickly nightshades have often been confused with it, making careful identification especially useful.
identification: Check for yellowish prickles, broad sometimes lobed leaves, small clusters of white flowers, and orange-scarlet berries. Detailed fruit and seed features help specialists separate related species.
actions: Photograph the leaves, prickles, flowers, and fruit without tasting them. Wear gloves if handling a confirmed plant, and seek local advice before controlling a larger patch.
researchNotes: PlantNET's older treatment uses Solanum aculeatissimum as a synonym; Kew distinguishes the names. Draft uses shared morphological evidence and keeps the broader tropical-American origin instead of conflicting narrower origins.

sources.title: Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney: Solanum capsicoides

claims: Tropical American origin and confusion with other prickly nightshades.
Prickles, white flowers, orange-scarlet berries, and disturbed moist habitats.

proposedDescription: Cockspur coral tree brings clusters of vivid red, pea-shaped flowers to a branching shrub or small tree. Its leaves are divided into three leaflets, and the branches carry prickles. Native to South America, it is grown as an ornamental in warmer regions and has been introduced well beyond its original range.
identification: Look for three-part leaves, prickly branches, and elongated red flowers held in clusters. Photograph leaves and flowers together; several cultivated coral trees share similar features.
actions: Note whether the tree is planted or growing wild. Ask a local botanist or extension office to identify unexpected seedlings before deciding on management.
researchNotes: RHS supplies horticultural morphology; Kew supplies native and introduced ranges. The draft does not extrapolate invasive impacts from ornamental cultivation or introduced status alone.

claims: Prickly branches, three leaflets, scarlet flowers and ornamental habit.
South American native range and introductions.

proposedDescription: Taro is the plant behind a familiar tropical food crop and many garden elephant ears. Its large, heart- to arrow-shaped leaves rise from a thick underground corm. In warm wetlands, escaped plants can spread into dense patches along streams, ditches, and marshes, shading smaller vegetation. Pieces of the underground plant can help establish new patches when moved. Its value in cultivation and its ability to invade some waterways are both part of the story; the local setting matters.
identification: The leaf stalk attaches to the underside of the blade, inward from its edge. Photograph that attachment and the whole plant to distinguish similar elephant ears.
actions: Keep garden waste out of waterways. Wear gloves during removal and collect underground pieces; consult local wetland managers for established patches. Do not eat raw plant material.
researchNotes: NC State documents food and ornamental use and raw-plant irritation; UF documents Florida wetland escape and vegetative spread. Cultivation is not treated as proof of harm at every recorded location.

claims: Wetland stands, shading, underground fragments and removal precautions.
Corm-forming food and ornamental crop, large leaves and raw-plant hazards.

proposedDescription: Coconut palms are a familiar part of tropical coastlines, with a ringed trunk, long feather-like fronds, and large fibrous fruits. People have carried them widely for food, fiber, and useful materials. They also grow outside cultivation in suitable coastal habitats, where their ecological role depends on the place. Florida's assessment, for example, treats the palm differently across the state and identifies invasive behavior in the south with limited approved uses. A coconut record therefore needs more context than a garden label.
identification: Look for a single ringed trunk, a crown of long divided fronds, and large husked fruits. Young palms may still have the attached germinating nut.
actions: Before planting near natural shorelines, check local guidance. Record whether a palm is planted or self-established; have a qualified professional handle removal of large palms.
researchNotes: NParks provides morphology and uses; UF's regional assessment supports the Florida distinction. The draft avoids a definitive ancestral origin because long cultivation complicates that history.

claims: Palm morphology, fruit structure, coastal cultivation and uses.
South Florida invasive with limited approved uses; caution in central Florida; undocumented problem status in north Florida.

proposedDescription: Coconut scale is a tiny sap-feeding insect that can gather in pale, closely packed patches on leaves. Coconut and banana are familiar hosts, but it also feeds on many other tropical crops and ornamental plants. Heavy infestations yellow and weaken foliage. Young insects, called crawlers, move before settling beneath a protective covering; infested nursery plants can carry them to new places. Predators and tiny parasitic wasps help suppress populations, so visible scales do not automatically mean broad insecticide treatment is needed.
identification: Look beneath leaves for small, flat, translucent covers with yellowish centers and nearby yellowing. Confirmation requires a specialist examining adult females under a microscope.
actions: Keep suspect plants from being moved or shared. Send clear photographs to extension or a plant clinic, and seek treatment advice that protects beneficial insects.
researchNotes: UF supplies diagnostic limitations and its own observations; Hawaii extension supplies host damage and natural-enemy management. Old pesticide lists and conflicting reproduction claims are excluded.

claims: Armored covering, crawler stage, host distribution and microscopic identification requirement.
Leaf yellowing, nursery movement and beneficial-insect suppression.

proposedDescription: Codling moth is best known for the caterpillar that tunnels into an apple or pear and feeds around the seeds. Adults are small, mottled moths that blend into bark; the damage inside fruit is usually more noticeable than the moth itself. It also attacks walnuts and some other fruit crops. Several generations can develop during a growing season, depending on climate. Successful management combines watching for moth activity with timely fruit protection and removing infested fruit before more insects emerge.
identification: Adults have a coppery patch near each forewing tip. Larvae become pale pink with a brown head; entry holes may have crumbly brown waste around them.
actions: Collect infested and fallen fruit promptly. Ask local extension about monitoring traps, fruit bagging, and seasonal management; timing varies with local weather and orchard conditions.
researchNotes: UC and Utah State independently cover orchard biology and management. Generation counts and treatment schedules are not generalized nationwide, and no pesticide rates are prescribed.

sources.title: University of California IPM: Codling moth
Utah State Extension: Codling moth in Utah orchards

claims: Fruit hosts, tunneling damage and home-orchard management.
Copper-tipped adult wings, pink larvae, frass, monitoring and sanitation.

proposedDescription: Hairy willow-herb is a tall perennial with fuzzy stems and pink-purple flowers, often growing where the soil stays moist. Introduced from Eurasia, it can form dense patches along wetlands, ditches, and stream edges in North America. Underground stems help a patch expand, while silky-haired seeds travel on the wind. Its flowers can be attractive, but a crowded stand can leave less room for other wetland plants. Native willow-herbs and fireweeds make careful identification worthwhile before any removal.
identification: Look for hairy stems, opposite toothed leaves, four notched pink petals, and a pale four-part stigma. Photograph the flowers and leaf arrangement to separate lookalikes.
actions: For a confirmed small patch, seek permission and local advice before digging, remove underground growth, and prevent seed release. Avoid disturbing sensitive wetland vegetation.
researchNotes: Wisconsin DNR supplies identification and control; Native Plant Trust independently describes regional ecology and morphology. No legal status or nationwide abundance is inferred from occurrence records.

claims: Rhizomes, seeds, diagnostic flowers and patch management.
Eurasian origin, dense wetland stands and opposite toothed leaves.

proposedDescription: Cogongrass is a spreading perennial grass that can turn varied vegetation into dense stands. Its extensive underground stems help it survive disturbance and move outward, while fluffy seeds and contaminated soil or equipment carry it farther. In the southeastern United States, it invades roadsides, pastures, and natural areas. The buildup of dry grass also increases fire danger and can change how habitats burn. Because a patch can regrow from underground pieces, controlling it usually takes a coordinated effort and repeated follow-up.
identification: Look for upright blades with a pale midrib noticeably off center and silvery, fluffy seed heads. Other grasses resemble it; have a specialist confirm suspected patches.
actions: Avoid mowing seed heads or moving soil from the patch. Clean equipment and contact local extension or land managers. Burning alone is not a solution.
researchNotes: UF and Mississippi State support identification, rhizome spread, fire effects and persistent management. The draft avoids chemical prescriptions and treats large infestations as a professional planning task.

sources.title: Mississippi State Extension: Cogongrass identification and control

claims: Off-center midrib, dense rhizomes, equipment spread and fire effects.
Persistence after disturbance, fire concerns and repeated control.

proposedDescription: Colocynth, sometimes called bitter apple, is a trailing relative of watermelon adapted to dry landscapes. Its rough, deeply divided leaves and small yellow flowers spread close to the ground, followed by round fruits that change from mottled green to yellow. Unlike a sweet watermelon, the fruit has intensely bitter flesh. The plant is native across parts of Africa and Asia and adjacent regions. Its desert ecology is well documented, but a record outside that range does not alone establish local invasive damage.
identification: Look for a sprawling vine with deeply lobed leaves, tendrils, yellow flowers, and small round yellowing melons. Do not use tasting as an identification test.
actions: Photograph leaves, flowers, and fruit, and ask a botanist to confirm unexpected plants. Keep unidentified melons out of food and avoid spreading their seeds.
researchNotes: Kew's regional floras support detailed morphology; Flora of Israel independently supports desert habitat. The draft does not claim documented U.S. ecological impacts or offer medicinal or food uses.

sources.title: Kew: Citrullus colocynthis, regional flora descriptions

claims: Trailing perennial, lobed leaves, yellow flowers, bitter yellowing fruit and range.
Independent desert habitat and perennial life-form account.

proposedDescription: Colombian waxweed is a small, branching herb with rough, hairy leaves and tiny purple to pink flowers. It can be easy to overlook among grasses in a damp, disturbed patch. Native from Mexico through tropical America, it has become established in other warm regions, including parts of the southeastern United States and Hawaii. The flower's narrow tube and the plant's sticky hairs help distinguish it from superficially similar weeds. Its introduced presence alone does not tell us how strongly it affects a particular habitat.
identification: Look for a low, branching, hairy plant with small oval leaves and tiny purple flowers emerging from narrow tubes. A close photograph is more useful than a distant patch view.
actions: Have unfamiliar plants identified before removal. Where management is warranted, address small patches before seed develops and avoid moving seed-bearing material into nearby natural areas.
researchNotes: Kew supports range; the independent Flora Malesiana treatment supplies morphology. The draft does not infer serious U.S. ecological impacts from naturalized status.

claims: Native tropical-American and introduced ranges.
Branched glandular-hairy herb, small rough leaves, tubular purple/red flowers.

proposedDescription: Colonial bentgrass, also called Rhode Island bentgrass, is a fine-leaved perennial introduced from Europe and nearby regions. Its airy flower clusters can give an unmown patch a soft haze. It has long been used in lawns, but also grows in fields, roadsides, and other open ground beyond cultivation. In some regions it becomes an invasive grass rather than staying a lawn plant. Separating it from related bentgrasses takes a closer look at the flowering branches and the small membranous flap where a leaf blade meets its sheath.
identification: Look for narrow leaves and a loose, branching flower cluster. The short membranous flap (ligule) at the blade-sheath junction helps distinguish it from creeping bentgrass and redtop.
actions: Keep lawn seed and soil from spreading into nearby natural grasslands. Ask a grass specialist to confirm suspect wild patches before choosing a restoration approach.
researchNotes: Native Plant Trust supplies regional ecology and diagnostic comparisons; Kew independently supports native range and perennial habit. The common name does not indicate North American nativity.

claims: Introduced lawn grass, open habitats and short ligule diagnostic.
Native Eurasian range and perennial grass habit.

proposedDescription: This colonial sea squirt forms thin living sheets over surfaces such as dock structures, ropes, rocks, and shellfish. Each sheet contains many tiny animals that filter food from the water. Colonies often look pale or marbled, but their appearance changes with conditions. It has spread through warm-water ports and can overgrow other organisms, creating concerns for aquaculture and some natural habitats. Its original home remains uncertain in parts of the scientific literature, even though introductions are documented in several regions.
identification: A thin, pale encrusting colony may be a clue, but color cannot confirm the species. Specialists examine microscopic structures and sometimes use genetic evidence.
actions: Photograph suspect growth and report it to local marine biosecurity staff. Follow approved hull and gear cleaning practices; avoid scraping live fouling into the water.
researchNotes: Smithsonian treats much of the range as cryptogenic; NIMPIS labels Caribbean origin. Draft retains uncertainty and uses NIMPIS's regional observations and explicit identification caution, without claiming all U.S. records are equally secure.

claims: Colonial filter feeder, uncertain origin, fouling habitat and overgrowth impacts.
Independent Australian monitoring, variable appearance and aquaculture fouling.

proposedDescription: Symplegma reptans is a colonial sea squirt that spreads as a low covering of many small animals joined within a shared outer layer. Native to the Indo-West Pacific, it has established in Southern California harbors, where it grows on docks, hulls, and other submerged surfaces. Colonies expand by producing new individuals through budding. At some sites they can cover large areas and compete for space with other attached organisms. Its resemblance to related sea squirts has complicated identification and some early records.
identification: Look for flattened individuals visible within a thin, nearly transparent colony. Species-level identification requires a tunicate specialist; photographs alone may not separate related Symplegma.
actions: Record the location and photograph the colony. Ask local marine specialists about identification and follow marina guidance for cleaning fouled equipment without releasing living material.
researchNotes: Smithsonian supports invasion history and resemblance to congeners. Independent developmental research supports budding; only its accessible abstract was used, not unseen full-text claims.

sources.title: Kawamura and Nakauchi: Development of buds in Symplegma reptans

claims: Indo-West Pacific origin, Southern California introduction, fouling habitat and identification history.
Direct observations show colony members develop through budding.

proposedDescription: Coltsfoot sends up yellow, dandelion-like flower heads before its broad leaves unfold. Later, the leaves form a low cover, with a pale, woolly underside that helps distinguish them from dandelions. Native across parts of Eurasia and North Africa, this perennial grows in moist disturbed ground and can spread into nearby habitats. Underground stems allow it to form persistent patches, while its fluffy seeds provide another route of dispersal. Removing only the visible leaves often leaves the living network below intact.
identification: Look for early yellow flowers on short, scaly or woolly stalks, followed by broad heart-shaped leaves with white-felted undersides. Dandelion leaves are differently shaped.
actions: For confirmed small patches, remove underground growth before seed spreads and monitor regrowth. Ask local land managers about established patches, particularly near wetlands.
researchNotes: Kew independently supports native range; Wisconsin DNR supports identification, spread and management. Outdated chemical recommendations in the source are deliberately excluded.

claims: Flowers before leaves, woolly leaf undersides, rhizome persistence and removal guidance.
Eurasian and North African native range and perennial habit.

proposedDescription: Comb bushmint is a branching, aromatic herb whose tiny pale flowers line curved clusters like the teeth of a comb. It can grow tall enough to look like a small shrub, with toothed, hairy leaves and angular stems. Native to tropical America, it now occurs in other warm regions, often around disturbed ground, thickets, and moist edges. Although it appears in weed records, Florida's assessment does not document it as a problem species there. Its local behavior deserves attention without assuming severe impacts everywhere.
identification: Look for toothed, hairy leaves and branching clusters of small whitish to pale mauve flowers arranged along one side. Confirm against other bushmints.
actions: Photograph flowering branches and the whole plant. If it is spreading into a managed habitat, seek identification and local guidance before deciding whether control is needed.
researchNotes: Hyptis pectinata is now Mesosphaerum pectinatum in Kew and UF. Kew provides regional-flora morphology; UF independently provides a bounded Florida assessment. Queue identifier remains unchanged.

sources.title: Kew: Mesosphaerum pectinatum, regional flora descriptions

claims: Comb-like inflorescences, aromatic herb, toothed hairy leaves and habitat.
Florida problem status undocumented; synonym and growth form.

proposedDescription: Rangoon creeper is a woody climber best known for fragrant flowers that change from white through pink to red as they age. Hooks formed from leaf stalks help it climb over supports, and its broad leaves grow in opposite pairs. Its native range includes Tanzania and tropical and subtropical Asia through northern Australia. Widely cultivated in tropical gardens, it has also been introduced elsewhere. The mix of flower colors on a single vine makes it especially distinctive when in bloom.
identification: Look for opposite oval leaves, hooked climbing structures, and clusters containing differently aged white, pink, and red flowers. Quisqualis indica is an older name.
actions: Record whether the vine is cultivated or spreading outside a garden. Contain prunings and ask local extension about management of confirmed escapes.
researchNotes: NParks supports floral changes and climbing morphology; Kew supports accepted name, broader native range and introductions. No unsupported blanket U.S. invasion impact is asserted.

claims: Flower color changes, woody climbing habit, hooks and opposite leaves.
Native and introduced ranges; Quisqualis indica synonym.

proposedDescription: Common asparagus-fern looks soft and fern-like, but it is a flowering climber rather than a true fern. Its fine green sprays are familiar in houseplants and floral arrangements. Outside cultivation in warm regions, thorny shoots can climb through other vegetation, and birds carry seeds from its dark berries. Persistent underground growth makes established plants difficult to remove completely. Native to eastern and southern Africa, it has escaped cultivation elsewhere; Florida guidance recommends preventing escape and managing existing plants carefully.
identification: Look for fine, feathery sprays on wiry climbing stems, small flowers, and berries that ripen dark. Check for thorns and distinguish it from other ornamental asparagus species.
actions: Wear gloves, prevent berries from scattering, and remove the crown and underground growth where appropriate. Recheck for regrowth and keep discarded plants out of natural areas.
researchNotes: UF documents escape and practical control; Kew independently supports native and introduced ranges. The draft identifies it as a flowering plant and avoids treating all asparagus-ferns as one species.

claims: Climbing habit, dark bird-dispersed berries, persistent roots and removal precautions.
Eastern and southern African origin and introduced distribution.

proposedDescription: Lemon balm is a perennial herb with wrinkled, toothed leaves that release a lemon scent when bruised. A member of the mint family, it produces small pale flowers visited by pollinators and has long been grown for kitchen and garden use. Native from the Mediterranean toward Central Asia, it has become established well beyond that range. Plants can spread and self-seed around gardens, so keeping an eye on seedlings is useful. Its familiar usefulness and occasional weedy behavior are both worth recognizing.
identification: Look for opposite, wrinkled oval leaves, square stems, and small pale two-lipped flowers. Scent can support identification but should not replace checking the plant's features.
actions: Remove unwanted seedlings and trim flowers before seed forms if spread is a concern. Keep garden waste contained and confirm identification before using any wild herb.
researchNotes: NC State provides morphology, garden uses and spread management; Kew independently supports range. The draft avoids medicinal promises or assuming serious ecosystem damage from naturalization alone.

claims: Lemon-scented leaves, flowers, garden use, self-seeding and spread.
Mediterranean to Central Asian origin and widespread introductions.

proposedDescription: Common bamboo forms large clumps of tall, jointed canes topped by leafy branches. Native to parts of Asia and widely planted in warm regions, it supplies material for buildings, tools, and crafts as well as garden screens. It is a clumping bamboo, so its growth differs from the long-running bamboos familiar in some gardens. That distinction matters when evaluating a sighting or planning management. Florida's completed assessment for its southern region does not document an invasive problem there; other regions need their own assessment.
identification: Look for a dense clump of substantial jointed canes and narrow, pointed leaves. Cane colors vary among cultivars; a bamboo specialist may need sheath and branching details.
actions: Record whether the clump is planted and whether it is expanding beyond its intended area. Seek experienced help with large canes, and contain discarded rhizome pieces.
researchNotes: NParks supports habit, morphology and uses; UF independently distinguishes regional assessment status, including incomplete northern and central assessments. This is not Phyllostachys aurea, also called golden bamboo.

claims: Large clumping bamboo, jointed canes, narrow leaves and material uses.
Regional assessment results and incomplete-assessment distinctions.

proposedDescription: Common Barberry is a deciduous shrub with branched spines, hanging yellow flower clusters, and red berries that can remain into winter. It grows in woodland, pasture, hedgerows, and disturbed ground, tolerating both sun and shade. Dense stands can crowd other vegetation, while birds carry its seeds to new sites. The shrub also serves as an alternate host for black stem rust, a disease of cereal crops. Its persistence comes from both long-lived seed and underground stems that send up shoots, so removing the visible branches alone rarely settles an established infestation.
identification: Look for a many-stemmed shrub roughly 8–10 feet tall, sometimes taller, with gray bark and two- or three-branched spines. Small oval leaves grow in clusters and have conspicuous sharp teeth. Spring flowers hang in elongated yellow clusters; the later fruits are oblong and red, with one to three seeds. Japanese barberry is a frequent confusion, but Common Barberry has toothed leaf margins and typically three-pronged spines. Hybrid plants can combine characters, so one spine or a distant photograph may be misleading. Photograph a complete branch, a leaf edge in focus, several spine junctions, and flowers or fruit. Include overall height and the date.
actions: Wear sturdy gloves and eye protection when working among the spines. Prioritize isolated young shrubs and fruiting plants near fields or uninvaded habitat. Dig manageable plants carefully, keeping the root crown and attached underground stems together as far as possible; chopped fragments can produce new growth. Contain berry-bearing branches before carrying them away, and avoid shifting infested soil. Larger shrubs need a planned root-focused treatment and repeat inspections rather than a single cut. Ask local Extension or a weed specialist about suitable methods and reporting expectations in your area. Check the cleared ground for seedlings and returning shoots over subsequent growing seasons.

sources.title: University of Minnesota Extension: Common barberry
Minnesota Department of Agriculture: Common Barberry

researchNotes: Sources differ in maximum height and native-range wording; draft avoids precise origin. Management is conservative inference from documented rhizome regeneration; no herbicide prescription or nationwide legal claim.

claims: Shrubs have toothed leaves, branched spines, drooping flower clusters, and persistent red berries.
Severed rhizomes can reproduce; seed persists for years.
An alternate host of black stem rust.
Birds spread seeds; Japanese barberry is distinguished using leaves and spines.

proposedDescription: Common barley is the cultivated cereal familiar from grain fields, brewing, and livestock feed. This cool-season annual sometimes appears along roadsides or in disturbed ground after seed escapes cultivation. Such plants should not automatically be described as a damaging invasion: the USDA guide describes volunteers as generally not persistent. The compact seed head often carries long bristles, although some cultivated forms lack them. Two-row and six-row barley differ in how many spikelets develop grain, a useful reminder that variation within this crop can change its appearance without indicating another species.
identification: Plants generally stand 2–4 feet tall, with hollow, jointed stems and flat leaves. At the point where a leaf blade meets its sheath, look for two overlapping, ear-like projections clasping the stem. The unbranched seed head has groups of three spikelets; long bristles may extend from them. In two-row forms only the middle spikelet produces grain, while all three are fertile in six-row forms. Wheat and cereal rye have single spikelets at each attachment point, rather than barley's groups. Photograph the leaf collar, an entire mature head, and a close side view of its attachments. Young plants without heads can be difficult to separate from other cereals.
actions: First establish whether the plants are a planted crop, a cover crop, or unwanted volunteers. Avoid removing a farmer's planting without checking its intended purpose. For a few escaped plants on your own ground, pull them before grain matures and collect any developed heads so seed is not scattered. Check nearby spilled feed, seed-storage areas, or recently disturbed soil for the source. In a production field, discuss volunteer management with the grower or Extension because timing depends on the crop rotation. Record repeated establishment outside cultivation if it appears to persist; isolated seedlings after a grain spill are a different situation from an expanding naturalized stand.

sources.title: Native Plant Trust Go Botany: Hordeum vulgare

researchNotes: Catalog's widespread-invasive label conflicts with NRCS description of nonpersistent volunteers; editorial classification review recommended. Actions are proportionate prevention recommendations inferred from annual crop biology.

claims: Cool-season annual bunchgrass reaches 2–4 feet.
Clasping overlapping auricles distinguish seedlings from other cereals; volunteers are generally not persistent.
Escapes occur in roadsides, fields, and disturbed soils.
Two-row and six-row forms differ in lateral spikelet fertility.

proposedDescription: Common bird's-foot is a small annual legume also called French serradella. Its softly hairy stems spread along the ground or rise above it, carrying leaves divided into many small leaflets. Small pink or whitish pea flowers develop into slender, jointed pods. Each pod segment holds a seed, giving mature fruits a beaded appearance. It is native to southwestern Europe and has been introduced elsewhere. The mature pods provide a useful way to recognize an unfamiliar patch after the flowers fade. A nearby planting or seed mixture may help explain an occurrence, but the plant itself still needs identification.
identification: Look for a branched, hairy annual up to about 50 centimeters high, often much lower because stems spread outward. Leaves have numerous paired, narrow oval leaflets and a terminal leaflet. Small groups of pink to white flowers sit above a conspicuously leafy bract divided into leaflets. Flowers are approximately 7 millimeters long. The flattened pods are about 12–30 millimeters long, slightly curved or straight, with constrictions separating three to seven seed-bearing segments. These fruits are more useful than a general photograph of the foliage. Photograph a whole leaf, the leafy bract below a flower group, and mature pods beside a scale. Identification among other Ornithopus species should use a regional botanical key.
actions: For an unexpected patch, record its location, approximate extent, and whether the ground was recently sown. Keep a photograph of mature pods for identification before deciding on removal. Where the plant is unwanted, lift small annual plants before pods harden and seeds separate. Collect fruiting material rather than dragging it through neighboring vegetation. Check seed mixtures or transferred soil if new plants repeatedly appear in the same place. Avoid distributing saved seed from an unidentified patch. For occurrences in conservation land, ask the land manager or a herbarium to confirm the species and determine whether management is warranted; management should reflect the habitat and observed spread rather than an assumption based on its presence alone.

sources.title: Flora of New Zealand: Ornithopus sativus

researchNotes: Morphology verified independently in two floras. Their seasonal dates are Southern Hemisphere and are not transferred to the US. Species-specific US impact/control evidence remains limited; actions are explicitly cautious annual-seed prevention inference.

claims: Annual with hairy leaves and white-to-pink flowers.
Pods are constricted into three to seven one-seeded segments.
Ascending to prostrate herb to 50 centimeters.
Leafy pinnate bracts subtend flower groups; native to Spain and Portugal.

proposedDescription: Common borage is an annual garden herb with bristly leaves and bright blue, star-shaped flowers. Native to the Mediterranean region, it is grown in herb and flower gardens and attracts bees. Plants often return through self-sown seed, rather than surviving as the same individual from year to year. Escapes beside a garden may therefore reflect ongoing seed production. The dark central cone of each nodding flower is especially distinctive against the blue petals. Flowers open in sequence as the curled clusters unfold, extending the display through summer. A persistent garden escape deserves attention without assuming that every volunteer damages surrounding habitat.
identification: Common borage grows roughly 1½–3 feet tall and has coarse gray-green leaves and stems covered with stiff hairs. Leaves alternate along the stem; lower leaves have stalks, while upper leaves become smaller and attach directly to the stem. Flowers are open stars about three-quarters of an inch across, with five pointed blue lobes and a prominent dark central cone formed by the anthers. Photograph a flower face and side view, the hairy stem, and a complete lower leaf. Other borage-family plants also have blue blooms, so color alone is insufficient. A hairy rosette without flowers should remain provisional until the leaf arrangement and eventual flower structure can be checked.
actions: Where seedlings are unwanted, remove them while small and before they produce another generation of seed. Wear gloves if the stiff hairs irritate your skin. Inspect the ground around the original planting and any place where garden debris was deposited, rather than treating a single seedling as the entire source. If retaining a garden plant, remove spent flowering stems before seed dispersal and check for volunteers beyond the bed. Do not move seed-bearing waste into natural areas. Ask local Extension about an expanding escape in sensitive habitat. Keep removal material separate from food crops and do not infer safe consumption from a visual identification; some botanical accounts flag potentially harmful plant compounds.

sources.title: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox: Borago officinalis

researchNotes: Initial single-institution evidence gap resolved with independently read Maryland, Washington and Oxford content. Wisconsin/RHS attempts were inaccessible and are not counted. Morphology and self-seeding are corroborated; containment follows annual seed production and makes no broad ecological-harm claim.

claims: Mediterranean annual with bristly gray-green leaves and blue star-shaped flowers.
Self-seeds and attracts bees; account includes toxicity cautions.
Annual commonly two to three feet tall with coarse hairy foliage and star-shaped blue flowers.
Readily self-seeds and attracts pollinators.
Alternate leaves become smaller and stalkless upward; flower has five pointed blue lobes.
Taprooted annual occurs in disturbed soil; flowers are about two centimetres across.
Five anthers form the dark central cone; flowers open progressively along curled clusters.
Plant contains small amounts of hepatotoxic pyrrolizidine alkaloids.

proposedDescription: Common brassbuttons is a low wetland plant named for its small yellow flower heads, which resemble buttons without surrounding petals. Fleshy stems can creep and root where they touch the ground. It occurs along streams and in both fresh and salty marshes, so a coastal location is helpful context but not a requirement. Introduced populations are widespread, though the Smithsonian account does not describe it as a highly aggressive invader. Local abundance and the plants growing alongside it matter when judging an occurrence. Its wetland setting also makes careless trampling or soil disturbance a concern during investigation.
identification: Plants commonly stand or spread about 5–25 centimeters, sometimes taller. Smooth, somewhat fleshy stems may lie flat and root at the joints. Leaves sit directly on the stem, with their bases forming a sheath; individual blades may be narrow and entire or irregularly toothed and lobed. Yellow flower heads are usually about 6–12 millimeters across and have no petal-like rays. Photograph the leaf bases around the stem, one entire leaf, a flower head from above and below, and the surrounding wetland. These details are more informative than yellow color alone. Other small wetland daisies require comparison, and a detached flower without leaves is unlikely to support a reliable determination.
actions: Photograph the patch from firm ground and note whether it is in freshwater, brackish water, or a tidal area. Ask the land manager to confirm identification and local priorities before disturbing a marsh or protected shoreline. For a small confirmed patch where removal is permitted, lift connected stems carefully and collect loose pieces, because rooted joints can maintain the plant. Keep seed-bearing or rooted material out of drains and waterways, and clean mud and plant fragments from footwear and tools. Revisit the marked location to check for surviving stems or seedlings. Larger wetland infestations need a site-specific approach that protects neighboring vegetation and avoids unnecessary sediment disturbance.

sources.title: Flora of North America: Cotula coronopifolia
Smithsonian Environmental Research Center NEMESIS: Cotula coronopifolia

researchNotes: FNA direct page timed out; substantial indexed treatment was read and is labeled accordingly. Native-range accounts differ; omitted exact origin. Smithsonian page says details under review. Wetland actions are conservative inference, not trial-verified control claims.

claims: Fleshy stems can root at nodes; leaves have sheathing bases.
Rayless yellow heads occur in saline and freshwater marshes and along streams.
Salt-tolerant and also occurs in fresh water.
Widely introduced but not regarded in the account as highly aggressive.

proposedDescription: Common brighteyes is a Mediterranean daisy-family herb with yellow flower heads and somewhat fleshy, often lobed leaves. The useful clue is beneath the flower: small bracts have a distinctive broad shape and pale, thin margins. It occurs in disturbed places such as field edges and roadsides in its native region. A familiar-looking yellow flower is not enough to identify an introduced occurrence, because many unrelated daisies look similar from above. Descriptions of related annual and perennial forms require care, especially when matching a plant found far from the area covered by a particular flora.
identification: Common brighteyes is described in horticultural accounts as roughly 4–20 inches tall. Look closely at the green bracts wrapping each flower head and continuing down its stalk. They resemble small inverted hearts, with thin, translucent margins. Leaves can be somewhat fleshy and blue-green, with variable lobing or teeth. The typical Mediterranean form is described as perennial with a thick persistent stem base, but annual relatives or infraspecific treatments complicate comparison. Do not use the life cycle alone to assign an unfamiliar specimen. Photograph the whole plant, basal and upper leaves, the side of a flower head, and mature fruits. A regional herbarium should check an unexpected record rather than relying on a flower-only match.
actions: Document a suspected escape before removing it: record the location, patch size, and nearby plantings or disturbed soil. If identification is confirmed and the plant is unwanted, remove a small plant with its persistent base, while collecting developed flower heads and seed-bearing material. Watch the same site for renewed growth rather than assuming that cutting the stalk removes the plant. Avoid sharing seed or putting reproductive waste in natural vegetation. For a new regional occurrence, submit clear photographs to a herbarium or local botanical recording program. There is insufficient species-specific control evidence here to recommend a broad treatment or to claim that every introduced population is harmful.

sources.title: University of the Balearic Islands: Reichardia picroides
Kew Plants of the World Online: Reichardia picroides

researchNotes: Additional RHS text supplies height and self-seeding but itself has conflicting annual/biennial versus perennial labels. Balearic account describes the typical subspecies, not necessarily every taxonomic treatment. Retain gap for reconciled life-history/application to US records; species-specific management efficacy remains untested.

claims: Broad, thin-margined bracts occur on the head and flower stalk.
Typical form is perennial with somewhat fleshy lobed leaves.
Accepted species name; taxonomic account lists infraspecific names.
Profile gives 0.1–0.5 metre height, heart-shaped bracts, fluffy seedheads and self-seeding.
Narrative calls it perennial while the displayed life-cycle label also lists Annual Biennial.

proposedDescription: Common Buckthorn is a large shrub or small tree that can form a dense understory in woodland and along forest edges. It opens its leaves early and retains them late, extending the period when it shades plants beneath it. Female plants produce dark fruits eaten by birds, which carry the seeds elsewhere. Introduced as an ornamental and hedging plant, it has become a significant woodland invader in parts of North America. It also provides an overwintering host for soybean aphids. Removing a mature patch is a continuing project because cut stems can resprout and new seedlings can appear.
identification: Look for a shrub or small tree reaching roughly 20–30 feet, often with several stems. Oval leaves have fine teeth and several prominent veins curving toward the tip. Their placement is often opposite or nearly opposite, but vigorous shoots may show alternate leaves. Short, sharp points occur at the ends of many twigs. Small greenish flowers precede clustered black fruits on female plants. Native cherries and plums can resemble young buckthorn in bark appearance, so inspect leaves and twig tips rather than bark alone. Photograph leaf veins, attachment positions, terminal buds or spines, and fruit if present. Late-season green leaves are a useful search clue, not a diagnosis by themselves.
actions: Start with an inventory of fruiting shrubs and the least invaded areas. Removing berry-producing plants first limits further seed input. Small seedlings can be pulled from suitable soil; use a shrub-pulling tool for larger manageable stems, minimizing disturbance around desirable plants. A single cut of a mature stem commonly leads to resprouting, so arrange an appropriate stump treatment or a sustained follow-up plan with a local specialist. Work in sections if the infestation is extensive, then restore ground cover suited to the site. Walk the area each year for seedlings and sprouts, particularly in early spring or fall when buckthorn foliage is easier to notice.

sources.title: Minnesota Department of Agriculture: Common or European Buckthorn
University of Minnesota Extension: Common buckthorn

researchNotes: Three institutional accounts support morphology, extended leaf season and sustained removal. Berry-producing plants and subsequent seedlings are management priorities. Minnesota-specific legal duties are not generalized nationally.

claims: Leaves are finely toothed with curved veins and often opposite or nearly opposite.
Twigs may end in short thorns; shrub can reach small-tree size.
Management is a multi-year commitment.
Prioritize berry-producing plants; pull seedlings and revisit for new growth.
Early and late foliage creates dense shade.
It hosts overwintering soybean aphids.

proposedDescription: Common Burdock begins as a cluster of large, heart-shaped leaves, then sends up a branching flowering stalk. Its purple flower heads develop into the familiar hooked burs that cling to fur and clothing. This is an effective way for seeds to travel beyond the original patch. The plant commonly occurs in pasture, fence lines, and other disturbed ground, where its broad leaves can shade neighboring plants. A deep taproot supports its growth. Finding young rosettes before burs develop makes management easier and helps prevent painful tangles in animals' coats.
identification: First-year leaves can be 6–18 inches long, with wavy or coarsely toothed edges and pale, hairy undersides. The lower leaf stalks are hollow. In the flowering stage, the ridged, branching stems commonly reach about 5 feet. Purple to lavender flower heads are surrounded by narrow bracts ending in hooks; these remain as brown burs after flowering. Thistles may have similar purple flowers, but their surrounding bracts do not make the same hooked attachment mechanism. Greater burdock can be separated in part by its solid lower leaf stalks. Photograph a basal leaf on both sides, the leaf stalk, a flowering head, and a mature bur without pressing it into clothing.
actions: Remove small rosettes before the flowering stalk develops. Dig out the crown or sever the deep taproot below the crown using a suitable tool; pulling leaves alone leaves the growing point behind. Repeated cutting before flowering can prevent seed production, but inspect for replacement stems. Carefully collect any formed burs and keep them out of animal bedding, hay, and garden waste intended for spreading. Check clothing, pets, and tools after working in a patch. Re-establish suitable competing vegetation on disturbed ground and revisit during the following growing season. If burs are lodged in an animal's eye or sensitive tissue, arrange appropriate animal care rather than pulling them forcibly.

sources.title: University of Missouri WeedID: Common Burdock
Invasive Species Council of British Columbia: Common burdock

researchNotes: Animal-care sentence is precautionary practical advice, not a treatment claim. No legal requirements imported from Canada.

claims: Biennial rosettes have large leaves, hairy undersides, and hollow petioles.
Second-year stems bear hooked purple flower heads.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Invasive Species Council of British Columbia
claims: Preventing bur development limits spread.
Cutting the taproot below ground and restoring competing vegetation are advised.

proposedDescription: Common Carp is a large, deep-bodied fish introduced to North America from Eurasia. It often feeds in shallow water, sucking material from the bottom and sorting out food. Where populations are abundant, this activity can uproot aquatic plants and stir sediment, reducing water clarity and changing habitat for other fish and waterfowl. It lives in lakes, rivers, ponds, and wetlands. Ornamental and cultivated forms vary in color and scale coverage, so a bright koi or partly scaled mirror carp can belong to this same species. An unfamiliar capture should be identified carefully before any management decision.
identification: Look for a stout body, a long dorsal fin, and two pairs of short, whisker-like barbels around the upper jaw. Typical fish are bronze, olive, or brown with large scales, but color and scale coverage vary. Adults are often 12–24 inches long and may grow much larger. Native buffalo fishes and suckers lack carp's mouth barbels; grass carp also lack them and have a shorter dorsal fin. Photograph the fish's whole side and the mouth area, with the dorsal fin visible where possible, and record its measured length and waterbody. Juveniles or unusual cultivated forms may require expert review. Do not identify or remove a native lookalike solely from body color.
actions: Never release aquarium, pond, or bait fish into a new waterbody. Dispose of unwanted bait appropriately rather than emptying it into the lake or stream. If you find Common Carp in a waterbody where it is unexpected, record the exact location, date, photographs, and approximate number, and contact the fisheries agency. Follow local fishing and possession rules for any fish already caught; release and harvest requirements differ by jurisdiction. Do not attempt to drain, poison, or net an entire waterbody yourself. Effective population management depends on the connected waters, spawning habitat, and other fish present, and should be planned with the responsible landowner and fisheries professionals.

sources.title: Missouri Department of Conservation: Introduction to Missouri Fishes

researchNotes: USGS snippet says one barbel per side; multiple state agencies explicitly confirm two pairs. Draft follows convergent agency diagnostic evidence. Source material read as substantial indexed content, not assumed full text.

claims: Bottom feeding can uproot plants and resuspend sediment.
Cultivated forms include mirror carp, leather carp, and koi.
Two barbels occur on each side of the mouth.
Deep body and long dorsal fin are diagnostic features.
Bigmouth buffalo lacks barbels.
Do not introduce carp to new waters; bait release can spread them.
Two pairs of upper-jaw barbels and a long dorsal-fin base are confirmed; native bigmouth buffalo lacks barbels.
Bottom feeding disrupts aquatic plants and water clarity.
Do not release into new waters; the source's same-water angling rule is Minnesota-specific.
Typical adult length is 12–24 inches.

proposedDescription: Common catchfly is a small annual of fields, roadsides, and other disturbed ground. Its narrow flowering stems carry white, pink, or occasionally red-marked flowers above opposite leaves. The plant is introduced from Europe and has been recorded in scattered parts of North America. Short sticky hairs and longer ordinary hairs occur together around the flowers, a useful clue that is easy to miss in a distant photograph. Records of introduction do not by themselves demonstrate substantial ecological damage; the practical concern at a garden or restoration site is whether an unwanted patch is producing seed and expanding.
identification: Plants commonly stand about 15–45 centimeters tall and grow from a taproot. Lower leaves are broader toward the tip, while upper leaves become smaller and narrower. Leaves occur in pairs. The flower's green outer tube is about 7–10 millimeters long and has ten visible veins, short glandular hairs, and longer hairs without glands. Five petals may be white, pink, red, or spotted; their tips are entire or shallowly notched. Silene pendula has a longer fruiting flower tube, only short glandular hairs there, and more deeply divided petals. Photograph the flower tube and hairs closely, plus a whole stem and mature capsule. Petal color alone is unreliable.
actions: Check a suspected patch while flowers and capsules are present so identification can be documented. Where removal is appropriate, pull these annual plants before capsules open and contain any seed-bearing stems. Revisit disturbed ground for later seedlings, especially if soil has recently been moved or reseeded. Keep garden debris and contaminated soil from spreading into adjacent habitat. If the plants occur on conservation land, confirm identification with the manager before removing a small native pink-family plant by mistake. For persistent or extensive occurrences, ask Extension about a plan suited to the site; removal timing and follow-up should account for both newly germinating plants and mature seed already present in the soil.

sources.title: Native Plant Trust Go Botany: Silene gallica
Flora of New Zealand: Silene gallica

researchNotes: Identification content read in substantial indexed floristic treatments. Actions inferred conservatively from annual seed reproduction; no regional impact claim.

claims: Mixed short glandular and long nonglandular hairs distinguish the species.
Silene pendula has a longer calyx and more deeply divided petals.
The named S. pendula comparison is confirmed: longer fruiting calyx, only short glandular hairs and deeper petal division.
Taprooted annual generally 15–45 centimeters tall.
Ten-veined calyx measures 7–10 millimeters; petals vary in color.
Taprooted annual generally 15–45 cm tall; 7–10 mm ten-veined calyx bears both short glandular and longer nonglandular hairs.
Petals may be white, pink, red or spotted and entire or shallowly notched.

proposedDescription: Common Chickweed is a low annual that often makes bright green mats in gardens, lawns, and other moist ground. It grows particularly well during cool, wet weather and can complete a generation quickly. Its tiny white flowers appear to have ten petals, but each of the five petals is deeply divided. Seeds allow repeated flushes of growth during favorable weather, so a patch can return after a quick weeding. Young plants may flower while still quite small. In vegetable beds it competes for space, nutrients, and light.
identification: Look for smooth, pointed, oval leaves arranged in opposite pairs along soft stems. A single band of hairs along the stem is a useful close-up feature. Plants may remain only about 2 inches high in turf, becoming 4–6 inches high and more open in a garden or shade. The tiny white flowers have five deeply split petals. Mouse-ear chickweed and sticky chickweed have much hairier leaves and stems; the former is perennial, while sticky chickweed is annual. Photograph a stem section close enough to show its hair line, a pair of leaves, and an open flower. A mat seen from standing height can conceal several different weed species.
actions: Remove seedlings promptly, ideally before flowers appear, because plants can begin producing seed within weeks. In a small bed, shallow weeding works best while plants are young and the surface is relatively dry. Collect flowering or fruiting material instead of leaving it scattered across the bed. Where appropriate, replenish mulch and close gaps in desired ground cover. Review unnecessary irrigation if the same wet corner repeatedly fills with chickweed. Inspect during the cool growing season for another flush, rather than waiting for a dense mat. Mature patches with capsules need careful collection to avoid spreading seeds into freshly cleared soil.

sources.title: University of Maryland Extension: Common Chickweed

researchNotes: Early removal and debris handling are directly supported by UC IPM. Maryland corroborates the cool-season annual life cycle and hairy mouse-ear lookalike. UC describes rooting at nodes whereas Maryland's newer comparison says it does not; the public draft omits this disputed trait. Identification and seed-prevention advice do not depend on resolving that discrepancy.

claims: Single stem hair band, paired smooth leaves, deeply divided white petals.
Early weeding and removal of debris prevent seed and rerooting.
Winter annual can have multiple generations in cool wet conditions.
Hairy perennial mouse-ear chickweed is a lookalike.

proposedDescription: Common comfrey is a perennial garden escape with broad leaves and hanging tubular flowers. It can persist around old homes, ditches, and damp disturbed ground long after a planting is abandoned. Pieces of its substantial root system can produce new plants, making soil movement and incomplete digging important routes of persistence. Garden plants sold as comfrey may also be hybrids or other species, so the familiar name does not settle identification. Historical medicinal use explains some cultivation, but it should not be presented as evidence of safety: extension sources warn that comfrey is unsafe to consume.
identification: Plants commonly reach 30–120 centimeters. Leaves are hairy and extend down the stem as narrow, flattened wings, especially useful when checking a flowering shoot. The hanging flowers may be whitish or purple and are about 12–18 millimeters long. Rough comfrey, Symphytum asperum, lacks the long leaf-base wings; Russian comfrey, S. × uplandicum, can have intermediate features and requires closer checking. Photograph the leaf attachment and the stem below it, a flower from the side, and mature fruits if present. Color is not sufficient to distinguish the species. An established garden clump with unusual characters should be checked against a botanical key rather than assumed to be this species.
actions: Before moving soil around an established clump, decide whether the plant is being retained or removed. If removing it, lift the crown and recover root pieces carefully; rotary cultivation can turn a localized clump into scattered regenerating fragments. Keep excavated roots out of soil or compost destined for other garden beds. Mark the spot and remove regrowth while small, repeating inspections through subsequent growing seasons. For a retained planting, watch its margins and avoid distributing unidentified root divisions. If an escape is spreading beyond a garden into damp habitat, document it and seek local advice. Do not use removed leaves or roots as a homemade medicinal preparation.

sources.title: NC State Plant Toolbox: Symphytum officinale
Native Plant Trust Go Botany: Symphytum officinale

researchNotes: Actions infer fragment-containment practices from documented regeneration; no tested eradication guarantee. Cytotypes and hybrids retained as identification caveats.

claims: Root fragments left during removal can sprout.
Consumption is not regarded as safe.
Roots left after removal regenerate; division and root cuttings propagate the plant.
Upper leaf bases extend down winged stems.
The source warns against consumption.
Plants 30–120 centimeters; leaves form wings down stems.
Related species and hybrids complicate identification.
Root fragments can spread garden escapes.
Its detailed hybrid discussion describes S. × uplandicum as lacking long decurrent leaf wings or having only short ones.

proposedDescription: Common corncockle is a slender annual with large pink to purple flowers, once a frequent weed of grain fields. Improved crop-seed cleaning and other farming practices have made it much less common in many agricultural areas. It also occurs in disturbed ground and may be grown as a flower. Long green points extending beyond the petals give the blooms a recognizable outline. The plant produces numerous seeds and is poisonous to people and livestock, making contamination of harvested grain or feed a more relevant concern than its attractive appearance suggests.
identification: Expect an upright, hairy plant roughly 2–3 feet tall with narrow leaves in opposite pairs. Leaves attach directly to the stem and may reach about 6 inches long. Solitary flowers are about 1–2 inches across, with five broad petals and five exceptionally long, pointed green sepals extending beyond them. Fine darker lines may mark the petals. The fruit is a capsule containing black, pitted seeds. Photograph a flower from both the face and side, the leaf pairs, and any capsule. Other pink-family plants can share hairy stems and pink flowers, so confirm the long sepals and narrow leaves together. Cultivars may vary in flower color.
actions: Keep suspected corncockle out of grain, hay, and animal feed. Document plants in a crop and alert the grower before harvest so contamination can be assessed. On your own noncrop ground, remove unwanted annual plants before capsules mature, collecting any developed capsules separately. Avoid sharing seed from an unidentified ornamental mixture and check future seed purchases for reliable labeling and cleanliness. Revisit the patch for seedlings after soil disturbance. Keep pulled material away from livestock and children. If a substantial area occurs in a field, obtain crop-specific advice rather than applying a garden treatment; control timing must account for the crop and the risk of seed entering the harvest.

sources.title: NC State Plant Toolbox: Agrostemma githago
Native Plant Trust Go Botany: Agrostemma githago

researchNotes: No blanket invasive status asserted. Preventive management is inference from annual seed biology and crop-contamination history.

claims: Hairy annual 2–3 feet tall; long sepals extend beyond five petals.
Poisonous plant; capsules hold black pitted seeds.
Formerly abundant crop weed declined with improved seed cleaning and modern farming.
Occurs in fields, roadsides and disturbed sites.

proposedDescription: Common crupina is a winter annual of open grassland and rangeland. It starts as a low rosette, then produces upright branching stems with narrow purple flower heads. Dense infestations can replace desirable forage and reduce plant diversity. Its seed is relatively large and carries a dark ring of bristles. Two named varieties occur in North America; their differences are most useful on mature fruits, not in a distant photograph. Preventing seed production and movement is central to containment because the species reproduces by seed.
identification: Plants are usually 1–3 feet tall. Young seed leaves are thick and rounded, sometimes with a reddish midvein; later leaves are deeply divided and have small teeth and stiff hairs. Slender flower heads develop at branch tips and contain only a few purplish-pink florets. Their surrounding bracts lack the conspicuous spines or fringes seen in many knapweeds. Mature fruits are dark and barrel-shaped with a ring of stiff bristles. Photograph rosette leaves, stem leaves, several heads, and mature fruits with a scale. Ask a specialist to confirm a new occurrence, particularly if assigning a variety: rosette color and growth angle are not reliable field separators.
actions: Report a suspected new patch to the relevant weed program and record its boundaries before disturbing it. Keep vehicles and livestock from carrying seed-bearing material away. Small confirmed plants can be hand-pulled before seed maturity where soil and access allow, but established infestations need repeated checks and a coordinated plan. Collect reproductive material securely; clean soil and plant debris from tools, boots, and equipment. Use clean hay and seed when managing surrounding land. Do not move plants to another site for identification without checking the receiving agency's instructions. Maintaining desired vegetation and watching the patch after removal are important parts of preventing renewed establishment.

sources.title: Washington Noxious Weed Control Board: Common crupina written findings
USDA ARS and WSU: Common crupina history and ecology

researchNotes: Historic board findings were used for morphology and biology, with the newer USDA–WSU account corroborating ecology. Old legal categories and distribution statements are not presented as current. Variety-specific measurement issues are tracked in their separate records.

claims: Winter annual reaches 1–3 feet.
Varieties differ in seed-head bristle length.
Common crupina displaces forage and spreads by seed.
Rosette color and position are unreliable varietal characters.

proposedDescription: Common crupina variety brachypappa is one of the named forms of a purple-flowered annual that grows in rangeland and other open sites. It shares the divided leaves and small flower heads of Common crupina as a whole. The main reported distinction lies in the mature fruits: their attached bristles are shorter than those assigned to variety vulgaris. Published accounts differ or are unclear about the exact measurements, so photographs of leafy plants cannot establish this variety with confidence. A botanist may need mature fruit and a carefully chosen identification key.
identification: Common crupina generally reaches 1–3 feet tall, with divided leaves and small purple flower heads. Those features identify a candidate for closer examination, not variety brachypappa by themselves. Photograph mature fruits with an accurate millimeter scale, showing both the fruit body and its attached bristles. The bristles are described as shorter than those of variety vulgaris, but published measurements are not consistent enough to use as a simple identification rule. Leaf color and whether the rosette lies flat are unreliable in the field. Do not assign variety brachypappa from geography, green shade, or an immature flowering plant. Expert examination of mature fruits is needed.
actions: Contain suspected Common crupina while keeping the varietal identification provisional. Map the patch and contact a local weed program for identification and a site-specific handling plan. Keep loose mature heads off boots, tools, vehicles, and livestock equipment that will enter clean ground. Where removal is appropriate, deal with a small patch before seed matures and revisit for later seedlings. If a specimen is requested, follow the recipient's instructions rather than carrying uncovered fruiting plants. The reported difference in fruit bristles does not by itself justify a different homeowner treatment. Preventing seed movement remains useful even when a specialist cannot yet assign the plant to a variety.

sources.title: Washington Noxious Weed Control Board: Common crupina written findings
USDA ARS and WSU: Common crupina history and ecology

researchNotes: Research gap: conflicting or ambiguous numerical fruit-bristle wording between 1999 board treatment and 2024 USDA/WSU factsheet. Exact variety requires mature fruit and specialist confirmation; shorter draft intentionally avoids fabricated precision.

claims: Winter annual reaches 1–3 feet.
Varieties differ in seed-head bristle length.
Common crupina displaces forage and spreads by seed.
Rosette color and position are unreliable varietal characters.

proposedDescription: Common crupina variety vulgaris is a named form of the same purple-flowered annual found in rangeland and other open sites. It has divided leaves, small flower heads, and fruits bearing bristles. North American treatments distinguish this variety mainly by the relatively long bristles attached to mature fruits. Older literature uses the name variety typica for a longer-bristled form, while newer material uses variety vulgaris. Those names and measurements need careful comparison before they are applied to a specimen. The shape and color of a young rosette do not reliably resolve its variety.
identification: Common crupina generally reaches 1–3 feet tall and has divided leaves and small purple flower heads. Document those features, then photograph mature fruits with a millimeter scale. The newer USDA–WSU account illustrates variety vulgaris with bristles noticeably longer than the fruit body; the older Washington treatment reports longer bristles under variety typica. The sources' numerical statements need reconciliation before a precise cutoff can be applied. Pale versus dark green leaves and upright versus flat rosettes are not reliable separators. Neither locality nor a photograph of flowers alone resolves the variety. Have a herbarium or weed specialist check mature material using the taxonomic treatment appropriate to the record.
actions: Record an uncertain plant as Common crupina until a specialist confirms its variety. Photograph and map the infestation, avoid moving seed-bearing plants, and contact the local weed program for a handling plan. Where removal is appropriate, taking out a small patch before seed maturity can reduce spread, but follow-up is necessary. Do not transport a loose specimen through uninfested ground; ask the receiving specialist how to submit it. Inspect footwear and equipment after entering a mature patch. A longer bristle does not establish a different management need. Continue watching for new plants around the original patch while the exact identification is being checked.

sources.title: Washington Noxious Weed Control Board: Crupina written findings
USDA ARS and WSU: Common crupina history and ecology

researchNotes: Exact infraspecific treatment unresolved; old typica/new vulgaris naming and ambiguous length wording require botanical review. Short provisional text intentional.

claims: Older treatment uses variety typica for the longer-bristled form.
Newer treatment recognizes variety vulgaris and warns against relying on rosette color.

proposedDescription: Common dandelion subspecies officinale is an introduced member of a difficult group whose boundaries differ among floras. The familiar plant has a basal leaf rosette, yellow flower heads, a deep taproot, and wind-carried fruits. Its flowering stalk rises directly from the rosette, and the rounded seed head breaks apart as individual fruits drift away. That general appearance can identify a dandelion without proving this exact subspecies. Native North American dandelions are treated differently by different authorities, so applying an introduced label to every dandelion in a natural area would be misleading.
identification: Yellow heads, toothed basal leaves and rounded white seed heads suggest a dandelion. Check for a single head on each hollow, leafless, unbranched stalk; catsear commonly has branched flower stalks. These features still do not establish subspecies officinale. Photograph the complete rosette, the underside of a flower head, a flowering stalk, and mature fruits beside a scale. The outer bracts surrounding the head and small fruit characters are important in dandelion keys and may require specialist examination. Older broad species concepts have included both introduced Eurasian and native North American plants. A field identification must therefore follow a regional treatment that explicitly distinguishes the relevant taxa. A lawn photograph or the fact that a plant grows beside a path is insufficient.
actions: For familiar unwanted lawn dandelions, a weeding tool can lift the crown and deep taproot; simply mowing the leaves does not eliminate the plant, and remaining root pieces can regrow. Revisit the spot and maintain suitable turf or ground cover if preventing new seedlings is the aim. In native meadow or alpine habitat, confirm the taxon before removing a dandelion on the assumption that it is introduced. Keep photographs and location details for a local botanist. Avoid carrying ripe seed heads through a cleared planting. Treat the exact subspecies name as provisional until a regional key and the necessary plant features support it.

proposedDescription: Common dogmustard is a yellow-flowered mustard of fields, roadsides, railway margins, and other disturbed ground. Introduced from Europe, it can be a weed of cereal and oilseed crops. Its flower stalks often have small leafy bracts beneath them, a useful difference from several superficially similar mustards. Plants usually complete their life cycle in one season, although some floras include biennial behavior. Like many crop weeds, it spreads through seed. A new occurrence near a planting deserves identification and attention to seed movement, without assuming that every roadside plant causes the same level of harm.
identification: Plants range from small individuals to about 80 centimeters tall. Leaves are alternate, hairy, and often divided into lobes; their shape can change upward along the stem. Flowers have four pale yellow or whitish petals. Slender seed pods measure roughly 10–45 millimeters. Most or all of the flower and fruit stalks are subtended by small leafy bracts. In tall hedge-mustard, Sisymbrium loeselii, most such stalks lack bracts, and each pod valve has three veins rather than one. Photograph the flowering stem from the side, lower leaves, pod attachments, and a mature pod. A close view of those bracts is more useful than flower color alone.
actions: Remove isolated unwanted plants before pods mature, taking care to collect any stems already carrying ripe fruit. Inspect the surrounding disturbed soil for additional plants rather than relying on one visible flowering stalk. Avoid moving pod-bearing vegetation with mowing equipment or contaminated crop material. In a field, notify the grower and seek crop-specific management advice, since control options and timing depend on the crop being protected. Use clean planting seed and check suspicious seed contamination with a diagnostic service. Record persistent patches along access routes where seed can be redistributed, and revisit after the next period of germination.

Plants may reach 80 centimeters and occur in disturbed habitats.
Pods are 10–45 mm long.
