The introduction and cereal/oilseed weed context is stated.
Annual introduced from southern and central Europe; widely naturalized in North America.

proposedDescription: Common flax is the cultivated annual grown for linen fiber and linseed oil. Escaped plants can occur in fields, along roads and railways, and around disturbed places where seed has been moved. Its slender stems carry narrow leaves and blue flowers with five petals, followed by rounded capsules. An introduced crop volunteer is not automatically a major ecological invader; a few plants beside a grain-handling site may have a different significance from repeated establishment in natural vegetation. Other blue-flowered flaxes are perennial and can look similar, making life history and small flower details important when checking an unfamiliar plant.
identification: Plants generally reach 30–120 centimeters. Narrow leaves, usually 15–40 millimeters long, attach alternately and have smooth edges. Five blue petals surround the flower center, and rounded dry capsules are about 6–10 millimeters long. Compared with perennial flax, Linum perenne, Common flax is annual, typically has three leaf veins, and has longer sepals, about 7–9 millimeters at maturity, with tiny hairs along the edges of the inner sepals. Photograph a whole plant, the leaf veins, a flower from the side, and a ripe capsule. A blue flower viewed from above cannot establish the species, and a cultivated bed may contain another flax.
actions: Determine whether the plants are intentionally grown before treating them as volunteers. For unwanted escapes in a small garden or restoration plot, pull plants before capsules ripen and collect developed seed heads. Check recent seed mixtures, imported soil, and nearby cultivation if plants repeatedly appear. Keep seed-bearing waste out of adjoining natural ground and avoid spreading unidentified flax seed. Where an occurrence is well outside cultivation, record its extent and persistence so local botanists can assess whether it is naturalizing. In production fields, coordinate with the grower rather than removing or treating a crop; the appropriate response depends on why flax is present.

Capsules are 6–10 mm long; crop use for fiber and oil is documented.
Recorded habitats include roadsides, railroads, fields, and other disturbed sites.

proposedDescription: Common frogbit is a floating aquatic plant that resembles a miniature water lily. Rounded to heart-shaped leaves collect in rosettes, and small white flowers may rise above them in summer. Plants can form crowded surface mats among other shallow-water vegetation. Besides growing shoots, the plant produces compact overwintering buds that detach and start new plants. These buds help it persist even when much of the visible foliage disappears. It is often called European frogbit, which helps distinguish it from American frogbit and other plants sold under similar common names.
identification: Leaves are typically about ½–2½ inches across, round or heart-shaped, and may have reddish-purple undersides. Plants usually float freely, though roots may reach the bottom in shallow water. Flowers have three white petals and a yellow center. Photograph a whole rosette, the leaf underside, connecting stems, roots, and any flowers or detached buds. American frogbit, Limnobium spongia, is a lookalike; comparison includes the amount of spongy tissue beneath the leaf, leaf shape, and root characters. These are easier to examine than to infer from an overhead photograph. Ask an aquatic-plant specialist to verify unfamiliar records, especially where native floating plants occur together.
actions: Report a suspected new occurrence with photographs and a precise waterbody location. Keep plants and detached buds from leaving on boats, anchors, boots, or sampling gear; inspect and clean equipment before visiting another waterbody. Do not empty aquarium or water-garden plants into drains or natural water. Hand removal may provide temporary control for a small patch, but should be coordinated with the landowner or aquatic-plant authority so fragments are collected and follow-up is arranged. The USGS account favors early-season removal after buds begin growing, before dense mats form. Large mats need an approved site-specific plan; do not introduce grazing fish or alter water levels on your own.

Native American frogbit comparison remains qualified; no local legal requirement is generalized nationally.

claims: Floating rosettes have 0.5–2.5 inch leaves and three-petaled white flowers.

Floating rosettes have 0.5–2.5 inch leaves and three white flower petals.

Spring or early-summer hand removal can help small populations but must be repeated.
Manual harvesting is temporary control; spring timing may improve it.

proposedDescription: Common globe amaranth is a warm-season garden plant with rounded pink, purple, or white flower heads. Most of the visible color comes from firm, papery bracts surrounding tiny flowers. Those bracts retain their color when dried, explaining the plant's popularity in arrangements. Hairy opposite leaves and stiff branching stems complete its appearance. It is usually grown as an annual and may produce self-sown seedlings. A garden volunteer is not necessarily a damaging invasion. Watch whether new plants remain within the bed or repeatedly establish in surrounding unmanaged ground.
identification: Plants commonly grow about ½–2 feet high, depending on cultivar. Leaves are simple, opposite, oblong to elliptical, and hairy, usually around 2–4 inches long. The compact heads look somewhat like clover but are made largely of dry-textured colored bracts; tiny whitish or yellowish true flowers may be visible between them. Photograph the full plant, a leaf pair, and a close-up of a head showing those small flowers. Red and orange globe amaranths may be selections of Gomphrena haageana or hybrids, so common names and color alone are inadequate. Retain nursery labels when available, but have naturalized specimens checked if their identity is uncertain.
actions: If plants are confined to an intentional flower bed, assess actual spread before deciding that control is necessary. Remove unwanted seedlings while small and collect spent heads before they scatter seed into nearby unmanaged ground. Keep discarded dried arrangements and seed-bearing garden waste out of natural areas. When a patch occurs beyond cultivation, record its location, size, and whether new plants return in later seasons. A herbarium can help distinguish this species from related ornamental globe amaranths. Inspect again after favorable germination weather and close gaps in the bed with suitable planting or mulch, keeping management proportionate to the observed escape and habitat.

sources.title: NC State Plant Toolbox: Gomphrena globosa

researchNotes: No unsupported ecological-impact claim. Management is cautious seed containment inferred from self-sowing.

claims: Colored bracts surround tiny true flowers.
Opposite hairy leaves and compact habit; introduced US occurrences.

proposedDescription: Common gorse is a dense evergreen shrub with stiff spines and golden-yellow pea flowers. Mature plants can form nearly impenetrable stands that displace grassland vegetation. Older bushes often accumulate dead material inside the living outer growth, and their oily foliage contributes to a serious fire hazard. Hairy pods split open and throw seeds away from the branches. Seeds can remain viable in soil for decades, so an apparently cleared patch may keep producing seedlings. Introduced for ornamental use, gorse is especially challenging where a long-established seed supply has built up beneath a thicket.
identification: Shrubs commonly reach several feet tall and can exceed 10 feet. Green angular shoots end in sharp spines, and mature foliage is strongly spine-like. Bright yellow flowers, about ½–¾ inch long, occur near branch tips. Their pea-flower shape may suggest Scotch broom or Spanish broom, but those shrubs lack gorse's dense array of obvious spines. Pods are short, flattened, and densely hairy, becoming brown at maturity. Photograph the branch structure, a flowering tip, and pods from a safe distance; include the bush's overall height. Young plants may have softer three-parted leaves, so the absence of a fully developed spiny thicket does not rule out gorse.
actions: Wear protective clothing and plan access before working near mature spines. Dig small plants with their crowns where feasible, then inspect for regrowth. Established shrubs can resprout after cutting, so a large patch needs a coordinated treatment and follow-up plan with local weed and fire-management advisers. Avoid leaving a pile of dry cut gorse against buildings or other vegetation. Prevent seed-bearing pods from being carried away on equipment or with soil. Re-establish appropriate cover on disturbed ground, and continue searching for seedlings over the long term. Do not use an improvised burn as a cleanup shortcut; fire and the persistent seed bank complicate safe management.

sources.title: Oregon State University Landscape Plants: Ulex europaeus

researchNotes: University morphology and state management guidance agree on dense spines, persistent seeds and resprouting. Fire hazard is relevant to access and debris management; the draft provides no improvised burn instructions or nationwide legal claim.

claims: Evergreen spiny shrub with golden flowers and hairy seed-ejecting pods.
Introduced ornamental naturalized in disturbed sites.
Dead interior foliage and oils create fire hazard; seed remains viable over 30 years.
Small plants can be dug; cut plants resprout and require follow-up.

proposedDescription: Common Groundsel is a fast-growing annual of garden beds, nurseries, and disturbed soil, especially during cool conditions. Its small yellow flower heads soon open into white seed tufts carried by wind. Plants can flower when quite small, and several generations may develop in a favorable year. A particularly important detail is that flowers on pulled plants can still produce viable seed. Groundsel competes with young garden and crop plants, and it is also a livestock hazard because eating it can cause liver poisoning. Removing it promptly matters more than letting a patch reach a conspicuous size.
identification: Look for an upright, often branched plant up to about 2 feet tall, with alternate leaves that become deeply lobed. Upper leaves attach directly to the stem; young lower leaves have short stalks. The narrow yellow flower heads are wrapped in green bracts with conspicuous dark tips. Later, each head opens to show a white tuft of wind-dispersed fruits. Photograph leaves at two heights and the side of several unopened or flowering heads so the dark bract tips are visible. A tiny flowering individual may already be capable of setting seed. Other yellow-flowered members of the daisy family need comparison, particularly when flowers are absent or the image is distant.
actions: Pull or hoe young plants before flowering, then check the bed regularly during cool growing periods. If flowers are already present, remove the entire plant from the site rather than leaving it on the soil, because seeds may finish developing after pulling. Keep all removed material out of hay, feed, and livestock access. Inspect incoming nursery pots and nearby neglected corners that can supply windblown seed. Suitable coarse mulch can reduce establishment in garden beds, while keeping desirable plant cover reduces open space. Repeated small removals are usually more useful than waiting for a large flush. Seek local advice for extensive crop or pasture infestations.

Cool moist nutrient-rich conditions permit several generations, and plants flower at small size.

proposedDescription: Common hawkweed is a yellow-flowered perennial whose scientific name is used differently among North American references. Some authorities recognize Hieracium vulgatum, while the Pacific Northwest flora uses Hieracium lachenalii and regards the former name as misapplied. These treatments may refer to different taxonomic boundaries rather than a simple spelling change. The plant described in the regional key has toothed basal leaves, several leaves along the flowering stem, and a group of small yellow heads. Native hawkweeds can look similar, so an unfamiliar plant needs both close examination and a clear choice of identification reference.
identification: The regional key describes plants about 20–80 centimeters tall, usually with four to seven stem leaves and four to twelve yellow heads. Basal leaves are gray-green, strongly toothed, and taper to stalks. Flower-head stalks and bracts carry combinations of simple hairs, star-shaped hairs, and dark gland-tipped hairs that need magnification. Smooth hawkweed generally has more stem leaves and more heads in the same key, but hair characters remain important. Photograph basal and stem leaves, the entire inflorescence, and close views of head coverings. Do not identify the species merely because a yellow hawkweed lacks runners; this group includes native lookalikes and difficult name usage.
actions: Document a suspected occurrence and avoid assigning an introduced-species label to all nearby hawkweeds. Request identification from a regional herbarium or weed specialist, providing close-ups of the leaf and flower-head hairs as well as the site location. Once a nonnative plant is confirmed and removal is appropriate, prevent mature seed from scattering and inspect the marked patch for returning growth. Work carefully among native vegetation rather than applying a broad treatment to every yellow flower. Record which scientific name and regional key were used for the determination. Keep uncertain plants marked for follow-up so that a later flowering or fruiting stage can supply missing evidence.

proposedDescription: Common Houndstongue is a biennial or short-lived perennial whose long hairy leaves form a low rosette before a flowering stem develops. Dull reddish-purple flowers produce four small hooked fruits that cling firmly to fur, clothing, and equipment. This makes trails, livestock movement, and contaminated material important opportunities for spread. It grows in pasture, roadsides, and other disturbed ground and can compete with forage. The plant is poisonous to livestock, including when dried in hay. A soft-looking rosette is therefore worth identifying before a mowing or haymaking operation carries it farther.
identification: Flowering plants reach roughly 1–4 feet. The first-year rosette has long, hairy, tongue-shaped leaves, often 4–12 inches long; leaves become smaller and attach directly to the stem higher up. Small burgundy to reddish-purple flowers have five lobes. Each flower develops four nutlets, each containing one seed and covered with tiny hooks. Photograph both the rosette and flowering stem, a leaf attachment, and the four-part fruit cluster. Other hairy rosettes can look similar before flowering, so record the leaf shape and hairs clearly rather than relying on texture alone. The mature hooked fruits are particularly helpful, but handle them carefully to avoid carrying them away.
actions: Prioritize plants in hay fields, livestock areas, and along travel routes before seed develops. Dig or pull small plants, removing the crown and as much root as practical, or sever rosettes below the crown. Recheck for sprouts and seedlings. Collect flowering or fruiting stems and keep even dried material away from livestock. Brush hooked fruits from clothing, animal coats, tools, and equipment before leaving the site, containing the removed seeds. Restore suitable competing vegetation where bare ground remains. For extensive pasture infestations, work with the local weed program and livestock adviser on a continuing plan; do not use grazing as a control method for this poisonous plant.

proposedDescription: Common house gecko is a small nocturnal lizard often seen on walls near lights, where insects gather. Broad toe pads let it climb smooth surfaces, and its pale gray to brown coloring can make it difficult to notice by day. Native to Asia, it has established introduced populations in parts of the United States and on many islands. Several other house geckos share buildings and look similar, so a gecko near a porch light is not automatically this species. Cargo and transported belongings are practical places to watch for accidental movement.
identification: Adults have a body length of about 42–60 millimeters from snout to vent, with a tail of roughly similar length when intact. The body is slightly flattened, the limbs are well developed, and a dark side stripe may run from the snout backward. The tail has rings of enlarged, pointed scales. Toe-pad scales are divided over much of each toe. Mediterranean and tropical house geckos can be confused with it, and diagnostic scale arrangements may need specialist examination. Obtain clear side and back photographs, including the tail and toes, without grabbing the animal or forcing it onto its back. A blurry silhouette or variable body color cannot establish species identity.
actions: Reduce entry into buildings by repairing screens and sealing gaps around doors, windows, and service openings after checking that animals are not trapped inside. Address indoor insect problems and unnecessary insect-attracting lights. Inspect boxes, nursery plants, and outdoor equipment before moving them to another region. Do not relocate a captured gecko to new outdoor habitat or release a pet. If one arrives unexpectedly in a shipment, keep the item contained where practical and ask local wildlife authorities for identification and handling advice. For persistent indoor problems, use exclusion-focused professional help. Photographs and shipping origin are useful evidence; broad insecticide spraying is not a reliable gecko-management plan.

proposedDescription: Common iceplant is a spreading succulent with broad fleshy leaves covered in clear, bead-like cells. These cells catch the light and give the plant its crystalline appearance. It often grows on disturbed coastal or salty ground, forming a low mat that may turn reddish as it ages or dries. In invaded coastal habitats, accumulated salts and persistent dead material can hinder other plants. This species differs from the large, familiar iceplants with thick triangular leaves. It usually completes its life cycle quickly, although its lifespan varies with conditions.
identification: Look for flat, oval to spoon-shaped leaves rather than thick three-angled blades. Leaves may be several inches long, with wavy margins and stout bases, and both leaves and stems carry conspicuous clear bladder-like cells. Trailing stems are green or red, and the plant may spread about a meter across. Small flowers have many narrow white to pinkish petal-like parts. Small iceplant, Mesembryanthemum nodiflorum, also has the clear cells but tends to be smaller throughout; use a regional key when both occur. Photograph an entire leaf, the sparkling surface cells, a flower and fruit, and the plant's spreading habit. Red color alone is not diagnostic.
actions: On accessible ground, remove small unwanted plants before fruits mature, lifting rather than scattering the succulent stems. Collect reproductive material and avoid adding it to soil or garden debris moved elsewhere. On coastal bluffs or sensitive dunes, coordinate with the land manager and work from stable ground; stripping a broad area can expose soil and disturb native plants. Mark the cleared patch and watch after rains for seedlings. Because the plant can alter surface salts and leave persistent litter, successful restoration may require more than removing green growth. Do not assume methods for large Carpobrotus iceplants have been tested for this species; use a cautious, monitored approach.

The page states that its assessment does not include management information.

proposedDescription: Common kochia is a bushy summer annual of crop fields, roadsides, and other open disturbed places. It tolerates dry and salty soils, helping it establish in arid and semiarid landscapes. The plant was grown ornamentally before spreading beyond cultivation, and modern sources commonly call it Bassia scoparia. Narrow leaves and many branches create a dense outline, sometimes becoming reddish late in the season. It competes with crops for light, water, and nutrients. Some populations resist several herbicide groups, so preventing seed production and maintaining plant competition are especially valuable.
identification: Mature plants are commonly 2–5 feet tall and branch near the base. Leaves are alternate, narrow, smooth-edged, and often covered with soft pale hairs. Small green flowers lack showy petals and sit in clusters where reduced leaves meet the stem. Fruits have short wings or knob-like projections. Fivehook bassia, Bassia hyssopifolia, is very similar, and UC IPM says their seedlings cannot reliably be separated. Mature branching pattern and fruit details are more useful: kochia typically branches from the base, while fivehook bassia branches along the main stem. Photograph the lower branching, leaves, and mature fruits, keeping seedling-only records provisional. Retain flowering or fruiting material when requesting an expert determination.
actions: Pull or hoe small plants before their stems become woody and before seed develops. In larger patches, plan mowing or other removal before seed maturity and check for surviving branches that can still flower. Keep field margins and disturbed access areas under observation, since unmanaged plants can replenish treated ground. Maintain suitable competitive vegetation; in crops, planting dates and cover-crop choices need to match the production system. Do not repeatedly rely on a failing herbicide treatment, because resistance is documented. Ask Extension to help diagnose poor control and design a broader plan. Do not put unidentified plants in livestock feed. If kochia is present in forage, seek Extension or veterinary advice and appropriate forage testing before feeding it.

sources.title: Montana State University Extension — Nitrate Toxicity of Montana Forages, revised March 2024

Seedling separation from fivehook bassia remains explicitly limited; no forage dose or pesticide recipe is inferred. Independent follow-up audit: Supports the parent's proposed correction. Do not add a safe dose, dilution recipe, or home veterinary treatment. The recommendation is to identify and evaluate forage before use, not a claim that all correctly identified kochia is unusable as managed forage.

claims: Bassia scoparia is former Kochia scoparia, a Eurasian summer annual.
Early pulling, competition, and integrated management help; resistance is documented.
Young plants can be pulled or hoed; seed prevention and plant competition are supported.
Competition strongly changes branching architecture, so mature fruit is stronger evidence than branching alone.
The page states that it is an excerpt of the GROW integrated management account.
Plants 2–5 feet; seedlings indistinguishable from fivehook bassia.
Mature branching and fruit characters support identification.

claims: Kochia can accumulate high nitrate concentrations, particularly under adverse growing conditions.
Chronic toxicity can follow small amounts of high-nitrate forage consumed over time; acute toxicity can occur after a large short-term intake.
Forage testing and an appropriate feeding program are needed to assess risk.

proposedDescription: Common lilac is a deciduous shrub best known for fragrant spring flower clusters. Long cultivated around homes, it can persist at former garden sites and spread locally through shoots arising around the base. Its flowers vary widely among cultivars, including white, pink, and purple forms. A surviving old shrub is not evidence by itself of rapid invasion, but expanding suckers can move it beyond an intended planting. The plant prefers climates with substantial winter chilling, which helps explain its familiar presence in cooler gardens. Records beyond cultivation should distinguish an old planting from newly established growth.
identification: Typical shrubs reach about 8–16 feet tall and carry opposite, smooth-edged, heart-shaped to broadly oval leaves. Spring flowers form dense branched clusters at shoot tips. Individual flowers have a tube ending in four spreading lobes, although double cultivars alter that appearance. Japanese tree lilac, Syringa reticulata, differs in having stamens that project beyond the flower tube. Flower color alone is unreliable because cultivars and hybrids are numerous. Check paired leaf attachment, the broad leaf base, and a side view of an individual flower. If mapping an escape, note whether separate shoots are still connected to an old garden clump and whether seedlings occur farther away.
actions: If retaining a garden lilac, remove unwanted basal shoots regularly and monitor the outer edge of the clump. Keep pruned material and rooted divisions out of natural ground. When removing a small escaped plant, dig its crown and attached roots where feasible, then revisit for new shoots. A mature clump may need repeated work, so decide whether containment or removal best fits the site before cutting it down. On an abandoned homesite, confirm ownership and the intended vegetation plan before removing a longstanding ornamental. Document new establishment beyond the original planting; that distinction is more informative for local management than the mere presence of a familiar lilac.

sources.title: NC State Plant Toolbox: Syringa vulgaris
Native Plant Trust Go Botany: Syringa vulgaris

researchNotes: University guidance directly supports suckering and removal of unwanted shoots; regional flora corroborates naturalized occurrences. The draft distinguishes old plantings from new establishment and does not infer broad ecosystem harm from persistence alone.

claims: Opposite heart-shaped leaves; shrub 8–16 feet tall.
Remove suckers to prevent unwanted spread.
Naturalized in disturbed habitats and forest edges.
Japanese tree lilac has protruding anthers unlike common lilac.

proposedDescription: Common Mallow is a spreading annual or biennial with rounded leaves and small pale flowers. Its flattened ring of fruits resembles a tiny wheel of cheese, giving it the alternate name cheeseweed. Young plants can be easy to overlook, but they soon develop a strong taproot that becomes difficult to pull. The plant reproduces by seed, and the hard seed coat allows some seeds to persist for years. It occurs in gardens, disturbed soil, and cultivated ground, where larger patches can compete with desired plants and replenish a lasting seed supply.
identification: Leaves are alternate on long stalks, nearly round or heart-shaped, with five to seven shallow rounded lobes and a scalloped edge. Plants usually spread outward but can reach about 2 feet high. White to pale pink flowers grow from the leaf axils and have five notched petals, each about twice as long as the green sepals beneath them. The mature fruit is a smooth, flattened disk divided into roughly ten to twelve sections. Little mallow, Malva parviflora, has shorter petals approximately equal to the sepals and wrinkled fruits. A photograph of leaves alone often cannot distinguish them; include a flower side view and a mature fruit.
actions: Pull or hoe seedlings early, ideally while they have only a few true leaves and before the taproot becomes woody. For older plants, use a tool that removes or severs the crown below soil level; clipping leaves or mowing above low buds is often ineffective. Collect developed fruits so seed is not returned to the bed. Mulch suitable garden areas and maintain competing plants to reduce open germination sites. Recheck after rain or soil disturbance, since hard-coated seeds can emerge over time. Avoid assuming one cleanup has exhausted the seed supply. In crop fields, address patches before their size and tough stems interfere with harvesting equipment.

sources.title: University of Washington Burke Herbarium: Malva neglecta

researchNotes: Biological and nonchemical recommendations supported; avoids transferring little-mallow-specific timing to this species.

claims: Common mallow has longer petals and smoother fruits than little mallow.
Early pulling, crown removal, and mulch help; mowing often fails.
Leaves are rounded to heart-shaped, shallowly lobed, and long-stalked.

proposedDescription: Common mediterranean grass is a small annual grass that can be easy to overlook until many plants cover the spaces between desert shrubs. Its narrow leaves and short, pale or purple flower clusters grow close to the ground. Plants dry to straw color as moisture disappears. Originally from the Old World, it now occurs in disturbed dry ground in parts of the western United States. It is often discussed with the closely related Arabian schismus because the two grasses look similar and share habitats. Management deserves particular care in deserts, where disturbing the soil can create more opportunities for annual weeds.
identification: Look for small tufts with slender stems roughly 2–12 inches long and narrow leaves usually less than 4 inches long and about 2 millimeters wide. The flower cluster is compact to narrowly oval, roughly 0.4–2 inches long, with pale or purplish spikelets and no conspicuous long awns. A ring of hairs occurs where the blade meets its sheath. Common mediterranean grass and Arabian schismus (Schismus arabicus) require examination of the tiny floral scales for reliable separation; plant color or overall size is insufficient. A grass specialist can check the short, rounded teeth at the tip of the lemma, the scale enclosing each flower. Collect a close view of mature spikelets with a scale and a view of the leaf collar.
actions: Map small outlying patches before deciding how to treat a larger area. In desert habitat, avoid scraping, disking, or broad soil disturbance: these actions can remove competitors and improve conditions for Common mediterranean grass. Its fine, shallow root mat also makes extensive hand pulling disruptive and impractical. For a few plants in an already disturbed garden edge, remove them carefully before seed ripens and inspect the spot after subsequent rains. Keep vehicle tires, footwear, and equipment free of attached soil before leaving infested ground. Do not use burning as a household control method; the published management account reports that fire commonly favors these grasses. Seek local restoration advice for larger desert infestations.

sources.title: Schismus barbatus — Upper Newport Bay flora

researchNotes: Cal-IPC management and ecology cover both Schismus species jointly; draft makes that limitation explicit. Individual removal advice for a few garden-edge plants is cautious practical inference, not a field-scale efficacy claim.

claims: Schismus arabicus and S. barbatus are treated together; small annual grasses occupy disturbed desert sites.
Mechanical disturbance and prescribed fire can favor Mediterranean grasses; extensive hand thinning disrupts surface soil.
Tufted annual with stems 0.5–3 dm, narrow blades and 1–5 cm panicles.
Lemma teeth are minute and rounded; palea is as long as lemma.

proposedDescription: Common Mouse-ear Chickweed forms low green mats with small leaves covered in conspicuous hairs. Unlike the annual Common Chickweed, established plants often persist for several years and can spread as creeping stems take root. Small white flowers rise above the foliage, each with five notched petals. It grows in lawns, gardens, fields, and other disturbed places, especially where conditions stay cool and moist. Much North American weed guidance concerns the widespread subspecies vulgare within this species. A patch may remain green through winter in mild conditions, then resume growth before many neighboring plants become active.
identification: Examine the leaves and stems closely: both are hairy, and the opposite leaves are oval to oblong with smooth edges. Stems spread along the soil and can root at their joints. Common Mouse-ear Chickweed is usually only a few inches high when mown but may form taller mounds where left alone. The white flowers are about a quarter inch across, with five deeply notched petals that can resemble ten. View a flower from the side to compare petals with the green sepals beneath them; they are about equal in length. Common Chickweed has largely smooth leaves, while Sticky Chickweed has sticky glandular hairs. Field Chickweed generally has larger flowers with petals much longer than the sepals. Hairy foliage alone does not establish a subspecies.
actions: Lift small patches with a hand fork when the soil is moist, taking the roots and the stem sections that have rooted at their joints. Pulling only the upright flower stalks leaves much of Common Mouse-ear Chickweed in place. Remove plants before seed develops, and revisit the patch because seedlings can emerge over a prolonged cool season. In lawns, repair thin areas with suitable turf and adjust unnecessary irrigation that keeps the surface constantly moist. Mulch open garden soil after removing established plants, while keeping mulch away from desired plant crowns. Persistent mats may need several passes. Regional extension guidance can help distinguish this perennial from annual chickweeds before a lawn treatment is chosen.
researchNotes: Species-level entry. Most extension material uses C. fontanum subsp. vulgare or the older name C. vulgatum; do not equate this entire species entry with that subspecies. Two independent extension accounts read.

claims: Mouse-ear chickweed has hairy opposite leaves, roots at nodes, and petals approximately as long as sepals.
It is perennial, favors moisture, and can be removed with roots by hand in small infestations.
Low perennial reproduces through seeds and rooted branching nodes.
Common chickweed lacks the dense foliage hairs; small populations in beds can be removed by hand.

proposedDescription: Common Mullein starts as a broad rosette of thick, soft, gray-green leaves. Later it sends up a tall stalk topped with closely packed yellow flowers, often becoming one of the most noticeable plants along a sunny roadside. It usually flowers in its second year, though conditions can delay flowering. Introduced from Europe, it favors open disturbed ground, pastures, and waste places. A mature plant produces numerous tiny seeds, and the soil seed bank can outlast the visible stand. Preventing fresh seed and restoring dense vegetation are therefore more useful than simply removing old brown stalks.
identification: First-year Common Mullein forms a rosette up to about 2 feet across. Its oblong to lance-shaped leaves can reach a foot long and are densely covered with soft hairs on both surfaces. Flowering stems often reach 6 feet or more, carrying progressively smaller leaves and a long, dense terminal flower spike. The flowers are yellow and open a few at a time. Thick, uniformly hairy gray-green foliage is a stronger early clue than a tall dead stalk. Other mulleins can look similar when young, so photograph the rosette, a stem leaf and its attachment, and the flowering spike together. An isolated leaf or a distant winter stalk is a poor basis for a confident identification.
actions: Remove Common Mullein while plants are still rosettes or before flowers produce seed. Pull or dig small plants when soil is moist, taking the root crown and minimizing the amount of bare ground left behind. Work from scattered outlying plants toward the center of a larger infestation. If seed capsules have formed, contain the stalks before carrying them through clean areas. Mowing alone is unreliable because low rosettes can survive and later send up flowering stems. Reestablish suitable vegetation over disturbed soil and check again after future soil disturbance; dormant seeds can produce a new flush. Large infestations on conservation land warrant a site-specific plan that protects surrounding desirable plants.
researchNotes: Management directly supported by Wisconsin extension. No medical use recommendation. No unverified lookalike distinctions added.

claims: Biennial introduced from Europe; rosettes can be two feet wide and flowering stems six feet or taller.
Thick densely hairy gray-green leaves and yellow terminal flower spikes are diagnostic features.
Small infestations can be pulled, hoed or dug before seeding; dense cover and avoiding disturbance help.
Mowing is ineffective against surviving rosettes; populations can persist as dormant seed.

proposedDescription: Common nipplewort is a leafy herb with many small yellow flower heads on a branching stem. The lower leaves often have one broad end lobe and smaller side lobes, giving the plant a different outline from a lawn dandelion. It is native to Europe and Asia and has been introduced widely in North America, where it grows in fields and other disturbed places. Plants generally complete their lives as annuals, although short-lived perennial growth is also reported. The pale yellow heads contain only strap-shaped flowers; there is no contrasting central disk.
identification: Common nipplewort can grow about 3 feet tall. Leaves alternate along the stem, with larger lower leaves often divided into a large terminal lobe and two smaller side lobes. Upper leaves may be simpler. The branched, leafy flowering stems carry small pale yellow heads, commonly with 8–15 strap-shaped flowers. Flowering is typically in summer and early autumn, with timing varying by climate. Compare an open head with the entire stem: a dandelion has a leafless stalk bearing a single head, while Common nipplewort has leafy branches and numerous heads. Its fruits lack the conspicuous feathery parachute seen on many similar yellow-flowered members of the daisy family. Include lower leaves and mature fruit in identification photographs.
actions: In a garden or newly disturbed margin, remove small Common nipplewort plants before they set seed. Use a narrow hand tool to lift the root rather than repeatedly stripping off the upper leaves. If plants already carry mature fruit, contain the flower heads while moving the material and avoid shaking them over clean soil. Check nearby disturbed ground for younger plants, then cover open garden soil with mulch or appropriate vegetation. A few plants do not by themselves establish that a site needs broad treatment; focus on unwanted reproduction and competition with desired planting. For persistent or extensive stands, ask a local weed adviser to confirm the species and assess the site before choosing a larger intervention.
researchNotes: No species-specific field management trial was located. Actions are conservative small-scale seed prevention inferred from the documented life cycle; not presented as an eradication protocol.

claims: Native to Europe and Asia, widely introduced in North America.
Leaves alternate; heads have yellow ray flowers without disk flowers; fruits lack a conspicuous plume.
Annual or short-lived perennial about one metre tall with lower leaf terminal and lateral lobes.
Branched leafy stems bear pale yellow heads of 8–15 ray florets in summer to autumn.

proposedDescription: Common oat is the familiar cereal and forage crop, with loose, branching seed heads rather than the compact ears of wheat or barley. Plants may also appear outside fields after grain is spilled or cultivation ends. These escapes occur along roadsides and on disturbed ground across North America. Common oat is an annual, so management of unwanted plants centers on preventing another seed crop and identifying the source of new seed. Its presence alone does not show that a habitat is being invaded or damaged; an isolated volunteer and a deliberately planted cover crop need different responses.
identification: Common oat generally reaches a few feet tall, although the documented range extends from about 1 to 6 feet. Broad, flat grass blades have a thin, translucent membrane at the junction with the sheath and lack the clasping ear-like projections called auricles. The seed head is openly branched, with large hanging spikelets enclosed by long papery scales. Cultivated Common oat usually has two flowers per spikelet. Wild oat (Avena fatua) commonly has three and conspicuous brown hairs on the flower-enclosing scales, while Common oat has smoother scales. Some cultivated forms carry bristles and others do not, so the presence of an awn alone is unreliable. Mature spikelets are more useful than young leaves for separating these grasses.
actions: First establish whether Common oat was intentionally sown as forage, a cover crop, or part of a restoration mixture. Where it is unwanted, pull scattered plants or cut them before viable grain forms, then check for later seedlings. Collect mature seed heads before moving cut material through clean areas. Look for spilled livestock feed, birdseed, or grain-handling losses that could repeatedly replenish a small patch. Maintain desired ground cover after removal rather than leaving loose bare soil. In a cropped field, confirm whether the plant is Common oat or a more troublesome wild oat before changing management. Use local agricultural advice for volunteer control within another crop, where timing and crop tolerance matter.

sources.title: Pocket identification guide to conservation plants

researchNotes: NRCS oat identification details read in indexed excerpt; PDF opened but returned earlier pages rather than oat section. Volunteer prevention advice inferred from annual grain life cycle, not a claim of nationwide harmful invasion.

claims: Cereal, feed and forage crop escapes to fields, roadsides and disturbed soils.
Annual with branched inflorescences, two-flowered spikelets and membranous ligules; diagnostic comparison with wild oat is provided.
Oat is a cool-season annual grain typically two to four feet tall.
Leaf junction has a membranous ligule and no auricles.

proposedDescription: Common periwinkle is a marine snail found on rocky shores, pilings, and other surfaces exposed by the falling tide. It holds tightly with a muscular foot and scrapes algae with a ribbon of microscopic teeth. A small hard lid seals its shell opening when the animal withdraws, helping it retain moisture. Originally European, it is well established along much of northeastern North America; scattered Pacific-coast records have not always represented reproducing populations. Dense populations can change seaweed communities through grazing. Its empty shells also provide homes for hermit crabs and shelter for other small shore animals.
identification: Common periwinkle has a thick, solid, roughly turban-shaped shell with a pointed spire and usually six or seven turns. Adults commonly reach about 1.2 inches long, although larger specimens occur. Shells vary from cream or brown to nearly black and may carry fine dark spiral lines; color alone is unreliable. The shell opening has a brown interior and a pale central column, and the base lacks an open central hole. Photograph the opening and the opposite side beside a ruler, without removing living animals from the shore. Rough periwinkle (Littorina saxatilis) and marsh periwinkle (Littoraria irrorata) can be confused with this species. Small or worn shells need expert comparison rather than identification from a distant group photograph.
actions: Do not release purchased live Common periwinkle, aquarium animals, bait, or seafood packing material onto a shore. Avoid moving live snails on rocks, shellfish gear, or collected seaweed between coastal sites. If you find a suspected population outside its familiar local range, record the location, date, approximate abundance, and clear shell photographs, then contact the state marine resource agency or a local marine extension program. Leave the animals in place unless the receiving agency requests a specimen and explains how to handle it. Broad hand collection is not a demonstrated solution for an established coastwide population, and indiscriminate removal can disturb other intertidal organisms. Focus on preventing new introductions and documenting unexpected records.
researchNotes: NPS gives a simplified introduction story; draft follows Smithsonian's more qualified historical treatment. Prevention and reporting are conservative pathway-based advice, not a validated eradication protocol. Listed lookalikes from Smithsonian, without unsupported distinguishing measurements.

claims: European marine snail established in northeastern North America; Pacific occurrences have not necessarily established populations.
Heavy shell has six or seven whorls, brown aperture interior and no umbilicus; grazing can change algal communities.
Muscular foot attaches snail to rock; radula scrapes algae; operculum closes the shell opening.
Intertidal snails have shells up to about three centimetres; empty shells provide shelter and hermit-crab homes.

proposedDescription: Common Periwinkle is a creeping evergreen groundcover with glossy dark leaves and blue to lavender flowers. Long stems take root where their joints touch soil, allowing a small planting to become a connected mat. Native to Europe and the Caucasus, it has been widely planted around homes, old gardens, and cemeteries. Escaped patches can spread into nearby natural areas and crowd low-growing vegetation. Flowers are most noticeable in spring and early summer, but the persistent foliage makes patches visible in other seasons too. Cultivated forms may have pale-edged or golden leaves rather than solid green.
identification: Common Periwinkle usually holds its leaves only 3–6 inches above the ground, while its trailing stems extend farther. Leaves occur in opposite pairs and are firm, smooth-edged, and generally about half an inch to an inch and a half long. The flowers have five spreading lobes joined into a narrow tube at the center, creating a flattened pinwheel-like outline. Compare it with Bigleaf Periwinkle (Vinca major): Common Periwinkle has thicker leaves broadest near the middle and smooth, hairless edges; Bigleaf Periwinkle has thinner leaves broadest nearer a rounded or heart-shaped base, with tiny hairs along their edges. Check the margins with a hand lens. Photographs should show a leaf pair, its base and edge, and a stem joint touching the soil.
actions: Start at the advancing edge of a Common Periwinkle patch and trace runners back to every rooted joint. Lift the connected stems and roots with a hand fork, working carefully around desirable plants. Simply cutting off the visible shoots leaves rooted sections able to regrow, so revisit the site and remove new shoots promptly. Keep pulled runners off moist soil and out of dumped garden waste where they could establish again. Inspect adjoining woodland edges and the far side of paths or fences, where overlooked stems may continue the patch. Replace cleared areas with suitable groundcover and monitor through subsequent growing seasons. For a large mat among valued plants, seek a selective local management plan.
researchNotes: Manual removal sequence follows rooting growth form and extension regrowth advice. No claim that a single removal pass eradicates a mature mat.

claims: Evergreen creeping plant roots at nodes and can form dense mats.
Vinca minor has thick, unciliated leaves broadest near the middle; V. major has ciliate edges and broader bases.
Opposite glossy evergreen leaves, lilac-blue five-lobed flowers, and rooting vine-like stems characterize Vinca minor.
Non-native to North America and invasive in several states.
New periwinkle growth should be removed promptly to weaken remaining roots.

proposedDescription: Common Plantain grows as a low rosette of broad leaves with strong curved veins. Slender upright stalks carry tiny flowers and later crowded seed capsules. It is familiar in lawns, paths, gardens, and other frequently disturbed places, particularly where soil is compacted and stays moist. A tough crown at ground level allows an established plant to survive mowing and produce new leaves. Although unwanted in many lawns, a few plants do not automatically justify treatment. Accurate identification matters because other broad-leaved plantains, including native species, can occupy the same kinds of sites.
identification: Look for oval leaf blades roughly 2–7 inches long, gathered at ground level on distinct stalks. Several strong veins curve from the leaf base toward the tip, following the general leaf outline. Leafless flowering stalks can reach about 15 inches and bear long, narrow spikes rather than showy petals. Buckhorn Plantain (Plantago lanceolata) has much narrower leaves and shorter, more compact flower heads. Rugel's Plantain (Plantago rugelii) can be much harder to distinguish: its leaf-stalk bases are often purple, but mature capsules provide better evidence. Common Plantain has smaller capsules that open around the middle; Rugel's capsules are longer and open nearer the base. Photograph the leaf-stalk bases and mature fruit, and seek confirmation when those features are missing.
actions: Remove unwanted Common Plantain before seed ripens, using a narrow weeding tool to lift the crown as well as the leaves. Mature crowns can resprout after partial removal, so revisit the spot over the following months. Mowing alone usually misses the low leaves and does not eliminate the plant. In a lawn, address repeated traffic, compaction, and thin turf, then repair the opening with grass suited to the site. Avoid unnecessary irrigation that maintains a consistently wet surface. Mulch open ornamental beds after removal and check for seedlings along paths and bed edges. Confirm broad-leaved lookalikes before treating a natural area, particularly where a native plantain may be present.

sources.title: Rugel's plantain — comparison with Plantago major

researchNotes: Ontario page returned 403, so it is not counted as read evidence. Native lookalike comparison comes from the flora key. Identification is species-level, with no inference about an individual plant from habitat alone.

claims: Plantago major has oval leaves with curved parallel veins, fibrous roots and a persistent crown.
Mowing is ineffective; remove plants before seed and monitor for resprouting; healthy turf and mulch reduce recruitment.
P. rugelii commonly has purple petiole bases.
P. major capsules are mostly 2.5–4 mm and open near the middle; P. rugelii capsules are mostly 4–6 mm and open near the base.

proposedDescription: Common pricklypear is a shrubby to tree-sized cactus with flattened green stem segments that often droop toward their tips. Older plants can develop a woody trunk, while yellow flowers and reddish-purple fruit form around the edges of the segments. Native to South America, it has escaped cultivation in warm regions elsewhere. Broken segments can root when they reach soil, so garden waste and moved plant pieces can start new patches. Its spines and tiny barbed bristles make handling difficult. The name “prickly pear” covers many different cacti, including native North American species, making exact identification especially important.
identification: Common pricklypear commonly stands about 6–10 feet tall and can grow larger. The flattened segments are often elongated or egg-shaped, glossy green, and visibly drooping on older branches. Small raised points carry fine barbed bristles and usually one or two larger spines, with more spines possible on older growth. Flowers are yellow, sometimes red-marked on the outside, and fruit becomes red to purple. Common pricklypear differs from Opuntia stricta, which has thicker, duller pale-green or gray-green segments, and from Velvet Tree Pear (Opuntia tomentosa), whose stems and fruit have fine hairs. Cultivated forms may be distorted or variegated. Record the whole plant, segment surface, spine clusters, flowers, and fruit; a detached green pad is often insufficient.
actions: Do not distribute cuttings from an unidentified prickly pear. Before removing Common pricklypear, confirm the species and plan how every segment and fruit will be contained. Wear protective clothing and use long-handled tools rather than grasping the pads. Small isolated plants can be dug out, but collect detached pieces and inspect the ground afterward for missed fragments and new growth. Keep material away from bare soil and do not dump it along roads, waterways, or vacant land. Ask the local waste service or weed program for an accepted disposal route. Large trunked plants need experienced help. Do not import or release cactus-feeding insects; overseas biological-control instructions are not transferable to a home garden.
researchNotes: Australian agency evidence used for morphology and vegetative spread; Australian legal duties, pesticide directions, burning/burial prescriptions and biocontrol releases are not reproduced as US advice. Common name is ambiguous across Opuntia species.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: New South Wales Department of Primary Industries
claims: Glossy drooping pads and usually one or two spines characterize Opuntia monacantha.
O. stricta has thicker dull pads; O. tomentosa has hairy stems and fruit.
Small isolated plants can be dug with protective equipment; follow-up and safe disposal are necessary.
Shrub can reach five metres; yellow flowers form on segment edges and fruit bears fine barbed bristles.
Detached segments and fruit can root; human movement, waste disposal and water can spread them.

proposedDescription: Common rue is a small aromatic shrub with blue-green divided leaves and clusters of yellow flowers. Young stems are soft and green, becoming woody as the plant ages. It has long been grown in herb and ornamental gardens and can reseed around the parent plant. The foliage also serves as food for several swallowtail butterfly species. Common rue is associated with southeastern Europe and the Balkan region, but has been cultivated and naturalized elsewhere. It is not appropriate to assume that every garden planting causes ecological harm. Wear gloves and long sleeves when handling Common rue: skin contact followed by sunlight can cause a severe skin reaction.
identification: Common rue usually grows 2–3 feet tall and about as wide. Its alternate leaves are divided more than once into small rounded or oblong segments, giving the blue-green foliage a finely cut appearance. Leaves are hairless and dotted with glands; avoid crushing them against bare skin to test their scent. Small yellow flowers occur in upright terminal clusters, with four or five petals surrounding a prominent green center. Brown capsules split to release dark seeds. The woody lower stems distinguish an established plant from a purely herbaceous seedling. For identification, include the complete leaf structure and a close view of flowers or capsules. Finely divided blue-green foliage alone is not sufficient to separate rue from unrelated ornamental herbs.
actions: If Common rue is intentionally planted, watch for seedlings outside the bed and remove unwanted volunteers while they are small. To reduce reseeding, clip developing seed clusters before the capsules open. Wear gloves and long sleeves when pruning or lifting plants, keeping cut foliage away from exposed skin. Check the leaves for swallowtail caterpillars before removing an occupied plant, and avoid unnecessary broad insecticide treatments around this host plant. If the shrub is unwanted, dig out the crown and roots and inspect the area for later seedlings. Keep it clearly separate from edible herbs; traditional use does not establish that home ingestion is safe. No broad eradication treatment is warranted solely because it is introduced.

sources.title: University of Texas at El Paso — Rue herbal safety
Eickhorst, DeLeo and Csaposs 2007 — Rue-associated phytophototoxicity

researchNotes: No evidence found supporting blanket US invasive status. Garden containment follows documented self-seeding; no claim of a tested eradication protocol. Native-range wording avoids differing broad range summaries. Independent follow-up audit: This is an upgrade to an incomplete hazard description, not a finding that the current protective-clothing advice is unsafe. Retain the draft's caution against home ingestion; do not reuse NC State's small-amount edibility wording.

claims: Two-to-three-foot subshrub has aromatic divided blue-green leaves, yellow flowers and self-seeding reproduction.
Foliage hosts swallowtail butterflies; gloves and long sleeves are advised during handling.
Blue-green divided foliage, 2–3 foot size, yellow flowers and self-seeding are supported.
Swallowtail host use and gloves/long sleeves during handling are explicit.
Woody-based aromatic shrub has alternate divided leaves, four-to-five-petaled yellow flowers and lobed capsules.
Plant is toxic and can irritate skin; introduced as an ornamental and naturalized beyond its native region.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Supplemental audit: University of Texas at El Paso
claims: Rue applied to skin followed by direct sunlight can cause serious photodermatitis.
Contact dermatitis can also occur.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Supplemental audit: Eickhorst, DeLeo and Csaposs 2007
claims: The case-report abstract connects rue psoralens on skin followed by UVA exposure with a photoirritant reaction.

proposedDescription: Common rustic moth is a small, stout, night-flying moth whose brown forewings often show a conspicuous pale kidney-shaped mark. Adults rest among vegetation by day and may come to outdoor lights after dark. The caterpillars feed on grasses, including cereal crops. A Eurasian species, it was first documented in North America in the Pacific Northwest in 2016 and has since been recorded more widely in that region. European crop damage is known, but the regional university account does not currently recognize it as a North American pest. New records are therefore useful for tracking its spread without assuming damage.
identification: Adult Common rustic moth has forewings about half an inch long. Their color ranges from olive-brown to reddish or nearly black, and the pattern can be mottled or almost plain. A pale cream or white kidney-shaped mark is often the strongest visible feature. The hindwings are dark brownish gray. Adults are most often recorded in July and August in the Pacific Northwest. Native Mesapamea fractilinea can look nearly identical; definitive separation relies on specialist examination of reproductive structures. In Europe, Lesser Common Rustic (Mesapamea didyma) is another close lookalike. Take sharp upper-wing photographs with a size reference and preserve the date and locality. A brown moth at a porch light should remain a tentative identification unless the necessary distinguishing evidence is available.
actions: Photograph a suspected Common rustic moth and send the record to a regional moth recorder, university insect collection, or extension entomologist, especially if it occurs beyond known local records. Ask before collecting a specimen because expert examination may be needed to distinguish the species. Do not infer that nearby crop injury was caused by this moth solely because an adult visited a light. If grasses or cereals show damage, document the affected plants and any larvae together and seek a crop-specific diagnosis. Avoid broad spraying of lawn or garden vegetation in response to a single adult. The available North American account supports observation and identification, rather than a routine homeowner eradication program.

sources.title: Common Rustic — Butterflies and Moths of Northern Ireland

researchNotes: Confirmed species identity at catalog level; individual photo identification is limited, not a reason to invent external diagnostic certainty. No established US damage threshold or homeowner control protocol found; reporting remains useful and supported. Avoid treating M. didyma as an unqualified synonym.

claims: First North American records were in Vancouver and Bellingham in 2016; later records extend through western Washington into Oregon.
Forewing length is 12.5–14 mm; native M. fractilinea is very similar and genitalia provide definitive diagnosis.
Larvae use grasses and cereals; species is not currently recognized as a North American pest.
Adults vary from light to dark brown, have a pale kidney-shaped mark and dark hindwings.
Adults fly at night and come to light; larvae feed on grasses; M. didyma requires specialist separation.

proposedDescription: Common Sheep Sorrel is a low perennial with slender stems and leaves that often resemble small arrowheads. Groups of shoots can belong to the same spreading underground system, so a patch may persist long after its original crown has died. Tiny flowers and developing fruits can give a stand a reddish-brown cast. Introduced from Eurasia, it is widespread in temperate North America in fields, pastures, roadsides, and other open places. It tolerates acidic, low-fertility soils particularly well, but its presence does not prove that soil needs lime. Existing vegetation and growing conditions strongly influence how troublesome it becomes.
identification: Common Sheep Sorrel commonly reaches about 6–18 inches tall. Leaves vary with age and position: many middle leaves have two outward-pointing lobes near the base, while young or upper leaves may lack those lobes. Slender flowering stems branch toward the top. A thin papery collar surrounds each stem joint and becomes brown and torn with age, a useful clue to the buckwheat family. The flowers are tiny, followed by very small three-sided brown fruits. Male and female flowers usually occur on separate plants. Do not identify it by tasting. Show several leaves from the same plant, the stem collars, and mature fruit; an unlobed seedling can look quite different from the familiar arrow-shaped adult foliage.
actions: For a small unwanted patch, lift the crowns and trace the shallow horizontal roots as thoroughly as practical. Common Sheep Sorrel can produce new shoots from short root fragments, so simply snapping off stems or chopping the soil once is unlikely to finish the job. Remove flowering shoots before seed matures and check repeatedly for regrowth. In lawns or pasture, use a soil test to guide any lime or fertilizer, and improve the competitiveness of the vegetation you want to keep. Do not apply lime solely because sorrel is present. Avoid moving soil containing roots into clean beds. Where the patch occupies a natural area, assess the surrounding plant community before making broad soil amendments.

sources.title: Red sorrel — Ohio perennial and biennial weed guide
Rumex acetosella — Fire Effects Information System
Forb seedling identification guide — Rumex acetosella

researchNotes: WSU Hortsense page returned 403 and was not counted. Descriptions of flower sex/color vary among sources, so draft avoids using flower color to diagnose sex. Soil-testing advice prevents unsupported inference that sorrel proves acidity.

claims: Perennial spreads through shallow horizontal roots; fragments as short as half an inch can produce shoots.
Arrow-shaped leaves vary by age and position; stems have papery sheaths at nodes.
Species tolerates acid soils but also occurs on neutral or alkaline sites; improved competition can reduce dominance.
Eurasian species is naturalized across temperate North America and occupies fields, meadows, roadsides and disturbed open sites.
Thrives in acid low-fertility soils but tolerates a range of soil types.
Slender stems arise from spreading underground growth; triangular basal leaf lobes and small flowers are characteristic.
Plants and flower clusters become reddish-brown with maturity.

proposedDescription: Common Sowthistle is an upright annual with yellow flower heads, lobed leaves, and a hollow stem that releases white sap when damaged. It often begins as a ground-level rosette before growing taller and branching near the top. The flower heads later release small fruits carried by tufts of fine white hairs. It grows in gardens, crop fields, roadsides, and other disturbed places, and can complete its life cycle in either cool or warm seasons. In mild climates, plants may be present through much of the year. Seed prevention is especially useful because established plants reproduce by seed rather than a spreading perennial root system.
identification: Mature Common Sowthistle usually stands about 1–5 feet tall. Its smooth, hollow stem bears alternate leaves, with the upper leaves clasping the stem through pointed, angular lobes. Leaves are dull green to blue-green, often deeply cut, and commonly have a broad triangular terminal lobe. Their teeth may be prickly but are softer than those of Spiny Sowthistle (Sonchus asper), whose shinier leaves have rounded, curled stem-clasping lobes and sharper marginal spines. Yellow flower heads occur in small terminal clusters and become loose white seed heads. Seedlings are harder to separate. Photograph the upper leaf base where it wraps around the stem, a lower leaf, and an open head; these are more informative than a photograph of the yellow flowers alone.
actions: Pull or hoe Common Sowthistle while plants are small and before the white seed tufts develop. A hand fork helps lift the short taproot without scattering much soil. If heads are already ripening, contain them before moving the plant and avoid carrying uncovered seed heads across the garden. Check bed edges, fences, and nearby uncultivated strips for plants that could replenish the site. Maintain mulch or desired vegetation over open ground and revisit after rain or irrigation brings another seedling flush. In vegetable gardens, remove unwanted plants near crops as part of routine weed sanitation. Distinguish this annual from perennial sowthistles before assuming that the same removal strategy will control an extensive root-spreading patch.
researchNotes: Identification and annual life cycle well corroborated. Alaska assessment's manual-control statement cites UC weed literature; treated as supporting management evidence, not fully independent experimental replication.

claims: Winter or summer annual with hollow stems, milky sap, clasping leaves and seed reproduction.
Grows in crops and disturbed sites; seed heads carry fine white hairs.
Annual sowthistle has angular leaf-base lobes and dull, deeply divided leaves; spiny sowthistle has rounded clasping lobes and sharp spines.
Mature annual sowthistles have short taproots and commonly reach one to five feet.
Manual removal before seed release is cited as effective control.
Seeds may persist in soil for multiple years.

proposedDescription: Common Speedwell is a low perennial with trailing stems, opposite leaves, and short clusters of small pale blue to violet flowers. Its stems can rise at their tips while the lower portions remain close to the ground. It occurs in fields, woodland openings, and disturbed places, with early-summer flowering documented in northern climates. Regional floras describe it as introduced in New England; broader North American origin treatments are not entirely consistent. The name “speedwell” is shared by many species, including annual lawn weeds and other perennials, so a management decision should begin with the actual plant rather than the common name alone.
identification: Common Speedwell has hairy stems with the hairs distributed around them, opposite toothed leaves, and flowering stems that trail near the base. Plants are often roughly 4–20 inches in extent or height depending on their posture. The small flowers are about 4–8 millimeters across and occur in stalked clusters arising from leaf axils, where a leaf meets the stem. They usually have four unequal lobes and two projecting stamens. Germander Speedwell (Veronica chamaedrys) has more upright flowering stems and larger flowers, about 8–13 millimeters across. Inspect the whole growth habit as well as a close flower. Include a stem segment showing leaf arrangement and hairs; a lone blue flower is not enough to distinguish the many speedwells.
actions: Decide first whether Common Speedwell is causing an actual problem in the planting or habitat. Where a small patch is unwanted, gently lift the trailing stems and roots with a hand fork, keeping nearby desired plants intact. Recheck the patch for surviving shoots and seedlings rather than treating one removal as complete. Avoid moving rooted pieces in soil or garden waste. In a lawn or managed bed, repair sparse vegetation and reduce repeated disturbance that leaves open establishment sites. If it is growing in a natural area, seek local botanical advice before broad removal because regional origin treatments and similar species complicate blanket recommendations. No species-specific eradication trial was found to justify a more aggressive household treatment.

sources.title: Common speedwell — wild blueberry weed images

researchNotes: Regional-origin discrepancy remains: New England flora says European introduction while VASCAN indexed record includes Native. This does not prevent species identification but makes a nationwide introduced/invasive claim unresolved. Maine partly cites Go Botany; independent phenology sources are identified there. Manual advice is conservative inference.

claims: Introduced in New England; opposite toothed leaves, axillary flower clusters and 4–8 mm flowers.
Trailing flowering-stem bases and smaller flowers separate it from V. chamaedrys; hairs are distributed around stems.
Perennial with opposite leaves, flowering generally in June and July in Maine.
Occurs in disturbed areas, meadows and fields; V. chamaedrys is a potential confusion.
Accepted species is presented with native regional status in the Canadian database.

proposedDescription: Common St. John's Wort is a perennial with branching stems and clusters of bright yellow flowers. Held to the light, its small leaves show translucent gland dots that can look like pinholes. It grows particularly well in open disturbed places, including pastures, roadsides, and grasslands. Introduced from Europe, western Asia, and North Africa, it can spread through seeds and underground growth. Grazing animals that consume enough may become unusually sensitive to sunlight, making pasture infestations a practical concern. The name is also used loosely for ornamental Hypericum shrubs, so yellow flowers alone do not identify this particular species.
identification: Common St. John's Wort usually grows about 1–3 feet tall, with several smooth stems that become woody near the base and branch above. Leaves are small, opposite, and stalkless. Examine a leaf against light for translucent dots, then check the five yellow petals for dark dots around their edges. The numerous stamens form a conspicuous tuft in each flower. Stems have two subtle longitudinal ridges rather than a broad, leafy wing. Common Tansy and Tansy Ragwort also carry yellow clusters, but their heads consist of many tiny flowers rather than individual five-petaled flowers. Native Hypericum species can resemble it more closely; a local flora may be needed. Include leaf glands, stem ridges, and an open flower in the record.
actions: Prioritize new patches and scattered plants beyond an established Common St. John's Wort stand. Dig or pull small plants with their crowns and lateral roots before seed develops, then revisit because remaining underground parts can regrow. Remove the material from the site rather than leaving it where shoots or seeds could survive. Repeated cutting may limit seed production but is not a dependable one-time cure. Restore suitable vegetation after removal and avoid overgrazing that leaves open soil. Keep livestock away from heavily infested forage while a local adviser assesses the situation. For large pasture or conservation-land patches, use a coordinated management plan; biological-control insects should be handled through an established local program.

sources.title: Hypericum perforatum — Fire Effects Information System

researchNotes: Species-level diagnosis includes native Hypericum limitation. No medical-use or universal legal claim. Forest Service review read in full-text sections and indexed management passage; manual guidance directly supported by state agency.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Washington State Noxious Weed Control Board
claims: Perennial has opposite gland-dotted leaves, yellow five-petaled flowers with black marginal dots, and somewhat two-edged stems.
Small infestations can be repeatedly pulled with lateral roots; removed material should not be left onsite; desirable vegetation helps prevent reinvasion.
Native to Europe, western Asia and North Africa; disturbance favors spread in many invaded habitats.
Management requires persistence and attention to vegetative spread; outlier populations merit priority.
Regional impacts and responses to biological control vary.
Transparent leaf glands, black petal-edge dots and opposite leaves are useful clues.
Toxicity may produce photosensitivity in livestock.

proposedDescription: Common St. Paul's wort is an upright annual with paired leaves and small yellow flower heads surrounded by conspicuous spreading green bracts. The bracts carry sticky gland-tipped hairs, a useful feature when the tiny flowers are hard to see. It belongs to the daisy family and is unrelated to the familiar yellow-flowered St. John's Wort. Its broad native range includes parts of Africa and Asia, with differing historical interpretations in Australia, and it has been introduced elsewhere. It often grows in disturbed ground. Site conditions and local records matter more than the word “weed” in one of its alternate names.
identification: Common St. Paul's wort often reaches roughly 1–3 feet tall, with hairy stems and opposite leaves on short stalks. Leaves range from narrow and spear-shaped to broader triangular shapes, usually with toothed edges. The yellow flower heads are only about a quarter to half an inch across. Five elongated outer bracts spread beyond each head and carry conspicuous dark, stalked glands; these are more distinctive than the yellow color alone. Small yellow outer rays surround the central florets, followed by dark, slightly angled fruits about 2–3 millimeters long. Closely related Sigesbeckia species can require a botanical key. Photograph the bracts from the side, leaf bases, and a complete flowering branch rather than relying on the outline of a single leaf.
actions: Remove a small unwanted patch of Common St. Paul's wort before its heads develop mature dark fruits. Lift young plants with their roots, minimizing disturbance to nearby vegetation. If fruit is already present, contain the heads before transporting the plants and check clothing or equipment for adhering material. Avoid dumping garden waste where surviving seed could establish. Record the location and obtain a botanical confirmation for an unfamiliar occurrence in a natural area, especially where another Sigesbeckia species may be present. Revisit the cleared patch after favorable growing weather and cover bare garden soil with suitable planting or mulch. These are practical seed-prevention measures; widespread removal needs a local assessment of actual impacts.

sources.title: Sigesbeckia orientalis — Flora of New South Wales
Sigesbeckia orientalis — Plants of the World Online

researchNotes: Species diagnosis supported by two independent botanical institutions; Kew corroborates annual life cycle. No US species-specific treatment trial found. Actions are cautious seed containment, not a proven eradication claim. Native-range debate is explicitly regional.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Royal Botanic Gardens and Domain Trust NSW
claims: Herb with opposite leaves, small yellow heads and spreading outer bracts densely covered in dark stalked glands.
Fruits are black and 2–3 mm long; Australian native status has been debated.
Opposite leaves and five spreading persistent bracts characterize the plant.
Ray and disk flowers are yellow; pappus is absent.
Accepted annual species with a native range from Africa and the Indian Ocean through Asia to Australia.
Flora of Tropical East Africa describes annual herbs 20–120 cm high.

proposedDescription: Common Tansy is a tall perennial with finely divided leaves and dense, flat-topped clusters of yellow button-like flower heads. Several stems rise from a spreading underground system, and established plants can form substantial clumps. Originally from Eurasia, it was introduced as an ornamental and herb and now occurs along roads, fields, streambanks, and other open sites. Its foliage has a strong odor when disturbed. Dense stands can displace desirable pasture plants and other vegetation. Although the plant has a long history of use, it can be toxic to livestock and should not be treated as forage or a home remedy.
identification: Common Tansy commonly grows 3–4 feet tall, sometimes taller. Its alternate leaves are divided into many narrow, toothed segments, giving them a fernlike outline. Brownish to reddish stems support numerous rounded yellow heads, each roughly a quarter to half an inch across. Unlike a daisy, each head lacks the surrounding strap-shaped ray flowers that look like petals. This separates it from Tansy Ragwort, whose yellow heads usually have a clear ring of rays. Common St. John's Wort has individual flowers with five broad petals and small opposite leaves, not finely divided alternate leaves. Flowering is typically in summer into early autumn. Include both the flower cluster and a complete leaf; persistent brown seed heads can help locate old patches.
actions: Dig or pull small Common Tansy patches when soil is moist, removing the underground stems as thoroughly as possible. Wear gloves and return regularly to remove shoots arising from missed pieces. Cutting before flowering can prevent seed production, but mowing alone will not kill the established underground system and must be repeated. Contain mature flower or seed heads before carrying plants through unaffected areas. Clean seeds and soil from equipment before moving to another site. Replant disturbed ground with suitable vegetation and monitor over multiple growing seasons. On pasture or extensive natural-area infestations, arrange local weed-management advice rather than relying on livestock to graze it down. A sustained plan is more realistic than a single clearing.
researchNotes: Two state-agency accounts agree on identification and persistent underground spread. Their local legal requirements are not generalized to other jurisdictions; hand-removal and repeated follow-up are directly supported.

claims: Eurasian perennial grows in clumps, commonly three to four feet tall, with fernlike alternate leaves and yellow button heads.
Spreads by seed and underground stems; repeated removal and monitoring are needed; pasture capacity can decline.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Washington State Noxious Weed Control Board
claims: Flower heads lack ray flowers, unlike tansy ragwort; Hypericum flowers have five petals.
Gloves, digging small patches, repeated cutting before seed, and prompt revegetation are advised; mowing alone does not kill plants.

proposedDescription: Common thrip is a minute leaf-feeding insect more widely described in specialist sources as black vine thrips or castor thrips. It feeds and breeds on many plants, including grapevines, roses, castor bean, and tropical landscape trees. Older leaves are especially important feeding sites.
