The species is associated with the Old World tropics and has been recorded in Florida, the Caribbean, and Brazil. Its tiny size makes it easy to overlook on moved plants and cuttings. Leaf injury alone cannot establish which thrips species is present, and a confirmed identification is more useful than treating every damaged leaf as the same pest.
identification: Adult Common thrip is about 1.3–1.5 millimeters long, appearing dark brown to nearly black; newly emerged individuals may be more reddish. Young stages begin pale and become yellow-orange to red. Under strong magnification, adults have a broad middle body section and unusual blister-like swellings along the forewings. These structures, together with antenna details, are important to specialist identification and cannot usually be resolved in a phone photograph. Greenhouse Thrips (Heliothrips haemorrhoidalis) and other small leaf-feeding thrips can produce confusing observations. Inspect older leaves, including their undersides, and photograph both the insects and the affected foliage. Record the host plant and whether immature stages are present. A diagnostic laboratory may need preserved specimens or infested leaves to confirm the species.
actions: Keep a newly acquired plant with suspected Common thrip separate from other susceptible plants until the insects are identified. Inspect older foliage on neighboring roses, grapevines, or tropical ornamentals rather than checking only fresh shoots and flowers. Do not distribute cuttings or move visibly infested plants to another property. Ask extension or a plant diagnostic laboratory how to submit a contained sample, including the plant's identity and the location of the feeding injury. If treatment is warranted, choose it with an adviser for that host and growing setting; an outdoor tree, greenhouse crop, and household potted plant need different approaches. Reinspect after action because surviving immature stages may be missed in an initial check.

sources.title: Thrips new to Florida — Entomology Circular 365
Retithrips syriacus — Thrips of California key

researchNotes: Catalog display name retained although specialist sources use black vine thrips/castor thrips. Halle key timed out; its indexed text was read but not needed as separate evidence. FDACS PDF extraction exposes page one only; no page-two description claimed. Containment is pathway-based advice, not a species-specific eradication trial.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services
claims: Retithrips syriacus was collected on Terminalia catappa in Florida in September 1993.
A specimen was intercepted on Jatropha cuttings destined for Florida; multiple tropical tree hosts are documented.
Dark-bodied species has an unusually broad thorax and three swellings on each forewing.
Breeds on older leaves of many hosts; Heliothrips is a related genus.
Adults are approximately 1.3–1.5 mm; larvae progress from pale to yellow-orange and red.
Foliage, especially lower leaf surfaces, can be damaged; distribution includes Florida, the Caribbean and Brazil.

proposedDescription: Common Velvetgrass is a perennial grass covered in short, soft hairs that give its leaves and stems a pale gray-green appearance. Its branching flower clusters can be silvery green, pink, or purplish, changing shape as they open and mature. It often grows in moist meadows, pasture, lawns, and disturbed ground. Introduced to North America through forage seed and related pathways, it is more widespread in coastal regions than in the continental interior. Established patches can become dense, and seed left in the soil can complicate removal. The soft texture is useful for recognition, but it should be checked alongside the flower and leaf-junction features.
identification: Common Velvetgrass often reaches 3–4 feet tall when flowering. Short white hairs cover the leaf blades, the sheaths wrapped around the stems, and the stem joints. Gently separate a blade from its sheath to see the thin membranous ligule at the junction. The flower head is a branched panicle with numerous closely packed, pointed spikelets; it can appear narrow before opening into a broader triangular shape. Pinkish color is variable and should not be used alone. Creeping Velvetgrass (Holcus mollis) is a close relative, and hybrids have been reported, so unusual plants may need a specialist. Photograph the leaf surface, stem joints, ligule, and mature flower head together. A mown patch without flowering material can be difficult to confirm.
actions: Target small outlying Common Velvetgrass clumps before tackling a large stand. Lift or hoe unwanted clumps with their crowns and roots, taking care to avoid tearing up neighboring desirable grasses. Prevent seed production where possible and contain mature heads before moving cut material. Hand removal is laborious and may reduce abundance without exhausting the soil seed bank, so inspect the area repeatedly after rain and disturbance. Clean soil and grass seed from mowers and other equipment before entering uninfested sites. Reestablish appropriate vegetation over cleared patches. In wet meadows or conservation grassland, coordinate mowing or other treatment with the land manager so that timing protects desired plants and wildlife as well as limiting this grass.

sources.title: Holcus lanatus — Fire Effects Information System

researchNotes: Forest Service review is older and used for biological and management context, not current county occurrence. Close relative and hybrid caveat retained without inventing a complete vegetative key. Manual control described as reduction, not guaranteed eradication.

claims: Grass commonly grows three to four feet tall and is densely hairy across blades, sheaths, stems and nodes.
Has a membranous ligule and branched panicles with silvery-green to pink pointed spikelets.
Introduced forage grass is widespread in coastal North America and occurs in meadows, pastures and disturbed sites.
Hybridization with H. mollis is reported; hand-pulling and hoeing can reduce abundance but require effort.
Soil seed banks can permit rapid reestablishment after disturbance, making monitoring necessary.

proposedDescription: Common viper's bugloss is a bristly plant with vivid blue flowers and conspicuous projecting pink to red stamens. It usually spends its first year as a rosette of narrow leaves, then produces upright flowering stems before dying after seed production. Originally from Europe and central Asia, it occurs along roads, in pasture, and on other dry disturbed ground. Its coarse hairs can irritate skin, and dense growth can reduce more palatable forage. Each flower can produce four small nutlets. Preventing those seeds is an important part of managing an unwanted patch, especially where wildflower seed mixtures or moved soil could introduce it.
identification: Common viper's bugloss typically reaches 1–3 feet tall above a deep taproot. Lower leaves are long and narrow, often up to about 6 inches, while stem leaves become smaller upward. Stems and leaves feel harsh because of stiff hairs. Flowers are funnel-shaped with five unequal lobes, pink in bud and usually bright blue when open. Four long stamens project prominently, with a fifth shorter one. Patterson's Curse (Echium plantagineum) has larger purple-blue flowers with only two conspicuously projecting stamens and less harsh leaves. Young rosettes are harder to identify than flowering plants. Include the stamens, side of a flower, lower leaves, and stem hairs in close photographs, while avoiding bare-skin contact with the plant.
actions: Check wildflower seed lists before sowing and avoid adding Common viper's bugloss where it could escape into pasture or natural areas. Remove small unwanted rosettes while the soil is moist, digging deeply enough to lift the crown and taproot. Wear gloves and protective sleeves because the stiff hairs can irritate skin. Revisit plants that were incompletely removed, since they can regrow. Prevent flowering plants from releasing mature nutlets, and contain seed-bearing material before transport. Clean tools and footwear after working in a seeding patch. Keep removed plants out of livestock feed. A local weed adviser can help plan larger infestations and choose an accepted disposal route for the material.

sources.title: Echium vulgare — New Zealand Plant Conservation Network

researchNotes: Washington state page says toxicity not known while King County explicitly describes pyrrolizidine alkaloid toxicity. Draft avoids a detailed medical claim and retains practical exclusion from livestock feed; toxicity wording deserves specialist consistency review. No local legal rule generalized nationally.

claims: Biennial rosette-to-flowering life cycle, deep taproot and irritating hairs characterize Echium vulgare.
Seed prevention, checking wildflower mixtures and digging small plants in moist soil are advised; incomplete removal can regrow.
Bristly narrow-leaved herb has flowers pink in bud then vivid blue, with four long projecting stamens and one shorter.
E. plantagineum has larger flowers and two projecting stamens.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Washington State Noxious Weed Control Board
claims: Taprooted upright biennial reaches one to three feet; each flower produces four one-seeded nutlets.
Reproduces by seed in roadsides, pastures and disturbed sites.

proposedDescription: Common wall lizard is a small European lizard that now lives in several introduced North American populations. Sunny stone walls, rock piles, and similar sheltered places provide basking surfaces and hiding spaces. Its brown or gray colors can blend closely with masonry, although the sides often carry conspicuous dark markings. A sighting does not by itself establish damage to local wildlife: Indiana's wildlife agency describes ecological effects there as uncertain. The useful first step is documenting where the lizards occur, especially when a population appears well away from an already known introduction.
identification: Adults are roughly 5½–8 inches long, including the tail. Look for a slender, somewhat flattened body, long toes, and a long tail, with a brown or gray back and darker spots or bands along the sides. Some individuals have a netlike pattern across the back; underside colors vary and should not be treated as a single defining mark. Introduced Italian wall lizards can be confused with this species, so a distant photograph of a brown lizard is insufficient. Photograph the back, side of the head, and entire body without catching or restraining it. Include location and approximate length, and note whether several animals or young lizards were present.
actions: Record the location, date, number seen, and photographs, then share an unexpected population with the relevant state wildlife agency or local herpetology program. Indiana specifically requests photographed sightings through its wildlife survey contact. Do not move lizards to another garden or release captive animals outdoors. Before relocating landscape materials from an occupied site, inspect crevices where animals may shelter. Avoid glue traps or broad pesticide applications: neither provides a sound identification or population-management plan. If animals repeatedly enter a building, address gaps around doors and foundations and ask a wildlife professional about humane exclusion appropriate to the site.

sources.title: Center for North American Herpetology — Podarcis muralis

researchNotes: Population reporting is supported directly; material inspection and exclusion are conservative prevention recommendations, not a validated eradication method.

claims: Adults measure about 5½–8 inches and have brown or gray backs with side markings.
Photographed sightings help document introduced populations.
Native to Europe; introduced populations occur in several North American jurisdictions.

proposedDescription: Common wheat is the familiar cereal grown for grain, but plants also appear outside cultivation when spilled or surviving seed germinates. These volunteers occur in fields, roadsides, and other disturbed ground. Domestication favored large grains and seedheads that stay together for harvesting, helping explain why a wheat head looks different from many wild grasses. An escaped plant should not automatically be described as an ecological threat. Its importance depends on the setting: unwanted wheat can interfere with another crop, while a few roadside plants may simply mark a recent source of grain.
identification: Common wheat is an annual grass, often approaching 3 feet tall, with broad, flat leaves and a dense, unbranched grain head. At the junction of blade and sheath, look for small projections that clasp the stem; these often carry hairs. Heads may have conspicuous bristles or lack them, depending on the cultivar, so bristles alone cannot identify wheat. Barley has a different arrangement of its flower units: each barley spikelet contains one flower, whereas wheat spikelets contain several. Durum wheat and wheat–rye hybrids can require closer examination. Photograph the whole plant, the leaf collar, and a mature head from both sides; seedlings or a bag of detached grain may not resolve the species.
actions: If Common wheat is unwanted in a garden, pull or hoe young plants before the heads develop mature grain. Remove ripe heads carefully so seeds are not scattered during cleanup. Look for the source of repeated volunteers, such as spilled feed, seed mixes, or grain handling, and correct that source before treating the same patch repeatedly. In a crop field, ask local Extension about volunteer-wheat management suited to the crop rotation rather than applying a garden recommendation at farm scale. Keep useful records of when plants emerge and whether they set seed; ordinary planted wheat does not need removal merely because it is introduced.
researchNotes: Manual removal is a practical recommendation based on annual seed reproduction, not a species-specific control trial.

claims: Bread wheat escapes into fields and roadsides.
Cultivated wheat has large seeds and a seedhead axis that resists shattering.
Annual about one metre tall; heads and bristles vary.
Durum differs in seedhead-axis and glume characters.
Wheat has clasping projections at leaf bases.
Wheat spikelets have multiple flowers, unlike barley.

proposedDescription: Compact brome is a small annual grass introduced from the Mediterranean region. It grows in disturbed grassy places and produces bristly seedheads that may turn reddish purple before the seed is ripe. Its name needs care: some references combine it with red brome as two subspecies, while others recognize separate species. This profile uses Compact brome for Bromus madritensis in the narrower sense. Studies about red brome alone should not be transferred automatically to this plant, particularly claims about desert fire, abundance, or effects on native vegetation.
identification: Compact brome commonly reaches about 20 inches tall and has several stems from a fibrous root system. Lower leaves can be noticeably hairy while upper portions are less hairy. The seedhead branches and flower clusters spread enough that the supporting axes remain visible. Red brome, Bromus rubens, has a more tightly packed head, although both plants can develop reddish colors. The UCLA regional treatment also reports later flowering in Compact brome, but that local timing is not a reliable nationwide test. Photograph mature heads against a plain background, the lower leaf sheaths, and the whole plant. A botanist may need measurements of individual flower parts to separate these bromes confidently.
actions: Check a suspected patch while the heads are developing, before ripe bristly seeds can be carried on clothing or equipment. For a small confirmed patch, pull plants with their roots when the soil is workable and contain any developed seedheads. Clean footwear and tools before moving to an uninfested area. Revisit the patch after subsequent rains because removing visible annual plants does not remove seeds already in the soil. Retain or restore appropriate ground cover where repeated disturbance favors germination. For larger infestations, ask a local weed specialist to distinguish Compact brome from red brome before selecting a treatment or interpreting fire-risk advice.

sources.title: US Forest Service FEIS — Compact brome and red brome
Prigge and Gibson — Bromus madritensis subsp. madritensis

researchNotes: Uses the narrow Compact brome concept; no red-brome-only impact claims. Manual recommendations follow annual seed reproduction.

claims: Authorities differ in whether compact and red brome are species or subspecies.
The review distinguishes the two entities where the literature permits.
Plants reach about 50 cm in the regional flora.
Compact brome has more spreading spikelets on longer branches than red brome.

proposedDescription: Comstock mealybug is a sap-feeding insect that gathers on leaves, stems, bark, and fruit. Its white wax covering can make a colony look like small bits of cotton caught on a plant. Feeding can contribute to fruit drop, while the sticky honeydew it produces supports dark sooty mold. Ants attracted to that honeydew can provide a useful clue when the insects themselves are hidden. Fruit trees and ornamental plants deserve close inspection, but a white insect colony is not enough to name the species: several mealybugs and scale insects look similar.
identification: Adult females are small, oval insects covered in white wax, with short wax threads around the sides and longer threads at the rear. UC IPM describes the rear pair as about one-quarter of the body length and the wax covering as thicker than in citrus mealybug. Longtailed mealybug instead has tail threads longer than its body. Newly hatched young, called crawlers, have little wax and can be yellowish, orange, or pink. Inspect sheltered places around fruit stems, leaf joints, and bark crevices. Photograph an individual sharply enough to show its rear threads and record the host plant. Worn wax, immature insects, and crowded colonies can obscure identification, so a diagnostic laboratory may need specimens.
actions: Inspect new plants and keep suspect stock separate while identification is arranged. On established plants, follow ant trails and examine tender shoots and fruit stems for living insects rather than judging infestation from old mold alone. Remove heavily infested small plant parts when practical and collect orchard litter that can shelter overwintering stages. Preserve lady beetles and other natural enemies; indiscriminate insecticide use can work against them. For a persistent infestation, send close photographs and host information to Extension and ask about treatment timed to crawlers. Monitor the plant afterward, because hidden mealybugs and eggs can remain even when exposed colonies have been removed.

sources.title: Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada — Pear crop profile

researchNotes: Host-specific treatment should be confirmed locally. No pesticide product or application rate proposed.

claims: Comstock mealybug has a thick wax covering and short rear wax threads.
Crawlers initially lack wax.
Longtailed mealybugs have rear threads longer than the body; other wax-producing pests can look similar.
Comstock mealybugs produce honeydew and can cause fruit drop.
Shoot inspection, ant activity, and orchard sanitation support monitoring and management.

proposedDescription: Confederate jasmine is an evergreen woody vine known for glossy leaves and strongly scented white flowers. Despite its common name, it belongs to the dogbane family rather than the true jasmine genus. Twining stems can climb a support or spread across the ground, which explains its use on fences, trellises, and garden banks. Established plants tolerate periods of dry weather. Where it grows beyond a planting, evaluate the actual spread and nearby vegetation rather than assuming every cultivated vine is harmful. Its ability to root from stems makes garden cleanup important when containment is needed.
identification: A supported vine can reach about 20 feet, although clipped or ground-cover plants are much shorter. Leaves occur in opposite pairs and are simple, glossy, leathery, and smooth-edged. New foliage may be bronze or purplish. The small white flowers have five slightly twisted, overlapping lobes that give a pinwheel appearance, usually appearing most abundantly in late spring. Broken stems release milky sap; do not deliberately expose skin to it as an identification test. True jasmines can also have scented white flowers, so combine flower shape with leaf arrangement and stem characters. Photograph a flowering shoot, a pair of leaves, and the climbing habit; the similar Asian jasmine (Trachelospermum asiaticum) needs closer examination. HortFlora distinguishes it by a hairless flower throat, unlike the finely hairy throat of Confederate jasmine.
actions: Keep planted Confederate jasmine within its intended area by checking trailing stems and pruning after the main flowering period. Remove stems that have rooted beyond the bed, including the rooted portions rather than only cutting the connecting vine. Collect cuttings instead of leaving them on moist soil or dumping them along a woodland edge. Wear gloves and clean sticky sap from tools after pruning. If an escaped patch is covering valued plants, trace its stems to the base before removal so neighboring vegetation is not torn out with it. Recheck the area for rooted pieces and new shoots, and use a locally suitable replacement where repeated escape makes maintenance impractical.

sources.title: JC Raulston Arboretum — Trachelospermum jasminoides collections
Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria HortFlora — Trachelospermum jasminoides

researchNotes: NC State Extension and its arboretum share one institutional group. Independent HortFlora treatment corroborates flower and leaf features and supplies the T. asiaticum comparison; substantive indexed text read after direct fetch timed out. Removal advice conservatively follows documented layering and cutting propagation.

claims: Evergreen twining vine with opposite glossy leaves, white pinwheel flowers, and milky sap.
Can reach 20 feet; propagate by layering or cuttings; prune after flowering.
Collection records describe woody evergreen vines native to Asia.
Glossy leaves are pale beneath; fragrant white flowers are about 2–2.5 cm across.
Related T. asiaticum lacks the small hairs in the flower throat described for T. jasminoides.

proposedDescription: Conifer needle scale is an armored scale insect that feeds on conifer needles and twigs. The insect lives beneath a small protective cover, so an infestation may first look like scattered gray bumps rather than moving insects. Heavy feeding can lead to early needle loss and drying branches. Infested cut trees and ornamental greenery can transport it: Minnesota inspectors documented this species on Christmas trees in 2023. That finding illustrates a pathway, not a nationwide instruction to destroy conifers. Identification matters because several different scales occur on these hosts.
identification: Female covers are approximately 1.8–2.1 millimeters long, slightly oval and raised, with gray margins and a central light-brown or yellowish remnant of the insect's earlier skin. Male covers are smaller, more elongated, and paler. Look along needles and twigs with a hand lens and photograph the cover beside a millimeter scale. Include the conifer's name and pictures of affected branches. Elongate hemlock scale and other conifer-feeding armored scales can be mistaken for this species; host and needle damage alone will not separate them. Reliable confirmation may require an adult female removed from its cover and examined on a microscope slide, as nursery inspectors use specialist identification.
actions: Keep suspect nursery stock or holiday greenery separate from living conifers until the insect is identified. Do not carry infested branches to another property or leave them beneath outdoor host trees. Contact Extension or the state plant-health office with clear photographs and the source of the material, especially for recently purchased stock. Ask that office how to contain and dispose of confirmed infested greenery locally; an enforcement action in another state is not automatically the right instruction for your site. For a living landscape tree, have the infestation and tree condition assessed before pruning extensively or choosing a treatment timed to vulnerable young scales.

sources.title: Minnesota Department of Agriculture — 2023 Nursery Certification Report

researchNotes: Specific identification characters and interception evidence read in indexed source excerpts; no species-specific home treatment protocol established. Follow-up audit: ScaleNet supplies literature-based biology; Minnesota supplies a separate inspection and diagnostic event. These are independent for their respective claims.

claims: Female covers are gray, oval, and 1.8–2.1 mm long; microscopic adult characters diagnose the species.
Female and male covers differ in size and shape; conifer needle and twig injury is documented.
Feeding injures conifer needles and twigs.
Christmas-tree interceptions were confirmed by USDA specialists in 2023.
The 2023 Fraser fir interception received USDA confirmation and an agency response.

proposedDescription: Cooper's cyathea is an Australian tree fern with a single trunk topped by very large, finely divided fronds. Often sold as Australian tree fern, it can become a substantial plant rather than remaining a compact garden fern. It reproduces through spores, which are much smaller than seeds and can travel on the wind. In Hawaii, escaped plants compete with native forest vegetation, including native tree ferns. That documented impact should be distinguished from an assumption of equal harm everywhere it is planted. Escapes near moist natural areas deserve particular attention.
identification: Mature Cooper's cyathea can reach about 40 feet, with triangular fronds reported up to 20 feet long under favorable conditions. The trunk shows oval scars where old leaf stalks have fallen away, and the stalks bear pale or whitish hairs and scales. Hawaii's native hapuu tree ferns have reddish hairs and a thick fibrous covering around the trunk, providing useful local comparisons. Height alone is unreliable because young tree ferns have not developed their mature trunks. Photograph the entire plant, the trunk surface, a close view of the stalk covering, and the undersides of mature fronds. Identification outside Hawaii should use the locally present tree-fern species rather than assuming the hapuu comparison covers every lookalike.
actions: Check around an established planting for small ferns emerging beyond the garden, particularly in damp shaded ground. Have volunteers identified before removal so native ferns are not mistaken for this species. Avoid planting additional Cooper's cyathea beside vulnerable moist forest where local invasive-plant guidance advises against it. Small confirmed volunteers may be removed carefully with their growing base; a tall trunk needs an appropriate professional removal plan. Contain fronds and soil during cleanup and do not dump them in natural areas. Where a local program requests reports, send location and diagnostic photographs first; Hawaii specifically asks for reports of this fern on Molokai.

sources.title: Hawaii Invasive Species Council — Australian Tree Fern
Botanic Gardens of South Australia — Cyathea cooperi

researchNotes: Hawaii impact and native-lookalike comparison remain explicitly regional. Manual volunteer removal is an editorial practical inference, not a control-trial result. Follow-up audit: Hawaii invasive-species council and South Australian government botanic-garden accounts are separate institutional sources. The smaller garden height does not contradict a stated maximum.

claims: Tall tree fern has pale stalk hairs and oval trunk scars.
Windborne spores and competition with native ferns are documented in Hawaii.
White hairs and absence of the native hapuu's fibrous trunk covering distinguish the introduced fern; spores disperse by wind.
Australian evergreen tree fern grows rapidly and favors adequate moisture.
Australian tree fern is a fast-growing fern of moist sheltered conditions; garden dimensions are 5–6 m tall.

proposedDescription: Cootamundra wattle is a small Australian tree or large shrub grown for its gray-blue foliage and masses of yellow flowers. The leaves are divided twice into many narrow leaflets, giving them a fernlike outline. Escaped plants can grow in woodland, scrub, and disturbed ground. Seeds can persist in soil and germinate after heat or disturbance, so removing a mature plant may not end an infestation. Its ornamental origin helps explain many occurrences outside its native range; management should focus on places where it is reproducing beyond plantings or affecting valued habitat.
identification: Plants can reach about 33 feet tall and have smooth bark, finely divided gray to bluish leaves, and round golden flower heads borne in clusters. Young pods may have a bluish color. Some garden forms have purple foliage, so leaf color is not fixed. The lowest pair of main leaf divisions is shorter and can turn back around the stem, a useful detail to photograph. Silver wattle, Acacia dealbata, and other feathery-leaved wattles can look similar, and this species can hybridize with related wattles. Include close photographs of a whole leaf, its attachment to the twig, flower clusters, and pods. A broad canopy photograph alone generally cannot establish the species or exclude a hybrid.
actions: Remove small unwanted seedlings while roots can still be lifted without major soil disturbance, preferably before they produce flowers and pods. Collect seed-bearing branches and pods instead of moving them to another garden or dumping them along a roadside. Recheck around the parent tree and disturbed soil for new seedlings, including after hot conditions or fire. Large plants require a site-specific removal plan, especially near structures or native vegetation. Do not use fire as a casual control method: heat can stimulate seeds already in the soil. Replace escaping plantings with a locally suitable species and keep follow-up records, because the persistent seed supply can outlast the first cleanup.

sources.title: Australian National Botanic Gardens — Acacia baileyana
California Invasive Plant Council — Acacia baileyana
Plants of South Eastern NSW — Acacia baileyana

researchNotes: No herbicide or cut-stump prescription supplied; long-term seedling follow-up follows documented persistent seed behavior.

claims: Small tree to 10 m; gray divided leaves, golden flower balls, and bluish young pods.
Persistent seeds germinate after fire, heat, or disturbance.
Garden waste is one dispersal pathway.
Lower leaf divisions can embrace the stem; hybridization with related wattles complicates identification.

proposedDescription: This Copepod, Cyclops strenuus, is a freshwater crustacean requiring microscopic identification. Its reported North American distribution is difficult to interpret because several similar species have been confused. USGS explains that some Great Lakes specimens previously called Cyclops strenuus were later identified as Cyclops sibiricus, while other recent material proved to be Cyclops divergens. Earlier research also questioned whether some northern records belonged to Cyclops canadensis. These are consequential identification changes: records, native status, and impacts assigned to one species cannot simply be carried over to another.
identification: An unaided view of a tiny swimming copepod cannot establish Cyclops strenuus. Specialists examine adult body proportions and detailed structures of the antennae, swimming legs, and tail branches under a microscope. USGS describes the genus Cyclops as having 17-segmented first antennae and a particular two-segmented fifth leg, but those genus characters do not settle this species. Cyclops sibiricus, Cyclops divergens, and Cyclops canadensis are especially important names in the history of North American identifications. Preserve the collection date, waterbody, sampling method, and original identification with any specimen. A modern taxonomic key and review of archived material are needed; no single size range or photograph-based species distinction is asserted here.
actions: Treat a suspected record as a request for expert identification, not a reason to treat a pond or lake. Contact a freshwater invertebrate specialist, state aquatic-invasive-species program, or university laboratory and ask what specimen preservation and collection documentation they require. Do not move live samples or aquarium water into another waterbody. Clean and dry sampling equipment between sites as a general precaution against moving aquatic organisms. If the record came from an older dataset, retain its original name and evidence while flagging it for taxonomic reassessment. A change to the accepted identification should be documented explicitly rather than silently replacing the species name.

sources.title: USGS Great Lakes Copepods — What's New
Einsle 1988 — Cyclops canadensis and C. scutifer
USGS Great Lakes Copepods — Cyclops sibiricus identification

researchNotes: RESEARCH GAP: reconcile the exact US-RIIS occurrence and authority with modern Cyclops taxonomy; no verified species-specific size, US impact, or management supplied.

claims: Archived and recent Great Lakes material formerly called C. strenuus was reassigned to C. sibiricus and C. divergens.
Earlier North American C. strenuus records were considered potentially referable to C. canadensis.
Genus identification uses antenna and fifth-leg structures; Great Lakes records have undergone repeated reassessment.

proposedDescription: This Copepod, Harpacticella paradoxa, is a minute freshwater crustacean that mainly crawls on surfaces or lives among bottom sediments. It is known from Asian freshwater habitats and has been recorded in western North American reservoirs and estuaries. Smithsonian researchers consider the timing and separated distribution of those records evidence of introduction. Unlike larger conspicuous invaders, this animal is found through specialist sampling. The Smithsonian account reports no demonstrated ecological or economic effects, so its presence should not be presented as proof that a particular waterbody has been damaged.
identification: The body is slightly flattened and boat-shaped, narrowing toward a rear section that may bend beneath it. Adult females have short first antennae with seven segments, and the tail branches are roughly as broad as they are long. These are microscopic characters, not features a phone photograph of pond water will normally capture. Smithsonian lists the marine and estuarine Harpacticus pacificus and Harpacticus uniremis as possible confusions. Young stages need particular care because adult diagnostic features are not fully developed. Provide a calibrated microscope image, the complete specimen, sampling location, and whether it came from sediment or open water. Adult females are about 0.8 millimeters long and males about 0.7 millimeters.
actions: Do not attempt to remove this copepod by draining, chemically treating, or disturbing a waterbody on the basis of an unconfirmed observation. A useful contribution is a well-documented sample reviewed by an aquatic invertebrate specialist. Ask the receiving laboratory for its collection and preservation instructions before collecting or shipping material. Keep water and sediment from the sampling site out of other waterways, and clean and dry nets, boots, and containers between sites. Reports should distinguish a newly confirmed occurrence from a claim of ecological damage. There is no species-specific homeowner eradication method supported by the sources reviewed here.

sources.title: Ishida 1987 — Freshwater Harpacticoid Copepods of Hokkaido, Northern Japan

researchNotes: Smithsonian full text verifies adult sizes and diagnostic structures. Ishida's original 1987 field study independently records two females from a Hokkaido forest stream in July 1983 and illustrates Japanese material. North American introduction remains probable, and no local ecological damage or selective homeowner treatment is established.

claims: Bottom-associated freshwater copepod probably introduced in western North America; no reported impacts.
Adult shape, seven-segmented first antennae, and tail structures assist microscopic diagnosis.
Adult females are approximately 0.8 mm and males 0.7 mm; Smithsonian regards North American introduction as probable.
Harpacticella paradoxa is listed as a valid species.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Ishida Hokkaido Salmon Hatchery primary field study
claims: Two females were collected in a small Hokkaido forest stream in July 1983.
The study illustrates male and female material collected in Nikko, Honshu.

proposedDescription: This Copepod, Limnoithona tetraspina, is a tiny crustacean that drifts in estuarine water and feeds on microscopic organisms. First recorded in the San Francisco Estuary in 1993, it quickly became abundant in the low-salinity zone and largely replaced another introduced species, Limnoithona sinensis. Its small size matters to food-web research because a community dominated by tiny prey differs from one containing larger copepods. Researchers continue to examine those consequences. A dense population is evidence of establishment, but it should not be used alone to explain changes in fish populations.
identification: Adults are around half a millimeter long; females measured in the original California introduction report were 0.44–0.54 millimeters. The body has a broad front section and a narrower, segmented rear, with small appendages that must be examined under magnification. Limnoithona sinensis is a close lookalike. A taxonomic diagnosis uses the fifth pair of legs, including four spines or bristles on the free outer segment, rather than body color or swimming behavior. Early developmental stages are harder to assign. A useful record includes a calibrated microscope image, an adult specimen, collection date, location, and salinity if available. Ordinary photographs of water cannot confirm this species or distinguish it from other minute copepods.
actions: An apparent new occurrence should go to an estuarine plankton specialist or the state aquatic-invasive-species program for confirmation. Ask for instructions before collecting and preserving a sample; the net mesh and life stage affect what can be identified. Do not release live samples into a different creek, bay, pond, or aquarium outlet. Clean and dry sampling gear between sites and dispose of retained water away from connected waterways according to local guidance. For vessel operators, ballast-water management is the relevant prevention pathway. Removing these animals individually or adding chemicals to a waterbody is not a realistic landowner response to an established plankton population.

sources.title: Orsi and Ohtsuka 1999 — Asian copepod introductions

researchNotes: Agency and research sources support microscopic identification and estuarine ecology. Prevention advice addresses movement of untreated water and wet equipment; no selective household control or universal ecological-harm claim is made.

claims: Established in estuaries and replaced L. sinensis in San Francisco Bay.
Effects on larval-fish feeding remain a research question.
California females measured 0.44–0.54 mm; first recorded in 1993; ballast water was the likely pathway.
The fifth leg has four spines or bristles on its free outer segment.

proposedDescription: This Copepod, Mesocyclops pehpeiensis, is a small freshwater crustacean native to Asia. Introduced populations have been found in rice fields, ponds, and facilities growing aquatic plants. It has also been studied and moved for mosquito-control experiments, which should not be taken as encouragement for private releases. Older records may use Mesocyclops ruttneri, a name later placed in synonymy with this species. The connection with transported aquatic plants is especially useful for prevention: water accompanying an ornamental plant can carry organisms that are almost invisible during a casual inspection. Laboratory experiments show it suppresses populations of small freshwater prey, but these results do not measure damage in a particular lake.
identification: Adult females in the material summarized by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service measured about 1.21–1.52 millimeters; males were about 0.74–0.88 millimeters. These are adult measurements, not sizes for every immature stage. Mesocyclops edax and Mesocyclops americanus can look similar. Unlike M. edax, M. pehpeiensis lacks hairs along the inner tail branches and lacks an inward-pointing spine on the base of the first swimming leg. The plate joining the fourth pair of legs has long spine-shaped projections; M. americanus has much smaller pointed projections there. These features require a microscope and sometimes dissection. Supply intact adult specimens, calibrated images, collection date and waterbody, and details of any association with purchased aquatic plants.
actions: Keep water from purchased aquatic plants and aquarium cultures out of natural waterways. Do not transfer this copepod between ponds as a home mosquito-control experiment; choose locally recommended mosquito prevention instead. If a suspect population is associated with newly received aquatic stock, keep the stock contained and contact Extension or an aquatic-invertebrate laboratory before distributing plants. Clean and dry nets, buckets, and other equipment between waterbodies. For a reported new wild occurrence, preserve location and sampling details and obtain an expert identification. Avoid treating a whole pond for an unconfirmed identification; other small freshwater animals could be affected too.

sources.title: Connolly et al. 2019 — Asian cyclopoid copepod Mesocyclops pehpeiensis in western Lake Erie
Hwang, Kumar and Ku 2009 — Impacts of Mesocyclops pehpeiensis predation on four cladoceran species

researchNotes: USGS NAS and USFWS summaries overlap underlying references; they are not counted as two independent biological studies. Added the original Lake Erie identification study (substantive indexed text; direct PMC fetch challenged) and Hwang et al.'s laboratory experiment (abstract read). Laboratory predation is not represented as measured ecosystem damage.

claims: US records include rice fields, ponds, and aquatic gardens.
Diagnosis relies on microscopic structures.
Adult female and male size ranges differ.
Older M. ruttneri records refer to this taxon; imported plants and mosquito-control experiments feature in introduction history.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Connolly and collaborators original Lake Erie taxonomic study
claims: Native M. edax and M. americanus are lookalikes.
Tail hairs, a spine on the first leg base, and projections on the fourth-leg connecting plate distinguish these species.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Hwang and collaborators independent laboratory experiment
claims: In laboratory experiments the copepod suppressed population growth of all four tested cladoceran prey species.
Responses varied among prey species and experimental conditions.

proposedDescription: This Copepod, Nitokra hibernica, is a tiny crustacean associated with bottom surfaces and aquatic vegetation. Native to Eurasia, it tolerates both fresh and brackish water and has been recorded in the Great Lakes region. Its lifestyle makes nearshore plant beds and sediment samples more informative than a casual look at open water. This is a microscopic identification problem, not an animal most visitors will notice from shore. Older records may use the spelling Nitocra hibernica. Researchers have recovered this species from ballast water carried by ships within the Great Lakes, showing a route for transport between waterbodies.
identification: Females measure about 0.5–0.75 millimeters and males about 0.5–0.6 millimeters. Under a microscope, specialists look for a narrow forward projection on the head and tail branches approximately twice as long as wide. Other useful characters include a small rear plate edged with about ten teeth and the arrangement of spines on the swimming legs. Those characters cannot reliably be judged from a blurry image of a moving speck. Nitokra incerta is a documented lookalike; specialists compare the fifth legs and other microscopic structures. Size and habitat alone are insufficient. Submit an intact adult specimen or calibrated microscope images with the date, waterbody, and sampled substrate; juveniles may remain unidentified at species level.
actions: Focus on preventing transport with water, aquatic plants, and wet equipment rather than trying to remove individual animals from a lake. Clean and dry sampling nets, waders, buckets, and similar gear before taking them to another site. Keep collected sediment and water at the source or follow the receiving laboratory's disposal instructions; never empty a live sample into a different waterbody. If identification would extend the known range, ask a state aquatic-invasive-species program or specialist to review the specimen and its collection record. Do not apply pond chemicals on the strength of a suspected identification. The reviewed management synthesis offers no established physical removal method for this species.

sources.title: USGS and NOAA GLANSIS — Nitokra hibernica
NOAA — Management of established Great Lakes nonindigenous species
Briski, Wiley and Bailey 2012 — Role of domestic shipping in introduction or secondary spread
Bolduc et al. 2026 — Taxonomy and Functional Traits Modulate the Environmental Niche Dimensions of Crustacean Zooplankton Communities in Submerged Aquatic Vegetation Beds

researchNotes: USGS and NOAA overlap and are grouped as one synthesis. Original ballast sampling by Briski et al. (2012) documents the species aboard domestic vessels; substantive indexed table read after publisher fetch failed. Independent Bolduc et al. (2026) vegetation-bed sampling also includes N. hibernica. Neither study establishes a selective homeowner treatment. Follow-up audit: USGS and NOAA remain one synthesis group. The Briski and Bolduc study excerpts were not independently reread in this bounded audit; no upgrade is asserted for them.

claims: Adults are less than 0.8 mm; diagnosis uses tail, anal plate, and leg characters.
The species occupies bottom habitats in fresh and brackish water.
The species account reports no known physical control methods.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Briski and collaborators original ballast-water sampling
claims: Nitokra hibernica occurred in one of 72 sampled domestic ballast-water samples in the Great Lakes.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Bolduc and collaborators independent Lake Saint-Pierre field study
claims: The study sampled submerged vegetation beds in Lake Saint-Pierre during 2012–2014.
Nitokra hibernica was included in the sampled community and species-level analyses.
Adult measurements and microscopic characters agree with the draft; Nitocra is described as a frequent misspelling.
N. incerta can be confused with N. hibernica; fifth-leg morphology helps specialists distinguish variable individuals.

proposedDescription: This Copepod, Oithona davisae, is a small estuarine crustacean thought to originate in East Asia. It was formally described from introduced California material, a reminder that the place where a species receives its scientific name is not necessarily its native home. Ballast water can move it between ports. It feeds on microscopic food and can become very abundant, but the Smithsonian account separates possible food-web effects from demonstrated species-specific impacts. Small size and similar-looking relatives have complicated both historical records and efforts to determine its full distribution.
identification: Adult females are about 0.54–0.62 millimeters long, with males approximately 0.47–0.53 millimeters. Under magnification, females have a downward-pointing projection at the front of the head and may carry two egg masses. The slender rear body and tail bristles are useful structures to photograph, but are not unique by themselves. Specialists examine antenna segments, tail proportions, and small leg structures to distinguish Oithona davisae from Oithona brevicornis, Oithona nana, and other relatives. Males differ in head shape and antenna structure, so a female-only key cannot simply be applied to them. Provide adult specimens, calibrated microscope images, location, date, and salinity if measured; young stages require additional caution.
actions: Report a suspected new population through the relevant marine-invasive-species or plankton-monitoring program and obtain a specialist identification. Keep live samples contained, and do not discard them into a different bay, pond, or drain connected to surface water. Clean and dry sampling gear between sites. For commercial vessels, preventing transport in ballast water is the practical intervention; follow the applicable vessel-management process rather than improvising treatment. A shoreline landowner cannot selectively eradicate established microscopic plankton by hand. Avoid adding chemicals to estuarine water or treating all small crustaceans as this species, because native copepods occupy the same habitats and are important parts of aquatic food webs.

sources.title: Washington Invasive Species Council — Invasive Zooplankton

researchNotes: Uses Smithsonian's explicit uncertainty instead of attributing combined zooplankton impact statements specifically to O. davisae.

claims: Adults are around half a millimeter and require microscopic diagnosis.
Ballast transport is documented; species-specific food-web effects are uncertain.
O. davisae is an East Asian copepod present in regional waters.
Ballast-water prevention is the principal management focus.

proposedDescription: This Copepod, Tortanus dextrilobatus, is a small predatory crustacean native to Asian coastal waters. It eats smaller copepods rather than relying only on microscopic plants. Introduced populations were discovered in the San Francisco Estuary in 1993, and transport in ships' ballast water is considered the likely pathway. Its predation can change the numbers of other plankton, although the full consequences for the food web require further study. This is an animal identified through plankton sampling and microscopy, so an unaided observation from the shore is unlikely to establish its presence.
identification: Adults are roughly 1.5–2.3 millimeters long in the populations summarized by Smithsonian, with measured ranges differing among locations and studies. The feeding limbs are conspicuously clawlike under a microscope. Both sexes have an unevenly shaped rear body, and the right tail branch is slightly longer than the left. Females have distinctive right-side projections on rear body segments; males have modified antennae and an uneven fifth pair of legs. Tortanus discaudatus is a related comparison, but immature stages cannot be confidently assigned using an adult description alone. Photograph the whole adult and rear body at known magnification, preserve the specimen as directed by a specialist, and record the sampling site and salinity.
actions: A suspected occurrence outside an already documented estuary should be reviewed by a marine plankton specialist or state invasive-species program. Preserve the sampling record and ask for suitable specimen-handling instructions before shipping material. Prevent movement of live samples, retained water, and wet gear between estuaries; clean and dry equipment after sampling. Vessel operators should address the ballast-water pathway through their established compliance and treatment procedures. Do not attempt a chemical treatment of a bay or pond from an uncertain microscope identification. Monitoring abundance and distribution is a useful response, while claims about effects on fish should be tied to research rather than inferred solely from the copepod's presence.

sources.title: Orsi and Ohtsuka 1999 — Asian copepod introductions

researchNotes: Adult size expressed broadly to accommodate published population differences. Original paper and later synthesis share some evidence; no claim that a sighting proves fish-population harm.

claims: Predatory Asian coastal copepod established in San Francisco Bay.
Adults have asymmetric rear body structures and clawlike feeding appendages.
First California collection was in 1993; ballast water is the likely introduction pathway.
Measured adult sizes vary among populations.

proposedDescription: Coppery mesemb is a trailing South African succulent that can form a low, dense mat. Fleshy leaves store water, and bright flowers stand above the spreading stems. It has escaped ornamental plantings in California and other regions with suitable climates. Stems can root where they touch the ground, while seeds provide another means of spread. Water helps disperse the seeds. These traits make discarded garden pieces and runoff worth watching around an escaped patch. Its presence outside its native range does not by itself establish the same level of harm at every planted site.
identification: Plants generally form mats under about 14 inches tall, with stems that become woody as they age. The smooth, pale blue-green leaves occur in opposite pairs and are fingerlike, with a rounded triangular cross section and blunt tips. Flowers are commonly about 1–2 inches across, with many narrow petals; their upper surfaces may be orange, red, or yellow while the undersides are pinkish purple. Hottentot fig, Carpobrotus edulis, has more sharply triangular leaves and usually larger flowers, about 6–10 centimeters across. Flower color alone is insufficient. Photograph a flowering stem from above and below, a leaf pair, and a ripe capsule if available. A regional flora may be needed to distinguish related cultivated ice plants, especially nonflowering material.
actions: For a small escaped patch, lift the mat carefully and collect rooted stem joints as well as loose pieces. Avoid dragging fragments through adjacent vegetation or leaving them on moist bare soil. Contain seed-bearing material and dispose of it through an appropriate local green-waste route instead of dumping it on dunes, bluffs, or streambanks. Check the cleared area after rain for rooted pieces and seedlings. On slopes or among native plants, work in sections and arrange suitable replacement cover so removal does not expose an entire bank at once. Repeated garden escape is a reason to replace the planting rather than keep trimming the same advancing edge.

sources.title: Prigge and Gibson: Aizoaceae identification key

researchNotes: Manual containment advice follows documented rooting and seed dispersal; no specific eradication trial found. Follow-up audit: NSW flora and Cal-IPC are separate sources. The new family key and existing UCLA-authored species treatment share Prigge/Gibson authorship and must remain one group.

claims: Spreads by seed and rooting stem joints; water disperses seed.
Stem nodes root; seeds disperse in water.
Low mat-forming succulent has opposite blunt leaves and often differently colored petal surfaces.
Other ice plants may resemble it.
Mat height below 35 cm and flowers 30–50 mm support the rounded imperial measurements.
A South African perennial with woody older stems, opposite succulent leaves, and capsules.
Leaves are opposite, succulent and triangular in section; older stems become woody.
Malephora has bluntly three-sided leaves, while Carpobrotus has sharper angles; C. edulis flowers are 60–100 mm across.

proposedDescription: Coral vine is a perennial climber with heart-shaped leaves and long clusters of pink flowers. Tendrils let it grip fences and neighboring plants, and vigorous growth can cover vegetation at disturbed sites and forest edges. Below ground, enlarged roots store reserves that allow the vine to return after cutting or frost damage. It also produces seeds that can travel in water. Those two routes of persistence explain why cutting away the visible growth is often only a first step. In warm places where it escapes, preventing seed production and following regrowth are central to containment.
identification: Coral vine can climb 25 feet or more, although seasonal growth and cold damage affect its size. Leaves are alternate, simple, and usually heart-shaped to triangular, with long-pointed tips. Curling tendrils and clusters of many small pink flowers are useful visible features; white-flowered forms also occur. The flowers can continue over a long warm season, and dry flower parts remain around the small fruits. A heart-shaped leaf alone could belong to many unrelated vines, so photograph the tendrils, a flowering cluster, leaf attachments, and the base of the plant. Related ornamentals sold under names such as queen's wreath can create common-name confusion; confirmation should retain the scientific name Antigonon leptopus.
actions: Remove small plants before they produce mature seeds, collecting any developing fruits during the work. Trace cut stems back to the root crown and remove the enlarged underground roots when feasible; these are reserves from which new shoots can grow. Where digging would damage surrounding plants or soil, repeated cutting can weaken the vine but requires several visits. Keep cut material and seeds out of waterways and do not move them to new planting sites. Recheck after frost or an apparently successful cleanup. For a large infestation covering trees, seek a local invasive-plant specialist's plan and work carefully around the plants being rescued rather than pulling the whole canopy down.

sources.title: UF IFAS — Antigonon leptopus plant directory

researchNotes: Explains enlarged roots in plain language. No pesticide recipe; direct manual-control guidance from UF IFAS. Follow-up audit: UF and Missouri Botanical Garden are separate sources. The latter timed out when opened; its substantive indexed text was read and must remain indexed_excerpt.

claims: Tendril-climbing vine spreads by floating seeds and regrows from enlarged underground roots.
Repeated cutting and root removal require follow-up.
Floating seeds and underground reserves aid persistence; remove before seed production and revisit repeated cutting.
Heart- or arrow-shaped leaves, pink to white blooms, and tuberous roots characterize this tropical vine.
Flowers are pink to white; size and persistence vary with climate.

proposedDescription: Coralbush is a tropical ornamental shrub with deeply cut leaves and clusters of bright coral-red flowers. The narrow leaf divisions give the foliage a distinctive open outline, while the flowers stand on long stalks above it. It belongs to the spurge family and produces sap when damaged. Plants and seeds should not be eaten, and sap can irritate skin. Reports of cultivation or escape outside its native tropical American range do not establish severe ecological effects everywhere. A useful local assessment asks whether seedlings are appearing beyond the garden and spreading into surrounding vegetation.
identification: Coralbush is usually a shrub around 6–10 feet tall, though floras report larger plants under favorable conditions. Leaves are carried on long stalks and divided almost to the base into roughly 9–11 narrow, pointed lobes; individual lobes may themselves be cut or toothed. Small red flowers form relatively flat clusters at the ends of long stalks. Yellowish, three-angled fruit contains seeds. Other Jatropha species also have red flowers or lobed leaves, so the depth and pattern of leaf division are more informative than flower color alone. Photograph a complete leaf, its stalk attachment, the flower cluster, and fruit without opening it by hand. Do not taste any plant part to help identify it.
actions: Inspect beneath and beyond a planted Coralbush for unwanted seedlings and remove small confirmed volunteers before they develop fruit. Wear gloves when pruning or uprooting, avoid contact with sap, and keep collected fruit and seeds away from children and animals. Do not place cuttings or seed-bearing waste along roadsides or natural-area edges. If the plant repeatedly escapes, replace it with a suitable local alternative and revisit the old site for volunteers. Ask Extension to confirm uncertain plants before extensive removal, especially when only seedlings are present. Management should respond to documented spread at the site; an ornamental shrub's introduced origin alone is not evidence that all established specimens need removal.

proposedDescription: Cordgrass here refers specifically to Spartina × townsendii, the sterile hybrid between smooth cordgrass and small cordgrass. It is not the same taxon as the fertile species Spartina anglica that arose through chromosome doubling. That distinction is important because older literature sometimes combined the two, making invasion histories easy to misread. Both are salt-marsh grasses with spreading underground stems. A confirmed identification therefore requires more than recognizing a tall cordgrass patch. Records that lack evidence for the hybrid's identity should remain provisional rather than inheriting the distribution and seed-spread claims of Spartina anglica.
identification: This hybrid forms perennial marsh-grass stands with upright stems and narrow leaves. Plant height and leaf color change with growing conditions, so they cannot reliably separate it from related cordgrasses. A taxonomic treatment distinguishes this group from smooth cordgrass partly through longer flower units and broader flower-cluster axes, but Spartina × townsendii and Spartina anglica overlap strongly in outward appearance. The decisive distinction is fertility: the hybrid's pollen is sterile, whereas Spartina anglica is fertile. Pollen testing or other specialist work may be required. Photograph the whole patch, mature flowering heads, leaf collars, and site context, but do not claim a definitive hybrid identification from those images alone.
actions: Send a suspected nonnative cordgrass patch to the local estuary manager or invasive-plant program before digging or cutting. Record its location and extent from accessible ground, avoiding disturbance of marsh vegetation and wildlife. Specialist confirmation should distinguish this sterile hybrid from native cordgrasses and fertile Spartina anglica before a treatment plan is chosen. Do not transplant plants or move sediment and underground stem fragments to another shoreline. Where removal is approved by the responsible site manager, follow that program's timing, access, and disposal directions. A private effort based on a photograph can remove native marsh grass or move viable fragments without resolving the underlying identification problem.

Fertility testing separates the hybrid from S. anglica; older records require care.
Chromosome doubling produced fertile S. anglica from the sterile hybrid lineage.

proposedDescription: Cordgrass hybrid is the cross between introduced smooth cordgrass and native California cordgrass, also widely written as Spartina alterniflora × Spartina foliosa. In San Francisco Bay, fertile hybrids and their descendants form a variable population rather than one uniform-looking plant. They can spread into tidal habitat and complicate restoration because the native parent must be protected during control. The current Sporobolus wording reflects a change in genus classification, not a different hybrid. Accurate identification and coordinated management are especially important here: a broad label of nonnative cordgrass can conceal both native plants and mixed ancestry.
identification: These are perennial tidal-marsh grasses with upright stems, narrow blades, and flowering heads made of several slender branches. Size and leaf form vary considerably across the hybrid population and with marsh conditions; there is no single dependable height or color test. Some hybrids have reddish or purplish leaf bases, but others do not. Native California cordgrass can look very similar, particularly before flowering. The Invasive Spartina Project combines mature-plant measurements with genetic evidence to improve identification. Photograph the full patch, flowering heads, leaf bases, and position relative to the tide line without trampling into it. Treat an identification from appearance alone as provisional when native cordgrass is present.
actions: Report an unfamiliar or expanding cordgrass patch to the local marsh manager or an established cordgrass-control program. Provide location, photographs, and an estimate of patch size; specialist review is needed before removal to protect native California cordgrass. Do not transplant marsh plants or transport mud and underground stem pieces between sites. Avoid cutting or digging an unidentified patch independently, especially in wildlife habitat. Coordinated treatment needs to account for seed production, tides, access, and bird breeding, and the Invasive Spartina Project explicitly adjusts work around these factors. After professional treatment, support follow-up monitoring rather than assuming one visit has eliminated all hybrid seedlings or surviving plants.

proposedDescription: Coriander is an annual culinary herb whose fresh leaves are commonly called cilantro and whose ripe fruits supply the spice called coriander. The same plant changes noticeably as it grows: broad lower leaves give way to finer leaves on flowering stems. Warm conditions can bring early flowering, followed by rounded seed-bearing fruits. Plants sometimes grow outside cultivation after seed escapes or remains in a garden. That makes unwanted volunteers possible, but the sources reviewed do not justify treating every escaped plant as a serious ecological invader. Managing seed production is usually the practical issue.
identification: Coriander generally grows about 1–2 feet tall. Lower leaves have broad lobes resembling parsley, while upper leaves are much more finely divided. Small white or pinkish flowers occur in umbrella-shaped clusters, followed by round yellow-brown fruits. The changing leaf shape can make a flowering plant look unlike the cilantro sold as fresh bunches. Parsley is a useful comparison for the lower leaves, but leaf resemblance or smell alone does not establish identity among the carrot family. Photograph the lower and upper leaves, their attachments, flower clusters, and developing fruits. Do not taste an unidentified roadside plant; a known garden source and the combination of mature characters provide much stronger evidence.
actions: Where Coriander volunteers are unwanted, pull or hoe seedlings while they are small and remove flowering plants before mature fruits drop. If you want a contained herb crop, harvest or collect ripe fruits deliberately rather than allowing all of them to fall around the bed. Check nearby paths and recently disturbed soil for the next flush of seedlings. Keep seed-bearing garden waste out of natural areas and inspect seed mixes or spilled kitchen seed if plants repeatedly appear in the same place. There is no need for a broad eradication campaign against an ordinary managed herb planting; address actual escape and interference at the site.
researchNotes: Botanical and horticultural accounts support annual growth, flowering and edible-leaf/seed distinctions. No severe ecological-impact claim was established; manual removal and seed prevention follow its annual life cycle.

claims: Annual herb bolts readily in heat and may become weedy outside cultivation.
Lower and upper leaves differ; flowers are white to pink and fruits rounded.
Annual culinary herb propagated by seed; cilantro and coriander refer to different harvested parts.

proposedDescription: Cork oak is an evergreen Mediterranean tree best recognized by its thick, deeply ridged bark, the source of commercial cork. Its leathery leaves stay green through winter and have pale, hairy undersides. Mature trees produce acorns and can persist for a long time in parks and older plantings. Occasional self-sown trees are documented outside its native range, but cultivation and escape are not equivalent to a demonstrated ecological threat. For a tree growing outside its native range, useful questions are whether seedlings are spreading beyond a planting and whether they are displacing vegetation at that particular site.
identification: Mature Cork oak can approach 65 feet tall, though many planted specimens are shorter and branch low. Leaves are alternate, roughly 1½–3 inches long, dark green above and pale gray beneath, usually with several short teeth along each edge. Acorns sit in cups with elongated scales that can look loose or shaggy. The exceptionally thick corky bark is most useful on older trees; seedlings lack that conspicuous character. Holm oak and native evergreen oaks can resemble its foliage, so a leaf alone may not settle identification. Photograph both leaf surfaces, a twig showing leaf arrangement, bark, and acorns with their cups. Avoid stripping bark to expose an identification feature.
actions: Check beneath a planted Cork oak and beyond the maintained area for self-sown seedlings. Remove unwanted small seedlings while the roots can be lifted with limited disturbance, after confirming they are not locally native oaks. Collect fallen acorns where concentrated recruitment creates a recurring problem, and avoid moving acorn-bearing soil into restoration areas. A mature tree should be assessed in the context of documented spread, shade, habitat, and site use before removal is considered. Use a qualified arborist for work on large trees. Do not strip or damage the bark as an improvised control method; commercial cork harvesting is a specialized practice, not a homeowner removal technique.
researchNotes: No evidence supporting catalog-wide severe invasiveness found. Seedling containment is conservative advice; native oak confusion emphasized.

claims: Evergreen tree to about 65 feet with pale hairy leaf undersides and deeply corky bark.
Acorn cups cover a substantial part of the nut.
Native Mediterranean evergreen and commercial cork source.
Weak escape from cultivation is documented in Victoria.

proposedDescription: Corm dry rot has been associated with the name Rigidoporus vinctus, but identifying the fungus behind a particular case requires care. Older references describe a crust-forming wood-decay fungus and use names including Junghuhnia vincta. A recent taxonomic revision found that material called Rigidoporus vinctus included several distinct fungi, and treats the type-linked species as Lividopora vincta. This name history makes an old disease label an uncertain guide to the organism present today. Decayed corms alone cannot establish the species or show that a nearby wood-decay fungus caused the problem.
identification: Older treatments describe thin fungal crusts spreading across wood, with very small pores and pale pinkish, buff, or darker surfaces. Those features are not a dependable field diagnosis of Rigidoporus vinctus, because the name has covered multiple species. The recent revision distinguishes related fungi through microscopic tissues and spores together with taxonomic evidence. Rotten corms, discolored roots, or a photograph of a crust do not establish Rigidoporus vinctus. A useful diagnostic submission includes the host's scientific name, affected tissue, photographs of symptoms and any fruiting body, and collection location. A useful identification must connect the specimen to a current taxonomic description; color, season, and host symptoms alone cannot resolve this name's complicated history.
actions: Keep affected planting material separate from healthy stock while a plant-diagnostic laboratory evaluates it. Record where it came from, which plants are affected, and whether decay appeared in storage or after planting. Ask the laboratory what tissue to submit before discarding every symptomatic piece; material from the active margin of a lesion may be more useful than completely decomposed tissue. Do not distribute suspect corms, roots, or soil to another garden while the cause is unresolved. Avoid choosing a fungicide, destroying nearby trees, or assigning a quarantine status from this name alone. The first necessary action is confirming the organism and its relationship to the observed disease.

sources.title: Miettinen and collaborators — Revised Cerrenaceae classification
ACIAR — Heart rot and root rot in tropical Acacia plantations

Lividopora vincta and Junghuhnia vincta are discussed as literature concepts, not silently installed as catalog synonyms.

claims: The name Rigidoporus vinctus has encompassed several fungi.
Type-linked Lividopora vincta is distinguished using microscopic morphology.
