proposedDescription: Corn brome is an annual Eurasian grass found outside cultivation in fields, roadsides, and other disturbed places. Its relatively large, drooping flower clusters and outward-spreading bristles become most apparent as the seedhead matures. It can arrive with grain or other transported seed, which helps explain scattered occurrences away from established populations. Closely related bromes can look nearly identical, so records based only on a loose grass head deserve checking. Local abundance and behavior matter more than the common name: finding one Corn brome plant does not by itself establish a large invasive infestation.
identification: Plants commonly stand about 8–24 inches tall, with hairy leaf sheaths and narrow blades. The mature flowerhead is open and often one-sided, carrying a relatively small number of large, nodding spikelets. Their bristles twist and spread outward as they dry. Japanese brome, Bromus japonicus, is particularly similar; Corn brome usually has fewer, larger flower clusters, and the small enclosing flower scales have more sharply angled sides. These distinctions need ripe material and often a hand lens. Photograph the whole head, a close side view of several spikelets, the leaf sheaths, and a ruler. Seedlings and freshly emerging heads generally do not provide enough evidence for a confident separation.
actions: Confirm the grass before treating a mixed brome patch, especially where native grasses occur. Pull isolated plants before ripe seed is shed and collect any mature heads separately so their bristles do not catch on clothing or equipment. Inspect spilled grain, feed areas, and recently imported seed if the same site repeatedly produces plants. Clean mowing or collection equipment before leaving a seeded patch. For a larger stand, work with local Extension on timing and desirable replacement cover rather than leaving extensive bare soil. Recheck the site in the next growing season, since removing annual plants does not remove the seeds already present.
researchNotes: Manual and seed-source prevention recommendations inferred from annual life cycle and grain pathway; no national impact claim.

claims: Introduced grass of fields and disturbed sites with one-sided nodding heads and spreading bristles.
Corn brome is close to B. japonicus; mature spikelet and flower-scale shape help distinguish them.
Grain introduction is documented.
Typical plants are 20–60 cm tall with hairy sheaths.

proposedDescription: Corn buttercup is a small annual buttercup of cultivated and disturbed ground. Its yellow flowers are familiar in outline, but the developing fruits provide a stronger clue: each has conspicuous spines. Leaves also change along the plant, from broader lower leaves to narrow divisions higher on the stems. It can occur as a crop or field weed outside its native range. Because several native and introduced buttercups share yellow flowers, a patch should be identified before broad removal. Corn buttercup's annual habit means preventing a new seed crop is a useful management goal.
identification: Plants usually grow about 6–24 inches tall with upright, branching stems. Basal leaves have stalks and broad, toothed outlines; upper leaves divide into three narrow segments and may have little or no stalk. The small yellow flowers have five petals. After flowering, several flattened, spine-covered fruits form a compact head. Bulbous buttercup is a named lookalike, but it has a swollen base and does not share Corn buttercup's narrow upper leaf divisions. Photograph the whole plant, lower and upper leaves, and a mature fruit head with a ruler. A yellow flower alone is insufficient, and very young plants may need to be revisited when their upper leaves or fruits develop.
actions: Remove small confirmed patches before the spiny fruits mature, lifting plants and roots when soil conditions permit. If fruits have already formed, collect them carefully rather than shaking or mowing them across the site. Wear gloves during handling and keep removed plants out of livestock feed and harvested material. Inspect field margins and disturbed patches for new seedlings during the next growing period. In pasture or crops, ask Extension for management matched to the forage or crop and the infestation's stage. Maintain suitable cover after removal, and verify nearby buttercups individually rather than assuming every yellow-flowered plant belongs to the same species.

sources.title: University of Missouri WeedID — Corn Buttercup

researchNotes: No toxicity dose or treatment claims. Manual removal and feed segregation are conservative handling recommendations.

claims: Winter annual 6–24 inches tall with narrow divided upper leaves and spiny fruit.
Bulbous buttercup differs by its swollen base and leaf form.
Flattened fruits bear conspicuous spines; flowers have five petals.

proposedDescription: Corn chamomile is an annual, sometimes short-lived biennial, herb of fields, roadsides, and disturbed open ground. White outer flowers surround a yellow center, and the leaves are cut into many narrow segments. It resembles several plants called chamomile or mayweed, which makes the common name a poor basis for identification or use. The small dry fruits and the structures inside the flowerhead provide better evidence than the familiar daisy outline. Where it is an unwanted field or garden weed, recognizing plants before they shed seed makes removal more useful.
identification: Plants can reach about 2 feet tall, with branching stems and finely divided alternate leaves. Individual flowerheads are usually around an inch across, with white rays and many small yellow flowers in the center. As the head matures, the center becomes more raised. Stinking chamomile, Anthemis cotula, is a close lookalike. Corn chamomile has broader papery scales throughout the central flowerhead and relatively smooth-ribbed, squared fruits; stinking chamomile has narrower scales concentrated higher in the head and bumpier fruits. These differences may need a lens and mature material. Photograph leaves, a side view of the head, and dry fruits. Published descriptions disagree about scent, so smell is not used here as the decisive test.
actions: Pull small confirmed patches before flowerheads develop ripe fruits, taking the taproot where practical. Collect mature heads before moving plants so seed is not shaken across a path, lawn, or field. Inspect seed mixes and newly disturbed ground if plants appear repeatedly, and establish suitable ground cover after removal. In a crop, pasture, or large turf area, ask Extension to identify the chamomile and advise on timing appropriate to the setting. Do not assume a tea or ornamental chamomile is the same species. Keep a few clear photographs of the mature diagnostic parts so later seedlings can be linked to a verified identification rather than a general daisy appearance.

sources.title: Flora of New Zealand — Anthemis arvensis

researchNotes: Odor claims vary among floras, so omitted as a decisive feature. Manual prevention follows short life cycle and seed reproduction.

claims: Annual or biennial to 60 cm with divided leaves and white-and-yellow heads.
Broad head scales and squared ribbed fruits distinguish Corn chamomile from A. cotula.
Flowerhead has papery scales throughout; disturbed habitats are typical.

proposedDescription: Corn gromwell is a small annual or winter annual herb with narrow leaves and tiny pale flowers. It often grows in fields, pastures, lawns, and other disturbed ground, where the modest blooms can be easy to overlook. The plant belongs to the borage family and develops small hard nutlets rather than a showy seed capsule. Older references call it Lithospermum arvense; that name is useful when following historical records. Its use in modern oilseed development does not make an unidentified roadside plant appropriate for eating or home remedies.
identification: Plants range from about 4–28 inches tall, with simple or lightly branched stems covered in short hairs that lie close to the surface. Leaves occur alternately along the stem, have smooth edges, and become narrow and stalkless toward the top. Tiny white to bluish-white flowers sit among the upper leaves; each is a short funnel with five lobes. Four hard nutlets can develop from a flower. Other small borage-family plants may look similar before fruiting, so photograph a complete stem, close views of the hairs and leaf attachment, flowers, and mature nutlets. A young leafy plant or a distant image of white flowers does not provide the same confidence as those combined features.
actions: Look for Corn gromwell in thin ground cover and winter-crop margins while it is flowering, before the nutlets mature. Pull or hoe a small confirmed patch and collect fruiting stems so hard seeds are not scattered during cleanup. Avoid bringing seed-bearing soil or contaminated planting material into a clean bed. Revisit the patch after the next germination period and maintain suitable vegetation where repeated bare-ground disturbance favors annual weeds. For substantial populations in crops or pasture, use local Extension advice matched to the production system. Do not feed removed plants to animals or treat the plant's commercial oilseed use as a basis for consuming wild material.

claims: Annual or winter annual with alternate hairy narrow leaves and tiny spring flowers.
Lithospermum arvense is an older name.
Plants are 4–28 inches tall, with flattened hairs, five-lobed flowers, and four nutlets.
Introduced Eurasian herb of disturbed ground and fields; developed as an oilseed crop.

proposedDescription: Corn leaf aphid is a small sap-feeding insect found on corn, sorghum, barley, and other grasses. Colonies can shelter inside developing leaves and around tassels, where sticky honeydew may become more obvious than the insects themselves. Heavy infestations can interfere with plant growth or pollination, and the aphid can transmit cereal viruses. Effects depend on the crop and conditions: UC IPM notes that direct damage in small grains is usually minor and treatment is seldom needed. Checking plant condition and natural enemies is more informative than reacting to every visible colony.
identification: Wingless adults are roughly 2 millimeters long and usually bluish green to olive, with dark legs, short antennae, and two short black tubes near the rear. Dark or purplish patches surround the bases of those tubes. Young aphids resemble smaller adults, while winged forms occur when populations disperse. Russian wheat aphid can be confused with it because both are small and have short antennae; Corn leaf aphid has prominent dark rear tubes and lacks the extra rear projection described for Russian wheat aphid. Photograph several individuals with a scale, including side and top views, and record the grass or crop. Honeydew and yellow leaves alone do not identify the species.
actions: Inspect developing leaves, tassels, and nearby host grasses, recording whether colonies are increasing and whether the crop shows injury. Look for lady beetles, hoverfly larvae, and parasitized aphids before deciding intervention is needed; these natural enemies can suppress populations. In a small garden, monitor individual plants closely rather than spraying the entire planting automatically. In field crops, consult current Extension thresholds for the crop and growth stage, especially when virus risk or pollination is a concern. Avoid moving infested seedlings to new plantings. UC's small-grain guidance says this aphid seldom requires treatment, so the presence of a few insects is not a treatment threshold.

Heavy colonies can affect tassels and produce honeydew.
Distinguishable from Russian wheat aphid by rear structures.
Damage is usually minor in small grains; natural enemies and monitoring inform decisions.
Lady beetles, hoverflies, and parasitoid wasps attack this aphid.

proposedDescription: Corn poppy is an annual flower associated with fields, gardens, and disturbed ground. Its thin red petals and dark center are familiar, but ornamental forms can vary in color and petal number. The plant reproduces by seed, with capsules developing after the brief flowers fall. Introduced occurrences may reflect old plantings or seed mixtures rather than a spreading ecological problem. Its annual life cycle makes seed management the practical focus where volunteers are unwanted. A patch of red poppies should still be identified, because several poppy species and cultivars can look alike in bloom.
identification: Typical Corn poppy plants have branching, bristly stems around 1–2 feet tall, though size varies with conditions. Leaves are alternate and deeply lobed or divided. Flowers stand singly on long hairy stalks and usually have four broad scarlet petals, often with dark blotches near the base. Numerous dark stamens surround a disk-topped central capsule that becomes conspicuous after petals fall. Oriental poppy is a commonly grown perennial lookalike, whereas Corn poppy is annual; color alone cannot distinguish them. Photograph the leaves, hair direction on the flower stalk, and mature capsule as well as the open flower. Garden cultivars may obscure typical flower characters, so fertile fruit is particularly useful.
actions: If Corn poppy is unwanted outside its intended bed, remove seedlings early or collect developing capsules before seeds are released. Bag ripe capsules before handling whole plants so their small seeds do not scatter. Check the contents of wildflower seed mixes and choose locally appropriate alternatives when planting beside natural habitat. Revisit disturbed soil in later seasons, where seed left from earlier plants may germinate. A cultivated patch can be managed by deliberate seed collection and removal of volunteers rather than treating every flower as a serious invasion. For a persistent crop infestation, seek crop-specific advice rather than applying a garden cleanup method at field scale.

sources.title: Colorado State Extension — Poppy identification response

researchNotes: Capsule detail beyond a disk-topped form not asserted without a verified comparative key. No unsupported broad ecological-impact claim.

claims: Bristly annual with divided leaves and usually four scarlet petals.
Occurs in fields and disturbed ground outside its Eurasian origin.
Annual introduced poppy with alternate lobed leaves and upright stems.
Corn poppy is a self-seeding annual; Oriental poppy is perennial.

proposedDescription: Corn Speedwell is a low annual weed whose small blue flowers can appear among grass before taller spring plants draw attention. It often grows in lawns, fields, and disturbed edges, particularly where turf is thin. Plants commonly begin growth in the cool season, then flower and set seed as conditions warm. The lower and upper leaves differ in shape and arrangement, which helps distinguish it from other speedwells. Its presence is often a ground-cover or maintenance issue rather than evidence of serious habitat damage. Addressing repeated bare spots can matter as much as removing the visible plants.
identification: Look for low, spreading or rising stems with small hairy leaves. Lower leaves occur in opposite pairs and are relatively rounded; upper leaves on flowering shoots are narrower and alternate. Tiny pale-blue to violet flowers occur on short stalks, and the developing capsules are heart-shaped and hairy. Creeping speedwell and purslane speedwell are useful named comparisons, but the combination of growth habit, hairs, leaf arrangement, and fruit is more reliable than flower color alone. Photograph the entire low plant, both lower and upper leaves, and a capsule beside a ruler. A close image of one blue flower can establish a speedwell-like plant without resolving which species it is.
actions: Hand-pull small patches while soil is moist and before the heart-shaped capsules release seed. In turf, inspect the reason grass is thin—such as unsuitable mowing, persistent shade, or repeated wear—and correct the condition where feasible before reseeding. Keep garden soil covered with suitable plants or mulch rather than repeatedly leaving open germination sites. Record where winter seedlings recur so the next check happens before flowering. Extensive lawn treatment is not automatically necessary for a few plants. If the weed is persistent or mixed with other speedwells, ask Extension to verify it and recommend management compatible with the turf species and the site's intended use.
researchNotes: No reliable numeric size range recovered; description explicitly uses low habit rather than an invented measurement. Ready for editorial review with this bounded limitation.

claims: Hairy winter annual with opposite lower leaves and alternate upper leaves.
Creeping and purslane speedwell are similar species.
Low hairy plant with small blue flowers and heart-shaped hairy capsules.
Turf conditions and acceptable weed levels should inform management.

proposedDescription: Corn Spurry is an annual plant with narrow leaves clustered around its stems and small white flowers. It grows particularly well in disturbed, sandy ground and can become troublesome among crops when many plants form a dense cover. An introduction once grown as forage in North America, it now occurs in fields, roadsides, and cultivated places. Its small size can disguise how quickly it replaces itself: plants can flower and set seed within a single growing season, and buried seed can survive for a long time. Preventing fresh seed is more useful than judging a patch only by its height.
identification: Look for branching plants about 5–70 cm tall, with slender, somewhat fleshy leaves that appear in rings or crowded clusters at the stem joints. Individual leaves are about 15–50 mm long but less than 1 mm wide. The stems and leaves may carry gland-tipped hairs. Flowers have five separate white petals, each roughly 2.5–4 mm long, followed by small capsules that open to release seeds. Young seedlings already have needlelike first leaves. Several other spurries occur, including Spergula morisonii and S. pentandra; a distant photograph of white flowers is insufficient to separate them. Photograph the whole plant, leaf clusters, flowers, and mature capsules, and retain close views of seeds for a botanical identification.
actions: In a garden or small cultivated patch, remove Corn Spurry while plants are young and before capsules mature. Collect seed-bearing material rather than shaking it over clean ground. Check again after rain and soil disturbance, because a surviving seedbank can produce another flush. Clean soil and plant debris from equipment before moving between fields, and avoid transferring infested topsoil into beds. In cropped ground, use soil testing and crop-specific advice to address conditions that favor the weed; changing soil acidity without a test is not a useful blanket remedy. Record whether the patch is spreading or competing with the crop so management addresses an actual problem.

sources.title: AHDB: Distribution and biology of corn spurrey

researchNotes: Removal and soil-movement prevention are cautious applications of annual seed biology; no locally tested control efficacy asserted. Exact distinguishing seed characters for congeners not verified.

claims: Annual introduced plant of cultivated ground; 5–70 cm tall; narrow clustered leaves, five white petals and seed capsules.
Sandy low-pH soils favor the weed; dense growth competes with cereals; persistent seeds move with machinery and animals.

proposedDescription: Corndaisy is a yellow-flowered annual associated with cultivated fields, disturbed ground, and occasional garden plantings. Both the outer ray flowers and the central disk are yellow, giving each flowerhead a single strong color. Its fleshy, often blue-green leaves vary from toothed to lobed, so different parts of one plant may look surprisingly different. The species is native around the Mediterranean and has spread beyond that range. An escaped plant may simply be a short-lived visitor, while repeated seedlings can become a crop or garden weed. Records under Chrysanthemum segetum refer to the same species under an older scientific name.
identification: Corndaisy usually stands about 20–80 cm tall, with smooth, fleshy stems and leaves. Flowerheads are commonly 3–6 cm across and have yellow rays around a yellow center. Lower leaves may be lobed or coarsely toothed; the upper leaves attach directly to the stem and partly clasp it. This combination matters more than a yellow flowerhead alone. Crown daisy, Glebionis coronaria, generally has much more deeply divided leaves and may have white rays with yellow bases. Photograph a lower leaf and an upper clasping leaf, as well as the entire flowering plant. Mature fruits can help a botanist: outer fruits have narrow wings, and the fruits lack a tuft of bristles. Seedlings are less distinctive than flowering plants.
actions: If Corndaisy is unwanted in a bed or field margin, pull or hoe young plants before flowerheads produce mature fruit. Gather mature heads carefully so the seeds do not spill into nearby soil. Revisit disturbed patches through the growing season and record whether seedlings return the following year. Where the plant is intentionally grown, deadheading provides a simple way to limit self-sowing. Check purchased seed mixtures before sowing near natural areas or production fields. A scattered ornamental escape does not by itself justify treating a whole site; focus on established patches that are spreading or interfering with the intended vegetation, and keep soil movement from carrying their seeds elsewhere.
researchNotes: Practical prevention inferred from annual seed reproduction, not a species-specific field trial. Southern Hemisphere flowering dates not transferred to a US profile.

claims: Annual 20–80 cm; smooth fleshy stems; yellow heads 3–6 cm; partly clasping leaves; winged outer fruits without pappus.
Yellow annual of cultivated fields and clearings; fleshy toothed or lobed leaves; G. coronaria has more divided foliage.

proposedDescription: Cornflag is a perennial with upright, sword-shaped leaves and a tall stalk of red, orange, or yellow flowers. Each flower has a prominent upper hood, often above a contrasting yellow throat. The plant survives between growing seasons in a corm, a compact underground stem that stores reserves, and can produce smaller corms around it. Native to a broad part of Africa and extending into Arabia, it has long been cultivated and sometimes escapes gardens. It also contributed to garden gladiolus breeding, which makes a colorful roadside flower worth checking carefully before assigning it to this wild species.
identification: Plants are often 60–120 cm tall and can approach 2 m. Leaves are roughly 1–2.5 cm wide, with conspicuous midribs and margins, and rise in a loose fan. The usually unbranched flower spike carries flowers mainly to one side. Flowers are unscented, with a curved tube about 3.5–5 cm long; the upper hood is larger than the lower lobes. Color varies, so red petals alone are not diagnostic. Garden gladiolus hybrids can overlap in appearance and require careful floral measurements. Photograph the whole spike, a side view showing the flower tube, leaf width, and the flower face with a scale. A dormant corm without leaves or flowers will rarely support a confident species identification.
actions: Keep Cornflag plantings within a managed bed if they are producing volunteers nearby. Remove spent flower stalks before capsules release seed, and inspect the bed edge for new shoots. When removing an unwanted clump, lift the corm and the small corms around its base; cutting leaves alone leaves the underground stem in place. Recheck the site during subsequent growing seasons for overlooked corms and seedlings. Do not discard corms, excavated soil, or garden waste along roadsides or in natural areas. For an apparent escape, photograph flowering plants before removal so a local herbarium or extension office can distinguish the species from cultivated hybrids.
researchNotes: Catalog species includes variation; no subspecies diagnosis asserted. Corm removal and seed prevention are cautious garden measures derived from growth form, not quantified eradication claims.

claims: Cormous perennial to 2 m; broad African native range; swordlike leaves and hooded variable flowers; long history in hybrid breeding.
Corms bear cormlets; leaves 10–25 mm wide; one-sided flower spikes; curved tube 3.5–5 cm; occasional garden escape.

proposedDescription: Cosmopolitan powderpost beetle is a small beetle whose larvae develop inside dry hardwood. An infestation may first become visible as fine wood dust and tiny round exit holes in flooring, furniture, or stored timber. The adult beetles do little of this damage; the hidden larvae tunnel through suitable wood while feeding. This species has been recorded from a range of hardwoods, including oak, ash, and walnut. A hole in an old piece of furniture is not proof that beetles are still active, however. Other wood-boring beetles leave similar signs, and the insect itself is needed for a reliable species determination.
identification: Adults are slender, brown to dark brown beetles about 2.5–5 mm long. The wing covers have orderly rows of punctures, and the head is visible from above. Larvae are pale, curved grubs with darker heads, usually concealed in the wood. Lyctus cavicollis is a close lookalike; specialist keys distinguish the single rows of wing-cover punctures and prominent frontal lobes of Cosmopolitan powderpost beetle from its features. Lyctus brunneus is another similar household species. Photograph any adult from above beside a ruler, and retain it in a closed container for an entomologist. Also photograph the wood, exit holes, and fresh debris. Dust or holes alone cannot identify the beetle or reliably establish that an infestation remains active.
actions: Isolate a suspect movable wooden item from other unfinished hardwood while arranging identification. Note and photograph existing holes, clear away loose dust, and check later for newly formed holes or fresh accumulations; vibrations can also dislodge old debris. Inspect incoming lumber and secondhand furniture before bringing them into storage or use. Finishing exposed wood helps prevent new egg laying, but it does not remove larvae already inside. A small affected component may be replaceable; valuable furniture, widespread damage, or structural concerns deserve a wood-pest professional's assessment. Do not choose treatment solely from an old hole or attempt improvised heating of furniture.
researchNotes: Management source addresses lyctid powderpost beetles as a group; species-specific morphology supplied separately. No household heat or pesticide recipe included. Follow-up audit: UCR, Swedish heritage authority and Kentucky extension are separate sources. UCR's historical chemical advice is not adopted.

claims: L. linearis attacks numerous hardwood products; differs from L. cavicollis in puncture rows and frontal lobes.
L. linearis identification includes single rows of wing-cover punctures; related lyctids require close examination.
Adults 2.5–5 mm, slender and brown; pale curved larvae; hardwood sapwood infestation.
Adult length 2.5–5 mm; larvae are pale and curved with brown heads.
Fresh holes and dust help assess activity; old dust may be dislodged; inspect wood, finish exposed surfaces and consider localized replacement.
Distinguish fresh activity from old dust; sealed surfaces prevent much new infestation, while preexisting insects may emerge through finishes.

proposedDescription: Cotton seed bug is a small, dark insect that gathers around the seeds of cotton and related plants such as hibiscus and okra. Adults have pale, translucent wings, while young bugs have reddish abdomens and no developed wings. Feeding can reduce cotton seed quality, and crushed bugs can stain cotton fibers during processing. The species can also hide on non-host plants, packing materials, and other objects between feeding periods. That ability makes transported plants and cargo important routes of spread. Finding a cluster on a garden plant is a reason to obtain an identification, especially where the insect has not previously been recorded.
identification: Adults measure about 3.5–5 mm long and are brown to black with translucent whitish wings. Nymphs are smaller, wingless, and red through the abdomen. Inspect mature seed pods and open cotton bolls, where groups can look like small fleas moving between seeds and fibers. Cotton seed bug does not normally pierce intact closed cotton bolls, although damage by another insect may give it access. Several Oxycarenus species look similar. Expert screening uses wing and body coloration, leg spines, and male structures; some specimens require dissection. Photograph adults from above and from the side, their size, the host plant, and the seed pod. A red nymph or a blurry cluster is not enough for confirmation.
actions: Report a suspected Cotton seed bug to your county extension office or state plant regulatory office and provide the location, host plant, and clear photographs. Ask how to preserve or submit a specimen before shipping any live insects or plant material. Inspect seed pods repeatedly as they mature, especially on cotton, okra, and ornamental mallows near a detection. Hold suspect nursery plants, used sacks, and plant debris at the site while seeking advice rather than passing them to another property. Check nearby non-host plants and sheltered packing areas too, since resting adults can hide there. Use the confirmed identification and local response advice to decide further action.

sources.title: USDA APHIS: Cotton Seed Bug Pest Alert
UC Davis Calinvasives: Oxycarenus hyalinipennis scorecard

researchNotes: APHIS and CAPS are one agency source family, not independent confirmation. UC source adds independent local review. No unverified current county boundary or legal restriction asserted.

claims: Adults 3.5–5 mm; nymphs red and wingless; seeds of mallows support feeding; hitchhiking pathways and official reporting guidance.
Close Oxycarenus species require expert morphological identification, sometimes male dissection; adult specimens important.
Human-assisted movement is important; cotton and mallows are hosts; southern California detections documented.

proposedDescription: Cottony camellia scale is a sap-feeding insect found on camellias, hollies, yews, and numerous other woody plants. Its most noticeable sign is a white egg sac on the underside of a leaf, often with a small tan female at one end. Sticky honeydew and black sooty mold may draw attention before the insects themselves are noticed. Heavy, persistent populations can yellow foliage and reduce growth, but a few scales do not necessarily require treatment. Old egg sacs also remain after the female dies, so checking for living insects and newly hatched young is more useful than counting white patches alone.
identification: Mature females are oval, yellowish tan with a brown border, and reach about 3 mm long. The white egg sac extending behind the body is approximately 6 mm long. Look beneath leaves, particularly on camellia, holly, and yew; immature scales may overwinter on evergreen foliage or on the bark of deciduous hosts. Newly hatched crawlers are pale yellow and need a hand lens to see well. Cottony maple leaf scale, Pulvinaria acericola, and other cottony scales can occupy overlapping hosts, so host identity and white wax alone are not decisive. Photograph the female body, its attached sac, and the leaf underside with a size reference. Preserve a representative adult for an extension specialist if the exact species matters.
actions: Inspect several branches and leaf undersides to determine whether Cottony camellia scale is scattered or widespread. On a small plant, manually remove accessible scales and egg sacs; prune a badly infested branch only where this will not seriously damage the plant. Keep removed material away from healthy nursery stock. Look for lady beetles and other natural enemies before considering a spray. Recheck for pale yellow crawlers, since egg sacs can remain empty and hatching may continue over an extended period. If foliage continues to yellow or new growth weakens, ask extension staff to confirm the scale and suggest timing appropriate to the local climate and host.

sources.title: University of Maryland: Cottony Camellia Scale
Rutgers Nursery IPM: Cottony Camellia Scale

researchNotes: Regional emergence calendars intentionally not generalized nationally. Specific differential characters for P. acericola require a specialist.

claims: Females to 3 mm with 6 mm egg sacs; pale yellow crawlers; leaf undersides and overwintering sites; old sacs persist; heavy infestations yellow leaves.
Manual removal, pruning selected infested branches, population monitoring and conserving natural enemies are cultural measures.
Cottony camellia, maple leaf and maple scales are distinct similar insects; host associations and emergence differ.

proposedDescription: Cottony cushion scale feeds on the sap of citrus and many ornamental shrubs and trees. The insect is best known for the long, white, ridged egg sac attached behind its orange-brown body. Large populations can weaken plants, while the sticky honeydew they release supports black sooty mold. Its history also includes a notable success in biological control: the vedalia beetle helped suppress severe citrus infestations after being introduced from Australia. Today, predators and parasitic flies can still keep populations low where they are established. Protecting those natural enemies is often more effective than reacting to every visible egg sac.
identification: A mature Cottony cushion scale with its egg sac can approach 13 mm in total length. The actual body is much shorter and orange, yellowish, or brown beneath varying amounts of wax. The sac has conspicuous lengthwise ridges and can be two or more times the body length. Newly hatched crawlers are red with dark legs and antennae; young stages often line leaf veins, while larger insects occur on twigs and branches. Unlike many familiar scales, this insect retains legs and can move throughout life. Other wax-producing scales and mealybugs can look similar at a glance. Photograph the ridged sac from the side, the body at its front, young insects, and the host plant rather than relying on a white patch alone.
actions: Check whether Cottony cushion scale numbers are increasing and whether the host shows leaf loss, weak growth, or twig dieback. Look closely for red-and-black vedalia beetles, their larvae feeding among the sacs, or small emergence holes left by parasitic flies. Preserve these natural enemies and address ants tending the scales, using locally appropriate ant management. Avoid unnecessary broad-spectrum spraying, which can remove the insects already suppressing the scale. Inspect new citrus and ornamental plants before placing them beside established plants. For a severe infestation without effective natural enemies, obtain extension advice based on the host and the presence of newly hatched crawlers before selecting any treatment.

sources.title: UF IFAS: Cottony Cushion Scale, Icerya purchasi

researchNotes: Natural enemy presence and effectiveness vary by location; no universal need for insecticides asserted. Biological control history is descriptive, not authorization to release organisms.

claims: Ridged sacs extend to total length near 13 mm; mobility retained; natural enemies, ant management and avoiding disruptive sprays support control.
Australian origin; colored bodies and red crawlers; citrus and Pittosporum hosts; feeding and honeydew damage; vedalia biological control history.

proposedDescription: Cottony grape scale is a soft scale insect that spends part of its life on grape canes and part on leaves. Mature females produce conspicuous cottony egg masses, while younger stages can be easy to overlook against the bark. Their honeydew can attract ants and leave fruit or foliage coated with sooty mold. The significance of an infestation is not limited to direct feeding: this species can transmit certain grapevine leafroll viruses. A healthy vine with a few scales may tolerate their feeding, but scales near known virus infections deserve a different response. Accurate identification and the condition of neighboring vines both matter.
identification: Overwintering scales on canes are flattened, oval, and brownish to dark, commonly only a few millimeters long. Mature females can reach roughly 6 mm, with a white egg sac extending well beyond the body and tilting it upward. Crawlers later settle beneath leaves; mature egg sacs may persist after the female dies. European fruit lecanium, Parthenolecanium corni, also lives on grapes but has a more rounded brown body and lacks the conspicuous projecting cottony sac. Cottony maple scale is another lookalike, and some illustrated guides mix their images. Photograph the female, egg mass, cane, and leaf undersides with a size reference. Have an adult checked before assigning an unfamiliar infestation to Cottony grape scale.
actions: Inspect canes during normal dormant pruning and note whether scales also occupy the permanent trunk or main arms. Removing infested canes as part of appropriate pruning may reduce a small population without further treatment. Check leaf undersides for crawlers and watch for honeydew or ants during the growing season. Keep planting material from affected vines separate and seek advice before distributing cuttings. If leafroll virus is known or suspected in the vineyard, ask a grape extension specialist about identification, virus testing, and scale management together. Treating the insect alone does not cure an infected vine, and visible leaf symptoms alone do not establish the virus responsible.

sources.title: Pacific Northwest Handbook: Grape—Cottony grape scale
British Columbia Best Practices Guide: Soft Scale

researchNotes: PNW article includes P. innumerabilis image captions and inconsistent cottony-maple wording; used P. vitis narrative only and cross-checked with independent BC guide. Regional dates omitted; vineyard virus response requires diagnostic advice.

claims: Scales overwinter on canes, grow to about 0.25 inch and produce long cottony sacs; pruning can remove much of an infestation; virus concern.
P. vitis differs from fruit lecanium by cottony egg mass and elongated form; leafroll-virus transmission, honeydew, seasonal leaf-to-cane movement and monitoring.

proposedDescription: Cottony grass scale is an elongated soft scale associated especially with grasses, including sugarcane. Living adult females can be pinkish with two red lines running along the back, a feature reflected in the alternate name red-striped sugar-cane scale. Unlike scales with large, conspicuous white tails, this species produces only a short egg sac beneath and around its body. Published accounts describe it as a minor sugarcane pest in many circumstances. More serious sugarcane damage has been reported in colonies associated with the tawny crazy ant, Nylanderia fulva. Its presence on a plant should therefore prompt a check of the population and damage, rather than an assumption of severe harm.
identification: Adult females in the original description were about 3.5–6 mm long, very narrow or elliptical, with both ends tapering. Fresh individuals ranged from pale crimson to pink, usually with two brighter red lengthwise lines. The short white egg sac projects only slightly beyond the body margin; dried specimens can become buff or brown and lose their useful live colors. The species can resemble Aclerda scales in overall shape. Historical New World records under Pulvinaria iceryi also include misidentifications, so that name should not be substituted automatically. Photograph fresh adults on their host, the underside if safely accessible, and a ruler. A scale specialist must examine fine hairs, pores, and ducts to confirm the identification.
actions: On a suspected Cottony grass scale host, record the grass species, where scales sit on the plant, and whether leaves are yellowing or growth is declining. Photograph any ants tending the colony without assuming their identity. Keep infested potted grasses or sugarcane planting pieces separate from clean stock and avoid sharing them until the scale is identified. For a small ornamental planting, removing a few heavily occupied leaves may reduce insects while preserving a sample for diagnosis. Recheck the remaining growth. In a production field, use an extension or crop adviser to assess the scale and ant association before treatment.

sources.title: Tanaka and Kondo 2015: key to Colombian Pulvinaria

researchNotes: Modern catalog confirms identity; original description supplies visible size and color. ScaleNet draws on original literature, so not wholly independent. Practical containment is precautionary; no unsupported treatment threshold. Follow-up audit: ScaleNet repeats Newstead and later studies; separate URLs do not make repeated facts independent. The 2015 key explicitly derives the elongata/iceryi distinction from Mamet 1958, a different diagnostic lineage from Newstead 1917. Caballero 2017 was accessed only as abstract, so it does not independently reverify the ant-impact statement here. The Australian diagnostic PDF returned 404 on follow-up. Its original indexed-excerpt evidence remains documented in the audit trail; the failed link was removed from the candidate source list and replaced by the accessible Tanaka and Kondo diagnostic key. No universal damage threshold or home treatment program was established.

claims: Grass and sugarcane hosts; minor pest except some ant associations; historical P. iceryi misidentifications; P. longisqua synonym.
More serious sugarcane damage is specifically associated with Nylanderia fulva; literature documents identity confusion.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: University of Liverpool / original taxonomic study
claims: Original adult description gives 3.5–6 mm length, elongated pink body with crimson lines and short egg sac; resemblance to Aclerda.
The visible adult measurements and Aclerda resemblance are explicit.
P. elongata has medial thoracic multilocular pores and lacks medial thoracic tubular ducts; P. iceryi has the opposite arrangement.
Abstract lists P. elongata among Colombian sugarcane scales and states that species biology and mutualistic ants are covered.

proposedDescription: Cottony pigface scale feeds on the fleshy leaves of iceplants and related succulents. Young adult females are greenish, then become reddish brown as they mature and produce a white egg sac. On a dense groundcover, infestations may be hidden among growing tips before damaged patches become obvious. Historical outbreaks affected iceplant plantings, and natural enemies introduced in a coordinated biological control program helped reduce them. The name Pulvinariella mesembryanthemi appears in older studies, while current taxonomic catalogs place the same insect in Pulvinaria. This name change does not make every cottony scale on an iceplant this species.
identification: Adult females are approximately 2–5 mm long, oval to nearly circular and moderately domed. Their color changes from green or yellow-green to reddish brown. A white egg sac forms beneath and behind the body, often with a groove along its middle; it may be as long as the body or longer. Check succulent leaves and new shoot tips. Pulvinaria delottoi is a very similar iceplant scale that often uses older growth, but feeding position is not a secure identification feature. Microscope examination distinguishes the thinner, mostly curved hairs along the body edge of Cottony pigface scale from the thicker, straighter hairs of that lookalike. Photograph adults, sacs, plant tips, and the host, and retain an adult for specialist confirmation.
actions: Inspect new iceplant and succulent cuttings before adding them to a collection, and keep visibly infested material separate. Avoid distributing cuttings from a colony until identification and management are settled. In a small planting, remove heavily occupied shoots into a contained waste stream and inspect adjacent new growth repeatedly. Preserve beneficial insects rather than spraying an entire groundcover at the first sight of white sacs; historical control depended strongly on natural enemies. If the host itself is an unwanted spreading iceplant, coordinate its removal rather than encouraging it to recover. Do not transport or release the scale as an improvised biological control agent.

sources.title: UCR: Biological Control of Ice Plant Scales
IUBS: Insects and Spiders, scale insect account

researchNotes: Clear nomenclatural change, not unresolved identity; retain catalog ID and supply modern combination separately. Small-scale removal advice is precautionary and not a quantified treatment trial.

claims: Oval green-to-brown females; white posterior egg sacs; succulent hosts; microscopic marginal-hair distinction from P. delottoi.
P. mesembryanthemi favors new terminal growth; historical outbreaks and successful parasitoid establishment reduced spray need.
Female body length 2–5 mm; fleshy iceplant hosts and egg-sac color changes.
Current combination is Pulvinaria mesembryanthemi; former genus retained in historical literature.

proposedDescription: Council tree is a large evergreen fig with broad, glossy leaves and pale gray bark. It can begin life on another tree or a stone surface, then develop roots that reach the ground and support a substantial trunk. Small yellow to orange figs enclose its flowers, as in other members of the fig family. Native to tropical Asia, it is planted for shade and as an ornamental, but has escaped in some warm regions. Its effects depend on local conditions: Florida assessments identify concern in the south, while the presence of a cultivated tree elsewhere does not establish the same ecological risk.
identification: An outdoor Council tree can reach about 25 m tall and develop buttressed or multiple trunks with aerial roots. Leaves alternate along the stem, are leathery and hairless, and may reach 20 cm long. Mature figs are oval, smooth, and up to about 2 cm across, becoming yellow to orange. The native Florida strangler fig, Ficus aurea, is an important lookalike. Council tree generally has broader, more egg-shaped leaves; the lowest pair of side veins leaves the midrib at a narrow angle and extends a third or more of the way up the blade. Photograph leaf shape and veins, both leaf surfaces, figs, and the whole trunk. A juvenile ornamental or a tree without figs may require a botanical specialist.
actions: Check around planted Council trees for seedlings, including in branch forks, palm crowns, walls, and other places where small figs may establish. Remove accessible seedlings while their roots are small, taking care not to injure a supporting tree. Larger plants rooted into another tree or a structure need an arborist's assessment before cutting or pulling. Where local agencies identify the species as invasive, choose an alternative for new planting and report escapes in nearby natural areas. Retain photographs before removal so native figs are not mistaken for this species. Monitor cleared spots for regrowth and new seedlings, and keep discarded plant material out of unmanaged habitat.

sources.title: University of South Florida FLIP: Ficus altissima
UF IFAS: Integrated Management of Invasive Plants in Natural Areas of Florida

researchNotes: Manual seedling guidance is cautious practical prevention, not a quantified control trial. No blanket US-wide harmful status or pollinator-presence claim. Follow-up audit: USF's morphology cites the UNC/Weakley flora and FNAI; UF assessment is separate. The two UF pages remain one institutional source group.

claims: Evergreen tree to 25 m; aerial roots; glossy broad leaves and yellow-orange figs; distinction from F. aurea using leaf shape and basal veins.
Council tree has broader ovate leaves than F. aurea; its lowest secondary veins extend at least one third of the blade at a narrow angle.
Assessment distinguishes invasive status in southern Florida from other zones; council tree and false banyan names.
South Florida assessment is invasive; central and north assessments are incomplete and report no current problem.
Epiphytic figs require care to protect host trees and nearby native figs during management.

proposedDescription: Cow sandbur is a tufted perennial grass adapted to hot, dry conditions. Its short, dense seedheads contain small burrlike units rather than the long, spreading spines familiar from some other sandburs. It has been used as forage in dry regions because established plants withstand drought and grazing, yet it can also spread beyond plantings and become a weed in suitable environments. Rain can prompt rapid growth and seed production. You may also find it under the scientific name Cenchrus setigerus; that different ending does not mean it is a separate grass.
identification: Plants commonly stand about 20–80 cm high, with narrow flat or folded leaf blades and a stout perennial base. Upright cylindrical seedheads are roughly 1.5–12 cm long. Each burrlike unit is about 3–7 mm long, with inner bristles fused into a small tough cup and only short outer bristles. Under magnification, the rough points on the inner bristles face toward their tips. Cenchrus echinatus and C. biflorus have backward-pointing barbs, an important distinction that ordinary landscape photographs may miss. Photograph the whole clump, leaf bases, and a mature seedhead, then obtain close views of individual burrs with a ruler. Avoid identifying non-flowering plants solely from drought tolerance or a resemblance to pasture grass.
actions: Where Cow sandbur is unwanted, identify a flowering clump before removing similar grasses. For a small patch, contain mature seedheads before digging out the plant base; mowing the top alone leaves a perennial plant capable of regrowth. Recheck after rain, when surviving plants and new seedlings may become visible. Brush seed units and soil from footwear and equipment before leaving the patch. Do not move seed-bearing hay or collected seed into uninfested areas without checking its contents. For an established pasture, weigh its intended forage use against escape into surrounding land with a local adviser. Do not assume treatment recommendations for buffelgrass apply unchanged to this species.
researchNotes: Treatment text in Tropical Forages explicitly extrapolates from C. ciliaris, so it was not adopted. Seed prevention and small-clump removal are practical inferences from perennial seed-producing habit. Follow-up audit: NSW species account and NSW genus key are one group. Tropical Forages is independent but remained indexed_excerpt during this audit.

claims: Perennial to 0.8 m; dense cylindrical seedheads; short outer bristles and fused inner bristles.
The draft's size ranges and burr structure agree with the flora.
Same naming variant; dryland forage, drought and grazing tolerance, seed spread; forward-pointing barbs distinguish C. biflorus; weediness varies.
C. biflorus has oppositely directed barbs; the alternate ending setigerus is a naming treatment, not a distinct taxon.
C. setiger burrs 3–7 mm with forward-pointing barbs; C. echinatus barbs point backward.
Direction of burr barbs separates C. setiger and C. echinatus.

proposedDescription: Cow soapwort is an annual with smooth, blue-green foliage and small pink flowers on branching stems. The green cup around each flower has five pronounced ridges, giving it an angular, almost inflated appearance that remains useful for identification after the petals fall. Native to Europe and neighboring regions, the plant occurs as an introduced weed in cultivated and disturbed ground in North America. It is also grown ornamentally, so a few plants may mark a past planting rather than a spreading infestation. Its life cycle centers on seed, making mature capsules and returning seedlings the main things to watch.
identification: Look for a hairless annual about 20–100 cm tall, usually branched above, with opposite leaves that attach directly to the stem. The leaves are lance-shaped to broadly oblong and often have rounded or heart-shaped bases. Flowers have five pink petals with shallowly notched tips. The surrounding calyx, the joined green sepals, is about 9–17 mm long and has five strong, often winglike ridges. Round capsules stay enclosed within it and contain dark, roughly 2 mm seeds. These ridges are especially useful when comparing Cow soapwort with other pink-flowered members of the carnation family. Photograph a flower from the side, the leaf attachment, the whole plant, and an old fruiting calyx; flowers alone provide less useful evidence.
actions: Remove unwanted Cow soapwort before capsules ripen, taking the taproot with the plant when the soil allows easy pulling. If mature capsules are present, collect the tops carefully before handling the rest so loose seeds remain contained. Check disturbed beds and field margins for another generation the following season. In a planned ornamental planting, deadhead to limit self-sowing and keep collected seed clearly labeled. Use clean crop seed and avoid moving seed-contaminated soil or harvest debris to a new site. A few isolated plants need not prompt broad treatment; document repeated establishment or crop interference and obtain local advice if a field-scale problem develops.

sources.title: World Flora Online: Vaccaria hispanica, Flora of North America treatment

researchNotes: Annual seed-prevention guidance is inferred from verified life history. Alternative modern generic placement was not needed to establish catalog identity; only verified older synonym listed.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Flora of North America / World Flora Online
claims: Hairless annual to 100 cm; five winged calyx ridges; pink petals, enclosed capsules and 2–2.5 mm seeds.
Blue-green erect herb of cultivated and waste ground; European origin; pink flowers, persistent fruits; V. pyramidata synonym.
Slender taprooted annual with opposite unstalked leaves and smooth stems.

proposedDescription: Cowpea witchweed is a small parasitic plant that attaches to another plant's roots and draws resources from it. Its own leaves are reduced to tiny scales, and clusters of short flowering stems may be the first visible sign above ground. Different forms use different broadleaf hosts, including cowpea and several wild or introduced legumes. This host specialization matters: damage documented on cowpea elsewhere should not automatically be assigned to every population. Florida records include plants associated with hairy indigo and alyce clover. A suspected new occurrence deserves expert attention because tiny seeds and an underground phase make casual removal an incomplete response.
identification: Plants are often about 10–35 cm high, with somewhat fleshy stems branching near the base. They may be greenish yellow or reddish purple. The very small leaves, commonly 5–10 mm long, lie close against the stem rather than forming a broad leafy canopy. Tubular flowers vary from pale or creamy white to pink, blue, or purple, so color is unreliable by itself. Cowpea witchweed differs from the familiar cereal-associated Striga asiatica and S. hermonthica in its reduced, scalelike foliage and broadleaf host associations, but confirmation requires a botanical key. Photograph the whole plant, flowers from the front and side, leaves, and neighboring potential hosts. Do not dig up roots or carry seed-bearing samples elsewhere merely to improve a photograph.
actions: Record the exact location and contact your state plant regulatory office or extension service before disturbing a suspected Cowpea witchweed patch. Send photographs and list nearby crops or legumes, while distinguishing a plant growing nearby from a proven root host. Keep soil, harvested seed, nursery plants, and muddy tools from moving off the affected spot until you receive guidance. Avoid mowing or pulling mature plants in ways that scatter capsules. If sampling is requested, follow the receiving specialist's directions for containment. A control plan may need repeated inspections and seedbank management; disappearance of visible stems alone does not demonstrate that the parasite is gone.

sources.title: Kew: Striga gesnerioides, African flora treatments

researchNotes: Florida host records dated explicitly in evidence; no unverified current range or US regulatory status. Reporting and containment are precautionary, not a legal claim. Genus-level movement guidance separated from species-specific biology.

claims: Small succulent branching parasite; scalelike leaves; variable flower color and host-associated forms.
Species attacks broadleaf hosts; underground infection precedes emergence; host and morphological diagnosis needed; contaminated commodities require inspection.
Florida detections associated with introduced legumes; multiple host-associated strains and crop hosts described.
Witchweed seeds spread with contaminated soil, machinery and planting material; S. gesnerioides distinguished from cereal witchweeds.

proposedDescription: Crack willow is a large deciduous willow associated with moist ground, riverbanks, and planted landscapes. The multiplication sign in Salix x fragilis identifies the hybrid between white willow and the willow treated as Salix euxina in current regional floras. Its branches can break at their bases, and detached pieces may root on wet ground. That allows a tree to spread along waterways without relying on seed. Older sources have used the name crack willow for different parts of this willow group, so records and management advice need to be checked against the hybrid concept rather than matched by common name alone.
identification: Trees are commonly about 3–20 m tall, with narrow, finely toothed leaves and upright to spreading or drooping branches. The leaf undersides are often pale, while hairs can range from sparse to nearly absent as leaves age. Young leaves may be noticeably silkier. Brittle branch bases are useful evidence but are not a stand-alone test, and deliberately snapping branches is unnecessary. White willow, Salix alba, and other tree-willow hybrids can be difficult to separate; leaf hairiness overlaps. Photograph mature and young leaves on both sides, leaf stalks, current-year twigs, the tree's form, and spring catkins when available. A botanist may need flowering material and multiple shoots to confirm a record, especially one originally labeled simply Salix fragilis.
actions: Do not leave pruned Crack willow branches on wet soil or in a stream, where fragments can take root. Collect cut material and arrange disposal that prevents contact with suitable rooting sites. Small seedlings or newly rooted fragments can be removed with their roots where this will not disturb a streambank. Mature trees near water or structures need a coordinated assessment: cutting alone may lead to regrowth, and abrupt removal can destabilize a bank. Consult a local land manager or arborist about staged removal and replacement vegetation where spread is a problem. Revisit the site for stump shoots and rooted fragments after floods or pruning.

proposedDescription: This Crambid moth, Duponchelia fovealis, is widely known as European pepper moth. Its caterpillars feed on many kinds of plants, including bedding ornamentals and vegetables, and can hide near the soil surface, among damp debris, or inside damaged stems. A greenhouse plant may therefore decline before the feeding caterpillar is noticed. Adults are small brown moths with pale curved lines across the wings. Although peppers are one host, the common name should not narrow an inspection to that crop. The species can also use decaying plant material, making sanitation and careful inspection of incoming plants important parts of nursery management.
identification: Adults have a wingspan of about 19–21 mm and gray-brown forewings crossed by two pale lines. The outer line bends outward in a conspicuous fingerlike projection. Males have a relatively long, slender abdomen that often curves upward at rest. Mature caterpillars are about 17–19 mm long, cream-colored with rows of darker spots and a shiny dark head. Look for silk, droppings, chewed lower leaves, and damaged stems near the potting-medium surface. Many crambid caterpillars look similar, so feeding damage alone cannot confirm this species. Photograph an unworn adult from above, a side view of its abdomen, the larva, and its feeding site. Keep a specimen available for an extension diagnostician when nursery stock is affected.
actions: Separate suspect plants from clean nursery stock while arranging identification. Inspect their lower leaves, crowns, pot rims, and the surface of the growing medium for larvae or silk. Remove accumulated dead leaves and leftover plants from benches and beneath containers, and correct unnecessarily wet conditions without stressing the crop. These steps reduce the moist hiding places used by the caterpillars. Examine neighboring pots and incoming shipments rather than checking only visibly wilted plants. In a nursery, ask an extension specialist about monitoring traps and a crop-specific management plan. A moth at a porch light is an observation worth recording, but does not by itself show that nearby plants are infested.

claims: Adults 19–21 mm wingspan with pale transverse lines; male abdomen curves upward; larvae 17–19 mm with spots and dark heads; broad hosts.

proposedDescription: This Crambid moth is recorded in current North American sources as Nacoleia charesalis; Lamprosema charesalis is an older combination for the same named species. It is a small brown moth native to the Asian and Australasian tropics and first detected in Florida in 2012. Caterpillars feed in decaying vegetation and have also been recorded boring into turmeric stems in their native range. Those habits do not establish that every adult near a garden is causing damage. The insect resembles several other crambids, including a related banana pest, so an identification should come before conclusions about affected plants.
identification: An adult has forewings about 9–11.5 mm long, brown with darker gray-brown lines. The outer cross-line makes two rounded outward bends, resembling a broad letter B, and a circular hollow spot lies nearer the wing center. Hindwing lines resemble those on the forewings; the mouthpart projections curve upward. Unworn adults can be identified from good photographs, but worn specimens may need specialist examination. Nacoleia octasema, the banana scab moth, is a related species whose damage should not be attributed here without confirmation. Caterpillars are pale with brown heads and darker spots; current regional guidance calls for rearing to an adult for larval identification. Photograph the moth's upper wings, body, size, and the place it was found.
actions: Record a suspected adult with the date, location, and clear photographs, particularly outside an already documented area. If caterpillars occur in a nursery shipment or turmeric stem, keep that material separate and ask an extension entomologist how to submit it for identification. Record actual feeding or tunnels rather than assuming that a moth resting on a plant uses it as a host. Removing decaying nursery debris and inspecting affected stems are reasonable sanitation steps, but the reviewed evidence does not justify routine garden spraying for an isolated adult. Do not transfer caterpillars or infested cuttings to another site, and let a diagnostic service manage any rearing needed for confirmation.

proposedDescription: Crapemyrtle is a deciduous shrub or small tree familiar for summer clusters of crinkled flowers and bark that peels to reveal smooth patches beneath. Cultivars range widely in height and flower color, from compact garden shrubs to small shade trees. The species comes from Asia and has been planted extensively beyond its native range. It sometimes persists or produces volunteers near old plantings, but introduced status alone does not make it a damaging invader. Regional assessments describe it as a limited escape in some areas. Many modern landscape plants are hybrids, so a familiar garden appearance does not always establish pure Lagerstroemia indica.
identification: Typical trees and large shrubs may reach roughly 5–10 m, although dwarf cultivars remain much shorter. Look for smooth, peeling bark; simple, short-stalked leaves with unlobed margins; and branching clusters of six-petaled, distinctly crinkled flowers at shoot tips. Pink, red, purple, and white flowers occur in cultivated material. Brown woody capsules follow flowering and split open when mature. Leaf arrangement can be opposite, alternate, or occasionally in threes. Hybrids involving Japanese crapemyrtle, often labeled Lagerstroemia fauriei or L. subcostata var. fauriei, overlap strongly with this species. Photograph bark, leaves, flower clusters, capsules, and the whole plant, and retain cultivar labels or planting records. Those records may be needed to resolve hybrid identity.
actions: A planted Crapemyrtle does not need removal simply because it is nonnative. Check nearby beds and disturbed ground for unwanted seedlings, and pull those while small if they are spreading beyond the intended planting. Remove unwanted seed clusters where practical. For a retained tree, choose pruning that preserves its natural form; repeated severe topping is not needed to manage a well-chosen plant's size. If a tree must be removed, monitor the site for new shoots and seedlings. Photograph any plants establishing away from cultivation and ask a local botanical or extension service whether they warrant recording. Keep cultivar information with observations so garden hybrids are not automatically recorded as the species.

researchNotes: Pure species versus cultivated hybrids remains an observation-level limit, not a taxon gap. UF page open redirected repeatedly; indexed content read. Regional low-impact assessments not generalized as proof of harmlessness everywhere.

claims: Deciduous tree or shrub, peeling bark, six crinkled petals, capsules, cultivar size variation and numerous hybrid parentages; severe topping unnecessary.
Tree to 5–10 m; terminal colored flower clusters; oval dry capsules and Asian distribution.
Commonly cultivated, persistent near plantings and only weakly spreading in the regional flora.
Regional assessment does not consider it a problem species.

proposedDescription: Cream narcissus is a bulb-forming perennial that produces clusters of fragrant flowers above upright, strap-shaped leaves. A short yellow or orange cup sits in the center of each flower, usually surrounded by pale outer segments. The bulbs can survive for years at old home sites and garden edges, making a spring clump a possible trace of former cultivation. This species is widely grown and sometimes naturalizes, but persistence alone is not evidence of aggressive spread. Names used for cultivated narcissus can be loose: some plants called paperwhites belong to another species, while garden hybrids further complicate identification.
identification: Flowering stems are often around 30–50 cm tall, with flat or slightly channeled leaves roughly 20–50 cm long and 5–25 mm wide. Several fragrant flowers share one stem, commonly four to ten, although cultivated forms vary. The central cup is short, about 3–6 mm high, and yellow to orange. Paperwhite narcissus, Narcissus papyraceus, typically has a white cup as well as white outer segments; older references sometimes combine these names. Photograph a fresh flower face and side view, the entire flower cluster, and the width and cross-section of a leaf. Record the cup's actual color in daylight. Bulbs or dormant clumps alone are difficult to identify, and unusual cultivated forms may require specialist review.
actions: Where Cream narcissus is wanted, keep it within the intended planting and check adjacent ground for new clumps. Remove spent flowers before seed develops if limiting spread is the goal. To remove an unwanted patch, lift the bulbs and their smaller offsets rather than cutting foliage alone, then inspect the spot in the next growing season. Keep discarded bulbs and bulb-bearing soil out of natural areas. Handle and label lifted bulbs as ornamental plants, keeping them separate from edible bulbs and out of reach of children and pets. If recording a naturalized population, photograph flowers before removal and note whether it occupies an old garden or is spreading farther away.

sources.title: NC State Plant Toolbox: Narcissus tazetta

researchNotes: Species-level entry; no subspecies chosen from flower color alone. NCSU common-name treatment is broad, so papyraceus comparison independently checked. Bulb removal is practical prevention, not a claimed eradication trial.

claims: Bulbous perennial with 20–50 cm leaves, several fragrant flowers, short yellow-orange cup, cultivation escapes and persistent old gardens.
Bulb-forming perennial, division and seed propagation, spreading clumps and toxic bulbs.
N. tazetta has yellow-orange cups; N. papyraceus has white cups; both may be called paperwhites.

proposedDescription: Cream-anther field pepperwort is a small mustard-family plant that often begins as a low rosette, then sends up flowering stems in spring. Its tiny pale flowers give way to crowded, oval seedpods that are easier to notice than the blossoms. The stems and leaves carry short hairs, and upper leaves clasp the stem with pointed bases. Native to Europe and western Asia, it is introduced in North America and occurs in disturbed ground, gardens, orchards, and fields. It reproduces by seed and may behave as an annual or biennial, so preventing mature pods is the central task where it is unwanted.
identification: Flowering plants can reach about 60 cm tall. Lower leaves form a rosette and may be toothed or lobed, while upper leaves are unstalked and clasp the stem with arrowlike bases. Short hairs cover leaves and stems. Flowers have four small white to greenish-white petals. The oval pods are about 5–6 mm long, relatively plump, and winged toward the notched tip. Virginia pepperweed, Lepidium virginicum, has non-clasping stem leaves and rounder, flatter fruits. Field pennycress, Thlaspi arvense, is generally hairless and has much flatter pods. Photograph the leaf bases, stem hairs, and mature pods with a ruler. A basal rosette without fruit is less reliable because many mustard-family weeds have similar young leaves.
actions: Remove Cream-anther field pepperwort while it is still a rosette or before its pods mature. In a small bed, pulling the taproot after rain or shallow hoeing of young plants can prevent that plant from setting seed. Collect mature fruiting stems carefully rather than scattering pods while mowing or carrying them. Inspect the patch again in fall and early spring, when new seedlings often appear. Maintain the intended groundcover and limit unnecessary soil disturbance around an affected bed. Use clean seed and check soil or plant debris before transferring it elsewhere. In crops or hay fields, match follow-up work to the crop schedule and local advice rather than assuming one cutting has exhausted the seedbank.

Annual or winter annual reproducing by seed; emergence often fall or early spring; crop competitiveness evidence variable.

proposedDescription: Creeping Bentgrass forms low, fine-leaved patches linked by stems that travel across the soil surface. Each rooted joint can extend the patch, which explains why pulling a few blades seldom removes it. This perennial is cultivated for turf but also occupies disturbed ground and damp margins. It tolerates a wider range of soils than its association with wet lawns suggests. Its presence alone does not show that a natural area is being damaged; the practical concern is whether the patch is expanding into vegetation that the landowner wants to retain.
identification: Unmown shoots commonly stand about 8–40 cm tall. Look for slender, pointed, green to gray-green leaves and horizontal aboveground runners with roots at their joints. The blades are rolled inside young shoots. At the junction of blade and sheath, a thin, relatively long membrane is visible; there are no clasping ear-shaped projections. Flowering stems carry many tiny spikelets on branching heads. Common bentgrass, Agrostis capillaris, and rough bluegrass, Poa trivialis, are documented lookalikes. Photograph a runner still attached to its shoots, the leaf junction, and an open flowerhead. A closely clipped patch lacks several useful features, so color or texture alone cannot confirm the species.
actions: Trace the runners beyond the center of an unwanted patch before removing it. For a small lawn or bed infestation, lift the rooted mat and collect attached runners; detached shoots can establish again. Keep removed material out of soil being moved to another bed. Recheck the margin during active growth and remove new shoots while they are easy to trace. Correct avoidable overwatering where it contributes to thin turf, then restore suitable groundcover so the opening does not remain available. For a large patch, ask a turf or restoration adviser to plan renovation around the plants you want to keep.
researchNotes: Independent flora and university evidence support the spreading-stem diagnosis. Management is a conservative synthesis of documented vegetative spread; no chemical prescription or promise of eradication is made.

claims: Introduced perennial reproduces by seed and stolons; leaves rolled in bud; no auricles; membranous ligule.
Plants commonly 8–40 cm; detached shoots spread; broad soil tolerance.
Common bentgrass and rough bluegrass listed as similar species.

proposedDescription: Creeping Buttercup is a perennial of damp lawns, pasture edges, and other moist ground. Its yellow flowers rise above spreading leaves, while runners put down roots at their joints and create new plants. Seed adds another route of spread. A patch can therefore persist even when its flowers are cut off. It is especially noticeable in spring and early summer, when flowering makes scattered plants easier to find. Dense patches can crowd thin turf. In grazing areas, identification matters because fresh buttercup material can be harmful to livestock.
identification: Look for dark green leaves divided into three main sections, often with pale blotches. The middle leaflet commonly has a short stalk, and leaflet edges have coarse teeth and deep cuts. Mature leaves are roughly 1.5–3 inches long; stems can trail much farther than the upright flowers suggest. The bright yellow flowers have five or more petals, and rooted runners are a stronger clue than flower color alone. Tall buttercup, Ranunculus acris, is a documented similar species. Photograph a whole leaf, its stalk, a flower, and a runner joining two rooted plants. A flower-only photograph cannot reliably distinguish the many yellow buttercups.
actions: Work through small patches when the soil is moist enough to release the roots. Follow each runner and lift its rooted joints rather than pulling only the flowering stem. Collect the pieces and watch for regrowth around the patch. Reduce avoidable compaction and overwatering in lawns, and repair thin turf after removal. Where buttercups are abundant in a pasture, arrange identification and forage-management advice before turning animals into the affected area. Keep removed plants away from feed. A veterinarian should assess suspected poisoning; plant removal is not a substitute for treatment. Larger recurring infestations need a plan that addresses both established plants and seedlings.

USDA NRCS: plant materials field guide
Canadian Food Inspection Agency: Creeping buttercup seed
Penn State: Weed Management in Pasture Systems

Moist-area perennial; stems to 40 inches; five or more yellow petals.
