proposedDescription: Edible fig is a spreading deciduous shrub or small tree with broad lobed leaves and the familiar fleshy figs. Its flowers are hidden inside the developing fig rather than displayed as an open blossom. Many cultivated varieties can form a crop without pollination, but fruit production and viable seed production are different processes. The tree also sends up shoots from its roots, and discarded branches can take root. In parts of California it forms dense patches along waterways. An established fruit tree in a garden should be assessed by its local spread, not by fruiting alone.
identification: Look for a multistemmed woody plant that may reach about 3–10 meters tall, with pale gray bark and large alternate leaves. The leaves commonly have three to five broad lobes and a rough upper surface; their size and degree of lobing vary. Figs develop where leaves join the branches and may ripen green, yellowish, brown or dark purple according to the cultivar. A small opening at the far end is a useful detail. The plant loses its leaves in cold seasons, making bare shoots less distinctive. Photograph a leafy branch, bark, fruit and any shoots emerging away from the main trunk. A photograph does not reliably establish cultivar, pollination requirements or whether a small shoot is a seedling rather than a root sucker.
actions: Watch for young Edible fig plants beyond the planting area, especially along drains or moist ground. Remove unwanted small seedlings while their roots are manageable, but check whether they are attached to a larger root system. Avoid skin contact with the milky sap; wear gloves and protective clothing when cutting. Collect fallen fruit and keep fresh branches or root pieces out of waterways and dumped garden waste. Cutting an established plant can produce vigorous new shoots, so plan follow-up rather than treating one cut as removal. For large trees or thickets beside a stream, ask a qualified local adviser about removal that protects the bank and surrounding vegetation.
researchNotes: NC State and John Randall's Cal-IPC treatment independently support size, leaves, sap precautions, root suckering and discarded-branch rooting. NC State's general statement that North American fruit forms without pollination is narrowed to many cultivated varieties, consistent with the detailed Cal-IPC pollination discussion. Historical control recipes and current legal status are not reproduced. The native-range wording differs among older accounts, so no unnecessarily precise origin is asserted.

sources.title: California Invasive Plant Council — Edible Fig, by John M. Randall

claims: Deciduous multistemmed tree with lobed leaves, variable fruit colors, suckers and skin-irritating milky sap.
Fig flowers develop within a receptacle; cultivars differ in pollination needs; root sprouts and fallen branches can establish; young plants can be removed but cutting triggers regrowth.

proposedDescription: Eel pest, here referring to Gyrodactylus anguillae, is a small parasitic flatworm associated with the skin and gills of eels. Its common name is also used for other eel parasites, making the scientific name important. Researchers have identified it on more than one eel species, and movement of live eels has helped carry parasites between regions. Infection does not automatically explain a sick or dying fish: a study of affected young European eels found several parasites together and could not attribute the deaths to this species alone. Diagnosis therefore needs an examination of the fish and its surroundings.
identification: This is a microscopic identification rather than one made from a photograph of an eel. Gyrodactylus has a rear attachment organ armed with hooks, and specialists compare the shapes and measurements of those hardened parts. Gyrodactylus anguillae and G. nipponensis have both been reported from cultured European eels, so the host's identity alone cannot separate them. Other organisms can occur on the same skin or gills. Useful information for a diagnostic laboratory includes the eel species, where and when it was acquired, water conditions, recent movements and the onset of any symptoms. Ask the laboratory how it wants samples collected and preserved; damaged or deteriorated worms can lose the features needed for a reliable species identification.
actions: Do not move suspect eels into another pond, aquarium or natural waterbody while arranging a diagnosis. Keep records of the source of each group and any recent additions so a fish-health professional can assess possible transmission. Use a separate quarantine setup for new arrivals and equipment that is not shared with established fish. For affected animals, arrange prompt professional examination rather than trying to identify the parasite from behavior alone. Report unusual illness or deaths in wild eels to the local fisheries authority with the location and date. Follow the diagnostic service's instructions for specimens and wastewater; an improvised salt bath or medication is not a substitute for determining the cause.
researchNotes: Two independent studies were read at abstract level: the Australian morphology/host study and the Spanish mixed-infection study; full text of the latter was blocked at Stirling and PubMed opening presented a verification page. The Ogawa/Egusa abstract independently supports G. nipponensis as a host-overlapping comparison. No unverified hook measurements, U.S. prevalence or single-agent mortality claim is included. UF/IFAS supports general diagnostic/quarantine practice. Earlier Australian native-origin hypotheses are not presented as settled global origin.

sources.title: Ernst, Fletcher and Hayward — Gyrodactylus anguillae from Australian Eels
Hirt-Chabbert and colleagues — Infection of Glass Eels in Spain
Ogawa and Egusa — Gyrodactylus Infestations of Cultured Eels in Japan

claims: Hook morphology supported identification from two Australian eel species; native versus introduced status was posed as a hypothesis.
G. anguillae occurred with other parasites; mortality could not be attributed to one pathogen.
Both G. anguillae and G. nipponensis occurred on European eels; the former was considered introduced with eels from France.
Quarantine and diagnostic examination help prevent parasite introductions; fish may look healthy while carrying parasites; treatment must account for parasite life cycle and husbandry.

proposedDescription: Eel pest, in this entry Pseudodactylogyrus anguillae, is a small flatworm that attaches to eel gills. It shares its common name and its host fish with several other parasites, including Pseudodactylogyrus bini. The two can occur together, but they differ in their attachment structures and some habitat tolerances. P. anguillae has been studied on eels in both fresh and brackish water. Live-fish movements are an important concern because an eel can carry small parasites without an obvious external change. A fish-health examination is more informative than assuming that clear-looking skin means the gills are parasite-free.
identification: Adults are around 1–1.5 millimeters long in the University of Tokyo comparison, although preserved specimens and life stages differ. A microscope reveals the rear attachment organ, or haptor, and the hooks that hold the worm to a gill. Pseudodactylogyrus anguillae has relatively long, slender anchors and a roughly heart-shaped haptor; P. bini has shorter, stouter anchors and a more oval haptor. These are specialist characters, not features visible on a swimming eel. The similar Australian species P. rohdei requires additional comparison of internal structures and the attachment apparatus. Provide the diagnostic service with host identity, origin, salinity and recent transfer history. General gill irritation, excess mucus or breathing difficulty cannot establish which parasite, if any, is responsible.
actions: Pause transfers of eels from an affected holding system and contact a fish-health veterinarian or diagnostic laboratory. Record whether fish came from fresh or brackish water, their supplier and any shared equipment or water connections. Quarantine new eels separately, including apparently healthy arrivals. Avoid moving used nets or untreated holding water between systems. Because this parasite has an egg-laying life cycle, removing visible worms from a fish does not demonstrate that its environment is clear. Have the professional plan follow-up checks as well as any treatment. For unusual illness in wild eels, report the site and observations to the fisheries authority without transporting live fish elsewhere.
researchNotes: Tokyo's direct comparative account and Saraiva's independent workshop treatment support practical dimensions, attachment morphology and brackish occurrence. The 2015 revision is abstract-only because the full Folia PDF timed out; it is used to flag P. rohdei rather than to invent a simplified key. Species is accepted, and historical Australian misidentifications do not make this catalog taxon unresolved. No chemical recipe, universal salinity cure or blanket impact on wild eels is claimed.

sources.title: University of Tokyo Fish Parasite Database — Pseudodactylogyrus bini
Saraiva — Origin, Distribution and Morphology of Pseudodactylogyrus
Ogawa and colleagues — Three New Species of Pseudodactylogyrus from Australian Eels

claims: Gill parasite with direct transmission and egg-laying development; bini is about 2 mm with smaller anchors than anguillae, which is about 1–1.5 mm; heavy infection damages gills.
P. bini has an oval attachment organ and stout anchors; P. anguillae has a heart-shaped organ and longer slender anchors; eel trade has spread these parasites.
Earlier Australian identifications as bini and anguillae included separate species now named P. gusevi and P. rohdei; reproductive and attachment structures distinguish them.
Quarantine and diagnostic examination help prevent parasite introductions; fish may look healthy while carrying parasites; treatment must account for parasite life cycle and husbandry.

proposedDescription: Eel pest, here Pseudodactylogyrus bini, is a gill-dwelling flatworm best known from studies of cultured eels. It anchors to the delicate gill tissue and can interfere with breathing when infections become severe. Young eels may be especially vulnerable, while an infected fish can show little change on its outer body. The parasite lays eggs and develops without needing a different animal as an intermediate host. That life cycle makes the movement of eels and their holding environment important. The shared name “Eel pest” should always be paired with the scientific name when discussing a laboratory result.
identification: An adult is approximately 2 millimeters long in the University of Tokyo account. Under magnification, its rear attachment organ bears a pair of substantial anchors, around 50–60 micrometers long in that description. Pseudodactylogyrus bini has a broadly oval attachment organ and shorter, stouter anchors than P. anguillae, whose anchors are longer despite its often smaller body. Size alone is inadequate because age and specimen preparation affect measurements. Another close relative, P. gusevi, was separated from some older Australian records using reproductive and attachment structures. A fish photograph cannot resolve those distinctions. A laboratory needs suitable gill material and the eel's identity and origin. Let trained staff obtain samples; handling or cutting gills without appropriate expertise can harm the fish.
actions: For a suspected infection, keep the affected group separate and ask a fish-health professional to examine the gills. Tell the service about recent arrivals, water temperature, mortality and any previous treatment. Do not sell, release or transfer suspect eels to clear space in the tank. Have a professional assess the entire holding system, because eggs and developing stages may persist beyond the worms currently found on the fish. Clean and manage empty equipment or ponds under that plan rather than applying an unverified treatment to occupied water. Maintain separate nets for separate groups and document follow-up results before resuming transfers. Healthy-looking skin alone is not a clearance check.
researchNotes: The Tokyo account was read in full and supplies species-specific life cycle and pathology; Saraiva independently corroborates the oval haptor/stout-anchor contrast. The 2015 revision was read as an abstract and prevents old P. gusevi records from being transferred indiscriminately to P. bini. The Tokyo page's historical pesticide dose is omitted. System-level containment and follow-up are bounded fish-health practice, not a claim that a particular household treatment eradicates the parasite.

sources.title: University of Tokyo Fish Parasite Database — Pseudodactylogyrus bini
Saraiva — Origin, Distribution and Morphology of Pseudodactylogyrus
Ogawa and colleagues — Three New Species of Pseudodactylogyrus from Australian Eels

claims: Gill parasite with direct transmission and egg-laying development; bini is about 2 mm with smaller anchors than anguillae, which is about 1–1.5 mm; heavy infection damages gills.
P. bini has an oval attachment organ and stout anchors; P. anguillae has a heart-shaped organ and longer slender anchors; eel trade has spread these parasites.
Earlier Australian identifications as bini and anguillae included separate species now named P. gusevi and P. rohdei; reproductive and attachment structures distinguish them.
Quarantine and diagnostic examination help prevent parasite introductions; fish may look healthy while carrying parasites; treatment must account for parasite life cycle and husbandry.

proposedDescription: Eggplant is a warm-season crop grown for its smooth, fleshy fruits, which range from familiar dark purple forms to white, green, striped, round and slender varieties. The plants have broad leaves and violet, star-shaped flowers with a yellow center. They are sensitive to cold and are commonly grown for a single season, though they can live longer in warm conditions. A volunteer beside a garden or discarded fruit is not evidence that the crop is invading natural habitat. Confirming the plant and observing whether it persists beyond cultivation is more useful than treating every cultivated food plant as a removal target.
identification: Most garden Eggplant plants grow about 60–120 centimeters tall and develop several branches. Leaves are alternate, broadly oval and sometimes shallowly lobed, with branched, star-shaped hairs best seen through a hand lens. Stems, leaves and the green cup around a fruit may carry prickles in some varieties. Flowers generally have five or more pointed violet lobes around yellow anthers. Fruit size, shape and color vary too widely to use one supermarket form as a universal guide. Other Solanum species also have star-shaped flowers and hairy or prickly foliage, so do not identify an unfamiliar wild nightshade as Eggplant from the flower alone. Photograph a complete branch, leaf hairs, the fruit's attachment and several developmental stages; a known planting history is especially helpful.
actions: Keep deliberate Eggplant cultivation within managed beds or containers, and collect unwanted ripe or damaged fruit rather than dumping it on unmanaged ground. Remove a confirmed unwanted volunteer with its roots while it is small, then check for further seedlings. If the plant's identity is uncertain, photograph it and obtain horticultural advice before eating any fruit. Leaves and other non-fruit parts should not be used as food. In an established vegetable bed, harvest by clipping the fruit stalk rather than pulling and tearing the plant. Diagnose unusual leaf damage or wilting before taking action; insect feeding, disease and growing conditions can produce different problems that need different responses.
researchNotes: NC State's detailed morphology and University of Minnesota's independent cultivation guidance support a crop-focused profile. Fruit shape and color are explicitly variable, and the draft does not use an unsupported native-range claim or allege national ecological harm. No named wild-nightshade lookalike key was verified, so identification remains bounded to a full plant with provenance. Volunteer removal is modest garden prevention, not an invasive-weed efficacy assertion.

sources.title: University of Minnesota Extension — Growing Eggplant

claims: Cold-sensitive crop with star-shaped hairs, violet flowers, variable fruits and sometimes prickles; vegetative parts should not be eaten.
Warmth is important; clip fruits with shears; plant symptoms need diagnosis before management.

proposedDescription: Egyptian broomrape is a parasitic flowering plant that obtains water and nutrients from another plant's roots. Much of its development happens underground; the yellowish or purplish shoots become noticeable when they emerge to flower beside the host. It has tiny scale-like leaves rather than ordinary green foliage. Agricultural hosts include tomato and other broadleaf crops. Its numerous minute seeds make accidental movement in soil a concern. Native broomrapes are also part of North American vegetation, so an unfamiliar parasitic plant needs expert identification before it is disturbed or treated as this agricultural pest.
identification: Look for upright, sticky-hairy shoots near a possible host plant, sometimes hidden beneath its leaves. The stems may be simple or branched and carry small triangular scales. Flowers are tubular and purple to pale, with an upper lip divided into two lobes and a lower lip divided into three. Flowers about 20–35 millimeters long are typical of Egyptian broomrape; the similar branched broomrape (Phelipanche ramosa) usually has flowers no longer than about 20 millimeters. There is overlap, so flower length is a clue rather than a final determination. Photograph the plant in place, nearby hosts and flowers from several angles with a scale. Native broomrapes and borderline Phelipanche specimens require a botanist's examination; do not dig up the attachment to prove the association.
actions: Leave a suspected Egyptian broomrape in place and promptly send photographs and its precise location to your state agriculture department or local agricultural extension service. In California, the county agricultural commissioner is the reporting route given by CDFA, which specifically advises against collecting specimens. Avoid walking or driving through the patch and pause movement of soil, plants or equipment from the affected area until you receive instructions. Keep others from mowing or composting the shoots. Removal of a visible stalk does not address seeds or the underground parasite. Let the responding specialist confirm the species and coordinate containment with the grower or landowner, particularly where crops or planting materials are involved.
researchNotes: CDFA's diagnostic sheet and UC weed-science comparison were read in full. CDFA explicitly says not to collect specimens; the public actions preserve that instruction. UC's simplified genus-level branching rule is not used because CDFA documents unbranched Egyptian broomrape as well. Measurements distinguish typical plants but do not erase overlap. Current legal listings and historical pesticide trials are unnecessary to the bounded reporting advice and are not asserted.

sources.title: California Department of Food and Agriculture — Egyptian Broomrape
UC Agriculture and Natural Resources — Broomrape Species

claims: Root parasite with simple or branched sticky shoots, reduced leaves, purple two-lipped flowers and many small seeds; report without collecting specimens.
Egyptian broomrape flowers typically 20–35 mm versus usually at most 20 mm in branched broomrape; related crop hosts and serious agricultural effects.

proposedDescription: Egyptian Goose is a sturdy waterbird with pink legs, a dark eye patch and a pale gray-brown body. It grazes beside ponds and lakes, often in pairs or family groups, but also feeds in shallow water. Despite its name, it belongs closer to shelducks than to the familiar true geese. Native to Africa, it has established introduced populations in parts of the United States. Pairs can use tree holes, ledges or abandoned bird nests as well as ground sites, and may defend the nest vigorously. A bird standing well above the water is therefore no surprise.
identification: Adults measure about 63–73 cm long. Look for a reddish-brown patch surrounding a pale orange eye, pink bill and legs, and a dark mark on the breast. A flying bird shows large white areas across the front of otherwise dark wings. Young birds retain the pink bill and legs but lack the adult eye mask, so a family photograph can help. Muscovy Duck also has conspicuous white wing patches, but typical adults are much darker and have red, wartlike skin on the face. Photograph the head, breast, legs and, if the bird opens its wings naturally, the wing pattern. Sex is less reliably judged from a distant photograph than species; males and females look similar.
actions: Observe from a distance and give pairs with young plenty of room; keep dogs from approaching or pursuing them. Do not release captive waterfowl or move free-living birds to another pond. Avoid feeding birds at a site where they are congregating, and secure spilled grain or pet feed. For a new local occurrence, record the date, location, number of adults and young, and clear photographs; a bird-recording project or state wildlife agency can assess the observation. If nesting birds create a recurring access or safety problem, contact the property manager and wildlife agency for a humane, site-specific response before handling birds, eggs or nests.
researchNotes: Cornell and Animal Diversity Web provide independent natural-history support. ADW contains an implausible wingspan figure and inconsistent incubation wording; neither is used. Actions are conservative observation and attractant management, not a claim of a nationwide removal requirement.

claims: Adults are 63–73 cm with pink bill and legs, eye masks and white forewings; young lack the eye mask.
Muscovy Duck is typically darker with red facial skin despite sharing white wing patches.
Pairs nest on ground or elevated sites; birds eat grasses and grains and defend breeding territories.

proposedDescription: Egyptian grass is a low, spreading annual whose seedheads resemble small crow’s feet. Several short branches radiate from the top of a stalk, each lined with tightly packed spikelets. The lower stems can lie along the ground and root at their joints, producing mats in disturbed soil. It grows especially well in warm conditions and occurs in fields, paths and other open ground. Its origin is in Africa and Asia, and its behavior varies by place: Florida’s assessment distinguishes greater invasion concerns in the central and southern regions from a caution rating in the north.
identification: Plants commonly stand about 15–60 cm high, with flat, narrow leaves and hairs along at least part of their margins. The flowering head usually has two to five short branches, each about 1–5 cm long. Look closely for a bare, pointed extension beyond the last spikelets at each branch tip. The small flap where the blade meets its sheath has a membranous base and a hairy fringe; magnification helps. Goosegrass, Eleusine indica, has a similar fingered head, but commonly carries a branch below the main cluster and has a conspicuously pale, flattened center to its clump. Photograph the entire head, its branch tips, leaf bases and rooted lower joints. Immature plants without seedheads are harder to separate confidently.
actions: For a small confirmed patch in a garden, loosen moist soil and lift the whole plant before its seedheads mature, including lower joints that have rooted. Gather any developed seedheads before carrying plants across the site. Check the surrounding bare ground for seedlings during warm weather and restore suitable ground cover rather than leaving open soil. Avoid moving soil or turf from a seeded patch into clean beds, and remove clinging material from tools and mower decks before moving elsewhere. Larger infestations in turf or crops warrant local extension advice matched to that setting. These steps limit spread; one pulling session does not establish that the site is clear.
researchNotes: Texas flora, FAO and UF provide independent support for morphology, annual life history and region-specific concern. Goosegrass comparison comes from an indexed UF turf-guide excerpt, explicitly labeled. Hand removal is bounded preventive guidance based on rooted joints and seed production, not a tested eradication claim.

sources.title: UF turfgrass pest-control guide: grass identification

claims: Annual stems root at lower nodes; heads have two to five bristle-tipped branches and hairy leaf margins.
Annual grass is 15–60 cm tall, reproduces by seed and occurs in warm disturbed ground.
Florida assessment distinguishes central/southern invasive status from northern caution.
Goosegrass often has one head branch below the tip and a white flattened clump center; crowfootgrass has pointed head branches.

proposedDescription: Egyptian starcluster brings clusters of small, five-pointed flowers to warm-season gardens. Each apparent star ends a slender floral tube, and the clusters attract butterflies and hummingbirds. Red, pink and white forms are familiar, with other colors available among cultivars. The plant is a tropical shrub from eastern Africa and southern Arabia, but gardeners often grow it as a seasonal bedding plant where winters are cold. In warm places it can persist for several years. Its presence in a garden is not, by itself, evidence of harmful spread; plants appearing independently beyond cultivation are the observations worth distinguishing.
identification: Most garden plants are roughly 60–90 cm tall, although cultivar and climate affect their size. Leaves grow in opposite pairs and are pointed, oval to lance-shaped, commonly 8–14 cm long. Their veins are conspicuous and the surfaces hairy, rather than smooth and glossy. Look at an individual flower from the side to see its tube, then from the front to count five spreading lobes. Small dry capsules, about 4–5 mm long, follow flowering. Many unrelated bedding plants have clustered blossoms, so cluster color alone is weak evidence. Include a whole-plant photograph, a leaf pair with the stem junction visible, and a close view of a single flower. A nursery label can help distinguish cultivars but does not replace these features.
actions: Keep Egyptian starcluster within maintained beds or containers and watch nearby disturbed ground for independent seedlings, particularly where winters allow plants to persist. If unwanted volunteers appear, remove them while small and before they form mature capsules. Collect seed-bearing trimmings and avoid dumping living cuttings or garden waste at woodland edges, drains or vacant land; this species can be propagated from both seed and stem cuttings. A managed flowering plant does not automatically require removal. Where plants repeatedly establish outside the bed, document their distance from the planting and ask local extension whether the behavior is unusual for the area. Choose locally suitable replacements if continued containment becomes difficult.
researchNotes: NParks supplies diagnostic leaves, flowers and capsules; UF independently supports garden size, cold response and pollinator use. No evidence of nationwide ecological harm was established, so the profile distinguishes cultivation from escape and offers bounded prevention rather than an eradication mandate.

claims: Opposite hairy leaves are 8–14 cm; five-lobed flowers and 4–5 mm capsules occur; propagation uses seed and cuttings.
Garden plants often reach two to three feet; freezes cause dieback; flowers attract butterflies and hummingbirds.

proposedDescription: Elecampane inula is a tall perennial with broad leaves and yellow flowerheads surrounded by many narrow rays. A leafy rosette can occupy a substantial patch before flowering stems rise above it in summer. The plant comes from Eurasia and has become established along roadsides, in fields and around former plantings in North America. Its large leaves and sunflowerlike heads make it conspicuous, but neither feature alone identifies it. The roots have a long history of human use, which helps explain its cultivation; that history should not be treated as advice to prepare or consume a wild plant.
identification: Flowering plants may reach about 0.6–1.8 m tall. Lower leaves are broad, generally 10–20 cm across, with tapering bases and stalks; upper leaves become smaller and clasp the stem. Check the hairy undersides and prominent midveins. Summer heads carry a yellow central disc and numerous slender yellow rays, with leafy bracts beneath. Inula salicina has much narrower lower leaves, only about 1.2–2 cm wide. Doronicum pardalianches has rounded to broadly oval lower leaves with heart-shaped bases, whereas elecampane’s lower leaves taper toward their stalks. A young rosette can resemble mullein, making flowering material especially useful. Photograph a lower leaf with a scale, an upper leaf attachment, and the front and underside of a flowerhead.
actions: Where this perennial is spreading beyond an intended planting, remove developing flowerheads before the bristled fruits disperse. Wear gloves when handling it, since skin irritation is reported. Small unwanted plants can be carefully dug with their crown and roots; revisit the spot for renewed shoots instead of assuming the first removal was complete. Keep divisions and seed-bearing debris out of dumped garden waste, and inspect any plants you share for unintended seedlings. Large established patches beside native vegetation deserve an extension or land-manager assessment before extensive soil disturbance. Do not use uncertain identification as a basis for harvesting roots for remedies, flavorings or animal feed.
researchNotes: Go Botany independently supports morphology, North American introduced status and named comparisons. NC State supplies seasonal details, size and contact dermatitis, but its recent contaminated-nursery introduction narrative appears potentially conflated with another Inula and was deliberately excluded, as were its aggressive root-control claims.

claims: Introduced perennial of roadsides and fields; broad lower leaves distinguish it from I. salicina and leaf bases from Doronicum pardalianches.
Plants reach two to six feet, flower in summer and fall, have clasping upper leaves and may cause contact dermatitis.

proposedDescription: Elegant dutchman's pipe is a twining vine best recognized by its cream-colored flowers densely marked with purple. Their bent tube opens into a broad, heart-shaped face, giving the bloom its unusual outline. Native to South America, it was widely planted as an ornamental and has escaped in warm regions, including parts of Florida. Established vines can climb over and weigh down surrounding vegetation. The flower’s unpleasant odor attracts flies that pollinate it. References also use the scientific name Aristolochia littoralis for this plant. Its striking flowers do not make it safe to eat or use medicinally.
identification: Slender stems twine through supports, commonly reaching several meters; older stems become woody. Alternate, smooth-edged leaves are broadly heart-shaped, about 3–10 cm long, with paler undersides. Look for a small ear-shaped leafy flap at the base of the leaf stalk. The flower has one broad, purple-mottled opening, generally up to about 10 cm across. Brown, oblong capsules around 4–6 cm long release many flattened seeds. Giant dutchman’s pipe, Aristolochia gigantea, has much larger flowers and lacks the little ear-shaped flaps; Aristolochia ringens has a narrower flower divided into distinct upper and lower lobes. Photograph the entire flower, its side profile, leaf-stalk bases and any capsules. Leaves alone may not separate closely related ornamental vines.
actions: Prevent new escapes by avoiding planting or sharing this vine where it establishes outside gardens. On an existing planting, remove capsules before they open and contain them while working so seeds do not scatter. Small seedlings can be pulled carefully; established vines may regrow after cutting, so check the base repeatedly. Do not wrench a heavy tangle out of a supporting tree: seek help where removal could break branches or damage desirable vegetation. Keep cuttings and seed-bearing material out of dumped yard waste. For extensive growth, obtain a local management plan. Keep the plant away from food preparation and animal feed, and do not use it in home remedies.
researchNotes: UF and the independently authored Weeds of Australia account support recognition and spread pathways. Both link elegans with littoralis. Australian butterfly-host toxicity is not generalized to US butterflies; old Australian legal declarations are excluded. UF supports seedling pulling and warns that cutting may be followed by resprouting.

claims: Escaped climbing vine can weigh down vegetation; plant is toxic; prevent seeding, pull seedlings and expect possible resprouting.
Heart-shaped alternate leaves have ear-shaped stalk-base structures; flower and capsule measurements distinguish related ornamental vines.

proposedDescription: Elephant grass forms towering, bamboo-like clumps with long leaves and dense, bristly flowerheads. This African perennial was brought to the United States as a forage crop and has escaped into warm landscapes. Its rapid growth can produce useful biomass in managed settings, but unmanaged stands can crowd other vegetation and obstruct access along waterways. Pieces of mature stems and underground growth can establish new plants, making careless clearing a route of spread. Many older publications call it Pennisetum purpureum; that name refers to the same species now placed in Cenchrus.
identification: Flowering stems commonly reach 2–4 m tall and can grow taller. Leaves are long and narrow, up to about 1.2 m by 5 cm, with a conspicuous pale midrib and rough margins. A dense fringe of hairs marks the junction of the blade and its enclosing sheath. The flowerhead is a compact, bristly cylinder about 8–30 cm long, greenish, yellowish or purplish before browning. Mission grass, Cenchrus polystachios, can look similar; its flowerhead axis is angular rather than rounded, a detail best checked with magnification. Size alone is unreliable for young plants. Photograph the full clump, a head beside a ruler, the leaf-sheath junction and any lower stem joints rooting into the ground.
actions: Do not till an established clump: chopping mature stems and underground parts can distribute pieces that regrow. Avoid carrying living stems or contaminated soil to other properties, and clean equipment after work in a stand. Small seedlings are much easier to remove than mature clumps; lift their roots before they expand and revisit for new growth. Keep any cut mature material contained rather than using it as fresh mulch elsewhere. For a tall stand beside a canal, wetland or desirable vegetation, arrange a site-specific plan with extension or the land manager. Cutting can improve access, but it is a first step that requires follow-up, not evidence of eradication.
researchNotes: UF directly supports fragment-spread precautions and the distinction between seedlings and mature plants. The independent Australian account supports diagnostic details and mission-grass comparison. Seed versus vegetative dominance varies between accounts and settings, so no universal dominant pathway is asserted. No crop-specific chemical recipe is transferred.

claims: African perennial escapes cultivation; stems and underground fragments spread it; tilling mature plants may enlarge infestations.
Tall clumps have pale midribs, hairy ligules and bristly cylindrical heads; mission grass has an angular head axis.

proposedDescription: Elkhorn fern grows attached to trees or rocks, using its support as a place to live rather than drawing food from it. It makes two very different kinds of fronds: rounded shields that cover the base and long, repeatedly forked fronds that resemble antlers. The shields catch fallen material and help direct rain toward the roots. Often cultivated on boards or tree trunks, the fern can develop into a substantial colony. Brown areas beneath mature fertile fronds contain spore-producing structures; they are part of the fern’s life cycle, not automatically a disease or insect problem.
identification: Look for a clump with several growing points and rounded basal shields whose upper edges are lobed. Long foliage fronds, roughly 22–105 cm, divide into strap-shaped branches; mature fronds bear broad spore patches beneath their outer segments. Older shields turn coppery brown. Platycerium superbum usually has a single growing point, a large fanlike shield and a prominent spore patch at the first division of the fertile frond. Platycerium hillii has a shield with an unlobed upper edge. Platycerium veitchii is much more densely white-haired beneath, obscuring the veins. Photograph the whole colony, the shield’s upper margin and the underside of a mature fertile frond. Juvenile plants and cultivated forms may need specialist comparison before a species name is secure.
actions: Record whether a plant was deliberately mounted or appears to have established by itself; that distinction matters when documenting an escape. Leave normal brown shields and spore patches alone rather than treating them as pests. Keep cultivated plants on maintained supports, and do not place divisions on trees in natural areas or discard living fern material there. If an unwanted fern is small and safely reachable, seek advice on removing the entire attached base without damaging the supporting tree. Large colonies high in trees are a job for an arborist or land manager. A planted fern does not automatically warrant removal merely because the species is introduced.
researchNotes: Australian Tropical Herbarium provides a species key and detailed frond morphology; NParks independently confirms the two frond types and spores. Native-range treatments differ in breadth, so a precise extralimital native-range claim is omitted. Actions are observational and precautionary; no ecological harm or treatment-efficacy claim is invented.

sources.title: Australian Tropical Ferns and Lycophytes: Platycerium bifurcatum

claims: Colonial fern has lobed nest fronds and fertile fronds to 105 cm; key separates superbum, hillii and veitchii.
Tree-growing fern has shield and forked fertile fronds, with spores under fertile tips.

proposedDescription: Elliptic yellowwood is a tropical shrub or small tree with glossy leaves arranged around the stem and striking pairs of red fruits. Those paired fruits are the origin of another common name, bloodhorn. Small pale flowers precede them, and broken tissues release white sap. The species comes from coastal parts of northeastern Australia and nearby Pacific islands and is grown ornamentally in warm climates. Its attractive fruit should not be tasted: both fruit and sap are reported as poisonous. A planted tree and seedlings growing independently beyond a garden represent different situations when evaluating its local establishment.
identification: Expect a shrub or small spreading tree several meters tall; published accounts range from about 4 to 9 m. The smooth, leathery leaves occur in whorls, usually of three, sometimes four, and have numerous closely spaced side veins joining a vein near the margin. Leaf size varies, commonly about 5–20 cm long. Small white to yellowish flowers occur in clusters near the branch ends. The most useful feature is the paired, elongated red fruit, each with pointed ends and a length of roughly 3–6 cm across the accounts. Photograph an intact fruit pair, leaf arrangement and venation without breaking tissues to test the sap. Glossy leaves or red fruits alone are insufficient to distinguish other tropical ornamentals.
actions: Keep fallen fruits away from children, pets and food-growing areas, and use gloves when gathering them or pruning to avoid contact with the sap. Do not taste fruit or offer it to animals. If the tree is retained, check beneath it and along nearby garden edges for seedlings and remove unwanted young plants before they mature. Dispose of fruits and living cuttings through an appropriate garden-waste route rather than dumping them beside natural vegetation; the plant can be propagated from seeds and cuttings. Document self-sown plants beyond cultivation with photographs and locations for local extension or a herbarium. Obtain professional advice before removing a large tree.
researchNotes: PlantNET full text provides diagnostic leaf, flower and paired-fruit details. ANPSA indexed content independently supports larger dimensions, poisonous fruit, milky sap and propagation; repeated full-page requests timed out. Australian Tropical Rainforest Plants also returned 403, so it is not misrepresented as full text. No US-specific ecological impact or eradication method is asserted.

sources.title: Australian Native Plants Society: Ochrosia elliptica

claims: Glossy whorled leaves have parallel lateral veins; white flowers precede paired red pointed fruits.
Small tree can reach 5–9 m; fruits are poisonous, wounded tissues produce white sap, and propagation uses seeds or cuttings.

proposedDescription: Elm Leaf Beetle feeds on elm foliage, with adults and larvae leaving different signs. Adults chew holes through leaves, while larvae scrape away the softer tissue and leave a network of veins. Heavy feeding can turn a canopy brown and repeated severe defoliation can weaken a tree. This damage should be distinguished from Dutch elm disease, which has a different cause and management response. The beetles also enter buildings to shelter, sometimes in large numbers. Finding them indoors does not mean they are eating the house; the feeding stages depend on elm leaves.
identification: Adults are about 5–6 mm long, yellowish to olive green, with dark lengthwise markings including a stripe along each wing-cover edge. Yellowish eggs are laid in short double rows on leaf undersides. Newly hatched larvae are dark; older larvae become yellow-green with rows of dark bumps that resemble stripes, reaching about 8 mm. Yellow to orange pupae may collect near the tree base after larvae crawl down the trunk. European flea weevil, Orchestes alni, also makes holes in elm leaves, so holes alone do not establish this beetle’s identity. Photograph insects, eggs and feeding damage together, including leaf undersides. Browning without obvious chewing, especially with branch dieback, needs a tree-health diagnosis rather than an assumed beetle identification.
actions: Inspect accessible elm leaves regularly from spring onward and record whether larvae and new feeding damage are increasing. Keep the tree appropriately watered during drought and protect its roots and trunk from injury. Avoid routine insecticide use simply because a few beetles are present; natural enemies often help, and healthy trees can tolerate appreciable leaf damage. Ask extension or an arborist about repeated early-season defoliation or extensive branch decline. Indoors, remove beetles with a vacuum and repair screens, door sweeps and exterior gaps before the next sheltering season. Do not spray inaccessible wall cavities to kill hidden beetles; accumulated dead insects can attract other household pests.
researchNotes: UC IPM and Utah State provide independent diagnostic and management accounts. UC regional generation counts and historical pest-range statements are not projected nationally. Guidance separates foliar beetle injury from Dutch elm disease and uses monitoring, tree care and exclusion without prescribing pesticides.

claims: Adults chew holes, larvae skeletonize leaves; eggs occur in double rows; other pests and disease require different diagnoses; monitor and conserve natural enemies.
Adults are 3/16–1/4 inch with black wing-edge stripes; indoor beetles can be vacuumed and excluded by sealing entry points.

proposedDescription: Elmleaf blackberry is a scrambling bramble with arching canes, pale-backed leaflets and pink flowers followed by black fruit. Its canes can root where their tips touch soil, extending a patch without waiting for new seedlings. Native to Europe and northwestern Africa, it is one of several introduced blackberries recorded in California. Brambles provide food and cover, but dense growth can also block access or overtake wanted vegetation. The name blackberry covers many species, including native ones, so a thorny thicket should not be assigned to this species from its fruit alone.
identification: Look for angled, arching stems and leaves divided into three or five toothed leaflets, with dense fine white hairs beneath. Terminal leaflets are often about 3–8 cm long. Flowers are usually pink, with rounded, somewhat crumpled petals, and fruits pass from green through red to black. Many plants have stout prickles, but thornless forms exist, so prickles are not mandatory. Cutleaf blackberry, Rubus laciniatus, has deeply divided leaflets rather than simply toothed ones. Himalayan blackberry, Rubus armeniacus, also has pale-backed leaflets and robust canes and needs closer comparison. Photograph a complete leaf from a new cane, both leaflet surfaces, stem angles and flowers. Because blackberry names and hybrids are difficult, an uncertain photograph should remain identified only as Rubus until checked.
actions: Confirm the species before clearing a patch, especially where native blackberries occur. For unwanted young plants, work when the soil is moist and remove the crown and attached roots rather than snapping off the cane. Lift rooted cane tips as well, and keep discarded stems from lying on moist soil where they could establish. Wear protective clothing when working among prickly growth. Cutting a large thicket can restore access but usually needs repeated follow-up for regrowth; plan that work before opening a large bare area. Retain appropriate cover or replant with suitable vegetation. Seek local advice for streambanks, extensive infestations or mixed native and introduced brambles.
researchNotes: NZ Flora and the updated NSW flora independently support morphology. NSW explicitly corrects an older ulmifolius misapplication to R. anglocandicans; that historic account is not used. UC confirms California occurrence and supplies broader blackberry management, identified as group-level guidance rather than a species-specific trial. Exact specimen confirmation remains an observation-level limit, not an unresolved catalog identity.

sources.title: Flora of New Zealand: Rubus ulmifolius

claims: Arching angled canes, white-haired leaf undersides and crinkled pink petals characterize the species.
Leaves have three or five leaflets; canes root at tips; older NSW usage was misapplied to R. anglocandicans.
Elmleaf blackberry is introduced in California; cutleaf and Himalayan blackberries differ; moist-soil removal and follow-up address blackberry regrowth.

proposedDescription: Elongate Hemlock Scale is a tiny sap-feeding insect that spends much of its life sheltered beneath a protective cover on conifer needles. Hemlocks and firs are important hosts, with other conifers also affected. Infested foliage may develop yellow blotches, lose needles or look unusually white where male scales produce waxy threads. A light infestation can be easy to miss because the insects sit mostly on needle undersides, including older growth inside the canopy. Introduced from Asia, this pest can weaken trees when abundant, but discoloration alone is not enough to identify it.
identification: Turn over several needles and use a hand lens. Female covers are elongated, yellowish to orange-brown, roughly 1.5–2 mm long, with fairly parallel sides. Immature male covers are smaller and white, sometimes with projecting wax threads. Tiny yellow young stages, called crawlers, move before settling to feed; adult males are minute winged insects. Cryptomeria scale and pine needle scale can also cause mottling, and algae may resemble the white discoloration associated with males. Confirm the actual insects rather than judging the tree from a distance. Photograph needle undersides at high magnification, the affected branch and the whole tree; include its identity and location. A diagnostic service may need material to distinguish scale species or determine whether old covers still contain living insects.
actions: Inspect nursery conifers before planting, especially the undersides of older needles, and avoid moving visibly infested stock or branches to clean sites. If a tree is suspect, record which branches carry scales and have the diagnosis checked by extension or a forest-health office. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer, which can favor scale populations. Preserve lady beetles, lacewings and parasitic wasps by avoiding unnecessary broad-spectrum sprays. Large or persistent infestations need a treatment plan based on live stages and local timing because crawler emergence can overlap through the season. If removal is advised, contain infested branches during transport and clean equipment before working among uninfested trees.
researchNotes: Independent NC State scouting guidance and Penn State material hosted by Maine were read in full. The original Penn State HTML returned 403, so the accessible PDF is cited instead. Host lists differ on pine susceptibility; public wording does not resolve that disagreement by making a universal claim. Farm-scale culling advice is not generalized into mandatory forest-tree removal.

sources.title: NC State: Scouting for Elongate Hemlock Scale
Penn State: Elongate Hemlock Scale, hosted by Maine DACF

claims: Scales occur beneath multiple years of needles; males are white, females brown; Cryptomeria and pine needle scales require distinct identification; natural enemies occur.
Female covers reach 1.5–2 mm; nitrogen favors scales; inspect stock, contain infested material and clean machinery.

proposedDescription: Emerald Ash Borer is a small metallic-green beetle whose hidden larvae cause the most serious damage. They feed beneath ash bark, disrupting the tissues that move water and nutrients through the tree. A tree may carry an infestation before the canopy shows obvious decline. Native to Asia, the beetle has killed large numbers of North American ash trees and can attack otherwise healthy trees. Adults fly locally, while infested firewood, logs and nursery trees can carry it much farther. Early reporting and careful decisions about ash wood are therefore important even when only one tree appears affected.
identification: Adults are slender, about 8–13 mm long, widest just behind the head and tapering toward the rear. The wing covers are metallic green; the abdomen beneath is reddish purple. Emerging adults leave small D-shaped holes, about 3 mm across, while larvae make winding galleries under the bark. Watch for thinning at the crown, unusual shoots on the trunk, bark splits and increased woodpecker activity, but these signs are not individually diagnostic. Six-spotted tiger beetles are also green and similarly sized, yet have long running legs, conspicuous jaws and bulging eyes; their white spots vary and may be absent. Photograph a beetle beside a scale and the tree’s leaves, branching and visible damage. Confirm that the host is an ash and seek expert review.
actions: Use locally sourced or certified heat-treated firewood, and do not carry suspect ash logs, branches or nursery trees to another area. Report a possible new infestation to the state plant-health or forestry agency with the location and photographs. Avoid peeling healthy bark merely to search for larvae. Have an arborist assess a declining tree promptly, especially near buildings, roads or paths. Some valuable ash trees can be protected when intervention is timely; others need removal and a disposal plan. Ask about current local wood-handling requirements before arranging transport. Replacement planting should use a suitable mix of tree species rather than recreating a stand vulnerable to one pest.
researchNotes: USDA APHIS and University of Minnesota provide independent pest and prevention support; a separate UMN entomology account supports the tiger-beetle distinction. Federal domestic quarantine was removed, so no outdated nationwide quarantine claim is made. Regional emergence and wood-removal calendars are not presented as universal.

sources.title: University of Minnesota: Emerald ash borer
University of Minnesota: Six-Spotted Tiger Beetle

claims: Asian beetle damages ash through larval feeding; movement of infested wood spreads it; use local or certified heat-treated firewood and report suspect damage.
Adults are 1/3–1/2 inch, tapered and green with purple abdomen; emergence holes are D-shaped; protection and removal require planning.
Tiger beetles have long legs, large jaws and eyes; white spot number varies, including no spots.

proposedDescription: Emperor's candlesticks is a large tropical shrub with upright columns of yellow flowers. Orange bracts cover the unopened buds at the top, while flowers open farther down, creating the candlelike shape behind its name. Its long leaves carry rows of broad, rounded leaflets, and winged pods follow the blooms. Native to tropical America, it is widely grown as an ornamental and has naturalized in warm regions. In Hawaiʻi it can form dense pasture stands. Its history as a cultivated medicinal plant helps explain its spread, but does not establish that home preparations are safe or appropriate.
identification: Mature plants can reach about 3–5 m, though younger or seasonally grown plants are smaller. A complete leaf is commonly 30–60 cm long and carries numerous opposite leaflet pairs, often around six to fourteen. The broad, oblong leaflets have rounded or slightly notched tips and tend to be larger toward the leaf’s end. Flowers are densely arranged in an erect column, with yellow open blooms below orange-covered buds. The mature pods are dark, stiff and conspicuously winged, giving them an angular cross-section. Other sennas have yellow flowers and paired leaflets, so neither feature by itself is enough. Photograph a whole leaf, the upright flower cluster and a pod from both the side and end. Include plant height and whether it persists through winter.
actions: Remove developing pods before they split if a garden plant is producing unwanted seedlings. Keep collected pods contained and check beneath the shrub and nearby disturbed ground for new plants. Avoid dumping cuttings, rooted pieces or seed-bearing material along drains or natural vegetation. If an established shrub is unwanted, plan for follow-up: the University of Hawaiʻi account warns that mechanical removal alone often fails because plants produce replacement shoots. Repeatedly check treated ground rather than interpreting a cut stem as a finished removal. For a dense stand in pasture or near a waterway, seek local extension guidance matched to the site. Do not promote it as livestock forage or a home remedy on the strength of its common names.
researchNotes: NParks provides detailed morphology and explicit pod-removal prevention; University of Hawaii independently documents naturalization, pasture stands and suckering after mechanical control. Kew supplies the broader tropical-American native range. Conflicting leaflet measurements and NParks nectar claims are not repeated; no medical or livestock-use endorsement is inferred from traditional use.

sources.title: Kew Plants of the World Online: Senna alata

claims: Large compound leaves accompany upright yellow flower columns and angular winged pods; remove pods before splitting to limit spread.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: University of Hawaii Motooka et al 2003
claims: Naturalized ornamental forms dense pasture stands; mechanical control can fail due to suckering.
Accepted species native from southwestern Mexico through tropical America; Cassia alata is a synonym.

proposedDescription: English grain aphid is a small, soft-bodied insect that feeds on cereal crops and grasses. Its color varies from green to reddish brown, but its long dark rear tubes are a useful clue. Colonies occur on leaves and stems and often gather on wheat heads as grain develops. Feeding can matter when numbers are high, and the aphid can transmit barley yellow dwarf virus. The importance of those two risks differs with crop, growth stage and region. Predators and parasitic insects often keep colonies in check, so finding a few aphids is a reason to inspect more closely rather than automatically spray.
identification: Adults are about 1.3–3.3 mm long, with long antennae, dark leg joints and two conspicuous black tubes near the rear of the abdomen. These tubes are called cornicles; a hand lens is helpful for seeing their color and length. Both winged and wingless adults occur, and young aphids are smaller. Bird-cherry oat aphid, Rhopalosiphum padi, is typically olive-green with a reddish-brown patch near the rear, rather than relying on the long black tubes as its main field mark. Color alone can mislead because English grain aphid itself varies. Photograph several individuals from above and the side, their position on the plant and the crop’s growth stage. A sharp close-up or diagnostic sample is needed when the rear structures are not visible.
actions: Check several parts of a cereal planting, including wheat heads once they form, rather than judging the field from one crowded stem. Record aphid numbers together with crop stage and look for lady beetles, lacewing larvae and swollen, discolored aphid bodies left by parasitoids. Repeat observations to see whether the population is increasing. Use current local extension guidance before deciding on treatment: direct-feeding thresholds and virus-management decisions are different, and published thresholds do not transfer unchanged between regions. Avoid unnecessary broad-spectrum sprays that remove natural enemies. In a commercial field, share counts, crop stage and any yellowing pattern with an agronomist; plant symptoms alone do not establish virus infection.
researchNotes: AHDB supplies measured size and broader life-cycle variability; Purdue independently supports the bird-cherry oat comparison and structured scouting; UC supports head colonization and natural-enemy suppression. UK virus-risk assumptions, resistance prevalence and numeric thresholds are not imposed on US settings. Regional overwintering differences are deliberately not flattened into one national calendar.

sources.title: AHDB: Basic biology of the grain aphid

claims: Adults measure 1.3–3.3 mm and have black rear tubes; feeding and virus risks require different monitoring decisions.
Winged and wingless English grain aphids occur; bird-cherry oat aphids often show rear reddish patches; sample multiple areas and record natural enemies and crop stage.
Often colonizes wheat heads; transmits barley yellow dwarf virus and is usually suppressed by predators and parasitoids.

proposedDescription: English holly is an evergreen shrub or tree familiar from its glossy leaves and winter decorations. Many leaves have sharp marginal spines, while female plants can carry red fruits after pollination. Birds eat the fruits and move the seeds beyond gardens. Native to Europe, northern Africa and western Asia, the species has become established in parts of the United States and can spread through forest understories, particularly in the Pacific Northwest. A well-kept hedge and a self-sown woodland stand deserve different assessments. Escaped plants can persist in shade and grow into substantial woody plants.
identification: Leaves are simple, alternate along the twig, thick and glossy, usually about 2.5–7.5 cm long, with wavy, often spiny edges. Small pale flowers appear in spring; fruits commonly turn red by autumn and may remain into winter. A mature tree can reach roughly 9–15 m, although clipped shrubs are much shorter. False holly, Osmanthus heterophyllus, has leaves in opposite pairs instead of alternate positions. Oregon grape species have yellow flowers and blue to dark fruits, unlike English holly’s pale flowers and usually red fruits. Cultivars can have pale leaf margins or unusual fruit colors, so use several characters. Photograph a twig showing successive leaf attachments, both leaf surfaces, flowers or fruits and the whole plant before deciding that a spiny evergreen is this species.
actions: Prioritize small self-sown plants around woodland edges and beneath bird perches, where removal is easier than after a woody root system develops. Wear sturdy gloves and loosen moist soil to lift the root system. Cutting a mature shrub at ground level commonly triggers new shoots, so arrange repeated follow-up or a professional treatment plan before tackling a large plant. Keep berry-bearing branches and living trimmings out of dumped garden waste; stems can establish where they contact moist soil. Choose suitable alternatives when replacing a planting that repeatedly seeds into nearby habitat. Do not eat the berries or leave decorative branches where children or pets can chew them.
researchNotes: NC State and Washington's weed board independently support morphology, origin, bird dispersal and resprouting. False-holly comparison is verified in its own NC State account. Oregon-grape comparison uses flowers and fruit, avoiding the misleading leaf-versus-leaflet wording found on a county page. Legal classifications differ over time and are intentionally omitted from national actions.

sources.title: Washington State Noxious Weed Control Board: Common Holly

claims: Glossy alternate leaves, separate male and female plants and bird-attractive fruits; fruits are not safe food.
Birds spread seeds; plants grow in forest understory; young plants can be pulled and cut mature shrubs resprout; Oregon grape has yellow flowers and dark fruit.
False holly leaves are opposite, unlike alternate true-holly leaves.

proposedDescription: English Ivy is a woody evergreen vine that can spread across the ground or climb high into trees. Its familiar lobed leaves belong to the juvenile stage. Older flowering shoots have a different outline and produce dark berries that birds carry away. Long used as a groundcover, it has escaped into woodlands, with serious effects documented in the Pacific Northwest. Dense ground cover can prevent other plants from establishing. Climbing growth brings heavy vegetation into tree crowns, making early attention easier than dealing with an established canopy infestation.
identification: Look for thick, glossy, alternate leaves on stems that attach by small aerial roots. Juvenile leaves are lobed; adult flowering shoots bear unlobed leaves and clusters of greenish flowers, followed by blue-black berries. Vines may climb tens of feet, so leaves near ground level can look different from those in a tree crown. Cultivars vary in leaf size and markings. Other Hedera species, including Irish ivy, are easily confused with English Ivy and may require examination of leaf hairs by a botanist. Photograph both leaf surfaces, stem attachment, and flowers or fruit rather than relying on one lobed leaf.
actions: Start with vines climbing trees. Cut accessible stems without cutting the bark, and clear a ring of ivy from the ground around the trunk. Leave high growth to die in place rather than pulling heavy vines down from overhead. Pull ground runners and dig out rooted sections, then revisit for shoots from missed roots. Wear gloves because contact can irritate some people's skin. Keep cuttings off moist soil where they can root. Do not use ordinary home compost for live ivy; ask the receiving yard-waste facility whether it accepts invasive vines. Watch for bird-sown seedlings.
researchNotes: OSU removal guidance and NC State morphology were read. NC State includes Hibernica among cultivars while other treatments separate Irish ivy; species confirmation is qualified. Regional impacts are not generalized to every US planting. Manual containment requires follow-up.

sources.title: Ivy removal in a home landscape - OSU Extension
Hedera helix - NC State Plant Toolbox

claims: Remove accessible climbing stems and ground growth; canopy ivy dies gradually.
Cuttings can root and home composting is discouraged.
Evergreen vines have distinct juvenile and adult stages.
Adult shoots flower and produce dark berries.

proposedDescription: English walnut is the familiar cultivated walnut tree, grown for its nuts, shade, and wood. A broad crown and large divided leaves give it a substantial presence in a garden or orchard. Green husks enclose the nuts through summer. People have moved and cultivated this tree for thousands of years, making the edges of its original Eurasian range difficult to reconstruct. Finding an English walnut outside cultivation shows that it has established there; it does not by itself establish that the tree is damaging the surrounding habitat.
identification: A mature English walnut commonly reaches 40-60 feet, with gray bark that becomes ridged with age. Each leaf has several broad leaflets, usually with a well-developed terminal leaflet. Edges are mostly smooth, although young growth may show fine teeth. Male flowers hang in catkins; rounded fruits develop smooth green husks around a wrinkled nut shell. Shell thickness varies among cultivated forms. The combination of broad leaflets, terminal leaflet, husk, and nut is more useful than crown shape alone. Photograph a complete leaf and a mature fruit, including the shell if available; a seedling without fruit can be harder to place.
actions: First decide whether the tree is a wanted planting or an unwanted seedling. For a retained tree, allow room for its broad crown and keep the root zone from becoming waterlogged; this species favors a sunny, well-drained site. Remove unwanted seedlings while small, before deep roots make lifting difficult. Collect fallen nuts where repeated seedlings are a concern, and check adjoining beds the following season. Large trees close to buildings need an arborist's assessment before substantial pruning or removal. In natural habitat, ask the land manager about local priorities rather than assuming all walnuts require removal.
researchNotes: NC State and the International Dendrology Society independently describe morphology and cultivation. The latter discusses uncertain native-range boundaries after long human movement. Actions are conservative horticultural and seed-prevention advice, not evidence of invasive impact or an eradication study.

sources.title: Juglans regia - NC State Plant Toolbox
Juglans regia - Trees and Shrubs Online

claims: Trees have broad crowns, compound leaves and husked nuts.
Sun and drainage are preferred; deep roots complicate transplanting.
Leaflets are usually entire with a terminal leaflet.
Shell thickness varies and original distribution is debated.

proposedDescription: Erect Hedgeparsley is a slender member of the carrot family whose small fruits cling to clothing and animal fur. That hitchhiking habit helps it move along paths, woodland edges, and disturbed ground. Plants commonly begin as low rosettes before sending up branched stems with white flower clusters. Native to Europe and Asia, it has spread outside that range and can form troublesome stands in parts of North America. Its fine leaves and modest flowers can be overlooked until burr-like fruits start catching on a passing sleeve.
identification: Flowering Erect Hedgeparsley can stand about 2-6 feet tall. Leaves are alternate, finely divided, and somewhat hairy; lower rosettes may remain green late in the season. Tiny white flowers form small, open clusters with pointed bracts beneath the main cluster. Fruits are about 3-4 millimeters long and bear hooked hairs. Spreading hedgeparsley, Torilis arvensis, usually lacks conspicuous bracts beneath the main flower cluster. Wild carrot has hairier stems and leaves, but the wider carrot family includes dangerously poisonous lookalikes. Do not taste or rely on a crushed-leaf smell. Close views of bracts, fruits, and a whole leaf are especially useful.
actions: Pull small patches or cut them before flowering and fruit development. Check cut plants for regrowth rather than assuming one mowing has finished the job. Once hooked fruits form, work from clean ground toward the patch and contain fruiting tops. Brush seeds from clothing, boots, tools, and pets before leaving. Revisit paths and disturbed edges where people or animals may have carried fruits. For a large woodland infestation, coordinate with the land manager so repeated work protects desirable vegetation. Local weed staff can help confirm the species and plan treatment appropriate to the site.
researchNotes: Wisconsin DNR supports identification, dispersal and mechanical management; Native Plant Trust independently confirms fruit dimensions and habitat. Regional native-status labels for lookalikes are not transferred nationally. No food identification by odor is encouraged and chemical recipes are omitted.

claims: Hooked fruits attach to fur and clothing.
Bracts distinguish it from spreading hedgeparsley.
Pull or mow before flowering.
Native to Europe and Asia.
Fruits measure three to four millimetres.

proposedDescription: Ethiopian dogstooth grass is a robust perennial that spreads by thick surface runners. Its stiff flowering branches often form several tiers and may be red or purple. It has been moved from tropical Africa for forage and ground cover, and has escaped cultivation. Older records can be difficult to interpret because related stargrasses were often confused. Some current authorities combine this name with Cynodon nlemfuensis, while regional floras still distinguish it. That difference matters when using a pasture label or older record to identify a new find.
identification: Plants described as Ethiopian dogstooth grass have coarse, often woody stems about 40-140 centimeters tall, narrow leaves, and surface runners without underground rhizomes. Flowering heads usually have two or more separated tiers of stiff branches, although a single tier can occur. Flower units are about 2.5-3 millimeters long. Common bermudagrass, Cynodon dactylon, has underground rhizomes as well as runners. Traditional keys separate C. nlemfuensis by softer stems and usually fewer, less separated tiers, but the boundary depends on the taxonomic treatment. Photograph the stem base, runners, complete head, and close flower details; a lawn-like patch alone is insufficient.
actions: Keep unidentified stargrass runners and soil within the site until the plant has been checked. For a small unwanted patch, lift rooted runners carefully and revisit for pieces that remain alive; avoid scattering fragments with mowing or dumped debris. Larger pasture stands need a plan with a local forage or weed adviser, especially when the grass has a legitimate grazing role. Record the original planting name, but do not use it as proof of species. If growth is escaping a managed boundary, contain that edge and prevent further planting while identification and local priorities are resolved.
researchNotes: AusGrass and Bishop Museum distinguish C. aethiopicus from C. nlemfuensis, but current Kew incorporates its descriptions under C. nlemfuensis. The traditional catalog concept is described and flagged for reconciliation. Bishop specimens demonstrate historical misidentification as C. dactylon. Runner removal is conservative containment advice, not an eradication trial.

sources.title: Notes on grasses of Hawaii - Bishop Museum

claims: Woody stems, surface runners and no rhizomes characterize the traditional concept.
Heads commonly have multiple tiers.
Rhizomes, stems and flowering branches separate three species in the key.
Some specimens were misidentified as C. dactylon.
The account incorporates descriptions under synonym C. aethiopicus.

proposedDescription: Ethiopian rattlebox is an upright branching legume with three narrow leaflets and yellow flowers marked with reddish veins. Long narrow pods follow the flowers. Native to tropical Africa, it has been cultivated and introduced elsewhere. It is among the rattleboxes used as leafy vegetables in parts of East Africa, but that history is not a safe guide to eating an unfamiliar roadside plant. Related species look similar, and the genus includes plants with important toxicity concerns. Its presence outside cultivation should be assessed in its local setting.
identification: Ethiopian rattlebox is often about 0.5-2 meters tall, with ascending branches and short stem hairs. Leaves have three narrow leaflets, smooth above and finely hairy beneath; the small appendages called stipules are absent in formal flora descriptions. Yellow or cream flowers with reddish-brown veins form long terminal clusters. Pods are narrow and cylindrical, commonly about 4-5 centimeters long and several millimeters wide, containing many small seeds. Crotalaria ochroleuca can resemble it when fruit is absent. Record a complete three-leaflet leaf, flower from the side, and mature pod; flower color alone does not settle identification.
actions: Remove unwanted small plants before pods mature and check for further seedlings. Contain mature pods before moving plants or garden waste, since seed-bearing debris can establish new patches. Keep uncertain rattlebox plants out of harvested forage and away from casual food gathering until identification and suitability have been checked. For a cultivated stand, retain seed information and inspect nearby disturbed ground for escape. Large or persistent populations deserve local weed advice, but introduction alone does not mean every population needs eradication. Avoid importing control or toxicity claims wholesale from other Crotalaria species.
researchNotes: Kew's Flora of Tropical East Africa and Colombia's independent taxonomic account support morphology. Food use is documented without recommending ingestion. Conflicting informal claims about stipules and seeds were rejected in favor of formal floras. Species-specific control trials were not located; actions are seed containment and identification precautions.

sources.title: Crotalaria brevidens - Flora of Tropical East Africa via Kew

claims: Three leaflets, absent stipules and reddish-veined flowers characterize this species.
Morphology confirms trifoliolate leaves, short hairs and absent stipules.
The typical variety resembles C. ochroleuca without fruit.
Food use is recorded; forage evidence is limited and historical.

proposedDescription: Eucalyptus leaf beetle is a small, rounded Australian beetle that feeds on eucalyptus foliage. Adults chew older leaves, while groups of larvae concentrate on tender growth, leaving ragged edges that can look like caterpillar damage. It has become a pest of some landscape trees and cut-foliage plantings outside Australia. Several different beetles share the name eucalyptus tortoise beetle, so that common name alone can be misleading. This species is also placed in the genus Paropsisterna, a name increasingly used in taxonomic references.
identification: Adults are about 5-7 millimeters long, strongly domed above and flatter underneath, with gray to reddish-brown coloration. Greenish-gray larvae have dark heads and three pairs of legs near the front. Orange eggs occur in rows or groups on leaves. The similar Australian tortoise beetle, Trachymela sloanei, has darker brown adults and larvae; its larvae feed at night, while eucalyptus leaf beetle larvae feed during the day. Color and feeding time are helpful clues, not a complete species test. Photograph the adult from above and the side, any egg group, and the damaged eucalyptus leaves, noting the host tree if known.
actions: Check young eucalyptus growth for eggs and feeding larvae before damage becomes extensive. Record whether new leaves are being lost repeatedly or whether an older scar is simply remaining visible. Keep trees appropriately watered without leaving roots waterlogged. Avoid moving infested cut foliage to another planting. Before treating a large tree, obtain a confirmed identification and advice from a local tree-health professional. Broad-spectrum sprays can disrupt beneficial insects controlling other eucalyptus pests, turning one problem into several. Small, accessible infestations are easier to inspect and address than insects high in a tree crown; avoid climbing or improvised overhead spraying.
researchNotes: UCR biology and CDFA's diagnostic sheet provide independent substantive information; Hawaii extension adds plant-care advice but draws partly on California literature. The Hawaii PDF redirect failed, so only its indexed text is claimed. EPPO confirms Paropsisterna m-fuscum as the preferred combination. Older speculative pesticide efficacy language is not repeated as established treatment.
