proposedDescription: Eucalyptus longhorned borer is an Australian beetle whose larvae feed beneath eucalyptus bark. Here the name refers to Phoracantha recurva, one of two closely related borers established in California. Freshly cut wood and stressed trees provide breeding opportunities, especially when drought has weakened a planting. Larval tunnels can interrupt the tissues carrying water and nutrients, causing branch decline or killing a heavily attacked tree. An adult beetle is much easier to identify than a fading crown, since wilting and bark leakage can have several causes.
identification: Adults are elongated beetles roughly 14-30 millimeters long, with antennae as long as the body or longer. In Phoracantha recurva the wing covers are mostly cream to yellow, with darker areas concentrated toward the rear. The underside of the antenna segments bears long, dense golden hairs. Phoracantha semipunctata is predominantly dark brown and has sparse or absent golden antennal hairs. Pale, legless larvae live beneath bark and later enter wood to pupate. Holes, gum, dark staining, and tunnels packed with debris suggest borer activity but do not identify the species. A clear adult photograph should include both wing pattern and antennae.
actions: Reduce avoidable stress on retained eucalyptus trees, particularly prolonged interruptions to established irrigation during drought. Protect trunks and roots from injury. Have declining or hazardous limbs assessed promptly, and discuss disposal of infested wood before it is moved. Fresh eucalyptus logs can support beetle development; local guidance may call for chipping, debarking, or other treatment rather than leaving them beside living trees. Do not transport suspect firewood to new areas. An arborist can distinguish an active attack from other causes of decline and advise whether the tree can recover. Preserve natural enemies by avoiding routine broad-spectrum spraying.
researchNotes: UC IPM provides exact adult distinctions and management; FABI independently describes P. recurva biology and South African experience, although some underlying California work is shared. FAO's measurement account explicitly derives partly from UC, so it is not counted as a separate independent group. FABI's apparent exit-hole unit error is omitted. No universal seasonal pruning date is exported from California.

claims: P. recurva has mostly pale wing covers and dense golden antennal hairs.
Stress reduction and proper wood handling are central management measures.
Larvae tunnel beneath bark of stressed or recently felled eucalyptus.
P. recurva biology and parasitoid responses differ from P. semipunctata.
Adult size is approximately fourteen to thirty millimetres.
Movement of infested fresh wood is a dispersal pathway.

proposedDescription: Eucalyptus snout beetle is a leaf-feeding weevil associated with eucalyptus. This entry concerns Gonipterus platensis, one member of a group formerly treated as a single widespread pest. Adults chew leaf edges, while larvae scrape or consume young foliage. Repeated heavy feeding can reduce tree growth and leave a thin crown. The species originated in Tasmania and has spread with eucalyptus plantings to other regions. Older reports under Gonipterus scutellatus need careful interpretation because they may refer to this species or to a different, very similar weevil.
identification: Look for a gray-brown weevil with a short snout on eucalyptus leaves, alongside scalloped leaf edges, feeding tracks, or compact brown egg capsules. Weevils in this complex are commonly around 8-9 millimeters long, but external size and color do not establish Gonipterus platensis. Yellow-green larvae with dark markings may have a sticky coating. The similar G. pulverulentus and other members of the complex can be difficult to distinguish even from good photographs. Reliable species identification may require male internal structures or DNA testing. Record adults, larvae, egg capsules, host species, and locality together; damage alone cannot confirm the taxon.
actions: Inspect new eucalyptus foliage and nursery plants for adults, egg capsules, and fresh feeding before moving them. Do not distribute infested cut branches or plants to another site, and include their potting soil in any movement assessment because later stages can occur below ground. Report a suspected new local occurrence to a plant-health service and retain a specimen only as instructed. For established infestations, ask about local biological-control programs and conserve their beneficial wasps. Treatment decisions should reflect active damage and tree condition; blanket spraying can interfere with biological control. Large trees and nursery outbreaks require coordinated professional advice.
researchNotes: EPPO's revised complex-level account supplies field signs and prevention, explicitly separated from species confirmation. The independent North American adventive-weevil review supports the need for male-genital or molecular identification. Measurements are labeled complex-level, not an exclusive G. platensis diagnosis. Current exact-species distribution corroborates Tasmania and introduced ranges; no old G. scutellatus records are silently reassigned.

proposedDescription: Eugenia psyllid is a name with an important scientific mix-up. The insect widely reported from ornamental eugenia in the United States as Trioza eugeniae was shown by a taxonomic study to be Trioza adventicia. True T. eugeniae is a separate Australian species. The familiar garden pest makes young foliage blistered and pitted, but those observations should not automatically be assigned to the scientific name in this entry. Both insects are tiny sap feeders; separating their identities requires more than seeing a damaged hedge.
identification: Garden accounts describe small, winged psyllids and flattened immature stages on young eugenia leaves. That is useful for recognizing a psyllid problem, but it does not establish true Trioza eugeniae. The taxonomic revision distinguishes the two species using wing proportions, shading around particular veins, fine wing hairs, leg spurs, and male structures. True T. eugeniae has more elongated wings and lacks the dark shading around certain veins described for T. adventicia. These are specialist characters, not dependable phone-photo shortcuts. Record the host plant, both sides of affected leaves, and an adult if possible; an expert should reconcile the specimen with the corrected names.
actions: If an eugenia hedge has pitted leaves, first confirm that psyllids are still present on new growth. Old pits will remain even after the insects are gone. For the familiar garden pest, good plant care and conservation of natural enemies can reduce the need for treatment; pruning decisions should follow local guidance for that pest. Do not report true Trioza eugeniae solely from an older nursery label or a damaged leaf. Send host and specimen information to an extension diagnostic service, explaining the name confusion. Avoid moving infested nursery plants while the identification is being checked.
researchNotes: Research gap: the catalog's scientific identity conflicts with the established common-name pest. The 2019 revision demonstrates T. eugeniae and T. adventicia are distinct, not synonyms. UC guidance still uses the misapplied name; it supports management of the familiar garden pest only. No US establishment or treatment efficacy is attributed to true T. eugeniae. The revision abstract was read, not full text.

proposedDescription: Euphorbia pit scale is a small sap-feeding insect found on many ornamental plants, especially succulents. Despite its common name, its host range extends well beyond Euphorbia. Mature females remain fixed to the plant beneath a close-fitting cover, while young crawlers can move to new feeding sites. Heavy infestations may produce pits or raised calloused areas and weaken stems. Originally described from South Africa, it has been recorded in the Americas and elsewhere. Movement of infested cuttings and plants is an important way it reaches new collections.
identification: Look for rounded or oval yellow to light-brown scales, about 1.5-2 millimeters long, usually on stems. A translucent cover lies close over the insect, with a fringe of fine white wax around the edge; a hand lens may reveal a raised waxy crest along its center. A surrounding pit can be present but is not always obvious. Young crawlers look like much smaller yellow dots. Whitefly immature stages can also have waxy fringes, and other scales may share the host, so color alone is insufficient. Photograph several individuals with scale and their position on the plant; laboratory examination may be needed.
actions: Inspect stems and sheltered leaf junctions before adding a succulent or cutting to a collection. Keep suspect plants apart from clean stock, and stop sharing cuttings until the infestation has been identified and addressed. Check neighboring plants, since mobile crawlers can spread locally. Clean tools and remove loose plant debris before working elsewhere. A diagnostic service can distinguish this insect from other scales and advise on options suited to the host; succulent surfaces can react differently to treatments. Report a suspected new regional occurrence to plant-health staff. Continue inspecting fresh growth after action, rather than judging success only by old covers.
researchNotes: Queensland's full species account supports morphology, pathways and prevention. The independent Tennessee-authored Florida Entomologist record supports host breadth and introduction history. Environmental impacts are not generalized from Florida to other jurisdictions. Control remains isolation, clean propagation and diagnosis; no pesticide or alcohol recipe is inferred for sensitive succulents.

proposedDescription: Eurasian collared dove is a pale, fairly large dove often seen walking beneath feeders or calling from wires above towns and farms. Its thin black neck collar and broad, squared tail distinguish it from the familiar mourning dove. Introductions in the Bahamas preceded its spread into Florida and across much of North America. Grain and other seeds are important foods, and developed landscapes provide both feeding places and nesting trees. Its expansion is well documented; the presence of this introduced bird does not by itself establish that a particular yard needs wildlife control.
identification: Adults are about 29-32 cm long, with a plump body, small head, pale gray-brown plumage and a narrow black crescent across the back of the neck. The wings have darker tips, and the broad tail shows conspicuous white outer portions in flight. A mourning dove has a longer, pointed tail and dark spots on the wings. Young Eurasian collared doves may lack a complete collar, so use tail shape and the whole plumage pattern together. The repeated three-part coo is another useful clue. Escaped domestic ring-necked doves can complicate identification; record the call and photograph the tail as well as the neck before submitting an unusual record.
actions: For an ordinary backyard sighting, observation is a reasonable first step. Record the number of birds and whether they are simply passing through or regularly nesting and feeding. If large gatherings are causing problems, reduce the easy grain supply by removing spilled birdseed and adjusting how much seed is offered. This follows the species' feeding habits; it is not a promise that birds will leave immediately. Avoid relocating birds or disturbing occupied nests as an improvised response. A local wildlife office can advise on a persistent site-specific problem. Clear photographs and a short sound recording are more useful for documenting range expansion than a collar-only photograph.
researchNotes: Cornell and Audubon provide independent identification and life-history accounts; feeder adjustments are a conservative inference from documented grain feeding, not a tested population-control prescription. No nationwide harm, legal status or removal requirement is inferred from introduction. Domestic-dove confusion is retained as an identification limitation.

claims: Pale plump dove has a black neck crescent and square tail.
Mourning Dove has a pointed tail; juveniles may have an incomplete collar.
North American expansion followed introduction in the Bahamas and establishment in Florida.
Adults measure 29-32 cm; grain is important food.
Towns and farms provide habitat; young birds disperse long distances.

proposedDescription: Eurasian hemp moth is a small moth whose caterpillars feed inside hemp stems and developing flower or seed structures. The hidden feeding can leave swollen stems, wilted shoots and damaged buds even when few insects are visible on the leaves. Originally described from Asia, it is established in parts of North America, but its importance varies among growing regions. Several generations can occur in a season. Crop remnants matter because larvae can survive between crops in plant material, making this a pest for which careful inspection and residue management are particularly useful.
identification: Adults are dark brown to gray-brown with narrow white markings on the forewings; each forewing is roughly 4.5-6.5 mm long. At rest the wings fold over the body. Young larvae are cream-colored with a dark head, becoming orange or reddish-orange as they mature. Look for small piles of frass, the caterpillar's droppings, near an entry hole or swollen stem, then examine the affected tissue for a larva. Grapholita tristrigana can have a very similar adult wing pattern; reliable separation may require examination of reproductive structures by a specialist. European corn borer and corn earworm also damage hemp, so damage alone is not a species identification.
actions: Inspect leaves and tender shoots during the growing season, and check buds and stems at harvest. Set aside affected material for identification before disposing of it; include the larva when possible. Remove infested crop debris so it does not become an overwintering refuge, and avoid carrying infested stalks into clean production areas. Review volunteer hemp and nearby host weeds with the crop adviser, concentrating effort where the pest is confirmed. Larvae already inside stems are sheltered from surface treatments. If damage warrants treatment, use local hemp-specific advice to match timing to exposed young larvae rather than repeatedly spraying damaged stems.
researchNotes: USDA TortAI supports adult diagnosis and the difficult G. tristrigana comparison. Utah State supplies scouting and residue guidance; Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada independently supports avoiding movement of infested stems. Published regional occurrence statements are not extrapolated to a current nationwide range. Treatment thresholds remain incompletely established.

Larvae feed in stems, flowers and developing seeds.
Larvae become reddish-orange; stems may swell, split or wilt.
Inspect stems and harvest material; remove overwintering crop debris.

proposedDescription: Eurasian poplar leaf rust pathogen is a fungus that produces yellow-orange spore patches on poplar leaves. Susceptible trees can lose foliage early, and repeated severe infections reduce growth and may contribute to dieback. Wet conditions favor infection, so damage can differ greatly among sites and years. The fungus has a life cycle involving poplars and larches, although repeating infections on poplar can also sustain it under suitable conditions. Poplar varieties differ in susceptibility, and a variety that once resisted the disease may become vulnerable as the rust population changes.
identification: Examine both sides of affected poplar leaves for small yellow-orange pustules, sometimes with yellow angular patches on the opposite surface. Heavy infection can cause browning, curled margins and premature leaf fall; darker resting-spore areas develop later in the season. These are signs of poplar rust, not a dependable field diagnosis of this particular fungus. Melampsora medusae, M. occidentalis and hybrid rusts can cause similar symptoms. Microscopic spore features or a diagnostic laboratory are needed to distinguish them. Submit fresh affected leaves with the poplar species or cultivar, location, date and photographs showing the crown's condition. Note whether nearby larches are present without assuming they prove the diagnosis.
actions: Monitor susceptible poplars during summer, especially when repeated early leaf loss is occurring. Ask a plant-disease laboratory to identify an unfamiliar outbreak before making a removal or treatment plan. When replacing trees or establishing a planting, choose locally suitable cultivars with current rust-resistance information and avoid making the entire planting one susceptible clone. Maintain good growing conditions and track annual defoliation rather than judging severity from one orange leaf. A forestry or extension adviser can assess alternate-host placement and any justified fungicide program. Removing nearby larches indiscriminately is not an appropriate substitute for diagnosis and a site-specific plan.
researchNotes: Forest Research, Scion and Pacific Northwest extension independently support symptoms, variable susceptibility and monitoring. The PNW handbook combines several rust species; its general conifer-host statements are not assigned wholesale to this taxon. EPPO prefers the spelling M. laricis-populina. No inference of eradication by leaf cleanup or larch removal is made.

proposedDescription: Eurasian Watermilfoil is a rooted aquatic plant with finely divided leaves arranged around long underwater stems. Shoots can reach the surface and form dense growth that interferes with boating and changes habitat, although not every occupied lake develops a severe infestation. Small broken pieces can root and start new plants, which explains why fragments caught on boats and equipment deserve attention. This perennial survives from its rooted base and spreads readily within suitable waters. Its resemblance to native watermilfoils makes careful identification important before anyone begins removal.
identification: Look for feather-like leaves usually arranged in whorls of four around the stem. A typical leaf has 12 or more pairs of narrow segments along its central axis. Stems may extend several feet through the water, and the soft leaves tend to collapse when lifted out. Small flower spikes can project above the surface. Native northern watermilfoil, Myriophyllum sibiricum, usually has fewer leaf divisions, often ten or fewer pairs, but the two species can hybridize. Leaf counts alone therefore do not settle every identification. Photograph several mature leaves spread flat against a scale, the branching pattern and any flower spike; seek specialist confirmation for intermediate plants.
actions: Before leaving a waterbody, inspect boats, trailers, anchors, fishing gear and other equipment for attached plants. Remove fragments, drain retained water and follow the local cleaning and drying requirements before using another lake or stream. Report a suspected new population with its location and clear close-ups. In a confirmed small patch, trained hand or diver removal can collect roots and loose fragments, but careless pulling or cutting may spread pieces. Larger infestations need a lake-specific plan that weighs recreation, native vegetation and treatment effects. Do not assume every sighting calls for broad chemical treatment, and arrange any in-water work with the responsible local manager.
researchNotes: Wisconsin DNR supplies management cautions and native/hybrid comparisons; USGS supplies independent biological synthesis, though both draw on established aquatic-plant literature. Public wording avoids Wisconsin-only legal requirements and numerical prevalence estimates. Count-based identification is qualified because hybrid plants can be intermediate; management is not presented as automatic eradication.

claims: Leaf divisions and native hybrids complicate identification.
Removal must capture fragments; many occupied lakes do not need aggressive treatment.
Rooted perennial spreads from fragments and persistent root crowns.
Leaves commonly occur in whorls of four with numerous paired divisions; flowers extend above water.

proposedDescription: European Alder is a fast-growing deciduous tree associated with wet ground, stream margins and pond edges. Rounded leaves and small woody, cone-like fruits make it recognizable through much of the year. Microbes in root nodules help it obtain nitrogen, allowing growth on some relatively poor soils. It has been planted outside its native European, western Asian and northern African range and has spread into natural areas in parts of North America. Water carries its small seeds, while rooting branches and new shoots can help a stand expand locally.
identification: Mature trees commonly reach 40-60 feet tall and may have several trunks. The alternate leaves are broadly rounded or widest toward the tip, with toothed edges and often a conspicuous notch at the end. Young leaves feel sticky. Long male catkins hang from the branches before spring leaf-out; the smaller female clusters mature into woody structures that remain through winter. Native speckled alder and green alder are usually shrubbier and have more elliptical leaves, although size alone is unreliable on young plants. Photograph mature leaf tips, both leaf surfaces, twig buds and the persistent fruits together. Suspected hybrids or unusual foliage deserve a regional botanical check.
actions: Check damp ground and drainage routes around planted trees for seedlings and expanding shoots. If European Alder is spreading into a natural area, confirm it against native alders before removing it. Small, newly established plants are easier to address before they become substantial trees. Cutting established stems commonly triggers regrowth, so plan repeated checks rather than treating a single cut as completion. For larger trees, use a qualified arborist or local invasive-plant program to plan safe removal and follow-up. Work near banks should protect soil and existing vegetation from erosion. Avoid moving seed-bearing material into clean wet ground, and choose an appropriate local tree when replacing it.
researchNotes: NC State supports morphology, dimensions and native range; Wisconsin DNR supports dispersal, native comparisons and resprouting after cutting. Removal advice is conditional on confirmed local spread. Regulatory text on the DNR page is internally dated/proposed in places, so no current legal claim is repeated. No universal wetland herbicide or excavation prescription is supplied.

claims: Typical height is 40-60 feet; rounded leaves alternate on twigs.
Female catkins become persistent woody fruits; young leaves are resinous.
Water disperses seeds; roots have nitrogen-fixing partners.
Native alders generally have more elliptical leaves; mature European alder leaves are notched.
Cut stems commonly resprout.

proposedDescription: European beachgrass grows in tight clumps on coastal sand and spreads through buried stems called rhizomes. It was widely planted to hold dunes in place along the Pacific coast. That ability also changes the habitat: dense stands trap sand, alter dune shape and replace open areas used by native plants and animals. It is adapted to accumulating sand and can send new shoots upward as burial continues. On the Pacific coast, identifying the grass correctly matters because American beachgrass, their hybrid and native American dune grass can grow in similar settings.
identification: The leaves are narrow and usually rolled inward, and stems grow close together in dense clumps. The most helpful feature is the ligule, a small flap at the junction of the leaf blade and its sheath around the stem. In European beachgrass this flap is long and pointed, commonly about 20 mm. American beachgrass has a much shorter, flatter ligule, about 2 mm; hybrids can be intermediate. Native American dune grass, Leymus mollis, has much broader, often blue-gray leaves and a ligule less than 1 mm long. Photograph the leaf junction with a ruler, along with a whole clump and any flower head. Intermediate plants should be recorded as uncertain until reviewed.
actions: Do not transplant beachgrass from an established stand to another dune. Where removal is appropriate, join a coordinated dune-restoration effort so work accounts for nesting wildlife, native plants and sand movement. Small patches can be dug repeatedly, collecting the buried stems as well as the visible shoots. Expect follow-up: fragments left underground can produce substantial regrowth, and one pulling session rarely finishes the job. Keep excavated plant material from being scattered into clean sand. Large stands may need specialist methods and restoration planning. Mark treated areas and revisit them through the growing season to find new shoots while they are still small.
researchNotes: Oregon Sea Grant provides current species and hybrid distinctions. Cal-IPC summarizes field removal experience, while the NPS project independently documents regrowth after incomplete hand removal. These support persistent, coordinated work, not an arbitrary excavation depth for every dune. American beachgrass is introduced on the Pacific coast but native elsewhere in North America.

proposedDescription: European bird cherry is a small deciduous tree with fragrant white flower clusters in spring and dark cherries later in the year. Also called Mayday tree, it has been planted as an ornamental well beyond its northern European and Asian range. Birds eat the fruit and carry the seeds into surrounding vegetation. In Alaska, escaped trees can form dense thickets in natural areas, making garden trees an important source to watch. Cutting alone can encourage a flush of new shoots from trunks and roots, so successful removal requires more than taking down the visible crown.
identification: Trees commonly reach about 15-30 feet, with smooth gray-brown bark marked by small pores. Leaves are oval to elliptical, sharply toothed and pointed at the tip; two small glands occur near the blade's base. The white flowers form elongated, often drooping clusters, followed by small black fruits. Prunus virginiana can look similar, especially before flowering; fruit stones in European bird cherry are wrinkled, whereas chokecherry stones are smooth. The red summer foliage of 'Canada Red' helps identify that particular chokecherry cultivar, but ordinary green-leaved chokecherries require other characters. Amur chokecherry has conspicuous copper-colored peeling bark. Include flower or fruit clusters and bark in an identification request.
actions: Look beyond an ornamental tree for seedlings, especially along nearby woodland edges and drainage corridors. Small seedlings can be pulled where the soil allows removal without damaging other vegetation. Established plants readily resprout from remaining roots and stems, so arrange follow-up checks before cutting a larger tree. An arborist or invasive-plant adviser can help select a method suited to the site and nearby desirable trees. Avoid dumping living branches or root material where they can establish. Before purchasing replacements, check current local guidance and choose a suitable alternative. In Alaska, use the state invasive-plant program for current planting restrictions and confirmed escape reports.
researchNotes: Alaska Plant Materials Center provides exact-species biology and small-plant removal advice. USDA Forest Service and Fairbanks soil-and-water conservation guidance provide lookalikes. The 2021 FAQ's no-statewide-ban statement is outdated relative to the 2026 FWS report of a 2025 quarantine; no old legal claim is repeated. The Alaska impact context is intentional, not nationwide.

proposedDescription: European black currant is a deciduous shrub grown for dark berries used in juices, preserves and other foods. Its leaves and branches carry aromatic glands, giving the plant a distinctive scent. Native to Eurasia, it occurs in cultivation and as an introduced plant elsewhere; that history alone does not make every planted shrub an ecological problem. A particularly important consideration in North America is white pine blister rust. Susceptible black currants can serve as an alternate host for the fungus, whose most serious damage occurs on five-needle pines.
identification: A mature shrub can reach about 2 m tall. Leaves are roughly 5-10 cm wide with three to five lobes and an aromatic glandular surface. Drooping flower clusters usually bear several small, bell-shaped flowers, greenish outside and reddish-white within, followed by round black berries. American black currant, Ribes americanum, can look similar but has larger yellowish-white flower clusters and longer floral bracts, the small leaf-like structures associated with flowers. Cultivars and currant-gooseberry hybrids add variation, so fruit color alone is insufficient. Photograph flowers, the underside of a mature leaf and the whole shrub; retain a nursery label if available. An unknown berry should not be identified by tasting it.
actions: Before planting or sharing cuttings, ask local extension or agriculture staff which currants are allowed and which cultivars have appropriate rust resistance for the area. Consider nearby five-needle pines when choosing a planting site. Monitor leaves for unusual orange spore patches or premature leaf drop, and have suspected rust checked rather than assuming all leaf spotting is blister rust. For an unwanted garden escape, confirm the identification and remove it while small, then monitor the spot for additional seedlings. Do not clear native currants indiscriminately: historical attempts to eliminate all Ribes did not eliminate the disease, and individual sites need a more considered plan.
researchNotes: HortFlora supplies exact morphology and the R. americanum distinction; UC IPM supplies the black-currant/blister-rust relationship and resistance guidance. Illinois Extension qualifies the limits of broad Ribes eradication. This profile does not imply a nationwide planting ban or cultivar immunity. The attempted NC State species page was inaccessible and contributes no evidence.

Black currant is an efficient alternate host of white pine blister rust.
Resistant Ribes and pine selections are management options.

proposedDescription: European blackberry is a prickly, scrambling shrub with arching canes, soft-looking hairy foliage and clusters of dark fruit. It belongs to a difficult group of closely related European brambles, several of which have become established outside their native ranges. In the Pacific Northwest it occurs in scattered disturbed places and woodland edges. Dense growth can obstruct access and compete with surrounding vegetation, but species-specific impact information is less complete than for Himalayan blackberry. Correctly naming the plant helps keep local records and management expectations from being confused with those of its better-known relatives.
identification: Look for arching, often dark-purple canes with numerous prickles and conspicuous hairs, especially on young growth and flower-bearing stems. Leaves usually have three to five leaflets; the terminal leaflet is broad, often nearly round, with a pointed tip and toothed margin. The undersides are densely pale-hairy. Flowers have five white to pinkish petals, and ripe fruits form rounded blackberries about 1.5 cm across. Himalayan blackberry, Rubus armeniacus, generally has smoother, greener, more angular stems with larger, less numerous prickles. These are comparative clues rather than a reliable single-feature test. For expert review, include first-year canes, flowering branches and both leaf surfaces, with close-ups of hairs and glands.
actions: Wear sturdy gloves and protect exposed skin when working among the prickly canes. For a small confirmed unwanted patch, cut back enough growth to reach the crown and dig out the rooted plant where that can be done without excessive soil disturbance. Gather living cane and root pieces instead of leaving them on moist ground. Revisit the site for regrowth and new seedlings. Cutting or mowing can reduce access problems, but established blackberry roots commonly survive and need further attention. Avoid mowing ripe fruit into clean ground. Larger thickets benefit from a staged plan that protects nearby desirable plants and includes several seasons of follow-up.
researchNotes: Flora of New Zealand provides independent exact-species morphology. The Center for Natural Lands Management guide explicitly borrows many control methods from R. armeniacus because R. vestitus trials are scarce; public actions are therefore cautious blackberry-level practice. NSW includes R. vestitus in its managed aggregate. No aggregate-wide impact or treatment percentage is assigned to this species.

sources.title: Flora of New Zealand: Rubus vestitus
Center for Natural Lands Management: Rubus vestitus management guide

claims: Arching dark-purple stems are hairy and glandular.
Leaves have three to five leaflets with densely hairy lower surfaces.
Himalayan blackberry has smoother stems and larger fewer prickles.
Many control recommendations are borrowed from other blackberries.
Small patches can be dug with repeated attention to regrowth.
The aggregate includes R. vestitus.
Living stems can regrow on soil; mowing does not kill established plants.

proposedDescription: European bugleweed is a perennial of wet margins, ditches and marshy ground. Its upright stems carry toothed leaves in opposite pairs and small white flowers crowded where the leaves join the stem. Although it belongs to the mint family, it lacks the familiar mint scent. Seeds can travel in water or on muddy footwear and machinery, while spreading stems help patches expand. It is introduced in parts of North America and has become troublesome around some New Zealand lakes; those observations do not establish the same level of impact at every North American site.
identification: Stems are four-sided and may reach about 1 m tall. Leaves are green and strongly toothed, with lower leaves sometimes deeply cut near the base. Small white flowers, often spotted purple, sit in rings at leaf junctions rather than in a showy terminal spike. Spearmint has a distinct mint smell and flowers concentrated toward stem tips. The more difficult comparison is native American water-horehound, Lycopus americanus. A regional key separates them using underside hair length, flower structures and calyx size; European bugleweed generally has longer leaf hairs and a larger calyx. These details require magnification. Include lower and upper leaves and mature flowers in a botanical identification request.
actions: Clean mud and plant material from boots and maintenance equipment before moving between wetland sites. Do not move plants or soil from a suspected patch to another pond or ditch. Confirm the species before removing it, because native water-horehounds can be very similar. If a small confirmed patch is unwanted, discuss careful manual removal with the land manager, collecting spreading stems and checking afterward for new growth. Extensive digging among sedges or along soft banks can damage the habitat being protected. Record patch boundaries and revisit them during flowering to assess spread; broad treatment should follow a local wetland-management plan rather than the common name alone.
researchNotes: NIWA-authored NZPCN material supports habitat, dispersal and cautious manual management; Native Plant Trust independently supplies the L. americanus comparison. New Zealand environmental-weed status is explicitly regional. USGS direct access returned 403, so its brief search statement about chemical control is not used to establish a treatment gap or a universal absence of options.

sources.title: NIWA: Identification guide to freshwater pests of New Zealand

claims: Wetland perennial lacks mint scent; white flowers have purple spotting.
Seeds disperse by water, footwear and machinery; manual control can be appropriate.
Four-sided stems reach 1 m; spreading stolons aid expansion.
Spearmint differs in scent and terminal flowers.
L. americanus differs in lower-leaf hair length and floral measurements.
European species is introduced in New England.

proposedDescription: European centaury is a small upright herb with pink flowers held above a basal cluster of leaves. It grows in grasslands, roadsides and other open, disturbed places, sometimes becoming much more conspicuous in favorable seasons. Native across parts of Europe, western Asia and northern Africa, it has been introduced on several other continents. A flowering patch can look striking without necessarily being a high-priority invasive problem. Local abundance, the plants it is growing among and the purpose of the site are more useful management guides than its introduced status alone.
identification: Plants are generally under 50 cm tall, with smooth, opposite leaves and an evident rosette at ground level. Stem leaves become smaller upward. The flowers have a slender tube opening into five pink lobes, and the branching flower cluster is relatively flat-topped. Small centaury, Centaurium pulchellum, usually lacks the basal rosette and has flowers on clearer stalks, commonly 2-5 mm long. In European centaury the flowers are nearly stalkless, and the calyx surrounding the flower tube is substantially shorter than the tube. Photograph the plant base as well as the flowers: a close-up of pink petals alone omits one of the most useful distinctions.
actions: First decide whether the patch is actually interfering with desired vegetation or land use. A few plants in disturbed ground may warrant observation rather than broad treatment. Where removal is wanted, hand-pull or carefully hoe young plants before capsules mature, taking care not to uproot surrounding desirable plants. Gather flowering or fruiting material rather than scattering it through the site. Return during the next growing season to check for new plants and maintain the intended ground cover. In a diverse meadow, confirm the identification before working through the whole patch; other small pink-flowered gentian relatives may deserve protection.
researchNotes: Native Plant Trust and NSW Flora independently support morphology and lookalikes. Local NSW Landcare observations support easy manual removal and proportionate prioritization, but are not evidence of harmlessness everywhere. Seed-prevention timing is a conservative inference from the dry capsule and short-lived habit, not a species-specific eradication trial.

sources.title: Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney PlantNET: Centaurium erythraea

claims: Basal rosette and nearly stalkless flowers distinguish it from C. pulchellum.
Dry capsules open to release seeds; it occurs in disturbed habitats and fields.
Usually 15-50 cm tall with a persistent basal rosette.
Pink flowers have a calyx about half to two-thirds the corolla-tube length.
Seasonal abundance varies; local managers prioritize more damaging weeds.
Hand pulling or chipping is straightforward where removal is wanted.

proposedDescription: European chestnut is a large deciduous tree grown for its nuts, shade and timber. Long, sharply toothed leaves and densely spiny fruit husks are its most familiar features; older trunks develop deep grooves. The tree's cultivation outside its native range does not by itself call for removal. Tree health is often the more immediate concern: chestnut blight and chestnut gall wasp can damage it, and moving affected shoots or planting material can help pests travel. A well-identified, healthy tree and an escaping seedling present different management questions.
identification: Leaves are simple and alternate, usually about 15-25 cm long, with strong parallel side veins ending in coarse teeth. Yellowish catkins appear in early to midsummer, followed by nuts enclosed in very prickly husks. Mature trees become substantial, often exceeding 12 m in height. Horse chestnut, Aesculus hippocastanum, is unrelated and has opposite leaves divided into hand-like groups of leaflets, showier upright flower clusters and less densely spiny fruit cases. Distinguishing European chestnut from other Castanea species or cultivated hybrids is harder and may need twig, leaf-underside and fruit examination. Keep cultivar or nursery records when available; a nut alone does not establish the exact tree species.
actions: For a retained tree, watch for thinning foliage, dead branches, cracked or discolored bark lesions and unusual swellings on buds or leaves. Photograph symptoms and ask a local tree-health service for advice before moving suspect branches or propagation material. Pink or green leaf galls can indicate chestnut gall wasp, while bark cankers require a different diagnosis. Pull unwanted seedlings while they are manageable if the tree is spreading beyond the intended planting. Use an arborist for large branches or removal, and protect the trunk from unnecessary wounds. Select replacement trees or nursery stock with local disease risks and the available growing space in mind.
researchNotes: NC State and RHS independently support morphology and size; Forest Research's 2026 campaign supplies current pest symptoms and movement precautions. Its TreeAlert reporting destination and restrictions are UK-specific, so the public actions route readers to local services. No nationwide invasive designation or reliable separation of chestnut hybrids from a single photograph is claimed.

sources.title: Forest Research: Check a sweet chestnut

claims: Leaves are alternate, coarsely toothed and 6-10 inches long.
Summer catkins precede nuts enclosed in spiny husks.
A large deciduous tree exceeding 12 m has grooved bark and glossy serrated leaves.
Chestnut blight causes bark cankers; gall wasps cause colored bud and leaf swellings.
Infested shoots should not be moved; horse chestnut has opposite compound leaves.

proposedDescription: European chickweed is a small, hairy annual that flowers in spring on open, sandy or gravelly ground. Its white, shallowly notched petals and opposite leaves give it the familiar mouse-ear chickweed appearance, but identifying the exact species requires a closer look. North American floras have included quite variable plants under this name, including material also treated as the glutinosum subspecies or variety. A roadside patch therefore should not be assigned a narrow taxonomic identity from flower color alone. The available accounts describe an introduced plant of disturbed ground rather than establishing severe harm at every site.
identification: The Flora of North America treatment describes branching stems about 2-12 cm tall, small hairy leaves and loose clusters of several flowers. Petals are around 5 mm long and roughly equal the sepals; the fruit is a narrow capsule that extends beyond them. Gland-tipped hairs can make the plant sticky. Cerastium glomeratum can resemble it, but typically has entirely green flower bracts and longer non-glandular hairs on bracts and sepals. The narrow papery margins of upper bracts are useful in the European chickweed group. Count flower parts and photograph mature capsules, bracts and hair tips through magnification. Regional treatments differ, so uncertain plants need a specimen-based botanical determination.
actions: For a small unwanted patch in a garden or other already disturbed ground, removal before the capsules open is a reasonable way to limit further seed input. Lift the small plants carefully and collect fruiting material; avoid carrying seed-bearing soil to another bed. Recheck the area the following spring and maintain the desired vegetation rather than repeatedly creating bare soil. In natural vegetation, establish which chickweed is present before clearing a patch. Broad spraying is difficult to justify from an uncertain chickweed photograph. An herbarium or extension botanist can advise which flowering and fruiting details are needed for confirmation.
researchNotes: FNA uses a broad, variable C. pumilum concept including glutinosum material; InfoFlora offers an independent European treatment with somewhat different floral counts. Kew currently accepts glutinosum as a variety within C. pumilum. Species-level copy keeps that variation visible and does not assign a variety. Actions are conservative annual seed-prevention advice, not trial-backed eradication claims.

sources.title: Flora of North America: Cerastium pumilum
Kew POWO: Cerastium pumilum var. glutinosum

claims: Annual plants have small hairy leaves, loose flower clusters and narrow capsules.
North American material is variable and includes glutinosum forms.
C. glomeratum differs in bracts and hairs.
An annual of dry sandy ground with shallowly notched petals and narrow-margined upper bracts.
European treatment allows five to ten stamens.
Glutinosum is accepted as a variety of C. pumilum.

proposedDescription: European common reed is the introduced lineage of a very tall wetland grass also represented in North America by native relatives. Its dense stands can replace diverse marsh vegetation and obstruct shorelines or drainage routes. Upright canes carry long leaves and large purple-brown flower plumes that fade as the season ends. Buried stems and fragments help it spread, so moving soil or mowing equipment between sites can create new problems. The native common reed is not the target of this profile: confirming the lineage is an essential part of deciding what to do.
identification: Plants can exceed 15 feet tall, with long blue-green leaves and dense flowering heads. Introduced stems are commonly ridged or dull, and leaf sheaths remain tightly attached, including on older standing canes. Native Phragmites australis subsp. americanus more often has smooth, shiny, sometimes reddish stems and sheaths that loosen and fall. The tiny ligule at the leaf-blade junction is usually shorter in the introduced lineage, roughly 0.4-0.9 mm, compared with 1-1.7 mm in the native lineage. Use several features together; Gulf Coast lineages and unusual plants complicate simple comparisons. Photograph stem surfaces, attached sheaths, ligules and the whole stand, preferably with a scale and seasonal information.
actions: Map a suspected new stand and ask a wetland or invasive-plant specialist to confirm the lineage before treatment. Keep soil, cut canes and buried stem fragments from moving to uninfested ground, and clean machinery before it leaves the site. A single mowing is unlikely to eliminate an established stand; repeated cutting may reduce density but underground growth can persist. Plan control with the responsible land or water manager, including any required authorization for work in water and a way to protect native vegetation. Revisit treated sites for several years, remove new growth as the plan directs, and include restoration of the desired wetland vegetation.
researchNotes: Minnesota DNR supplies exact-subspecies management and field characters; USDA NRCS supplies independently assembled lineage keys including the Gulf Coast lineage. MSU documents mechanical-treatment limits. Morphology is presented as a combination, not an infallible ligule cutoff. Local permit requirements are not generalized into a national rule, and no taxonomic catalog status is changed.

sources.title: Michigan Natural Features Inventory: St. Martin Island invasive plants

claims: Introduced reed can exceed 15 feet and retains tight leaf sheaths.
Mowing reduces density; equipment cleaning and multiple years of follow-up are needed.
Native and introduced lineages differ in ligules, sheath persistence and stem surface.
The Gulf Coast lineage complicates a simple native versus introduced field key.
Mechanical treatment alone is ineffective for established invasive common reed.
Identification combines several vegetative and floral traits.

proposedDescription: European Corn Borer is a moth whose caterpillars tunnel into corn stalks and other sturdy plant stems. Feeding can weaken stalks, damage ears and leave broken tassels or wilted shoots. Corn is an important host, but peppers, potatoes, beans and some ornamental plants can also be attacked. The pest survives winter as a larva inside plant material. The number and timing of generations vary with region and weather, so a calendar date that works in one place may miss the vulnerable stage elsewhere. Local scouting is more useful than assuming every damaged stalk needs treatment.
identification: Mature caterpillars are roughly an inch long, light brown to pinkish-gray, with a dark head and rows of round dark spots on the body. Look for small holes in leaves, entry holes in stalks and brown frass, the insect's droppings, around tunnels. Adult moths have a wingspan of about 20-34 mm, with zigzag markings across yellowish to brown wings; males are generally smaller and darker. Corn rootworm can also cause plants to fall, but its larvae feed on roots rather than making stalk tunnels. Corn earworm and other caterpillars may share the crop, so include the larva and feeding location when seeking confirmation.
actions: Inspect corn for fresh leaf feeding and check damaged stems for larvae before selecting a response. Follow regional extension scouting guidance, because generation timing and pest pressure vary. Remove or appropriately manage infested stalk residues after harvest so they do not shelter overwintering larvae; choose a method that also fits the garden or farm's soil-conservation needs. Treatments aimed at young caterpillars must reach them before they tunnel deeply into the plant. Repeated applications to old, empty damage will not repair a stalk. For a small garden, concentrate on confirmed infested plants and cleanup; for larger crops, use crop-specific thresholds and resistance-management advice.
researchNotes: UF/IFAS supplies biology, adult measurements and residue-management evidence; Minnesota independently supports larval recognition, rootworm comparison and scouting. The UF source's broad insecticide schedules and tillage percentages are not copied as universal recommendations. A New Brunswick page returned 403 and is not counted. Regional Bt suppression does not mean the pest has disappeared.

sources.title: University of Minnesota: Corn plants fallen over
University of Minnesota: European corn borer in field corn

claims: Adults span 20-34 mm and males are darker; larvae overwinter inside stalks.
Host range extends beyond corn and generations vary geographically.
Stalk-residue management reduces overwintering habitat.
Spotted larvae, stalk holes and frass indicate corn-borer feeding.
Rootworm causes lodging through root injury rather than stalk tunneling.
Scouting guides whether treatment is worthwhile.
Biotypes differ in generation timing and overwinter in stalk residues.

proposedDescription: European dewberry is a low, trailing bramble whose dark fruit often carries a pale blue-white coating. Its slender prickly canes can root where their tips touch the soil, gradually extending a patch. White flowers and usually three-part leaves distinguish its appearance from many taller blackberries. It is native across a broad Eurasian region and occurs outside that range in scattered introduced populations. In a garden, the main practical issue may be keeping rooted canes within their intended space; an occurrence does not automatically carry the same impact as a large Himalayan blackberry thicket.
identification: Look for creeping or arching canes, commonly under about 1.5 m tall, with slender prickles and a pale waxy coating. Leaves usually consist of three broad, toothed leaflets. Ripe fruits remain attached to their central core and often contain relatively few, large individual fruitlets. Native northern dewberry, Rubus flagellaris, can look similar, but lacks the strongly coated stems and commonly has fruit with more fruitlets. Black raspberry, R. occidentalis, leaves its central core behind when the ripe fruit is picked. Hybrids with other brambles can blur these differences. Photograph young canes, leaf undersides, flowers and intact fruit, and treat intermediate plants cautiously.
actions: Watch the outer edge of a planting for cane tips that have rooted. Where containment is wanted, lift and remove these newly rooted sections before they extend the patch further. Prune old fruiting canes as part of routine garden care, and keep living cuttings from being placed on moist soil elsewhere. If removing an unwanted patch, trace the rooted sections rather than cutting only the visible canes, then revisit for regrowth. Confirm the plant before clearing native dewberries or other low brambles. For a natural-area population, document its extent and seek local botanical advice before deciding whether removal is a priority.
researchNotes: RHS provides exact-species containment by pruning and removing rooted tips. FNA and the University of Michigan independently support morphology, while Michigan synthesizes several floras. The source's loose description of the plant as biennial is not repeated: individual canes are biennial, while the rooted shrub persists. No medicinal claims or regional eradication claim is used.

sources.title: Flora of North America: Rubus caesius
University of Michigan CLIMBERS: Rubus caesius

claims: Canes fruit in their second year; stems naturally root at their tips.
Pruning and removing newly rooted sections can contain a planting.
Creeping prickly stems have a strong pale coating; leaves have three leaflets.
North American fruits commonly have few large fruitlets.
R. flagellaris lacks strongly coated stems; black raspberry fruit separates from its core.
Stems root at tips and can reach about 1.5 m.

proposedDescription: European earwig is the familiar brown garden insect with conspicuous pincers at the end of its body. It feeds at night and shelters in tight, damp spaces by day. Earwigs can damage seedlings, flowers and soft fruit, but they also eat aphids and other small insects, so their presence is not automatically a reason to control them. The scientific name has historically covered a complex of very similar species. Recent research separates several of those species, which means older North American records and garden advice do not always refer to Forficula auricularia in the narrow modern sense.
identification: Typical European earwigs are reddish-brown, roughly 13-14 mm long before the pincers are counted, with short wing covers concealing folded hind wings. Adult males generally have strongly curved pincers; females and young stages have straighter ones. These features recognize the familiar earwig group but do not reliably separate F. auricularia from the nearly identical F. dentata. Modern species-level work may require molecular evidence. For a garden problem, photograph the entire insect and record its location and the plant being eaten. Check at night: irregular holes alone can also come from slugs or other feeders, and slug damage may be accompanied by slime trails.
actions: Confirm that earwigs are causing the damage before reducing their numbers. If seedlings or flowers are being eaten, place rolled newspaper or short tubes near affected plants before dark and empty the shelter traps into soapy water the following morning. Repeat while damage continues, and reduce unnecessary damp hiding places immediately around vulnerable plants. Mature plants often tolerate some feeding, and earwigs hunting aphids can be useful. Indoors, focus on entry points and removing occasional insects rather than treating the whole garden. These practical steps apply to the commonly managed European-earwig group even where its exact species identity has not been resolved.
researchNotes: Research gap is exact taxon assignment, not absence of safe garden advice. Recent peer-reviewed work recognizes cryptic species; Iowa State-hosted BugGuide now excludes narrow F. auricularia from several western jurisdictions, while extension pages retain the historical broad name. UC management evidence is therefore labeled group-level and not assigned uncritically to narrow F. auricularia.

sources.title: Animal Biodiversity and Conservation: Revising western European Forficula distribution

claims: Pincer shape differs between adult sexes; young earwigs resemble small adults.
Night inspection distinguishes feeding causes; earwigs can be nuisance visitors indoors.
European-earwig group eats both plants and beneficially aphids.
Rolled-paper shelter traps emptied daily can reduce populations.
Typical adult body length excluding pincers is 13-14 mm; hind wings fold beneath short covers.
Most cryptic members of the auricularia complex cannot be identified without molecular evidence.
F. dentata is essentially identical; the account revises western North American assignments.

proposedDescription: European elm scale is a sap-feeding insect that can make the area beneath an elm sticky long before the insects themselves are noticed. Its honeydew, a sugary waste, supports black sooty mold on leaves and branches. Heavy infestations can cause yellowing, early leaf fall and twig dieback. Mature females sit on bark with a distinctive white fringe around a darker body, while young stages may feed along leaf veins. The insect is also widely called Gossyparia spuria in current references; those accounts concern the same elm pest.
identification: Look on twig forks, bark cracks and the undersides of small limbs for oval gray, brown or dark reddish females surrounded by a white waxy fringe. Large females may approach 8-10 mm. Tiny yellow-orange crawlers move onto leaves, where they settle along the main veins; later stages return to bark. Male immature stages form small elongated white coverings that can look like grains of rice. Sticky honeydew alone is not diagnostic because aphids and other scales also produce it. Examine the fringe and body shape with a hand lens, and include the elm's identity and leaf undersides in photographs. Old scale remains may persist after the insects have died.
actions: Check whether the scales are alive and whether the tree is declining before arranging treatment. Support tree health with appropriate watering during drought, and preserve the small predators and parasitic wasps that attack the scale. Round emergence holes in mature scales can indicate parasitoid activity. Avoid routine broad-spectrum sprays that remove these natural enemies. If damage is substantial, an arborist can monitor the mobile crawler stage and select a properly timed treatment for the tree's size and setting. Repeated use of the same systemic insecticide may fail where resistance has developed. Monitor the next generation rather than judging success only by old coverings left on the bark.
researchNotes: UC IPM, Utah State and Colorado State agree on the elm host, fringed females, honeydew and seasonal movement. CSU's webpage has an apparent reversal saying dead scales bleed; that wording is deliberately not used. Dates vary by climate. UC reports resistance in some locations, not universal resistance. Both scientific combinations are preserved without changing catalog taxonomy.

claims: Fringed dark females occur on elm bark; young stages may feed on leaves.
Natural enemies, tree health and crawler monitoring guide control.
Some populations resist repeatedly used neonicotinoids.
Females are about 5/16 inch; male coverings resemble white rice.
Yellow-orange crawlers settle along leaf veins.
Live infestation should be confirmed because old scales remain attached.
Severe infestations cause premature leaf loss and branch dieback.

proposedDescription: European fingernail clam is a tiny freshwater bivalve that lives among bottom sediments and aquatic vegetation. Unlike the larger mussels familiar from riverbanks, it is only about the width of a fingernail. It filters suspended food from water and occurs in lakes, ponds and slower-flowing waters. North American records have been treated as introductions from Eurasia, but the extent of ecological harm remains poorly documented. A recent U.S. risk assessment calls the evidence insufficient to determine invasion impacts; uncertainty should not be turned into either a claim of serious damage or a guarantee of harmlessness.
identification: The shell is broadly oval and somewhat swollen, commonly around 9-11 mm long and sometimes approaching 14 mm. It is yellowish, gray or brown, with rounded raised areas near the center of the hinge and very fine concentric growth lines. Sphaerium nitidum can look like a smaller version, and members of the S. corneum group, including S. nucleus, require close attention to shell shape, pores and hinge teeth. Size and color alone are inadequate. A specialist may need the shell under a microscope, including the hinge interior. Record waterbody, depth and substrate, and photograph both sides beside a millimeter scale before arranging any authorized specimen collection.
actions: Avoid transferring live clams, aquatic plants, sediment or untreated water between ponds and waterways. Inspect and clean mud from sampling gear, boots and other equipment before the next site, following local aquatic-hygiene guidance. If a clam may represent a new occurrence, send photographs and the exact location to an aquatic-biologist or invasive-species program and ask how they want a specimen handled. Leave surrounding native mussels and clams undisturbed. There is no basis here for household chemical treatment, dredging or draining a waterbody solely because a tiny clam resembles this species. Management should follow confirmed identification and a site-specific assessment.
researchNotes: USGS and FWS are treated as one source family where FWS derives biological material from USGS; MolluscIreland supplies independent morphology and habitat. Killeen's taxonomic discussion shows why historical S. corneum records can include related species. No species-specific eradication method was established, but prevention and diagnostic referral remain actionable. USGS shell-luster wording is inconsistent, so not used as a decisive character.

sources.title: US Fish and Wildlife Service: European fingernail clam risk summary
National Museums Northern Ireland: Sphaerium corneum
Ian Killeen: Notes on the Sphaerium corneum group

claims: Small oval shells reach about 14 mm and resemble S. nitidum.
Found in freshwater sediments and vegetation.
Introduced-population impact data are deficient and assessed risk is uncertain.
Broad oval shells commonly measure 9-11 mm, with central rounded umbones.
Occurs in sediments and climbs aquatic plants; favors slower freshwaters.
Distinction from S. nucleus and S. ovale uses pores, hinge teeth and shell form.
Pores may require high magnification and careful lighting.

proposedDescription: European fire ant is a small reddish ant that can form dense colonies in damp gardens, lawns and other sheltered places. Disturbing a nest can provoke painful stings, and the ants may make heavily occupied areas unpleasant to use. Nests are often hidden beneath stones, wood or roots rather than marked by obvious soil mounds. Colonies can spread locally by splitting into new nests, while moved soil, mulch and potted plants can carry them farther. Native to Europe and parts of Asia, the species has established troublesome populations in parts of North America.
identification: Workers are about 4-5 mm long, reddish-brown, with a shiny rear body and a more textured head and middle section. A hand lens reveals a two-part waist and two backward-pointing spines. These are useful clues but are shared by other ants, including native Myrmica species. Myrmica ruginodis is a particularly close comparison requiring attention to the waist profile and other small structures; color or a sting is not enough to decide. Photograph several workers from above and the side, and ask an identification service how to submit a securely contained sample. Do not handle live ants with bare fingers while trying to inspect the spines.
actions: Pause movement of soil, compost, mulch and container plants from a suspected infestation until the ants are identified. Inspect incoming pots and their drainage areas before planting them. Mark occupied areas so people working or playing nearby can avoid disturbing nests. Around buildings or heavily used garden space, reducing unnecessary damp shelter may make conditions less favorable, but it will not remove every colony. For confirmed infestations, seek a local program or experienced pest professional familiar with this species. Track ant activity after treatment and check neighboring patches, because colonies can persist or recolonize. Avoid assuming a product marketed for other fire ants will solve this different ant problem.
researchNotes: UF/IFAS and Maine publications share authors and research and are grouped together rather than counted as independent corroboration. Thompson Rivers University entomologist Higgins independently supports the difficult species comparison; Metro Vancouver practice supports follow-up and reinvasion monitoring. No homemade bait recipe, eradication promise or current national range boundary is supplied.

sources.title: University of Maine: European Fire Ant
Thompson Rivers University: Identification of Myrmica rubra
Metro Vancouver: European Fire Ant best management practices

claims: Workers are 4-5 mm with a two-part waist and backward spines.
Colonies favor humid shelter and spread in soil and potted plants.
Habitat modification can reduce suitability but does not eliminate colonies.
Nests are concealed rather than large soil mounds; identification should precede control.
M. ruginodis requires careful waist and other microscopic comparisons.
Monitoring and maintenance are required because treated sites can be reinvaded.

proposedDescription: European fruit lecanium scale feeds on the sap of many woody plants, including fruit trees and maples. The rounded brown females can look like little swellings in the bark. Large populations may slow growth or contribute to twig dieback, while sticky honeydew supports black sooty mold on leaves and surfaces below. An infestation does not automatically call for spraying: natural enemies often keep this soft scale in check. Its appearance changes with its host and age, which makes identification less straightforward than the common name suggests.
identification: Adult females form domed brown bodies that can reach about 6 mm across, sometimes with two noticeable humps. Smaller immature scales are flatter. Look along twigs and beneath leaves, especially near the veins, for the much smaller pale crawlers. On deciduous hosts the insects move between leaves and woody stems during their development. Related lecanium scales, including Fletcher scale (Parthenolecanium fletcheri) and oak lecanium (P. quercifex), can be difficult to separate by appearance alone. Record the host plant, photograph several occupied twigs, and include both adults and young stages when requesting identification. Honeydew reveals sap feeding but does not identify the species.
actions: Inspect affected branches before deciding whether treatment is needed. Check for living insects and fresh honeydew rather than treating old scale bodies alone. Preserve predators and parasitoids by avoiding unnecessary broad-spectrum sprays. If damage is increasing, ask extension staff to help track crawler emergence; these exposed young insects are easier to target than protected older females. Timing varies with local weather, so a calendar date from another region is unreliable. A local adviser can assess whether a dormant-season oil or another labeled treatment fits the host and infestation. Large trees and persistent dieback are good reasons to involve a qualified arborist.
researchNotes: Maryland and Massachusetts extension describe this insect as native despite its common name; this finding is retained for review without changing catalog status. Morphology varies by host, and related Parthenolecanium species require caution. Management combines independently read university guidance; regional crawler dates were deliberately not generalized.

sources.title: University of Maryland: European fruit lecanium scale
University of Tennessee: European fruit lecanium

claims: Soft scale with broad woody host range; females reach 6 mm and heavy populations cause reduced growth or dieback.
Crawlers settle along leaf veins and later return to twigs; inspect twig undersides and leaves.
Related lecanium scales are difficult to distinguish; conserve natural enemies.
Biological control frequently regulates populations; dormant or delayed-dormant oil may be appropriate when control is needed.

proposedDescription: European fruit scale is a small armored scale that lives on the bark of fruit trees and other woody hosts. Apple, pear, cherry, peach, and plum are among the plants it can infest. A gray cover protects each settled female, so colonies may resemble roughened bark rather than insects. Heavy feeding can weaken a tree, and feeding on leaves may produce reddish marks. This species is especially easy to confuse with San Jose scale, sometimes on the same plant; a reliable diagnosis matters before choosing a treatment.
identification: The female's cover is approximately circular, raised, and about 1.4-1.9 mm wide, with orange-yellow shed skins near its center. Beneath it, the female is yellow and pear-shaped. Male covers are smaller and more elongated; adult males have wings, while the yellow crawlers are the mobile young stage. These features separate it from an elongated, mussel-shaped oystershell scale cover, but not reliably from San Jose scale (Diaspidiotus perniciosus). Specialists distinguish those species using microscopic structures, including pores around the female's genital opening. Send a twig with intact scales for examination rather than relying on a distant bark photograph.
actions: Inspect nursery trees and grafting material before bringing them into an orchard. On an affected tree, note which branches carry living scales and whether new injury is appearing. Keep infested cuttings and prunings from being distributed to other growers. Have the species confirmed, then use local orchard guidance to monitor crawler emergence and decide whether treatment is justified. Dormant oils are one management option described by Michigan State, but host condition, season, and the product label determine whether they are suitable. A single treatment date copied from another climate can miss the vulnerable stage. Recheck marked branches to judge whether management reduced live scales.
researchNotes: Naturalis and the New Zealand fauna treatment independently support the circular cover and microscopic separation from San Jose scale. Michigan State supplies orchard context and management. A NSW page labeled with this scientific name describes an elongated oystershell scale; that conflicting identification was excluded rather than repeated.

sources.title: Michigan State IPM: European fruit scale

claims: Infests pome and stone fruits; gray circular covers resemble San Jose scale; dormant oils and crawler timing are management considerations.
Female cover is 1.4-1.9 mm, circular and gray; body is yellow; perivulvar pores separate it from D. perniciosus.
Specimen-based account describes gray cover and yellow body and confirms diagnostic pores absent in D. perniciosus.

proposedDescription: European gooseberry is a thorny, deciduous fruit shrub with lobed leaves and berries that may ripen green, yellow, pink, or red. Many cultivated forms have been selected for cooking or fresh eating, so fruit color and sweetness vary widely. Outside gardens it can persist or become naturalized, including in parts of New England. Its presence does not by itself demonstrate ecological harm. The flowers and spines are more useful for identifying a stray shrub than the familiar grape-sized fruit alone, especially where native gooseberries grow nearby.
identification: Most garden plants are roughly 1-1.5 m tall. Leaves are rounded and divided into three to five lobes; stout spines occur on the branches. Flowers appear singly or in pairs, with small petals inside longer sepals. Fruits often have bristles and retain the dried flower parts at their tips. In the New England flora, European gooseberry usually has sepals 5-7 mm long and strong nodal spines about 10-15 mm long. Northern gooseberry (Ribes hirtellum) has smaller sepals, about 3-4 mm, and generally shorter nodal spines. Garden hybrids and cultivars complicate identification, so document flowers and the points where spines join the stems.
actions: Before removing a wild gooseberry, distinguish it from native Ribes. Where an unwanted European gooseberry is confirmed, removing a small shrub and its root crown is a practical garden-scale option; check the spot for surviving growth. Wear gloves around the stout spines and keep fruit-bearing debris out of natural areas. For retained fruit plants, use open pruning and suitable watering to maintain a manageable shrub. Ribes can participate in the white pine blister rust cycle, so consult local extension guidance before planting near susceptible white pines. Disease resistance and local planting restrictions need checking for the particular cultivar and location.
researchNotes: PlantNET and Native Plant Trust provide botanical characters; RHS corroborates cultivated size and fruit variation. Minnesota guidance on Ribes and white pine blister rust supports planting caution, not a claim that every shrub is infected. Manual removal is a limited garden recommendation, not a verified landscape eradication protocol.

sources.title: University of Minnesota: White pine blister rust

claims: Naturalized in New England; floral and spine measurements help distinguish R. hirtellum.
Small spiny deciduous shrub with lobed leaves, paired or solitary flowers and often bristly berries.
Ribes grossularia is a synonym.
Cultivated plants reach 1-1.5 m; berry color and cultivar disease resistance vary; prune in winter and summer.
Ribes and susceptible white pines should not be planted together without considering resistant cultivars.

proposedDescription: European grain moth is a small, mottled moth whose larvae can spoil stored grain and other dry foods. Damp conditions are especially favorable, and the insect also uses fungi and decaying material. In grain, caterpillars feed near the surface and bind material with silk, leaving clumps of grain and waste. Its interests extend beyond cereal stores: a study in Italian wine cellars documented larvae tunneling into bottle corks. Finding a moth therefore calls for a search for the breeding material, rather than assuming that the nearest flour bag is the source.
identification: Adults have a pale, tufted head and white forewings heavily marked with dark brown or black. The Canadian Grain Commission gives a wingspan of about 9-14 mm. Mature larvae are approximately 7-10 mm long, whitish, with a darker head. Silk-bound grain or debris can reveal activity, but several stored-product moths make webbing. Other Nemapogon moths can look very similar, and worn wings lose useful pattern details. Keep an adult specimen if possible and record whether larvae were in grain, dried fungi, cork, or another material. A clear photograph of the spread wing pattern can assist identification, but difficult specimens may need specialist examination.
actions: Locate and isolate the infested material before cleaning. Remove accumulated grain dust, spilled food, and debris from shelves, machinery, and cracks; inspect adjacent stock as well as the visibly affected package. For bulk grain, repair leaks and use appropriate drying and aeration to prevent warm, moist pockets. Monitor stored grain regularly for insects and temperature changes. In a wine cellar, inspect corks and storage fixtures, and seek professional advice for affected bottles. Pheromone traps can support monitoring where a suitable lure is available, but catching adults alone does not remove larvae already feeding inside material. Use a grain-storage specialist for a substantial infestation.
researchNotes: Canadian and Argentine government accounts corroborate food associations and adult pattern. Their pest-category labels differ, so the profile avoids primary-versus-secondary classification. The wine-cellar study was read as an abstract only and supports sanitation and monitoring, not a general pesticide recipe or guaranteed household eradication.

sources.title: Canadian Grain Commission: European grain moth
IOBC: Corks damaged by Nemapogon granellus in Tuscan wine cellars
Canadian Grain Commission: Prevent infestations in stored grain

claims: Adult wingspan 9-14 mm; pale larvae reach 7-10 mm; prefers moist grain and leaves silk-bound material near the surface.
Mottled pale and dark wings with a tufted head; associated with fungi and stored products; Nemapogon granella listed as a synonym.
Larvae damaged bottle corks; integrated management included pheromone monitoring and thorough cleaning.
Clean storage and aeration systems, repair leaks, reduce grain moisture and temperature, and monitor stored grain.

proposedDescription: European green crab is a coastal crab that can live in sheltered bays, tidal marshes, eelgrass beds, and river mouths. Its tolerance of changing salinity helps it use habitats where freshwater and seawater meet. In invaded areas it can threaten native shellfish and damage eelgrass habitat. Despite its name, a green crab may be brown, orange, or reddish as well as green. The most dependable visible clue is the set of five points along each side of the shell behind the eyes. Prompt, well-documented reports help coastal managers locate newly occupied sites.
identification: Adults can reach roughly 4 inches across the shell. Count five pointed teeth on each side, starting just outside the eye; there are also three small projections between the eyes. Color is variable and should never be the deciding feature. Photograph the upper shell squarely enough to show both edges, and include a ruler or familiar object for scale when feasible. The native helmet crab can cause confusion in Alaska, but it has a conspicuously hairy covering unlike a green crab. An empty molt can also provide useful evidence. Juveniles and damaged shells deserve extra caution because counting the edge teeth may be difficult.
actions: Report a suspected crab or molt to the relevant state or provincial aquatic invasive-species program, with photographs, date, and an exact location. In Washington, managers specifically ask the public to report rather than kill suspected green crabs because native crabs are often mistaken for them. Do not carry a live crab to another beach or keep it as a pet. Follow the receiving agency's instructions if a specimen is needed; collection and possession rules vary. Coordinated trapping is used in response programs, but an unplanned private trapping effort can harm native animals and obscure where the crab was found.
researchNotes: NOAA supports habitat, size and visible shell features; Washington supplies reporting and native-crab protection guidance, and Alaska Fish and Game provides the helmet-crab comparison. No stale claim that Alaska remains uninvaded is included. Reporting advice is regional and does not imply uniform collection law across jurisdictions.
