researchNotes: Native Plant Trust and the New Zealand flora independently support perennial habit and leaf distinctions. Their fruit-size/tubercle treatments differ, so the reader-facing diagnosis avoids those potentially conflicting measurements. Actions are conservative rootstock and seed containment, not a tested eradication protocol.

sources.title: Flora of New Zealand: Rumex acetosa

claims: Fields and roadsides; backward-pointing leaf lobes distinguish it from typical sheep sorrel.
Dioecious perennial with woody rootstock, stems to about 1 m and backward-directed leaf lobes.

proposedDescription: Narrow-leaved sorrel is a perennial Eurasian plant recorded on disturbed ground, roadsides and open grassy sites in parts of North America. It has often been mistaken for common sorrel, so older names and records need care. A well-documented photograph of the mature plant is more useful than a report based only on a few narrow leaves.
identification: Several upright stems may arise from a stout, deep rootstock. The leaves are narrow and arrow-shaped, often with wavy edges. The most useful field clue is the broad, pyramid-shaped flower cluster: its side branches branch again, giving it a dense, full appearance. Common sorrel usually has a less repeatedly branched cluster. Mature fruit coverings are generally smaller in narrow-leaved sorrel, but the ranges overlap. Include the whole flowering stem, lower leaves and close views of ripe fruits, and seek botanical review when the two species remain difficult to separate.
actions: Document an unfamiliar patch before disturbing it, including nearby roads, fill or former cultivation that might explain its arrival. If confirmed plants need removal, prevent seed production and account for the persistent rootstock; cutting stems once is not the same as removing the plant. Check treated ground in following seasons. For a large patch, obtain a site-specific weed plan rather than transferring control advice from a different Rumex species. Avoid moving soil containing roots or ripe seed to clean ground.
researchNotes: Flora of North America supplies the diagnostic combination and explicitly describes frequent confusion with R. acetosa. Kew independently supports accepted identity and Eurasian range. Published North American collections support regional occurrence, not a current county determination. No species-specific controlled management trial was located; actions are labeled through conservative prevention rather than efficacy claims.

sources.title: Flora of North America: Rumex thyrsiflorus

claims: Deep stout rootstock, narrow wavy leaves and repeatedly branched pyramidal inflorescence distinguish this often-misidentified sorrel.
Accepted perennial Eurasian taxon introduced in parts of North America.

proposedDescription: Common thyme is a small woody herb grown for its aromatic leaves. It favors sunny, well-drained ground and can persist around old plantings. It is not interchangeable with every creeping thyme sold for ground cover. A garden clump or occasional escape does not establish that it is causing ecological harm, so observations should explain whether the plant is cultivated or growing independently.
identification: Look for a low, bushy plant with a woody base, small opposite gray-green leaves and tiny pinkish, lavender or white flowers. Leaves are roughly 6-13 mm long, with edges rolled underneath; young stems are hairy and square in cross-section. Common thyme tends to form an upright little mound, whereas some other thymes form low creeping mats. Cultivars and hybrids complicate identification. Record growth form, leaf edges and a flowering stem, and use the original nursery label as supporting information when available. Aroma alone does not identify the species.
actions: If a plant is spreading beyond an intended bed, remove unwanted rooted growth and prevent seed from reaching adjacent habitat. Do not dump live garden divisions or cuttings on open land. Keep a record of any independently established plants before removing them. For a planting that remains contained, routine pruning and monitoring are more appropriate than treating it as a major infestation. Confirm unfamiliar aromatic plants before using them in food; this profile is not a foraging identification guide.
researchNotes: NC State supplies the small revolute leaves, woody base, floral characters and approximate size. RHS independently distinguishes mounded common thyme from creeping thyme species. Ecological severity and herbicide efficacy are not inferred from culinary use or catalog inclusion.

claims: Woody low subshrub with tiny opposite aromatic leaves, rolled leaf margins and small two-lipped flowers.
Common thyme forms small mounded shrubs; other thymes have creeping growth forms.

proposedDescription: Tomatoes can appear as volunteers where fruit or compost has been discarded, as well as in deliberately planted vegetable beds. They are warm-season plants, usually grown as annuals where frost ends the season. A stray tomato is not equivalent to an established invasive population. Useful observations show whether plants are surviving, fruiting and producing another generation without cultivation.
identification: Tomato stems and leaves are noticeably hairy, often with sticky glandular hairs. Leaves are alternate and divided into several toothed or lobed leaflets. Small yellow, star-shaped flowers are followed by fleshy fruit whose size, shape and ripe color depend on the cultivar. Do not use red fruit alone as the identifying feature: other nightshades have red berries, and tomatoes need not ripen red. Photograph the divided leaves, flowers and fruit together. The strongly scented foliage supports identification but is not an invitation to taste an unfamiliar plant.
actions: Remove unwanted volunteers before ripe fruit drops, and contain discarded fruit in a managed waste or compost system. When reporting a plant outside cultivation, note whether it is near a garden, compost pile or deposited soil. Keep potentially diseased crop residues away from new tomato beds and seek a crop diagnosis if wilting or spotted leaves are the concern. Do not remove native nightshades on the assumption that all nightshade-like seedlings are tomato escapes, and do not eat berries from an uncertain identification.
researchNotes: NC State supports morphology, cultivar variation and warm-season cultivation. Native Plant Trust's independent key corroborates glandular hairs and compound leaves and uses the spelling Solanum lycopersicon. No claim of substantial ecological impact is added without regional evidence.

claims: Glandular hairy stems, divided alternate leaves, yellow flowers and cultivar-dependent fruit.
Tomato is distinguished by aromatic glandular hairs, compound foliage and characteristic fleshy berries.

proposedDescription: Common valerian is a tall perennial once widely planted as a medicinal herb. It can escape into meadows, stream edges and woodland openings, returning early in spring from underground growth and spreading by seed. Dense stands can crowd nearby plants. Its ecological significance is regional; Wisconsin, for example, identifies it as an invasive plant of concern. It is different from the purple-flowered ornamental commonly sold as garden heliotrope.
identification: Leaves are opposite and divided into many toothed, narrow leaflets. Small white to pale pink flowers form clusters near the stem tips. Plants may reach about 1.5 m, and the pale fleshy underground parts have a distinctive strong odor. Native valerian species require care: Valeriana uliginosa generally has simple basal leaves or just a few basal lobes, whereas common valerian has divided basal leaves. Photograph basal and stem leaves as well as flowers; a cluster of pale flowers alone is not diagnostic.
actions: Remove small confirmed plants with their underground growth and revisit the site for shoots or seedlings. Cutting or mowing before flowering can limit seed production, but a persistent patch needs follow-up. Keep ripe heads and living root pieces from being moved elsewhere. In wetlands or near native valerian, confirm identification and coordinate removal with the land manager before disturbing soil. Do not collect wild plants for self-medication. Where the species is regulated, follow the local weed program's disposal and control requirements.
researchNotes: Wisconsin DNR supports regional impact, rhizomes and pre-flowering control. Native Plant Trust independently provides the comparison with native V. uliginosa. The draft omits medical efficacy claims and pesticide instructions; the regional example is not presented as a nationwide legal designation.

claims: Perennial with divided opposite leaves, pale flower clusters and fleshy rhizomes.
Escapes into natural habitats; cut, pull or mow before flowering.
Non-native valerian of open disturbed habitats; divided basal leaves distinguish it from V. uliginosa.

proposedDescription: Common vetch is an annual legume used as a cover crop and also found growing outside cultivation. Its tendrils let it scramble over neighboring plants, forming a loose tangle rather than standing firmly on its own. Seed production can make it a persistent visitor around fields and gardens. A planted cover crop and an unmanaged escape should be described differently in a sighting record.
identification: Each leaf has paired leaflets and ends in a tendril. Pea-shaped flowers arise singly or in small groups close to the leaf axils. This differs from hairy vetch, which typically carries many flowers on longer stalks. Common vetch is part of a variable group that includes narrow-leaved forms; leaf width alone may not resolve a subspecies. Photograph the flower attachment, leaflets, the small stipules where leaves join the stem, and mature pods. A leafy tangle without flowers is harder to distinguish from native vetches.
actions: Where common vetch is unwanted, pull or cut young plants before pods ripen and scatter seed. Follow up along fences, bed edges and disturbed ground. When managing a cover crop, plan termination with crop-specific advice so it does not reseed into the next planting. Do not offer unfamiliar vetch seed or collected plants as animal feed; forage use requires the right species and management. In natural vegetation, confirm that the plant is an introduced vetch before removing it.
researchNotes: NC State independently supports annual cover-crop use and aggressive reseeding; UC IPM and NSW PlantNET provide diagnostic comparisons. This is the species-level profile; the separately queued nigra entry provides narrower diagnostic details. Management remains seed containment rather than a blanket chemical prescription.

claims: Annual climbing cover crop with aggressive self-seeding; occurs in disturbed fields and roadsides.
Common vetch has few flowers close to stems rather than the many-flowered stalks of hairy vetch; seed can spread in soil and equipment.
Vicia sativa has 1-4 axillary flowers and stipules usually with a prominent gland.

proposedDescription: Narrow-leaved vetch is a slender annual member of the common-vetch group, often listed under Vicia angustifolia or a subspecies name. It grows among grasses and along disturbed margins, using leaf tendrils to hold nearby stems. It can spread by seed, but distinguishing it from related vetches is important before assigning a precise name to a record.
identification: Upper leaflets are narrow, commonly 1-4 mm wide. The pea-shaped flowers are about 8-18 mm long and occur close to the leaf axils, usually in small numbers. Mature pods are roughly 2.5-5 cm long, generally smooth, and darken toward black without obvious constrictions between seeds. In the NSW treatment, the pointed teeth of the flower's green calyx are shorter than its tube. Broader common-vetch forms and several native vetches can overlap in appearance. Include ripe pods, flowers and upper and lower leaves in photographs rather than relying only on narrow foliage.
actions: Remove unwanted plants before the pods dry and split. Check equipment, soil and garden waste before moving them from a patch that has set seed. In a small bed, hand removal is usually more targeted than treating the surrounding vegetation. Revisit the site for later seedlings. If plants are mixed with native vetches or are being considered for forage, obtain a firm identification first; similar-looking vetches should not be treated as interchangeable.
researchNotes: NSW PlantNET provides subspecies-level measurements and the calyx/pod distinction. UC IPM independently recognizes narrowleaf vetch among escaped annual vetches. Naming varies among floras; the catalog subspecies is retained without declaring all Vicia angustifolia usages identical.

sources.title: NSW PlantNET: Vicia sativa subsp. nigra

claims: Leaflets 1-4 mm wide; flowers 8-18 mm; calyx teeth shorter than tube; smooth unconstricted pods 2.5-5 cm.
Narrowleaf vetch is an escaped cool-season annual; tendrils, few axillary flowers and seed dispersal are relevant.

proposedDescription: Garden loosestrife is a yellow-flowered perennial that spreads through long underground stems as well as seed. In wet ground it can build dense patches that replace other vegetation along shorelines and in marshes. A few visible stems may be connected to a much larger underground system, which is why one round of cutting rarely finishes the job. It is unrelated to purple loosestrife despite the shared common name.
identification: Leaves occur opposite one another or in small whorls, often three at a node. Five-petaled yellow flowers form branched clusters toward the tops of stems. Examine the green sepals beneath a flower: their edges are dark reddish or orange-brown. The similar ornamental Lysimachia punctata has flowers grouped more closely in leaf axils along the stem, with entirely green sepals and fine glandular hairs along the petal edges. Photograph the whole flower arrangement and the underside of a flower to show these differences.
actions: Report a suspected new shoreline patch to the land manager or weed program before digging. Small, newly established patches may be removable if all rhizomes can be recovered, but larger stands usually need a coordinated plan and repeated checks. Keep root pieces and seed-bearing material out of water and yard-waste piles. Cutting flowers can reduce seed production while a plan is arranged; it does not eliminate the rhizomes. Work in wetlands may require specialized methods and permissions, so use local guidance rather than applying ordinary garden products near water.
researchNotes: Washington's weed board provides spread and management limits; Native Plant Trust independently supplies the diagnostic comparison with L. punctata. County and state-hosted copies of the same fact sheet are not counted as separate corroboration. Regional regulation is not generalized nationwide.

sources.title: Washington State Noxious Weed Control Board: Garden loosestrife

claims: Spreads by seed and rhizomes in wetlands; small-patch digging is limited by extensive rhizomes and sensitive sites.
Dark-edged sepals and terminal flower clusters distinguish vulgaris from punctata.

proposedDescription: The Cuban brown snail feeds on a wide range of cultivated plants and is an established garden and nursery pest in parts of Florida. It can travel unnoticed with potted plants, making inspection of pots and growing media particularly useful. Chewed leaves alone do not identify this snail: slugs, other snails and insects can leave similar damage.
identification: Adults have a rounded brown to yellow-brown shell, usually about 25-30 mm wide, with four or five whorls and pronounced curved ribs. The opening has a pale edge rather than a broadly flared lip, and the underside lacks an open central hole. Zachrysia trinitaria looks similar but grows considerably larger; small or immature individuals still need expert examination. Photograph the top, opening and underside beside a ruler. Shell wear and age can obscure color, so include measurements and structure rather than relying on brown coloration.
actions: Inspect the bases and undersides of pots, moist hiding places and incoming nursery stock. Avoid moving infested plants or loose growing media to another property. Use gloves if handling snails and wash afterward; do not relocate them outdoors elsewhere. Photograph suspected new occurrences and ask an extension or plant-health service for identification and appropriate disposal advice. Where damage is confirmed, reducing damp debris and monitoring hiding places can support a locally recommended snail-management plan. Keep baits, if recommended, away from children and animals and follow their labels.
researchNotes: UF/IFAS supplies shell ribs, dimensions, plant damage and potted-plant transport. USDA IDtools corroborates the shell and the need for anatomical separation of similar Zachrysia, but its distribution statement for trinitaria conflicts with the newer UF account and is not repeated. Some foundational references overlap; this is diagnostic corroboration, not two independent impact trials.

sources.title: UF/IFAS: Terrestrial snails affecting plants in Florida

claims: Cuban brown snail damages many crops and ornamentals and travels with pots; shell 25-30 mm with ribs and no umbilicus.
Provisoria is smaller than trinitaria; similar shells may require reproductive anatomy to distinguish.

proposedDescription: Garden cress is a fast-growing annual cultivated for its young leaves. Plants allowed to mature produce branching stems, small flowers and numerous flat seed pods, and occasional escapes occur around gardens and disturbed ground. It is a terrestrial mustard-family plant, not watercress. A seedling crop in a tray and a self-sown outdoor population represent very different kinds of occurrence.
identification: Lower leaves are deeply divided, while upper leaves become smaller and narrower. Flowers have four small pale petals and six stamens. Mature pods are flat, oval and notched at the tip, usually about 5-6 mm long, with a winged edge. Virginia pepperweed, Lepidium virginicum, usually has smaller pods and only two, occasionally four, stamens. These small features need a close photograph or magnification. Include ripe pods and flowers together, because a leafy seedling alone is hard to separate from other small mustards.
actions: If cress is reseeding where it is unwanted, remove plants before the pods mature and check nearby bare soil for seedlings. Keep discarded seed trays and seed-bearing plants within managed garden waste. For an observation away from cultivation, note nearby gardens or soil dumping and document flowers and pods. Do not remove every similar pepperweed without checking the species; native relatives may grow in the same area. No broad treatment is needed for a contained food planting solely because this species appears in the catalog.
researchNotes: Native Plant Trust and the New Zealand flora independently agree on the six stamens, divided leaves and approximately 5-6 mm pods. The comparison with L. virginicum comes from Native Plant Trust. Advice focuses on annual seed containment and does not infer major harm from casual escapes.

sources.title: Flora of New Zealand: Lepidium sativum

claims: Six stamens and larger winged pods distinguish garden cress from Virginia pepperweed.
Annual with divided lower leaves, four petals, six stamens and notched 5-6 mm pods; casual garden escape.

proposedDescription: Garlic mustard is a woodland plant that usually spends its first year as a low rosette and flowers the following spring. It can crowd out native spring plants and leave a lasting supply of seeds in the soil. Removing a patch is therefore a follow-up project, not simply a matter of pulling the tallest stems once.
identification: First-year leaves are rounded or kidney-shaped, with scalloped edges. Flowering plants have more triangular, toothed leaves and small white flowers with four petals. Slender seedpods develop along the upper stems. Crushed foliage often smells of garlic, but smell alone is not a firm identification. Young violets and other woodland plants can resemble the rosettes. Photograph the lower leaves, stem leaves, flowers and pods; the transition between these features is more useful than a single leaf.
actions: Check a suspected patch in spring, before seedpods mature. In a small patch, pull carefully from moist soil and remove the root crown; broken plants can regrow. Flowering plants may still produce viable seed after pulling, so contain them and follow local disposal guidance rather than leaving them on the ground. Clean soil and seeds from boots and tools. Recheck the area for several years, protect nearby native seedlings, and avoid disturbing more soil than necessary.
researchNotes: Wisconsin DNR and University of Minnesota independently support the biennial life cycle, diagnostic leaves and flowers, and repeated seed-focused control. Their disposal rules differ by jurisdiction, so the draft directs readers to local guidance rather than declaring one nationwide disposal method.

claims: Biennial rosettes, triangular flowering leaves, four white petals, slender pods and root-crown regrowth.
Spring removal, seed maturation after pulling, repeated follow-up and equipment hygiene.

proposedDescription: Carnation spurge, also called false caper, is an introduced spurge that can form dense patches in disturbed grassland and coastal habitats. In California it has spread into places such as bluffs, dunes and open woodland. Its small greenish flowers are easy to overlook, so the branching stems and narrow leaves are often what first draw attention.
identification: Stems stand upright or lean outward and may become woody near the base. Narrow, stalkless stem leaves have finely toothed edges; the leaves around the flowering branches are broader and more triangular. The upper branches repeatedly fork. What looks like one tiny flower is a cup holding several reduced flowers, with greenish-yellow glands bearing two slender hornlike tips. Mature capsules are smooth. Many spurges share milky sap and green flower clusters, so photograph leaves, forks and close-up flower cups for confirmation rather than breaking the plant to test its sap.
actions: Avoid contact with the milky sap, especially around eyes, and keep children and animals away from cut material. Record the extent of a suspected patch and contact the local weed program if it is spreading in coastal or natural vegetation. For a small confirmed patch, plan removal before capsules release seed, using protective clothing and a disposal method appropriate to the site. Revisit disturbed ground for seedlings. Larger stands need a site-specific plan; cutting visible stems alone should not be assumed to finish control.
researchNotes: Cal-IPC documents California habitat concerns; NSW PlantNET provides a separate formal botanical description. No unverified herbicide rate or universal treatment claim is included. Australian flowering months and legal declarations are not transferred to U.S. readers.

sources.title: California Invasive Plant Council: Euphorbia terracina

claims: Dense patches in coastal and disturbed habitats; toxic sap warrants handling precautions.
Narrow finely toothed sessile leaves, broader flowering leaves, forked branches, horned glands and smooth capsules.

proposedDescription: The German cockroach is an indoor pest closely associated with kitchens, food storage and other warm places where food and moisture are available. It can arrive with belongings or deliveries and build a hidden population in narrow cracks. Seeing one does not tell you how many are present, which is why monitoring and removing food, water and shelter matter as much as treating the insects you can see.
identification: Adults are about half an inch long, light brown, and have two dark lengthwise stripes on the shield directly behind the head. Young cockroaches are smaller and darker, with a lighter stripe down the back and no fully developed wings. Females often carry an egg case at the end of the abdomen. Brown-banded cockroaches have crosswise pale bands, while some outdoor species can resemble German cockroaches more closely. Save a clear photograph or a contained specimen for identification before choosing a treatment.
actions: Use sticky monitors near likely hiding places, including beneath sinks and beside appliances, and note where catches are highest. Store food in sealed containers, remove crumbs and grease, repair leaks and reduce cardboard clutter. In an apartment building, tell the property manager so adjoining spaces can be considered together. Targeted baits and professional integrated pest management are generally more useful than repeatedly spraying visible insects. Follow product labels and keep bait placements inaccessible to children and pets; sanitation and follow-up remain essential.
researchNotes: UC IPM and University of Minnesota independently support identification and indoor habitat. UC IPM supplies the monitoring, sanitation and bait-centered management framework. The draft avoids equating a sighting with a measured infestation or making unsupported disease-transmission claims.

claims: German cockroach stripes, indoor food-preparation habitat, monitoring and integrated management; baits generally outperform sprays.
Adult size and pronotal stripes, dark nymphs with a light streak, warm humid hiding places.

proposedDescription: Bearded iris is a long-cultivated perennial that grows from thick, horizontal rhizomes. Garden forms come in many colors and sizes, and an old clump can persist after a garden has disappeared. A surviving planting is different from a population spreading into nearby habitat; recording that context helps explain what an observation means.
identification: Flat, sword-shaped leaves overlap in fans. Flowers have three upright inner segments and three outer segments that spread or hang downward; the outer segments carry the characteristic fuzzy beard. A flower's color alone is not reliable because there are many cultivars. Photograph an open flower from the front and side, the leaf fan and any naturally exposed rhizomes. Iris names in gardens can cover complex hybrids, so a cultivar or exact parentage should not be assigned from a photograph alone.
actions: If an unwanted clump is confirmed, remove the rhizomes rather than cutting only the leaves, and check for regrowth from pieces left behind. Do not dump divisions into natural areas or roadside soil. Wear gloves when handling cut plants, keep the material away from pets, and do not eat any part. If reporting an escape, note whether an old garden, cemetery or discarded planting material is nearby and whether new clumps occur beyond it.
researchNotes: NC State treats this plant as Iris x germanica and discusses broad cultivar variation; RHS independently supports clump growth, division and handling precautions. The catalog name is retained, while precise hybrid parentage and nationwide ecological harm are deliberately not asserted.

sources.title: NC State Extension: Iris x germanica

claims: Rhizomatous perennial, fan-arranged leaves, six-parted flowers, cultivar variation and irritant plant material.
Clump-forming iris propagated by division; harmful if eaten and gloves advised when handling.

proposedDescription: Annual knawel is a small, branching weed of open ground, lawns and fields. Its narrow leaves can make a patch look like thin grass or moss, but it is a flowering plant in the carnation family. It reproduces by seed and often grows through the cool season, though its timing varies with climate.
identification: Look for very narrow, pointed leaves in opposite pairs along spreading stems. The leaf bases meet in a thin, pale membrane. Tiny green flowers sit in clusters where leaves join the stem; they lack showy petals. The pointed sepals remain around a one-seeded fruit. Perennial knawel has more rounded sepals with broader white margins, and pearlwort usually has more noticeable white flowers and many-seeded capsules. A close photograph of the flower cluster and leaf bases is much more informative than a distant photograph of the mat.
actions: In a small bed or open patch, remove plants before seed matures and check again for later seedlings. Lift the central root rather than simply trimming the sprawling tips. In turf, confirm the identification before applying a product intended for grass weeds: knawel is not a grass. Reduce repeated bare-soil disturbance and maintain suitable ground cover for the site. If it is widespread in a crop or lawn, ask a local extension office about management matched to that setting.
researchNotes: Native Plant Trust supplies the annual-versus-perennial knawel distinction; Missouri and Michigan State independently describe the leaf-base membrane, mat-forming habit and seed reproduction. Actions are conservative small-patch seed prevention, not an unsupported selective-herbicide recommendation.

claims: Opposite narrow leaves, inconspicuous petal-free flowers, sharp sepals distinguish annual from perennial knawel.
Spreading mats, pointed leaves joined by a clear membrane, small green flowers and central taproot.
Seed reproduction and comparison with pearlwort; summer or winter annual habit.

proposedDescription: The German yellowjacket is a social wasp that nests in enclosed spaces, including wall cavities and underground sites. Workers hunt insects and also visit human food, which can bring a nest into conflict with people. A wasp visiting a picnic is not necessarily nesting nearby, and its yellow-and-black coloring alone does not distinguish this introduced species from native yellowjackets.
identification: Workers are about half an inch long, with a compact body and bold yellow-and-black markings. The first abdominal segment commonly has a dark spade-shaped mark, followed by separate dark spots along the sides of later segments. These markings vary and need to be considered together. A clear photograph of the face and the top of the abdomen can help an expert separate similar species. Watch from a safe distance for repeated traffic into one small opening; do not approach or disturb the entrance to obtain a better image.
actions: Keep food and sweet drinks covered, close garbage containers, and give foraging wasps space. If a nest threatens a doorway, play area or occupied building, contact a qualified pest professional. Do not plug an active wall-nest entrance yourself: wasps may find another route into the building. Traps can reduce some foraging workers but do not reliably remove an established colony. A nest away from people may not require immediate intervention; identification and location should guide the response.
researchNotes: Penn State provides species-level markings and building-nest information; UC IPM independently covers yellowjacket behavior and management. Trap limitations and the risk of redirecting an indoor colony are supported by Penn State's separate stinging-insect guidance. No pesticide application instructions are supplied.

sources.title: UC IPM: Yellowjackets and other social wasps
Penn State Extension: Managing stinging insects

claims: Worker size, abdominal markings and frequent nesting in human structures.
German yellowjackets occur in urban structures; food sanitation and site-based social-wasp management.
Traps do not eliminate established colonies; inappropriate sealing can redirect wasps indoors.

proposedDescription: Madwort is a rough-haired annual that sprawls or scrambles through disturbed ground and field margins. Its tiny blue flowers are less distinctive than the enlarged, leafy structures that later surround the fruits. Those structures make a fruiting plant much easier to recognize than a young seedling.
identification: The stems have backward-pointing prickles that help them catch on neighboring vegetation. Leaves are elongated and rough, with lower leaves more clearly stalked than upper ones. Small blue flowers appear close to the leaf bases. After flowering, the green calyx enlarges into a flattened, strongly toothed, clamshell-like enclosure around the nutlets. Photograph this fruiting structure from both sides. Forget-me-nots and other rough-leaved members of the same family can share blue flowers, but do not have this distinctive enclosing calyx.
actions: If a confirmed plant is unwanted in a small area, remove it before the fruits mature and handle the prickly stems with gloves. Keep fruiting material contained rather than dragging it through clean ground. Photograph mature features before disposal if the identification is uncertain, and check the site for later seedlings. Where it is mixed with native plants, remove individual plants selectively rather than clearing all rough-leaved vegetation.
researchNotes: University of Washington's Burke Herbarium and the Flora of China/Pakistan treatments corroborate the rough stems, small blue flowers and enlarged fruiting calyx. A species-specific U.S. management trial was not located; the draft offers limited annual-weed seed containment, not a claimed eradication protocol.

claims: Backward prickles, blue flowers and strongly toothed clamshell calyx are diagnostic.
Ribbed rough stems, leaf arrangement and small blue flowers.
Annual branched herb with enlarged fruiting calyx and four nutlets.

proposedDescription: Germander meadowsweet is a deciduous ornamental shrub with white spring flowers and new shoots that can arise from the ground around an established plant. It has been recorded outside cultivation in parts of New England. A persistent garden shrub and an expanding escape are different situations, so a useful report shows both the plant and its relationship to nearby plantings.
identification: Leaves alternate along the woody stems and have toothed edges. White flowers with conspicuously long stamens form small clusters on short side shoots. In the New England key, most clusters have their own stalk and about five to twelve flowers; the leaves have short but visible stalks. Some bridalwreath and Thunberg spireas have smaller, essentially unstalked flower clusters. Several forms of germander meadowsweet differ in leaf width and cluster shape, so photograph a flowering twig, leaf undersides and the base of the shrub.
actions: Check whether shoots are appearing beyond the original planting and whether they connect to its roots. If removal is needed, plan to address the root system and revisit for suckers rather than assuming pruning will remove the shrub. Keep rooted divisions and soil containing live roots out of natural areas. Ask for help with identification before removing an unfamiliar wild spirea, since native species occur in the same genus.
researchNotes: Native Plant Trust establishes regional escape records and a comparison with similar ornamentals. International Dendrology Society material independently describes variation and annual sucker growth. The sources do not establish equal ecological impact across the United States; the draft does not make that claim.

sources.title: Trees and Shrubs Online: Spiraea chamaedryfolia

claims: Introduced shrub in southern New England; alternate toothed leaves and stalked flower clusters distinguish related ornamentals.
Variable leaf and inflorescence forms, long stamens and renewal by ground-level sucker shoots.

proposedDescription: Germander speedwell is a low perennial with bright blue flowers. It spreads through slender underground stems and stems that root where they touch the ground, which can let it persist in lawns and garden edges. Sometimes sold as ground cover, it is also found outside cultivation. A few flowers can hide a more extensive connected patch.
identification: Look for opposite, coarsely toothed leaves and two distinct lines of hairs running along the stem. Blue flowers have a white center and four unequal lobes, with the lowest lobe narrower than the others. Flowers are carried in loose, stalked clusters from upper leaf axils. The capsules are flattened, notched and roughly heart-shaped. Other speedwells may have similar flowers; photograph the hair pattern, leaf attachment and whole flowering cluster rather than relying on flower color.
actions: For a small unwanted patch, work through the rooted stems and rhizomes instead of pulling only the flowering tips. Recheck the edges for regrowth and keep live fragments out of nearby beds. In lawns, avoid treating all small blue-flowered plants as the same weed: confirm the species and choose management suited to the turf and surrounding vegetation. When reporting it outside a garden, include the patch size and whether it is spreading into other ground cover.
researchNotes: The Illustrated Flora of British Columbia supplies the two hair lines, rooting stems, flower and capsule features. Native Plant Trust independently describes its introduced ground-cover use and disturbed habitats. No unverified local herbicide recommendation is included.

claims: Perennial rhizomes, rooting lower nodes, two stem-hair lines, opposite leaves, blue white-eyed flowers and heart-shaped capsules.
Introduced species sometimes sold as ground cover; occurs in disturbed habitats and fields.

proposedDescription: Ghost ants are tiny ants whose pale legs and abdomen can seem to disappear against a light surface. They nest both indoors and outside in warm regions, and may occupy small, temporary spaces rather than one conspicuous mound. An indoor trail can therefore come from a hidden nest inside the building or from a nest nearby.
identification: Workers have a dark head and middle body contrasting with a very pale abdomen and legs. Under magnification, the antennae have twelve segments and no distinct club; the waist node is low and often hidden by the abdomen. The ants lack a stinger. Size or a dark head alone is not enough to separate every small household ant, so a close photograph or securely contained specimen is useful. Look along a trail without disturbing it to see where ants enter cracks or approach food and moisture.
actions: Clean up sweet spills, store food securely and repair moisture problems. Inspect potted plants and other movable items before taking them to a new room or property. For an indoor infestation, identify the ant first and use a coordinated bait-based plan rather than repeatedly spraying the visible trail. If bait is used, check whether ants are actually feeding and follow the label for placement around children and pets. Persistent or scattered trails may need professional inspection to locate several nesting sites.
researchNotes: Mississippi State's museum treatment provides independent anatomical identification. UF/IFAS supplies nesting and bait-monitoring guidance; its HTML full-text retrieval failed, so the accessed source is honestly marked indexed_excerpt. Species-specific eradication success is not promised.

claims: Dark head and mesosoma, pale appendages and gaster, twelve-segment antennae, hidden waist node and no stinger.
Indoor and outdoor nests; bait feeding should be checked after placement.
Sanitation and removal of nesting materials support a longer-term ant management strategy.

proposedDescription: The giant ameiva is an active, ground-dwelling lizard introduced to southern Florida through the pet trade. It searches for food during the day and can be seen moving quickly through open or disturbed vegetation. Historical records under this name deserve careful checking because similar ameivas and whiptails can be confused, particularly when young.
identification: Look for a streamlined lizard with a long tail and well-developed legs, but do not use these general features as a final identification. Juveniles and adults can differ in pattern, and other Florida teiid lizards can look similar. Specialist keys examine scale arrangements, including the rows of large scales on the underside. Take clear photographs of the whole animal, head and sides from where you are standing, and include its approximate size. Do not catch or turn it over simply to obtain a scale count.
actions: Report an unfamiliar free-living ameiva with its location, date and photographs to the local wildlife agency or a qualified reptile specialist. Note whether you saw one animal or several and whether young animals were present. Do not release pets or move a wild-caught lizard to another location. If a captive animal needs rehoming, use an appropriate surrender or adoption route. Avoid glue traps and broad pest treatments that can injure native lizards as well.
researchNotes: Research gap: the Florida museum key and Animal Diversity Web support the general account, but a digitized Florida voucher carries original A. ameiva and updated A. atrigularis names. Record-level reconciliation is needed before presenting all historic A. ameiva observations as one current taxon. The draft avoids a definitive color formula or an unsupported statewide impact claim.

sources.title: Smith and Krysko: Florida teiid lizards and identification key

claims: Native and introduced teiids are easily confused, especially juveniles; scale characters support expert identification.
Diurnal terrestrial behavior, introduced Florida occurrence and variation between age classes.
Original scientific name A. ameiva and updated canonical name A. atrigularis occur in the same specimen record.

proposedDescription: The giant applesnail is a large freshwater snail that feeds on aquatic vegetation. Its bright pink egg masses are often the first sign people notice, attached above the waterline to plants or other solid surfaces. It can alter aquatic habitats, but several native and introduced applesnails look similar, so a large shell or pink eggs alone may not settle the species.
identification: The shell is rounded, with a short spire, deeply indented joins between whorls and a large teardrop-shaped opening. Color varies from yellowish to brown, often with dark bands. Fresh egg masses contain many small pink eggs and become paler as they develop. Florida's native applesnail has fewer, larger eggs, usually pale, and less deeply channeled shell joins. Pomacea canaliculata is harder to distinguish from P. maculata. Photograph the shell opening, side of the shell and an egg mass with a size reference; an expert may need more than photographs.
actions: Do not move snails, egg masses, aquarium plants or water between waterways. Inspect boats and equipment and remove attached material before leaving the site. For a suspected new occurrence, photograph it and report the location to the state aquatic-invasive-species program. Ask for local instructions before removing eggs, especially where native applesnails occur. Avoid bare-handed contact with eggs and wash after handling equipment from the site. Never release unwanted aquarium animals outdoors.
researchNotes: USGS provides the species comparison and warns that P. maculata and P. canaliculata are difficult to separate. Florida FWC independently documents large pink clutches and feeding; North Carolina provides reporting guidance. Older P. insularum usage is treated as an alias, not a separate corroborating species.

sources.title: North Carolina Wildlife: Aquatic nuisance species

claims: Rounded channeled shell, variable color, large pink clutches and comparison with native P. paludosa and P. canaliculata.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
claims: Large bright pink egg masses above water become pale before hatching; feeds on aquatic vegetation.
Photograph suspected applesnails or egg masses and report exact locations.

proposedDescription: The giant cave cockroach is a large tropical cockroach associated with dark, sheltered places such as hollow trees, caves and decaying wood. It scavenges organic material and is also kept in captivity. A sighting outside a collection should be documented, but it should not automatically be treated as evidence of a widespread household infestation or an established outdoor population.
identification: Adults have a broad, flattened oval body and long light-brown forewings; both sexes are winged. Large individuals can approach four inches in length. Young stages lack the adults' developed wings and can look quite different. Several Blaberus species resemble one another, and size or a dark patch behind the head is not a dependable species test. Photograph the whole insect from above and the side, include a scale, and record whether it was found indoors, outdoors or near a captive collection.
actions: If it may be an escaped captive animal, secure the enclosure and inspect nearby hiding places rather than releasing it outdoors. For an unfamiliar outdoor specimen, send photographs to an extension office or museum entomologist before using insecticides. Keep any specimen contained if a specialist requests it, and do not ship live insects without instructions. In a building, reduce access to food and damp hiding places while the identity and extent of the occurrence are checked.
researchNotes: University of the West Indies and Toronto Zoo corroborate morphology, tropical shelter use and scavenging. The literature notes confusion among captive Blaberus cultures. Research gap: these sources do not independently establish the current U.S. naturalized status or a species-specific domestic management protocol; no such claim is made in the draft.

sources.title: University of the West Indies: Giant cave cockroach

claims: Large flattened body, light-brown adult wings, wingless nymphs, nocturnal shelter use and scavenging.
Both sexes winged; tropical caves, tree hollows and loose bark; occasional entry into houses.
Similar appearance complicates identification of species held in cultures.

proposedDescription: Giant foxtail is a summer annual grass that produces a bristly seedhead and can compete strongly with crops. It spreads by seed rather than a creeping perennial root system. Preventing a new seed crop is important, especially where plants survive along field edges or after an early harvest.
identification: The seedhead resembles a fuzzy bottlebrush and usually bends or nods when mature. Leaf blades have many short hairs on the upper surface, while the underside is much less hairy. At the junction of blade and sheath, the ligule is a fringe of hairs rather than a membrane. Green foxtail generally lacks the same covering of short hairs across the blade, and yellow foxtail has conspicuous longer hairs near the blade base. Photograph the seedhead, both leaf surfaces and the collar area; an immature grass without these views is harder to name.
actions: Remove small patches while plants are young and before the heads shed seed. In cultivated ground, early control is easier than waiting until strong crown roots develop, and disturbed plants may reroot in moist soil. Check field margins and recently harvested areas for plants that could replenish the seedbank. Clean seed-bearing debris from equipment before moving fields. For larger infestations, combine crop competition and locally appropriate control rather than relying on one repeated herbicide treatment.
researchNotes: Ontario's identification guide and Cornell independently support the leaf-hair and seedhead characters. Cornell supplies management timing, rerooting and post-harvest seed prevention. An apparent yellow-foxtail yield-loss statement on the Ontario giant-foxtail page was not transferred into this profile.

sources.title: University of Maryland: Know your foxtails

claims: Annual seed reproduction, hairy upper leaf surface, hairless lower surface and hairy ligule.
Early control before crown roots, rerooting in moist soil, seedbank reduction and post-harvest control.
Giant foxtail has drooping seedheads and short fine leaf hairs; comparisons with green and yellow foxtails.

proposedDescription: Giant hogweed is a very large member of the carrot family whose sap can make skin extremely sensitive to sunlight, causing serious burns. Its size is striking, but young plants may be much smaller and still hazardous. A suspected plant should be photographed from a distance and reported for confirmation, not handled to test its identity.
identification: Mature flowering plants can reach roughly seven to fourteen feet tall. Look for huge, deeply cut leaves, broad umbrella-shaped clusters of white flowers, and stout green stems with purple blotches and coarse white hairs. Several plants, including cow parsnip and angelicas, can look similar. Size alone does not distinguish them, and some lookalikes also have irritating sap. Take separate photographs of the whole plant, leaf shape, flower cluster and visible stem markings without touching or entering the patch.
actions: Keep people and pets away and contact your state agriculture department or local invasive-plant program. Do not mow, string-trim or cut a suspected plant, because broken material can expose you to sap. If sap touches skin, wash promptly with soap and water, cover the area from sunlight and seek medical advice; eye exposure needs urgent medical attention. Leave removal to people equipped and trained for this plant, and follow the reporting program's instructions about access and follow-up.
researchNotes: New York DEC and Michigan's invasive-species program independently corroborate diagnostic features and reporting. New York Health supplies exposure guidance. The draft emphasizes distance and professional response rather than reproducing a hazardous do-it-yourself removal protocol or assuming a mature plant's height is required for identification.

sources.title: New York Department of Health: Giant hogweed health advice

claims: Large leaves and flower umbels, purple-blotched hairy stems, sap hazard and coordinated control.
Seven-to-fourteen-foot mature plants, coarse white stem hairs and exposure precautions.
Wash sap exposure immediately, avoid sunlight and protect eyes.

proposedDescription: Giant knotweed is a tall perennial that forms dense stands connected by underground rhizomes. It can crowd out streamside vegetation, and small pieces moved in soil or flood debris can start new patches. Its stems die back seasonally, but the underground system remains alive; a stand that looks cleared in winter may return strongly in spring.
identification: Hollow stems have swollen joints and carry very large, alternate leaves with rounded or heart-shaped bases. Mature leaves can exceed a foot in length. Small greenish-white flower clusters appear near upper leaf joints. Japanese knotweed usually has smaller leaves with a more squared-off base, while their hybrid, Bohemian knotweed, can have intermediate features. Size alone does not reliably separate all three. Photograph several mature leaves, their undersides, stem joints and flower clusters for an informed identification.
actions: Keep soil and cut stems from the patch from being moved elsewhere. Do not mow through it and carry fragments to another site. Mark the patch's extent and ask a local weed program for a multi-year plan, especially beside water. Small clumps can sometimes be excavated carefully, but missed rhizome pieces can regrow. Repeated cutting or other treatments need sustained follow-up, and disposal must prevent live fragments from rooting. Do not interpret one season without tall stems as proof that the patch is gone.
researchNotes: Washington's weed board provides giant-knotweed diagnostics and fragment precautions; Penn State independently explains the Japanese/giant/hybrid comparison. Older blanket statements about availability of biocontrol were not repeated. The profile retains Fallopia while acknowledging Reynoutria and Polygonum usage in sources.

sources.title: Penn State Extension: Japanese and giant knotweed

claims: Large heart-based leaves, hollow jointed stems, rhizome spread, tiny fragments and multi-year control.
Leaf-base comparison, hybrid intermediate features and interconnected rhizomes.

proposedDescription: The giant ramshorn is an applesnail with a flattened, disk-like shell. It eats aquatic plants as well as other organic material and can change vegetation in waters where it becomes abundant. Although it has been tested for weed control, releasing it to clear a pond can create a new invasive-species problem rather than solve the original one.
identification: The shell coils in a flat circle instead of rising into a tall spire. Adults commonly measure about one and a half to two inches across. Brown spiral bands often cross a yellowish shell, but some individuals are nearly unbanded. Egg masses are clear, jellylike clusters attached below the water surface, unlike the conspicuous above-water pink masses of some other applesnails. Native ramshorn snails can also have flattened shells, so photograph both shell faces, the opening and a size reference. Color alone is not enough.
actions: Keep aquarium snails, aquatic plants and tank water out of ponds, canals and streams. Inspect plants and equipment for small snails and submerged egg masses before moving them. If you find a suspected giant ramshorn in a new waterbody, photograph it and report the location to the state aquatic-invasive-species program. Do not move live specimens between waterways or release them as weed control. Any removal effort should first distinguish them from native snails and follow the receiving agency's advice.
researchNotes: USGS and the University of the West Indies account support shell form, feeding and submerged egg masses. Some foundational citations overlap, so those shared claims are not treated as separate field trials. Impacts are described conditionally rather than assigning a measured effect to every occurrence.

sources.title: University of the West Indies: Giant ramshorn snail

claims: Flat circular shell, variable bands, typical adult diameter and potential effects on aquatic vegetation.
Jellylike egg masses laid below water; aquatic-plant feeding and freshwater habitat.

proposedDescription: Giant reed is a very tall perennial grass that forms dense, cane-like stands along waterways and other moist ground. Its rhizomes make established patches difficult to remove, and dry stands can contribute to fire hazards. The thick growth can replace more diverse streamside vegetation and complicate access and restoration.
identification: Upright, jointed canes carry broad gray-green leaves that clasp the stem. The leaves can be about two feet long and several inches wide. Large feathery flower clusters develop above the foliage, changing from a reddish-brown cast toward pale silver as they dry. Bamboo and common reed can look similar at a distance. Include photographs of the leaf bases, cane joints, entire stand and flower plume; a close view of the clasping leaf base is more useful than height alone.
actions: Do not plant it for screening or erosion control where it could spread. For an existing patch, keep rhizomes and cut material from being carried downstream or dumped in new soil. Cutting canes alone does not remove the underground system. Work with a land manager or weed specialist on treatment, follow-up and replacement vegetation, particularly along streams. Biological control is available through organized programs in some places, but it is not a reason to collect or release insects on your own.
researchNotes: NC State independently supplies leaf and flower features. UC IPM supports the limits of cutting or hand removal and the role of organized biological control; USDA's information center summarizes habitat and fire concerns. Source statements about seed viability differ by setting, so seed spread is not used as the central U.S. explanation.

sources.title: NC State Extension: Giant reed grass
USDA National Invasive Species Information Center: Giant reed
UC WeedCUT: Giant reed biological control

claims: Broad clasping gray-green leaves and large reddish-to-silver flower plumes.
Rhizomatous arundo is not reliably controlled by hand-pulling or cutting alone.
Crowds out vegetation, alters riparian habitat and contributes to fire hazards.
Several permitted specialist insects are used in organized arundo biological-control programs.

proposedDescription: The giant river prawn is a large freshwater prawn widely raised in aquaculture. Adults live in fresh water, while early development normally involves brackish water. An animal found outside a farm or aquarium is worth documenting, but an isolated escape does not by itself demonstrate a self-sustaining population.
identification: Large males have exceptionally long second legs ending in claws, often blue or orange, that extend well beyond the head. The pointed rostrum projects forward and carries teeth on both its upper and lower edges. Identification keys also examine the tail tip and fine features of the claws. Females and young prawns do not have the same exaggerated male claws, and native Macrobrachium species can be confused with them. Photograph the whole animal, side of the head and claws with a scale; a specialist may need a specimen for confirmation.
actions: Never release aquarium or farm prawns, use them as live bait outside their approved setting, or move them between waterways. If found in open water, record the exact site, number seen and approximate sizes, then contact the state fisheries or aquatic-invasive-species program. Farm operators should review screens, drains and overflow routes after an escape. Follow agency instructions about retaining a specimen; do not transport live animals elsewhere simply to have them identified.
researchNotes: FAO provides a detailed morphological key; USGS independently compiles U.S. occurrences and life-history literature, though it also cites FAO. Numeric rostral-tooth counts differ among FAO treatments and are omitted from public identification rather than forcing a false exact range. Historical records are not described as current established populations.

sources.title: FAO: Identifying and farming giant river prawns

claims: Long toothed rostrum, male second chelipeds and tail characters distinguish species; widespread aquaculture introductions.
Freshwater adults and estuarine early stages; long blue or orange claws; occurrence records do not all indicate current presence.

proposedDescription: Giant salvinia is a floating fern that can rapidly cover sheltered water with dense mats. Those mats shade plants below, interfere with access and can reduce oxygen as vegetation dies and decomposes. It spreads through living fragments, so a small piece caught on a trailer or fishing gear can matter.
identification: Pairs of green floating leaves sit above a finely divided brown structure that hangs underwater. That submerged structure is a modified leaf, not a true root. Under magnification, hairs on the upper leaves branch and rejoin at their tips, resembling tiny eggbeaters. Common salvinia has hairs whose tips remain separate. Several other members of the giant-salvinia group share joined hairs, however, so this feature narrows the identification without always proving the exact species. Photograph both the floating leaves and the submerged parts.
actions: Avoid driving or dragging equipment through a mat if you can do so safely. Inspect boats, trailers, nets and other gear, remove all plant fragments, and follow local clean, drain and dry guidance before entering another waterbody. Report a suspected new patch promptly with photographs and a location. Do not move plants to an aquarium or garden pond. Established mats need a coordinated aquatic-plant plan; unplanned removal can scatter fragments and leave enough live material for regrowth.
researchNotes: USGS provides the modified-leaf anatomy and both the useful eggbeater-hair distinction and its limits within the auriculata complex. Texas A&M independently documents fragmentation and mat effects; TPWD supports equipment hygiene. The misleading root label in one AquaPlant summary is not repeated.

sources.title: Texas Parks and Wildlife: Clean, drain, dry

claims: Floating leaf pairs, submerged modified leaf, joined hairs and limits within related Salvinia species.
Fragmentation, rapid mat growth and possible oxygen depletion.
Inspect and clean equipment, drain retained water and dry before moving between waters.

proposedDescription: Giant taro is a large tropical perennial grown for its dramatic foliage. Its thick stem can persist and produce new growth, so discarded plants or divisions deserve care in climates where they survive outdoors. The name elephant's ear is also used for other plants; a large leaf alone does not establish which species is present.
identification: Leaves are held upright in a rosette and have a broad arrowhead shape. In this species, the notch where the leaf stalk meets the two rear lobes is open, without a bridge of leaf tissue across it. The similar Alocasia odora has a more closed notch and often more basal offshoots. Flowers are tiny and packed onto a pale central spike partly enclosed by a hoodlike spathe. Photograph the leaf-stalk attachment, entire plant and any flower structure. Ornamental hybrids and cultivars can complicate identification.
actions: Do not discard live stems, corms or divisions beside waterways or in natural vegetation. For an unwanted plant, arrange removal of the storage stem and check the site for regrowth rather than cutting off leaves alone. Wear gloves and avoid sap contact. Do not taste it or assume it is edible because it is called taro; Alocasia tissues contain irritating compounds and can harm people and pets. If reporting an escape, show how far it lies from a planting or dumped garden material.
researchNotes: Singapore NParks supplies species-level leaf-notch and floral distinctions; NC State independently supports Alocasia morphology and handling hazards, with the species included in its account. The draft distinguishes that genus-level safety evidence from species-specific ecological impact and does not prescribe food preparation.

claims: Upright rosette, open leaf sinus, thick storage stem and comparison with A. odora.
Large aroid leaves, spathe and spadix, and genus-level irritating/poisonous plant characteristics.

proposedDescription: Giant whitefly feeds on plant sap and can cover leaf undersides with long white wax strands. Sticky honeydew encourages black sooty mold, making an affected plant look worse even when the mold is growing on the residue rather than invading its tissues. Heavy infestations can weaken ornamentals, but the presence of wax does not mean the plant is beyond recovery.
identification: Adults are larger than many other whiteflies and have white wings marked with irregular pale-brown patches. Eggs are placed in waxy spirals on leaf undersides. Flat, yellowish young stages remain on the leaves and later produce long, hairlike wax filaments that give a bearded appearance. Other whiteflies and mealybugs also make wax. Photograph the adults, egg spirals and settled young stages together, along with the host plant, rather than relying only on the white coating.
actions: Inspect nearby plants, especially leaf undersides, and remove a limited number of heavily infested leaves if the plant can tolerate it. Washing colonies off with water can help. Preserve lady beetles, lacewings and tiny parasitic wasps instead of applying broad insecticide sprays that kill them too. Check for renewed colonies rather than judging success only by whether old wax remains. If additional treatment is needed, choose a locally appropriate labeled product with extension advice and cover the infested leaf surfaces carefully.
researchNotes: UC IPM and University of Florida independently support wax spirals, marked wings and nymphal filaments. UC IPM supplies washing, selective leaf removal and natural-enemy conservation. Exact adult size varies between the sources, so the draft uses a relative size statement rather than forcing one measurement.

claims: Waxy beards, honeydew and sooty mold; wash colonies, remove infested leaves selectively and protect natural enemies.
Marked adult wings, yellowish flat nymphs, spiral egg placement and long wax filaments.

proposedDescription: This catalog entry needs a name check before its history can be explained confidently. Lachnus tatakaensis is described in specialist aphid literature from willow trunks and branches in Taiwan, while the common name giant willow aphid is usually used for Tuberolachnus salignus. Some databases link the names, but the specialist treatments do not support simply combining all their biology and records.
identification: The original account describes wingless L. tatakaensis as a large, brownish-black aphid with rows of dark circular abdominal spots, black antennae and reddish-brown to black legs. These details are not enough for a reliable field identification. The familiar giant willow aphid, T. salignus, is often recognized by a raised, finlike structure on its back; that feature should not be transferred to this entry without resolving the name. Photograph the colony, host tree, individual aphids and the side profile, and seek specialist confirmation.
actions: Record the willow or other host, the part of the tree occupied and the date before considering treatment. Do not remove a tree or spray a colony solely because this catalog uses an introduced-species label. An extension entomologist can help determine which aphid is present and whether it is affecting plant health. If a specimen is requested, follow the specialist's collection instructions so the features needed for identification are preserved.
researchNotes: Research gap: Blackman and Eastop retain L. tatakaensis with uncertain generic placement and unknown life cycle; Aphid Species File lists historical T. salignus nomenclatural links, while RHS uses T. salignus for the giant willow aphid. The current common-name mapping and U.S. record concept need expert reconciliation. No borrowed life cycle, impact or pesticide claim is presented as L. tatakaensis fact.

sources.title: Blackman and Eastop: Lachnus species accounts
Royal Horticultural Society: Large willow bark aphid

claims: L. tatakaensis wingless morphology, Taiwanese willow host, unknown life cycle and uncertain generic placement.
Historical nomenclatural links include T. salignus usages and spelling variants.
Giant willow aphid common name is applied to Tuberolachnus salignus with a characteristic dorsal tubercle.

proposedDescription: Fusarium graminearum causes several cereal diseases, including Gibberella stalk and ear rot in corn and Fusarium head blight in small grains. In corn, weakened stalks can lodge before harvest. The fungus can also produce mycotoxins, so crop quality and feed safety need to be assessed separately from how much mold is visible.
identification: Gibberella stalk rot can leave the internal pith shredded and distinctly pink or red, with dark streaks on lower stem sections. Small black fungal structures may appear near lower nodes in moist conditions. Other stalk rots and plant stresses can produce similar collapse or discoloration. Photograph affected plants and the pattern across the field, then follow a plant diagnostic laboratory's sampling instructions. A visual diagnosis of Fusarium is not always a confirmed identification of F. graminearum, and appearance cannot measure toxin concentration.
actions: Scout for weak stalks and discuss harvest timing with a crop adviser if lodging risk is rising. Keep suspect grain or silage lots identified and arrange appropriate mycotoxin testing before feeding or blending them. Plan future management around hybrid resistance, plant stress, residue and crop rotation; rotating corn with another susceptible cereal may not break the disease cycle. Do not assume a late fungicide spray can repair rotted stalks or remove toxins already present.
researchNotes: Crop Protection Network provides stalk symptoms and the F. graminearum/Gibberella relationship. University of Minnesota independently describes lodging, stress and cereal-rotation limits; Penn State supports grain/silage toxin concerns. The catalog common name is retained, but the draft clarifies that it names a disease manifestation, not the fungus's only effect.

sources.title: Crop Protection Network: Gibberella crown and stalk rot
University of Minnesota: Corn disease management
Penn State Extension: Mycotoxins in grain corn and silage
Crop Protection Network: DON in corn silage

claims: Pink-red shredded pith, dark lower internodes, residue survival and harvest concern.
Stalk weakness and lodging; stress reduction; susceptible small-grain rotations can maintain inoculum.
F. graminearum causes Gibberella ear/stalk rot and may contaminate grain and silage with DON.
Research connects F. graminearum in stalks and ears with DON and changing detectable toxin during ensiling.

proposedDescription: Haplorchis pumilio is a tiny parasitic fluke with a life cycle involving snails, fish and fish-eating hosts. It has been found in introduced snails and freshwater fish at sampled sites in southern California. People can be exposed by eating infected fish raw or inadequately prepared, but finding the parasite in fish is not the same as documenting a local human infection.
identification: This parasite cannot be reliably recognized by looking at a fish from the outside. Encysted young stages are microscopic and can occur especially around fin bases; laboratory examination and sometimes molecular methods are needed to distinguish related flukes. The catalog's broad name gill fluke should not be taken to mean that every gill problem is this species. A fish with breathing difficulty, damaged fins or no visible symptoms cannot be diagnosed from those signs alone.
actions: Do not eat raw or undercooked freshwater fish, and do not rely on a healthy appearance to judge parasite safety. Follow established food-safety guidance for preparing fish rather than assuming a home marinade removes parasites. Keep aquarium snails, fish and water out of natural waterways. If you suspect a fish-health problem, contact a fisheries biologist or aquatic veterinarian and follow their sampling instructions. If you are concerned about illness after eating fish, tell a healthcare professional what you ate and where it came from.
researchNotes: UC San Diego field studies document infected snails and fish, while an independent Tanzania study confirms the limits of identifying small trematode eggs without molecular work. Research gap: the catalog's gill-fluke label needs correction or explanation because H. pumilio fin-base cysts differ from the gill-centered C. formosanus example. The studies demonstrate plausible U.S. transmission, not confirmed local human cases.

sources.title: Palmer and colleagues: Fishborne trematodes in California game fish
Metz and colleagues: Introduced snail and trematodes
Shin and colleagues: Molecular detection of H. pumilio

claims: H. pumilio cysts were predominantly at fin bases in sampled fish; findings support plausible rather than confirmed local human transmission.
Introduced Melanoides snails carried human-infectious trematodes at surveyed southern California fishing sites.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Korean and Tanzanian parasite research team
claims: Small trematode eggs required molecular confirmation; independent evidence for human infection outside the United States.

proposedDescription: Glabrous cabinet beetles are associated with stored grain, flour mills and, sometimes, food in homes. Their larvae feed on grain and other dry materials; the adults visit flowers for pollen and nectar. An adult near a window does not by itself show where an infestation began, so finding the food source matters more than treating the place where the beetle was noticed.
identification: Adults are oval, about 2 to 4 mm long, with dark wing covers clothed in a mixture of pale, golden and darker hairs. The clubbed antennae and hair pattern help specialists distinguish them from other cabinet beetles. Larvae are densely hairy, become reddish brown as they mature and have conspicuous hair tufts toward the rear. Cast skins in stored food are useful evidence, but larvae of related Trogoderma species look similar. Keep a contained specimen for identification rather than assigning a species from a small photograph alone.
actions: For a household infestation, inspect dry foods, pet food and spilled material near storage areas. Seal and discard infested food, vacuum cracks and empty the vacuum promptly, then protect unaffected supplies in tightly closed containers. These are general stored-food pest measures, not a substitute for identifying an unusual beetle. In a grain facility, keep the affected lot identifiable and ask a grain-storage specialist about sampling and treatment appropriate to the commodity; do not move suspect material simply to clear the bin.
researchNotes: Canadian Grain Commission provides the species-level morphology, feeding stages and storage associations. Agriculture Canada's identification guide independently describes the diagnostic hair pattern, although some historical records are shared. Minnesota Extension supports the household sanitation advice at the pantry-pest level. No current national distribution or quarantine status is inferred from these sources.

sources.title: Canadian Grain Commission: Glabrous cabinet beetle
Agriculture Canada: Beetles associated with stored products

claims: Adult and larval appearance, storage associations and separate feeding roles of larvae and adults.
T. glabrum diagnostic wing-cover hair pattern and historical grain-storage records.
General stored-food pest inspection, disposal, vacuuming and protective storage.

proposedDescription: Glenwood grass is a small annual grass of damp ground, including muddy edges of freshwater wetlands. Its narrow, compact flower heads can make it easy to overlook among other grasses. Finding it in a wet area is not enough to establish either its identity or an ecological impact; both depend on the plant and the site being documented.
identification: Look for slender stems that branch near the base and may lean before rising, with narrow, mostly smooth leaf blades. The small membrane where a leaf blade meets its sheath is very short. Flower heads are dense and spike-like, with closely packed green to purplish spikelets. Under magnification, the larger outer bract of a spikelet is strongly veined and swollen or curved near its base. Flower-head length varies between floras, so photographs of mature spikelets, the leaf junction and the whole clump are more useful than height alone.
actions: Photograph the flowering plant in place and record whether it is on a wet bank, disturbed ground or within established wetland vegetation. Ask a botanist to confirm it before removing similar-looking grasses. Avoid carrying muddy footwear, tools or seed-bearing plant material between wetlands. For a confirmed unwanted patch, agree on a small-scale approach with the land manager before seed disperses, while protecting the surrounding soil and vegetation. The sources here do not establish a species-specific herbicide program.
researchNotes: Flora of China and the Royal Botanic Garden Sydney flora independently describe annual habit, damp habitat and spikelet structure. Their reported plant and inflorescence dimensions differ, so the draft emphasizes shared diagnostic features. U.S. occurrence must remain tied to the catalog's underlying records; these floras do not establish local harm or treatment efficacy.

sources.title: PlantNET New South Wales Flora: Sacciolepis indica

claims: Annual branching habit, narrow leaves, short ligule, veined spikelets and moist habitats.
Dense spike-like inflorescences, curved inflated upper glume and freshwater wet-ground habitat.

proposedDescription: Globe candytuft is a Mediterranean annual grown for rounded clusters of pink, purple or white flowers. It can reseed and occasionally appear outside gardens on disturbed ground. Those escapes should be documented separately from intentionally planted flowers; the references here do not justify treating every garden planting as an invasive infestation.
identification: The four petals of each small flower are unequal, with the outward-facing pair larger. Smooth stems carry narrow, alternate leaves, and the flower clusters remain broadly umbrella-shaped as the flattened, winged seedpods develop. The pods have a notch at their tip. Bitter candytuft, Iberis amara, typically has hairier lower stems and fruit clusters that lengthen; evergreen candytuft, I. sempervirens, is a perennial with persistent leaves. Include mature fruit and lower stems in photographs, because flower color alone can be misleading.
actions: If plants are appearing beyond a bed, photograph the escape and nearby cultivated source before removal. Where reseeding is unwanted, remove the annual plants or spent flower heads before ripe pods shed seed, then check for new seedlings. Keep seed-bearing garden waste out of roadsides and natural areas. Ask the land manager before removing plants from a public site, and confirm the species if the plant is woody or remains evergreen through winter.
researchNotes: NC State Extension supports annual habit, Mediterranean origin, unequal petals, fruit and reseeding. Native Plant Trust independently documents occasional New England escapes and provides a key separating I. umbellata from I. amara and I. sempervirens. The draft uses prevention of unwanted reseeding rather than claiming demonstrated ecosystem damage.

sources.title: Native Plant Trust: Iberis identification key

claims: Annual ornamental, reseeding, unequal petals, narrow leaves and winged notched fruit.
Occasional garden escapes in disturbed New England habitats.
Stem, fruit-cluster and evergreen/perennial distinctions among three candytuft species.

proposedDescription: Globose scale is a sap-feeding insect associated with stone-fruit trees, particularly plums. Mature females resemble small dark bumps on branches. Dense colonies can weaken a tree and leave sticky honeydew that supports sooty mold, but a few bumps on bark are not enough to identify the insect or decide whether treatment is needed.
identification: Mature females are strongly rounded, roughly 3 mm across, and dark brown to nearly black, with a shiny, finely pitted surface. Look for colonies on woody growth and record the host tree. Other soft scales can become similarly brown and convex, so photograph several individuals with a size reference and ask an extension specialist to examine a sample. The tiny moving young stages, called crawlers, can help determine treatment timing, but their appearance alone is not a reliable species diagnosis.
actions: Inspect the tree's vigor and the extent of infestation before acting. Pruning a limited amount of heavily colonized wood may help where the tree can tolerate it. As general soft-scale management, protect predators and parasitic wasps, and address ants that tend the insects for honeydew. If treatment is warranted, monitor for crawlers and obtain advice for the tree, scale and local conditions. Do not copy a calendar date from another country or assume a spray aimed at mature rounded females will reach the vulnerable stage.
researchNotes: ScaleNet supplies species-level adult morphology and taxonomic references; Turkish agricultural guidance independently describes stone-fruit hosts, honeydew and pruning. UC IPM supports the explicitly general soft-scale advice. Turkish crawler months are deliberately omitted because they cannot establish U.S. treatment timing.

sources.title: Turkish Ministry of Agriculture: Apricot pests, plum scale account

claims: Hemispherical mature females, dark shiny finely punctate surface and diagnostic dimensions.
Stone-fruit hosts, feeding and honeydew damage, and selective removal of heavily infested branches.
General scale monitoring, crawler timing, natural-enemy conservation and ant management.

proposedDescription: Globular spider beetles are small scavengers found in buildings and stored materials. They can matter in museums and collections as well as food-storage areas, where their presence may lead to an overlooked pocket of dry organic debris. Their rounded shape and long legs resemble a tiny spider, but they are beetles with six legs and antennae.
identification: Adults are roughly 3 to 5 mm long, with a rounded body covered in uneven brown and golden hairs rather than a smooth, polished surface. The antennae are long and slender. Other spider beetles can look similar: the golden spider beetle is more uniformly golden, while this species has darker patches in its hair covering. Photograph the beetle from above and from the side, with a size reference, and retain a contained specimen if identification is important. A distant image of a brown dot will not reliably separate these species.
actions: Look for the source as well as the insects: inspect stored dry materials and accumulated debris around the affected area. For household food, isolate infested packages, remove the source and clean nearby cracks before protecting unaffected supplies in sealed containers. For books, textiles, dried plant specimens or other collection objects, isolate the item and ask a conservator about treatment. Do not spray an object or apply heat or freezing without checking whether its materials can tolerate the method. Keep a record of where beetles recur so hidden sources can be investigated.
researchNotes: National Museums Scotland supplies the distinctive patchy appearance and collection-care context. Agriculture Canada's stored-product beetle guide independently describes the dense mixed hair covering and storage records. Minnesota Extension supplies explicitly general pantry sanitation. Older names include T. globulum; the draft avoids an uncertain native-range claim and does not treat a museum record as a county-wide outdoor occurrence.

sources.title: National Museums Scotland: Identifying collection pests
Agriculture Canada: Beetles associated with stored products

claims: Globular spider beetle size and patchy brown-gold appearance; spider beetle collection damage and debris associations.
T. globulus mixed dense golden and dark hair covering and stored-material associations.
General food-source removal, cleaning and sealed storage for pantry infestations.
